The appellant's application in C.P.(IB) No. 139/BB/2022 is restored to the record of the National Company Law Tribunal, Bengaluru, and it shall proceed from the stage of passing of the order dated 16.02.2024.

acts_cited: Section 95 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016
Rule 7(1) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority for Insolvency Resolution Process for Personal Guarantors to Corporate Debtors) Rules, 2019
Part III, Chapter III of the IBC
precedents_cited: Dilip B. Jiwrajka v. Union of India 5, (2024) 5 SCC 435
Thansingh Nathmal v. Superintendent of Taxes, Dhubri, AIR 1964 SC 1419, para 7
United Bank of India v. Satyawati Tondon, (2010) 8 SCC 110, paras 43, 45
Commissioner of Income Tax v. Chhabil Dass Agarwal, (2014) 1 SCC 603, para 15
South Indian Bank Ltd v. Naveen Mathew Philip, 2023 SCC OnLine SC 435, para 14
Whirlpool Corporation v. Registrar of Trade Marks, Mumbai, (1998) 8 SCC 1, para 15
Harbanslal Sahnia v. Indian Oil Corporation Ltd, (2003) 2 SCC 107, para 7
Mohammed Enterprises (Tanzania) Ltd v. Farooq Ali Khan, 15
Union of India v. V.N. Singh, (2010) 5 SCC 579
Executive Engineer Southern Electricity Supply Company of Orissa Ltd. v. Seetaram Rice Mill, (2012) 2 SCC 108, para 80
Radha Krishan Industries v. State of Himachal Pradesh, (2021) 6 SCC 771, para 27.6
constitutional_provisions: Article 226 of the Constitution

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The High Court cannot invoke its writ jurisdiction under Article 226 to prematurely interdict personal insolvency proceedings under the IBC, 2016, at the stage where the Adjudicating Authority has merely appointed a resolution professional under Section 97. The Adjudicating Authority's functions under Sections 95-99 are facilitative, not adjudicatory, and the determination of the existence of debt, being a mixed question of law and fact, falls within the Adjudicating Authority's adjudicatory domain under Section 100, after the resolution professional's report.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: Statutory tribunals are established to adjudicate questions of law and fact, and High Courts should not substitute themselves as decision-making authorities during judicial review. While judicial review powers are critical, their exercise demands rigorous scrutiny and judicious application, especially when a complete code like the IBC provides sufficient checks and balances and remedial avenues.

special_directions.special_directions: The National Company Law Tribunal, Bengaluru, is requested to decide the matter (C.P.(IB) No. 139/BB/2022) as expeditiously as possible, given that it has been pending since 2021.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO.3829 OF 2025 [Arising out of SLP(C) NO. 24400 OF 2024]

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns a retired bank employee's belated application to join a pension scheme after the stipulated deadline and the High Court's interference with the dismissal of his writ petition.

judgements.case_summary: The first respondent, a retired employee of Bank of India (BoI), sought to join the BoI (Employees') Pension Scheme, 1995. BoI had published a circular in August 2010 inviting options from retired employees between September 1, 2010, and October 30, 2010. The first respondent, who was in the USA and claimed unawareness and surgery, submitted his option belatedly on March 19, 2011, which BoI rejected. A Single Judge dismissed his writ petition, holding that the option period had expired. The Division Bench, however, allowed his appeal, condoning the delay due to the beneficial nature of the policy and the surgery. The Supreme Court, in this judgment, found the Division Bench's interference unwarranted. It noted that BoI had given wide publicity to the scheme and that the first respondent was not diligent. The Court emphasized that beneficial policies with deadlines must be adhered to, and considerations of sympathy cannot override legal principles or create a legal right where none exists due to inaction. The Supreme Court concluded that the first respondent had no legal right to seek mandamus and that the Single Judge rightly dismissed the writ petition. Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside the Division Bench's order and affirmed the Single Judge's decision.

petitioner_key_arguments: The first respondent failed to exercise the option within the stipulated deadline of October 30, 2010.
The circular inviting options was widely publicized by IBA and BoI through various channels, including local and national newspapers.
The Division Bench erred in interfering with the Single Judge's dismissal of the writ petition, as there was no unreasonableness or arbitrariness in BoI's decision.
Sympathy, grace, or compassion have no place when a subject is called upon to exercise an option within a settlement's terms.
respondent_key_arguments: The first respondent was unaware of the circular due to being in the United States and undergoing surgery during the relevant period.
The policy to extend pension was beneficial, and the delay in submitting the application should have been condoned.
The Division Bench was justified in its interference with the Single Judge's order.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments prevailed. The court agreed that the respondent failed to act within the stipulated time, the circular was widely published, and the Division Bench erred in allowing the appeal based on sympathy, as there was no legal right to mandamus.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned judgment and order dated 7th March, 2024, passed by the Division Bench is set aside, and the judgment and order of the Single Judge dated 22nd November, 2023, dismissing the writ petition of the first respondent is affirmed.

precedents_cited: Calcutta Port Trust and Ors. vs. Anadi Kumar Das (Captain) and Ors.7
Mani Subrat Jain v. State of Haryana8
constitutional_provisions: Article 226 of the Constitution

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: A beneficial policy with a stipulated time limit must be strictly adhered to, and belated options cannot be accepted without a legal right. The employer's decision not to entertain a belated option is not unreasonable or arbitrary if proper publicity was given to the scheme. Mandamus cannot be sought without a judicially enforceable legal right, which is lost if the applicant fails to act diligently within the prescribed period.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: High courts, in exercising writ powers, should not come to the aid of the tardy, the indolent, and the lethargic. Exercise of discretion should not be colored by considerations of sympathy, grace, or compassion, as these are beyond the scope of writ powers, especially when no acceptable justification for the failure to act with expedition is proffered.

case_identification.petitioner_name: BERNARD FRANCIS JOSEPH VAZ AND OTHERS
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (Arising out of SLP (C) No. 10338 of 2023)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns land acquisition for the Bengaluru-Mysuru Infrastructure Corridor Project (BMICP), specifically regarding the determination of compensation and the appropriate date for market value assessment due to significant delays in the acquisition process.

judgements.case_summary: The appellants purchased residential sites in Gottigere Village between 1995-1997, which were subsequently acquired for the Bengaluru-Mysuru Infrastructure Corridor Project (BMICP) under a preliminary notification issued on 29th January 2003. Possession was taken in November 2005, but no compensation award was passed for 18 years. Following contempt proceedings for non-compliance, an Award was passed on 22nd April 2019, based on a legal opinion to postpone the preliminary notification date to 2011 to consider prevailing guideline rates, resulting in higher compensation. The Project Proponents challenged this Award, arguing compensation should be based on the original preliminary notification date. The Single Judge quashed the 2019 Award, directing fresh awards based on the original preliminary notification date, which effectively denied the appellants' plea for a later valuation date. The Division Bench dismissed the appellants' writ appeal as premature. The Supreme Court found the Division Bench's dismissal erroneous, noting the Single Judge had already decided against shifting the valuation date. Exercising its powers under Article 142, the Court directed the SLAO to pass a fresh award based on the market value prevailing on 22nd April 2019, acknowledging the State's delay and the need for fair compensation, while quashing the High Court's judgments.

petitioner_key_arguments: The Writ Appeal was not premature as the Single Judge had already rejected the plea to shift the market value assessment date.
More than 21 years passed since preliminary notification without compensation, necessitating determination based on current market value.
Compensation should be determined by notionally shifting the date of the Preliminary Notification to the date of the Award.

Compensation should be determined as per the provisions of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (2013 LA Act), as Section 30 of the KIAD Act makes the 1894 LA Act applicable mutatis mutandis for compensation determination.
respondent_key_arguments: (Respondents 6 & 7 - Project Proponents): If additional compensation is granted, the liability should fall on the State Government and/or KIADB, not them, as they deposited compensation as per agreement. Shifting the date can only occur in rare circumstances. Awarding compensation under the 2013 LA Act is a new case not argued before lower courts.

(Respondent 1 - State of Karnataka): Appellants' claims are premature and speculative as they are yet to exhaust remedies under ongoing award proceedings. The Division Bench correctly held that the issue of shifting the acquisition notification date could only be examined after the award is passed by the SLAO.

(Respondents 2-5 - KIADB/SLAO): The SLAO passed the 2019 Award based on the Advocate General's opinion regarding shifting the date. The Single Judge quashed this Award and directed fresh awards within a stipulated timeframe. If appellants are aggrieved by the new compensation, they can take permissible legal steps. The High Court's concurrent findings should not be interfered with.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that due to the inordinate delay by the State/KIADB in disbursing compensation, and to ensure fair compensation, the market value should be determined as of a later date (22nd April 2019), even though the SLAO lacked jurisdiction to shift the date. The court exercised its power under Article 142 to achieve this.

outcome.relief_granted: The SLAO is directed to pass a fresh award taking the market value prevailing as on 22nd April 2019 within a period of two months, after hearing the parties. The appellants are entitled to all statutory benefits as are available to them in law. The rights of parties to challenge the award in reference remain open. The judgment and order passed by the Division Bench of the High Court dated 22nd November 2022 in Writ Appeal No. 678 of 2022 (LA-KIADB) is quashed and set aside, and the writ petition filed by the appellants herein before the High Court being W.P. No. 1627 of 2021 is allowed.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 250 OF 2025

case_details.subject_matter: This case concerns an appeal against a conviction under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, specifically challenging the conviction based on alleged non-compliance with Section 52A of the Act regarding the disposal and sampling of seized contraband.

judgements.case_summary: The appeal challenged a conviction under Section 20(b)(ii)(c) of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (NDPS Act), which had been affirmed by the High Court, sentencing the appellant to 15 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 1 lakh. The appellant's primary contention was that the conviction was vitiated due to non-compliance with Section 52A of the NDPS Act, arguing that the investigating officer improperly mixed all 73 seized packets of Ganja and drew samples from the mixture, violating Section 52A and Rule 10 of the NDPS Rules, 2022. The Supreme Court extensively reviewed the legislative history and judicial precedents related to Section 52A, clarifying that while it provides a mechanism for early disposal and preservation of seized substances, its non-compliance does not automatically invalidate a trial or lead to acquittal. The Court distinguished between procedural irregularities and illegalities, asserting that irregularities do not nullify proceedings unless they create serious doubt about the physical evidence. It held that the initial burden to prove non-compliance rests with the accused, after which the prosecution must demonstrate substantial compliance or that the non-compliance did not prejudice the case. In the present case, the Court found the appellant's claim of non-compliance to be a bald allegation, concluding that the police had substantially followed the prescribed sampling process. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed, and the conviction upheld.

petitioner_key_arguments: The conviction was vitiated due to non-compliance with Section 52A of the NDPS Act.
The investigating officer mixed all 73 packets of seized contraband (Ganja) and drew two samples from the mixture, violating Section 52A of the NDPS Act, 1985 and Rule 10 of the NDPS Rules, 2022.
This non-compliance rendered the accuracy and reliability of the samples doubtful, thereby vitiating the trial.
respondent_key_arguments: The police officers duly followed the procedure prescribed for seizure and sampling, including identification tests, bunching of packets, and drawing representative samples.
The appellant's contention regarding non-compliance of Section 52A was a bald allegation without sufficient evidence.

Mere non-compliance or delayed compliance with Section 52A does not automatically vitiate the trial or entitle the accused to acquittal, especially when other material on record establishes recovery and conscious possession of contraband.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court accepted the implicit arguments of the respondent, finding that the police had substantially followed the prescribed sampling process and that the appellant's claim of non-compliance was a bald allegation. The Court reiterated that non-compliance with Section 52A is not automatically fatal to the prosecution's case unless it creates serious doubt about the physical evidence.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: Non-compliance or delayed compliance with Section 52A of the NDPS Act or its allied rules is not automatically fatal to the prosecution's case or a ground for acquittal. Such procedural lapses are considered irregularities, not illegalities, unless they lead to discrepancies in physical evidence that render the prosecution's case doubtful. The initial burden to demonstrate non-compliance lies with the accused, after which the onus shifts to the prosecution to prove substantial compliance or that the non-compliance did not affect the case.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court provided a detailed discussion on the legislative history and purpose of Section 52A, emphasizing its role in early disposal and preservation of seized substances. It distinguished between procedural irregularities and illegalities, noting that irregularities may be overlooked or corrected without affecting the outcome, whereas illegalities may nullify proceedings. The Court cautioned against being hyper-technical about minor discrepancies and stressed the need for courts to take a holistic and cumulative view of the evidence.

case_identification.respondent_name: Commissioner of Central Excise Nashik Commissionerate
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 5642 OF 2009

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the valuation of petroleum products for excise duty purposes, specifically whether the price fixed under a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) between Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) constituted the 'sole consideration' for sale, and the applicability of an extended period of limitation and penalty under the Central Excise Act, 1944.

judgements.case_summary:
The case involves Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd. (BPCL) and other Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) challenging excise duty demands. The OMCs had an MOU for product sharing/assistance, selling petroleum products to each other at Import Parity Price (IPP), which was lower than prices to their own dealers. The Revenue contended that the IPP was not the 'sole consideration' for sale under Section 4(1)(a) of the Central Excise Act, 1944, and invoked an extended period of limitation and penalty under Section 11AC, alleging suppression of facts.
BPCL argued that the IPP was the transaction value, parties were unrelated, and the MOU was government-directed. They also contended that previous Tribunal decisions, affirmed by the Supreme Court, should be binding, and that no suppression of facts occurred, making the extended limitation and penalty inapplicable.
The Supreme Court analyzed the MOU, concluding its primary purpose was to ensure smooth supply and distribution, not purely commercial sales, thus the price was not the sole consideration. However, on the issue of limitation, the Court found that the Revenue was aware of the MOU (evidenced by a 2007 circular and previous Tribunal decisions) and failed to prove fraud, collusion, willful misstatement, or suppression of facts by BPCL. Therefore, the invocation of the extended period of limitation and penalty was deemed unjustified.
Consequently, BPCL's appeal (Civil Appeal No. 5642 of 2009) was allowed, setting aside the demand and penalty. Other connected appeals filed by the Revenue were remanded to the Tribunals for fresh adjudication consistent with this judgment.

petitioner_key_arguments: The 'transaction value' under Section 4 of the 1944 Act (post-2000 amendment) refers to the actual price paid or payable for each removal of goods.
Assessees are permitted to charge different prices from different buyers.
The Import Parity Price (IPP) was the sole consideration for sales to other OMCs, with no additional amounts paid.
The parties to the MOU were not related, making Section 4(1)(a) applicable.
The MOU was entered into at the behest of the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas.
The summary dismissal by the Supreme Court of an appeal against the Tribunal's decision in Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. should be binding (doctrine of merger).

There was no fraud, collusion, willful misstatement, or suppression of facts, as the department was aware of the MOU (as per a 2007 Circular); therefore, the extended period of limitation and penalty under Section 11AC are not applicable.
respondent_key_arguments: The price fixed under the MOU was not the sole consideration for the sale of petroleum products between OMCs.
The OMCs did not produce a copy of the MOU, which justified invoking the extended period of limitation on the ground of suppression of material facts.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that the extended period of limitation and penalty under Section 11A/11AC could not be invoked because the Revenue failed to prove fraud, collusion, willful misstatement, or suppression of facts, as the department was aware of the MOU.

outcome.relief_granted: Civil Appeal No. 5642 of 2009 was allowed, and the impugned orders, including the demand and penalty, were set aside. Other connected appeals were remanded to the concerned Tribunals for fresh adjudication in light of the judgment's findings.

precedents_cited: Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Commissioner of Central Excise (2005) 187 ELT 479 (Tri-Bang)

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: For Section 4(1)(a) of the Central Excise Act, 1944, to apply, the price must be the sole consideration for the sale; if the transaction's primary purpose is product sharing/assistance for smooth supply rather than purely commercial sale, the price is not the sole consideration. However, the extended period of limitation and penalty under Section 11A/11AC cannot be invoked if the department was aware of the relevant facts (like the MOU) and there is no proven fraud, collusion, or willful suppression of facts with intent to evade duty.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: A summary dismissal of an appeal by the Supreme Court does not necessarily constitute a binding decision on all issues if those issues were not explicitly decided by the Tribunal below, especially regarding specific conditions like 'sole consideration' under Section 4(1)(a).

special_directions.special_directions: Civil Appeal No. 5642 of 2009 is allowed, and the impugned orders, including the order dated 8th December 2007 passed by the Commissioner of Central Excise, Nashik, are set aside. In the remaining appeals, the impugned judgments are quashed and set aside, and the appeals are remanded to the concerned Tribunals to decide the same in accordance with the law laid down in this judgment.

case_identification.petitioner_name: Bhudev Mallick Alias Bhudeb Mallick & Anr.
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO.2248 OF 2025 (@Special Leave to Appeal (C) No.21328 of 2023)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the execution of a permanent injunction decree, specifically the arrest and detention of judgment debtors and attachment of their property, and the High Court's failure to address jurisdictional errors in the execution process.

judgements.case_summary:
This appeal arises from a Title Suit No. 25 of 1965, where a permanent injunction decree was passed in 1976, restraining the appellants (judgment debtors) from disturbing the respondents' (decree holders) peaceful possession. After nearly 40 years, in 2017, the respondents initiated an execution case, alleging breach of the injunction. The executing court, without accepting the judgment debtors' written objections, ordered their arrest and detention for 30 days and attachment of property. The High Court affirmed this order, finding no jurisdictional error.

The petitioners argued that the execution petition was not maintainable after such a long lapse of time and that the executing court erred by ordering arrest without a mandatory affidavit as per Order XXI Rule 11-A of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and without properly considering their objections. The respondents contended that a permanent injunction decree has no limitation period for execution and that the High Court committed no error.

The Supreme Court analyzed the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, particularly Section 51, Order XXI Rule 32, and Rule 11-A, emphasizing the mandatory requirement of a finding of willful disobedience based on material evidence for arrest and detention. The Court found that the executing court proceeded on surmise and that the High Court failed to exercise its supervisory jurisdiction to correct this jurisdictional error. The Court highlighted the importance of affording an opportunity of hearing and proper procedure in such matters.

Consequently, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the orders of both the High Court and the executing court. It clarified that the decree holders could file a fresh application, which the executing court should decide on its own merits, keeping the Supreme Court's observations in mind.

petitioner_key_arguments: The execution petition was not maintainable after a lapse of almost 40 years from the date of the decree.

The Civil Judge committed a serious error by directing the arrest and detention of appellants and attachment of their property without a mandatory petition/affidavit stating grounds, as required by Order XXI Rule 11-A of the Code of Civil Procedure.
The High Court overlooked this mandatory requirement and failed to exercise its supervisory jurisdiction.
The High Court should have permitted the appellants to file their written objections to the execution case.
respondent_key_arguments: No error was committed by the High Court in passing the impugned order.

The contention that the execution petition could not be filed after 40 years is without merit, as a permanent injunction decree, once final, can be enforced whenever possession is disturbed, with no period of limitation.
The decree holders are entitled to seek appropriate relief from the court in accordance with law.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioners' arguments regarding the procedural errors in the execution process, specifically the lack of proper procedure for arrest and detention under Order XXI Rule 11-A and Rule 32, and the High Court's failure to correct this jurisdictional error.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal is allowed. The order passed by the High Court and the executing court are set aside. The decree-holders are permitted to file a fresh application if there is any interference, which the executing court shall decide on its own merits, keeping the Supreme Court's observations in mind.

The High Court committed a jurisdictional error by failing to correct the executing court's order which lacked such a finding and denied the judgment debtors an opportunity to be heard.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The judgment extensively discusses the evolving concept of "jurisdictional error" in judicial review, citing numerous Indian and English precedents, and legal scholars, emphasizing that even errors of law can be jurisdictional errors, especially when they lead to grave consequences like arrest and detention.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S).1408/2013

case_details.subject_matter: Appeal against conviction for dowry death (Section 304B IPC) and cruelty (Section 498A IPC) where the deceased was found in a burnt condition.

judgements.case_summary: The case concerns an appeal against the conviction of the appellants, the father-in-law and husband of the deceased, for offences under Sections 304B (dowry death) and 498A (cruelty) of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. The deceased, Kamla Devi, was found in a burnt condition on the night of 13th/14th June 1999. The prosecution relied on the testimonies of PW-1 (father of the deceased) and PW-2 (uncle of the deceased) to establish dowry demands and cruelty. However, the court found significant omissions and contradictions in PW-1's testimony regarding dowry demands and payments, noting that these details were not in the FIR and were contradicted by his own letters. Similarly, PW-2's testimony about a letter from the deceased and subsequent disclosures was deemed unreliable as the alleged handwriting was not sent for expert verification, and his statement to the Naib Tehsildar omitted crucial information. The court concluded that the prosecution failed to establish the necessary ingredients for conviction under Sections 304B and 498A IPC due to the lack of legally admissible and reliable evidence. Consequently, the High Court and Sessions Court judgments were quashed, and the appellants were acquitted.

petitioner_key_arguments: No legally admissible evidence to sustain the conviction.
Testimonies of prosecution witnesses (PW-1 and PW-2) are riddled with omissions and contradictions.
respondent_key_arguments: Appellants are guilty of offences under Sections 304B and 498A IPC based on witness testimonies.
Dowry demands and cruelty led to the death of the deceased.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The appellants' arguments that there was no legally admissible evidence to sustain the conviction, due to significant omissions and contradictions in the prosecution witnesses' testimonies, prevailed.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned judgments of the High Court and Sessions Court are quashed and set aside. The appellants are acquitted of the offences alleged against them. The bail bonds furnished by the first appellant stand cancelled.

acts_cited: Sections 304B and 498A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The court's decision is based on the finding that the prosecution failed to establish the necessary ingredients for conviction under Sections 304B and 498A IPC. This failure stemmed from the unreliability of the key prosecution witnesses (PW-1 and PW-2), whose testimonies were marred by significant omissions and contradictions, and the absence of other legally admissible evidence to corroborate the charges of dowry demand and cruelty.

special_directions.special_directions: The bail bonds furnished by the first appellant stand cancelled.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO.183 OF 2025 [Arising out of SLP(C) NO. 17120 OF 2022]

case_details.subject_matter: Challenge to disciplinary proceedings and a penalty (pension cut) imposed on a Senior Medical Officer for alleged misconduct, including leave without sanction and non-participation in a pulse polio program, shortly before his retirement.

judgements.case_summary:
The appellant, Bhupinderpal Singh Gill, a Senior Medical Officer, faced disciplinary action 11 days before retirement in March 2017 for alleged misconduct, including unauthorized leave and non-participation in a pulse polio program. An Inquiry Officer found most charges proved, leading to a 2% permanent pension cut by the Disciplinary Authority. The High Court's Single Judge dismissed his challenge, while a Division Bench modified the penalty to a 2% cut for five years.
The Supreme Court, in this appeal, found the charges of unauthorized leave and non-compliance lacked legal evidence, noting the Inquiry Officer's inconsistent application of proof standards. It also deemed the finding of guilt for a "perceived moral duty failure" extraneous. Crucially, the Court highlighted an Election Commission order exempting retiring officers from election duty, which applied to the appellant, suggesting the proceedings were a "ruse to wreak vengeance" due to his prior legal actions against government officials.
Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside all previous orders, directing full pension restoration with 6% interest on deducted amounts and awarded Rs. 50,000/- in costs to the appellant, with the option for the government to recover from responsible officials. The judgment underscored the necessity of legal evidence in disciplinary actions and condemned mala fide proceedings against public servants.

petitioner_key_arguments: Appellant did not commit any misconduct warranting punishment.
Disciplinary proceedings were initiated to "teach a lesson" for questioning actions before the High Court and were mala fide.
Findings of the Inquiry Officer and penalty order were perverse.
Governmental action of initiating proceedings days before retirement and imposing a pension cut was arbitrary and mala fide, especially given 34 years of blemish-free service.
The charges of leave without sanction and non-compliance with superior orders were not supported by legal evidence.
The Inquiry Officer's finding of guilt for a "perceived failure to perform a moral duty" was extraneous to the charges.
An Election Commission order exempted officers retiring within six months from election duty, making the charges against him baseless.
respondent_key_arguments: Inquiry was conducted with reasonable and adequate opportunity for defense, with no breach of natural justice.
Findings of the Inquiry Officer were based on legal evidence.
Disciplinary Authority's order demonstrated application of mind.
Limited notice was issued by the Division Bench, and the appellant's grievance was addressed by modifying the penalty, so no further grievance should exist.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the charges were not supported by legal evidence, the Inquiry Officer's findings were extraneous, and the disciplinary proceedings were mala fide, especially in light of the Election Commission's exemption for retiring officers.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned order of the Division Bench, the Single Judge's dismissal, and the Disciplinary Authority's penalty order were set aside. Appellant is entitled to full pension without any cut, with all deducted amounts returned within three months with 6% interest per annum. Costs of Rs. 50,000/- awarded to the appellant.

precedents_cited: Union of India v. H.C. Goel
Maneka Gandhi v. India
Madhayamam Broadcasting Ltd. v. Union of India
constitutional_provisions: Article 311 of the Constitution
Article 226 of the Constitution
Article 14
Article 16

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The Court held that disciplinary proceedings must be based on legal evidence, and findings cannot be sustained if they are based on hearsay, extraneous considerations, or a "perceived failure to perform a moral duty" not explicitly charged. It also emphasized that disciplinary actions initiated with mala fide intent, especially against retiring employees, are arbitrary and warrant judicial interference.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that issuing limited notice at the admission stage does not bar a Constitutional Court from enlarging the scope of an appeal to ensure justice, especially when fundamental rights are involved. It also strongly deprecated the "vile acts" of officials who punish senior doctors on the verge of retirement for taking legal action against the government, calling it a "ruse to wreak vengeance."

special_directions.special_directions: The appellant shall be entitled to costs assessed conservatively at Rs. 50,000/-, to be released within the aforesaid period. Should there be any default, the appellant is free to bring it to the court's notice for appropriate direction. The GoP has liberty to realize the amount of costs payable from the persons responsible after fixing responsibility in accordance with law.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 87 OF 2025 (Arising out of Special Leave Petition (Crl.)No.1337

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the interim release of a truck seized under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, after suspected heroin was found concealed within it, where the owner was not arrayed as an accused.

judgements.case_summary:
The appellant, Bishwajit Dey, purchased a truck for commercial purposes, which was seized on April 10, 2023, after police found 24.8 grams of suspected heroin concealed within it. The main accused, Md. Dimpul, was arrested, and a chargesheet was filed, but neither the appellant (owner) nor the driver was arrayed as an accused, with the police not finding evidence of their knowledge or connivance. The appellant sought interim release of the vehicle, arguing it was his sole source of income and was deteriorating while in police custody, citing Sections 451 and 457 of the Cr.P.C. and various precedents. The respondent-State argued that the NDPS Act is a special enactment that does not contemplate interim release of seized conveyances, which are material evidence and prone to reuse, citing other High Court judgments.

The Supreme Court, after considering divergent views among courts, held that there is no specific bar or restriction under the NDPS Act for the interim release of seized vehicles. It reasoned that the general powers under Sections 451 and 457 of the Cr.P.C. can be invoked, especially when the owner is not arrayed as an accused and no allegation of knowledge or connivance is made against them. The Court emphasized that keeping vehicles in police custody leads to deterioration and serves no purpose. Consequently, the Criminal Appeal was allowed, and the vehicle was ordered to be released on superdari, subject to conditions including video and photographic documentation, authentication by all parties, and an undertaking not to sell or transfer ownership until the trial concludes.

petitioner_key_arguments: The appellant purchased the truck for commercial purposes, and it is his only source of income.
Neither the appellant (owner) nor his driver was aware of the contraband.
The driver and helper were cited as witnesses, not involved in the offence.
The remand report states heroin was recovered from the possession of the accused, Md. Dimpul.
The seized vehicle is deteriorating in police custody.
Sections 451 and 457 of Cr.P.C. allow for interim release of property.
Cited Sunderbhai Ambala Desai V. State of Gujarat and Bhola Singh @ Ayush Singh vs. The State of Bihar.
respondent_key_arguments: The NDPS Act is a special enactment and a complete code, which does not contemplate interim release of seized conveyances.
The seized vehicle is critical material evidence for the prosecution.
Releasing the vehicle prematurely on zimma would jeopardize the trial.
There is a likelihood of the conveyance being reused for transporting contraband.
Releasing seized vehicles encourages misuse and undermines efforts to combat illegal activities.

Cited Smt. Narender Kaur vs. Arun Sheoran, B. Ganga Hire Purchase Pvt. Ltd. Vs. State of Punjab and Others, Union of India vs. Dinesh Kumar Verma, Shajahan vs. Inspector of Excise and Others, and Moumita Saha.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that there is no specific bar in the NDPS Act for interim release of vehicles, and that Cr.P.C. provisions (Sections 451 and 457) can be invoked, especially when the owner is not arrayed as an accused and no connivance is alleged.

outcome.relief_granted: The vehicle (Truck bearing Registration No.AS-01-NC-4355) is to be released in the interim on superdari, subject to specific conditions.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, does not contain a specific bar against the interim release of seized vehicles. In cases where the owner of the vehicle is not arrayed as an accused and there is no allegation of their knowledge or connivance in the offence, the general powers under Sections 451 and 457 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, can be invoked to release the vehicle on an interim basis, especially to prevent its deterioration.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that keeping seized vehicles in police custody for long periods leads to their deterioration and serves no useful purpose. Releasing such vehicles on interim custody benefits the owner, financier, and society by allowing the vehicle to be used for its intended purpose. The Court also discussed four scenarios for seizure and release, emphasizing that release is appropriate when the owner is not implicated.

special_directions.special_directions: The trial Court is directed to release the Vehicle on superdari after preparing a video and still photographs of the vehicle and obtaining all necessary identification information, authenticated by the Investigating Officer, owner, and accused. The appellant shall not sell or part with the ownership of the Vehicle until the conclusion of the trial and must furnish an undertaking to surrender the Vehicle within one week of being so directed and/or pay its determined value if ultimately ordered by the Court.
special_directions.interim_orders: The judgment itself constitutes an interim order for the release of the vehicle.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 2052/2014

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns an appeal against conviction for offenses under the Indian Penal Code and the Prevention of Corruption Act, focusing on the scope of appeal when limited notice was issued and the quantum of sentence.

judgements.case_summary: The appellant, Biswajit Das, was convicted for offenses under Sections 468 r/w 120(B), 271, 465 r/w 120(B), and 420 r/w 120(B) of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and Section 13(1)(d) read with Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. He was sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for varying terms, including three years for the PC Act offense. The High Court affirmed the conviction and sentence. The appellant approached the Supreme Court, which initially issued a limited notice on January 3, 2014, confined to the applicability of PC Act Section 13(1)(d) and the quantum of sentence for other offenses. The petitioner's counsel argued for expanding the scope of the appeal, citing precedents like Taherakhatoon, Yomeshbhai Pranshankar Bhatt, and Kutchi Lal Raeshwar Ashram Trust, emphasizing the Court's power under Article 142 to do complete justice. The respondent's counsel relied on Spring Meadows Hospital to argue for adherence to the limited notice. The Court, after reviewing jurisprudence, held that its jurisdiction under Article 142 allows for expanding the scope of appeal beyond limited notice in appropriate cases, especially in criminal matters, to ensure complete justice. The Court upheld the conviction under both IPC and PC Act, finding sufficient evidence. However, considering that the appellant had already served 22 months out of a 36-month prison term and the minimum sentence for the PC Act offense was one year, the Court altered the sentence to the period already undergone. The appeal was partially allowed, maintaining the conviction but modifying the sentence.

petitioner_key_arguments: Assailed the findings of the trial court regarding the offenses under the IPC.
Contended that the provisions of the PC Act would not be applicable to the appellant.
Argued that the scope of the appeal should be expanded beyond the limited notice issued, citing precedents like Taherakhatoon, Yomeshbhai Pranshankar Bhatt, and Kutchi Lal Raeshwar Ashram Trust.
Sought alteration/modification of the sentence imposed.
respondent_key_arguments: Invited attention to the order issuing limited notice, suggesting the scope of the appeal should not be expanded.
Relied on Spring Meadows Hospital to support the argument for adhering to the limited scope of notice.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments regarding the expansion of the appeal's scope and the alteration of the sentence were accepted by the Court. The Court maintained the conviction but modified the sentence to the period already undergone.

outcome.relief_granted: The sentence imposed on the appellant was altered to the period of imprisonment already undergone. The appellant is not required to serve the remainder of the prison term, and the bail bond stands discharged.

acts_cited: Life Insurance Corporation of India Act, 1956
precedents_cited: Taherakhatoon (D) by Lrs. vs. Salambin Mohammad (1999) 2 SCC 635

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The Court held that its discretionary power under Article 142 of the Constitution allows for the expansion of the scope of an appeal, even when a limited notice was initially issued, to ensure complete justice, particularly in criminal matters. While the conviction was upheld based on the evidence, the sentence was modified considering the period already served and the minimum statutory sentence, reflecting a pro-liberal and justice-oriented approach.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that the views expressed in Yomeshbhai Pranshankar Bhatt and Kutchi Lal Raeshwar Ashram Trust are in consonance with the rapidly changing times of liberty being given primordial consideration. It also noted the pro-liberal and justice-oriented approach of the Court to secure the liberty of citizens.

special_directions.special_directions: The appellant is not required to serve the remainder of the prison term. The bail bond shall stand discharged.
special_directions.interim_orders: Notice was issued on January 3, 2014, confined to the question of PC Act applicability and quantum of sentence. The appellant was enlarged on bail on October 12, 2015.

case_identification.case_number: Criminal Appeal @ SLP(Crl.) No. 3044 of 2021

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the conviction of an appellant for offences related to a fabricated marksheet for MBBS admission, specifically challenging the reliance on handwriting expert testimony without the original disputed document.

judgements.case_summary: The appellant, C. Kamalakkannan, was convicted in 2016 for offences under Sections 120B, 468, and 471 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, related to a fabricated marksheet used for MBBS admission. The conviction was affirmed by the appellate court in 2017 and the High Court in 2019. The prosecution's primary allegation was that the appellant prepared the postal cover in which the forged marksheet was transmitted, with the handwriting on the cover being his. The appellant argued that the trial court illegally relied on a co-accused's deposition, the original postal cover was never produced or exhibited, and the handwriting expert's report (PW-18) was inadmissible as its reasoning sheet was not brought on record. The respondent contended that the original cover was untraceable, making a photostat copy admissible as secondary evidence. The Supreme Court, after considering the arguments and citing Murari Lal v. State of M.P. on the cautious approach to expert evidence, found that the original postal cover was not available on record and thus could not be exhibited. The prosecution failed to lead primary evidence, rendering the handwriting expert's report redundant. The Court concluded that the prosecution miserably failed to prove the existence of the disputed postal cover and its connection to the appellant. Consequently, the appellant's conviction was set aside, and he was acquitted.

petitioner_key_arguments: The prosecution's sole allegation was that the appellant prepared the postal cover for the forged marksheet.
The trial Court's reliance on the co-accused's deposition was illegal.
The original postal cover was never produced or exhibited by the prosecution.
The handwriting expert's report (PW-18) is inadmissible as the reasoning sheet was not brought on record and proved.
Comparison of handwriting is not a complete/conclusive science.
respondent_key_arguments: The contention regarding reliance on PW-9 (Vijaya Kumar) is misplaced as his evidence was found unacceptable by the trial court.
The original postal cover was untraceable, making the photostat copy admissible as secondary evidence.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments that the prosecution failed to produce and exhibit the original disputed postal cover, and that the handwriting expert's report lacked evidentiary value without the original document, were accepted by the Court.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal is allowed. The impugned judgments dated 25th October, 2016 (trial Court), 23rd October, 2017 (appellate Court), and 16th April, 2019 (High Court) are hereby quashed and set aside. The appellant is acquitted of the charges.

acts_cited: Sections 120B, 468 and 471 (2 counts) read with Section 109 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860
precedents_cited: Murari Lal v. State of M.P.8, (1980) 1 SCC 704

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that for a conviction based on handwriting evidence on a disputed document, the original document must be produced and exhibited as primary evidence. Failure to do so renders the handwriting expert's report on a copy or unexhibited document redundant and insufficient to prove the prosecution's case beyond reasonable doubt.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court reiterated the principle that while corroboration may not invariably be insisted upon for handwriting expert opinions, a cautious approach is necessary, and the reasons for the expert's opinion must be carefully probed and examined, especially given the imperfect nature of handwriting identification science.

special_directions.special_directions: Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 ARISING OUT OF SLP (C) No. 29261 OF 2024

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the procedural distinction between condoning delay in filing an application to set aside an ex-parte decree and the actual setting aside of the ex-parte decree, and the jurisdictional limits of a High Court in revision.

judgements.case_summary: The appellants, as plaintiffs, obtained an ex-parte decree for specific performance. The respondents challenged this by filing applications to set aside the decree and to condone the delay in filing that application. The Trial Court dismissed the application for condonation of delay, consequently dismissing the application to set aside the ex-parte decree. The respondents filed a revision petition before the High Court, but only against the order refusing to condone the delay, not against the dismissal of the application to set aside the ex-parte decree. The High Court, however, not only condoned the delay but also proceeded to set aside the ex-parte decree and restored the suit. The Supreme Court, in this appeal, addressed whether the High Court committed a jurisdictional error by setting aside the ex-parte decree when that specific order was not challenged. The Court affirmed the High Court's decision to condone the delay, finding justifiable reasons. However, it held that the High Court erred in setting aside the ex-parte decree and restoring the suit without a specific challenge to that order, emphasizing that condonation of delay and setting aside an ex-parte decree are independent processes. The Supreme Court partially allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's order to the extent it restored the suit and directed the Trial Court to hear the application for setting aside the ex-parte decree on its own merits.

petitioner_key_arguments: The High Court committed a jurisdictional error by setting aside the ex-parte decree when there was no challenge to the Trial Court's decision on I.A. No. 1163 of 2021 (application to set aside ex-parte decree).
The circumstances, justification, consideration, and legal remedies for 'condoning the delay' and 'setting aside the ex-parte decree' are different and must be dealt with independently.
respondent_key_arguments: There was a justifiable reason to condone the delay in filing the application to set aside the ex-parte decree, including the value of the property, the counsel's failure to update status, and the need for an opportunity to contest the suit.
The High Court was justified in condoning the delay.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that the High Court committed a jurisdictional error by setting aside the ex-parte decree and restoring the suit without a specific challenge to the order dismissing the application to set aside the ex-parte decree. However, the court also accepted the respondent's argument that there was a justifiable reason to condone the delay in filing the application to set aside the ex-parte decree.

outcome.relief_granted: The High Court's finding that there is a justifiable reason for condoning the delay in filing the application for setting aside the ex-parte decree is affirmed. The High Court's conclusion that the suit is restored is set aside. I.A. No. 1163 of 2021 (for setting aside the ex-parte decree) is revived and the Trial Court is directed to dispose of it expeditiously, preferably within two months. Appellants are entitled to costs quantified at Rs. 50,000/-.

constitutional_provisions: Article 136 of the Constitution

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that the processes for condoning delay in filing an application and for setting aside an ex-parte decree are distinct and require independent adjudication. A revisional court cannot set aside an ex-parte decree if the order dismissing the application to set it aside was not specifically challenged, even if the delay in filing that application is condoned.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The High Court did not apply its mind to the justification for setting aside the ex-parte decree, which was a separate issue from condoning the delay.

special_directions.special_directions: The Trial Court is directed to take up I.A. No. 1163 of 2021 and dispose of it as expeditiously as possible, preferably within two months from the date of receipt of this order. The appellants shall be entitled to cost quantified at Rs. 50,000/- payable by the respondents.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NOS. OF 2025 (Arising out of SLP(C) Nos.14513-14514 of 2020)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the propriety of modifying a High Court order via an oral "for being spoken to" mention, three years after its original passing, without notice to the respondents, and the subsequent clarification by a Division Bench.

judgements.case_summary: The appellant's father was granted occupancy rights by the Land Tribunal in 1981. In 2004, the appellant sought rectification of this order, which was initially dismissed by the Tribunal but later remanded by the High Court. The Tribunal then granted the rectification in 2007. Aggrieved, the respondents filed a Writ Petition, which the Single Judge disposed of in 2013. Three years later, in 2016, the appellant sought and obtained a modification to the 2013 order via an oral "for being spoken to" mention, adding a sentence that confirmed the Tribunal's 2007 order. The respondents challenged this modification in a Writ Appeal, arguing it was made without notice and violated natural justice. The Division Bench clarified the order, leading the appellant to file a review, which was dismissed. The Supreme Court deprecated the practice of modifying judicial orders through informal oral mentions, especially after a significant delay and without notice, emphasizing the stability and finality of judicial pronouncements. The Court found the Single Judge's action improper and in violation of natural justice. Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside the Division Bench's judgment, the review order, the Single Judge's 2013 order, and the corrected order of 2016. The original Writ Petition (W.P. No.1331/2008) was restored to the High Court's file for fresh hearing, and costs of Rs.1,00,000/- were imposed on the appellant.

petitioner_key_arguments: Sought rectification/modification of the Land Tribunal's 1981 order regarding land extent and survey number.
Sought modification of the Single Judge's 2013 order via 'for being spoken to' to confirm the Tribunal's 2007 order.
respondent_key_arguments: Modification of 'paragraph 6' by the Single Judge was not in accordance with law.
Modification was made without opportunity for respondents to contest, violating natural justice.
The procedure of 'for being spoken to' for modification after three years was improper and circumvented legal processes like review.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the respondents' arguments that the modification procedure adopted by the appellant was improper, violated natural justice, and circumvented established legal processes for modifying judicial orders.

outcome.relief_granted: The judgment of the Division Bench in W.A.No.683/2018, the order in Review Petition No.535/2019, the Single Judge's order dated 25.02.2013 in W.P. No.1331/2008, and the corrected order dated 19.01.2016 in W.P.No.1331/2008 are set aside. W.P. No.1331/2008 is restored on the file of the High Court for fresh hearing. Costs of Rs.1,00,000/- are to be paid by the appellant to private respondent Nos.1 to 5.

precedents_cited: Supertech Limited vs. Emerald Court Owner Resident Welfare Association, (2023) 10 SCC 817

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: Judicial pronouncements possess stability and finality, and modifications to orders, especially after a significant delay, must adhere to established legal procedures like review petitions, not informal oral mentions without notice. Such unilateral modifications violate principles of natural justice and judicial propriety.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court deplored the practice of making oral mentions for modification of orders/judgments in the guise of a review, stating that it cannot be permitted as it circumvents the legal process of filing a review. Judicial verdicts are not like sand dunes subject to vagaries of wind and weather.

special_directions.special_directions: W.P. No.1331/2008 is restored on the file of the High Court and shall be heard in accordance with law and as expeditiously as possible. Costs of Rs.1,00,000/- (Rupees One Lakh Only) are to be paid by the appellant to the private respondent Nos.1 to 5.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 255 OF 2025 [ARISING OUT OF SLP (CIVIL) NO. 30532 /2019]

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns a claim for compassionate appointment by the dependent of a deceased bank employee, focusing on the assessment of financial distress, age relaxation, and the applicability of the compassionate appointment scheme.

judgements.case_summary: The case involves an appeal by Canara Bank against a High Court judgment that directed the bank to appoint Ajithkumar G.K. on compassionate grounds. Ajithkumar's father, a bank employee, passed away in 2001, and Ajithkumar applied for compassionate appointment in 2002 under the 1993 scheme. His application was initially rejected due to the family's financial position (receipt of family pension and terminal benefits) and his being overaged. After multiple rounds of litigation, including a High Court order in 2015 directing reconsideration, and a subsequent order in 2016 allowing the writ petition and directing appointment with costs, the bank appealed to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court examined the principles of compassionate appointment, emphasizing that it is an exception meant to alleviate immediate financial distress, not a right. It held that financial condition, including terminal benefits and family pension, must be assessed, and suitability criteria must be met. The Court disagreed with the High Court's view that terminal benefits are irrelevant and that appointment could be directed without a suitability assessment. While acknowledging the High Court's predicament in following a previous Supreme Court decision (Canara Bank supra) which was later referred to a larger bench, the Supreme Court found the High Court's orders unjustified in directing appointment without considering suitability. However, recognizing the respondent's two-decade long wait and the hope generated by the High Court's decisions, the Supreme Court, exercising its powers under Article 142, set aside the High Court's judgments but directed the bank to pay the respondent a lump sum of Rs. 2.5 lakh, in addition to Rs. 50,000 already paid.

petitioner_key_arguments: Reliance by the Single Judge and Division Bench on Canara Bank (supra) was misplaced as the facts differed, and paragraph 19 were mere observations, not binding precedent, and the decision is referred to a larger bench.
Terminal benefits and family pension must be accounted for when assessing the family's overall financial condition for compassionate appointment.
The question of age relaxation arises only if the applicant is otherwise eligible; the respondent was not eligible due to non-existence of indigent circumstances.
The High Court applied wrong tests to allow the respondent's claim.
respondent_key_arguments: The scheme of 1993 did not contain provisions to consider the applicant's family's financial condition before granting compassionate employment.
Rejection based on receipt of pension and terminal benefits contravenes the binding decision in Canara Bank (supra).
The appellant's contention of age-bar is untenable, especially after the quashing of the initial rejection, and the appellant had the power to relax age.
There was no bona fide assessment of the financial condition; the conclusion of financial soundness was based solely on pension and terminal benefits.
Substantial time has elapsed since the father's death, and the respondent should not be penalized for the delay caused by litigation.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court largely accepted the petitioner's arguments that financial condition (including terminal benefits and family pension) must be assessed for compassionate appointment and that suitability criteria cannot be overlooked. The court disagreed with the High Court's direct order of appointment without such assessment. However, the court also acknowledged the respondent's long wait and the hope generated by the High Court's orders, leading to a compensatory payment.

outcome.relief_granted: The civil appeal is allowed. The impugned judgment and order of the Division Bench as well as that of the Single Bench stands set aside. The appellant is directed to make a lumpsum payment of Rs.2.5 lakh to the respondent within a period of 2 (two) months from date. This is in addition to Rs.50,000/- already paid to the respondent in terms of an earlier order of another coordinate bench.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO.1876 OF 2016

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the jurisdiction of civil courts versus the Debts Recovery Tribunal (DRT) under the SARFAESI Act, specifically regarding the validity of a sale deed and mortgage, and the right to possession, when the plaintiff is not the borrower and claims independent title.

judgements.case_summary:
This case involves an appeal by the Central Bank of India against a High Court order that allowed a civil suit filed by Smt. Prabha Jain to proceed. Smt. Jain sought declarations that a sale deed and subsequent mortgage of her inherited property to the bank were null and void, and also sought possession. The property was allegedly illegally sold by her brother-in-law and then mortgaged to the bank. The bank initiated proceedings under the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 (SARFAESI Act) and argued that the civil court's jurisdiction was barred by Section 34 of the Act. The trial court agreed, but the High Court reversed this, holding that the DRT lacked jurisdiction to decide questions of title for third parties or to grant possession to non-borrowers.

The Supreme Court analyzed the scope of Section 34 and Section 17 of the SARFAESI Act, emphasizing that DRT's powers are limited to measures taken under Section 13(4) and do not extend to adjudicating pre-existing title disputes or granting possession to individuals not in possession or not claiming through the borrower. The Court clarified that the word "restore" in Section 17(3) implies returning possession to the person who was dispossessed, not "handing over" to a new claimant. Since Smt. Jain's claims (declaration of nullity of sale/mortgage and possession) fell outside the DRT's specific powers, the civil court retained jurisdiction. The Court also reiterated that a plaint cannot be partially rejected under Order VII Rule 11 CPC if even one relief survives. Consequently, the Supreme Court dismissed the bank's appeal, affirming the High Court's decision that the civil suit could proceed.

petitioner_key_arguments: The civil court's jurisdiction is barred by Section 34 of the SARFAESI Act.
The DRT has jurisdiction over matters related to measures taken under Section 13(4) of the SARFAESI Act.
respondent_key_arguments: The DRT has no jurisdiction to decide questions of title for persons other than the mortgagor.
The validity of the sale deed and mortgage deed are matters for the civil court, not the DRT.
The DRT's power to "restore" possession under Section 17(3) does not extend to "hand over" possession to a third party who was never in possession or is not a borrower.
A plaint cannot be partially rejected under Order VII Rule 11 CPC if some reliefs are within the civil court's jurisdiction.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the respondent's arguments that the DRT's jurisdiction under the SARFAESI Act is limited and does not extend to adjudicating title disputes involving third parties or granting possession to non-borrowers. Therefore, the civil court retains jurisdiction for such matters.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal filed by the Central Bank of India is dismissed. The interim order granted earlier by the Supreme Court stands vacated. The civil suits shall now proceed further expeditiously in accordance with law.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that the jurisdiction of civil courts is not ousted by Section 34 of the SARFAESI Act for matters that the Debts Recovery Tribunal (DRT) is not empowered to determine. case_identification.respondent_name: THE STATE OF JHARKHAND AND OTHERS
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO(S). 10389 OF 2024

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the interpretation of educational qualifications for the post of Food Safety Officer, specifically whether post-graduate degrees in relevant subjects are valid when the advertisement primarily mentioned a "degree" or Master's only for Chemistry.

judgements.case_summary:
The appellants, holding post-graduate degrees in science with microbiology, food, and technology subjects, applied for Food Safety Officer (FSO) posts advertised by the Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) in 2015. They cleared the written examination but were disqualified during interviews on the grounds that their Master's degrees were not considered valid qualifications, as the advertisement was interpreted to require only a graduation degree for subjects other than Chemistry, for which a Master's was specified. Aggrieved, the appellants approached the High Court, which dismissed their writ petition and subsequent intra-court appeal. The High Court held that the appellants did not possess a graduation degree in the specified subjects and that their post-graduate degrees did not meet the qualification criteria.
The Supreme Court, however, found that the term "degree" as defined in the UGC Act includes Bachelor's, Master's, and Doctorate degrees. It ruled that the FSS Act grants the Central Government exclusive power to prescribe FSO qualifications, and the FSS 2011 Rules, while specifically mentioning a Master's degree for Chemistry, do not exclude Master's or Doctorate degrees in other specified subjects like Food Technology, Biotechnology, etc. The Court noted that a 2022 amendment to the Food Safety and Standard Rules explicitly clarified that Bachelor's, Master's, or Doctorate degrees in these subjects are valid qualifications.
The Supreme Court concluded that the disqualification of the appellants was unjust, arbitrary, and unconstitutional. It allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's judgments, and directed that the appellants be allowed to participate in the recruitment process from the interview stage. To accommodate them, supernumerary posts are to be created if necessary, and while no back wages are granted, they are entitled to all notional service benefits.

petitioner_key_arguments: The term "degree" in the subject advertisement and FSS Act should not be restrictively interpreted to exclude post-graduation degrees in relevant subjects.
The UGC Act defines "degree" to include Bachelor's, Master's, and Doctorate degrees.
The Central Government has the exclusive power to prescribe qualifications for FSOs under the FSS Act, and the State Government cannot transgress this.
The Food Safety and Standards (First Amendment) Rules, 2022, clarified that Bachelor's, Master's, or Doctorate degrees in the specified subjects are valid qualifications for FSO.
A candidate possessing a higher degree should not be disqualified for not possessing the required lower degree.
respondent_key_arguments: Appellants participated in the recruitment process without challenging the conditions in the advertisement.
The advertisement and FSS 2011 Rules restricted Master's degree qualification only to the Chemistry subject, implying a graduation level degree for other subjects.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the term "degree" encompasses Master's and Doctorate degrees in the specified subjects, and that the State's restrictive interpretation was arbitrary and unconstitutional, especially given the Central Government's exclusive power to prescribe qualifications and subsequent clarifications.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned judgments of the High Court were quashed and set aside. Appellants are to be allowed to partake in the recruitment process from the interview stage. If vacancies do not exist, supernumerary posts shall be created. Successful appellants will be offered appointment below the last selected candidate in the 2016 process, with no back wages but all notional service benefits.

acts_cited: Food Safety and Standards (First Amendment) Rules, 2022
precedents_cited: Parvaiz Ahmad Parry v. State of Jammu and Kashmir and Others (2015) 17 SCC 709
constitutional_provisions: Article 246(2) of the Constitution of India
Article 254 of the Constitution of India
Seventh Schedule of the Constitution of India

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that the term "degree" in educational qualification requirements, particularly for posts like Food Safety Officer, should be interpreted broadly to include Bachelor's, Master's, and Doctorate degrees, unless a specific exclusion is provided. The power to prescribe such qualifications rests exclusively with the Central Government, and any restrictive interpretation by a State that contradicts this broad definition or the Central Government's rules is arbitrary and unconstitutional.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed that excluding candidates with higher degrees in relevant subjects is illogical and unjust, especially when the Central Government has clarified the inclusive nature of such qualifications through amendments.

special_directions.special_directions: The respondents shall create supernumerary posts to accommodate the appellants if vacancies do not exist in the 2016 recruitment process. Successful appellants shall be placed below the last candidate selected and appointed in the subject selection process to ensure seniority of already selected candidates is not disturbed.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 879 OF 2019

case_details.subject_matter: This case is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction and death sentence for murder, rape, kidnapping, and other related offences, primarily based on circumstantial evidence and the admissibility of electronic records.

judgements.case_summary:
The present appeal challenged the correctness of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay's judgment dated 20.12.2018, which upheld the conviction and death sentence of the appellant, Chandrabhan Sudam Sanap, for offences including murder (Section 302 IPC), kidnapping (Section 364 IPC), abduction to compel marriage (Section 366 IPC), rape (Sections 376(2)(m), 376A IPC), robbery (Section 392 read with 397 IPC), and causing disappearance of evidence (Section 201 IPC). The case was based entirely on circumstantial evidence. The prosecution alleged that the appellant was last seen with the deceased, EA, at Lokmanya Tilak Terminus (LTT) on 05.01.2014, and her burnt, decomposed body was found on 16.01.2014. Key evidence included CCTV footage from LTT, 'last seen' testimonies, an extra-judicial confession to PW-9, and recoveries of the deceased's articles and the appellant's motorcycle.

The appellant argued that the CCTV footage was inadmissible due to the lack of a Section 65-B(4) certificate, and even if admissible, it did not conclusively link him with the deceased. The defense also challenged the reliability of 'last seen' witnesses due to significant delays in recording statements and prior media circulation of the appellant's photograph, which vitiated identification parades. The extra-judicial confession was deemed unreliable due to the witness's questionable credibility and lack of corroboration. Recoveries were also contested as suspicious and not conclusively linked to the appellant.

The Supreme Court found significant infirmities in the prosecution's case. It ruled that the CCTV footage was inadmissible due to the absence of the mandatory Section 65-B(4) certificate, citing the precedent of Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer. The court also found the 'last seen' testimonies and the extra-judicial confession to be unreliable and lacking the necessary confidence for conviction. The recoveries were also not found to be sufficiently credible. The court concluded that the chain of circumstantial evidence was not complete and did not lead to the sole hypothesis of the appellant's guilt, failing the test laid down in Sharad Birdhichand Sarda. Consequently, the appeal was allowed, and the appellant was acquitted.

petitioner_key_arguments: CCTV footage is inadmissible due to the lack of a Section 65-B(4) certificate, as mandated by Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer.
The CCTV footage, even if admissible, does not conclusively identify both the appellant and the deceased together.

The 'last seen' testimonies of PW-20, PW-21, PW-18, and PW-19 are unreliable due to significant delays in recording statements, inconsistencies, and prior media circulation of the appellant's photograph, which vitiated identification parades.
The extra-judicial confession made to PW-9 is a weak piece of evidence, unreliable due to PW-9's questionable credibility, contradictions in his testimony, and lack of corroboration.

The alleged recoveries of the deceased's articles (identity card, spectacles, etc.) and the appellant's motorcycle were suspicious, not properly documented, and not conclusively linked to the appellant.
The prosecution failed to establish a complete chain of circumstantial evidence that leads to the sole hypothesis of the appellant's guilt, as required by Sharad Birdhichand Sarda.
Parallel investigations by different police units created procedural irregularities and potential for manipulation of evidence.
respondent_key_arguments: The deceased EA was last seen with the accused at Lokmanya Tilak Terminus (LTT) on 05.01.2014.
The death of the deceased was homicidal, with injuries to private parts, establishing rape.
An attempt was made to destroy evidence by burning the body.
CCTV footage from LTT showed the accused loitering and then leaving the station with the deceased.
The accused was seen near the crime spot with the deceased's trolley bag and backpack.
The subsequent conduct of the accused, including visiting an astrologer for a puja to wash off a sin committed on a woman, indicates guilt.
Recovery of the deceased's articles (identity card, spectacles, eye-liner, pencil) at the instance of the accused.
The accused made an extra-judicial confession to PW-9, admitting to rape, murder, and burning the body.
The medical examination of the accused (potency test and mental health) was part of the investigation.
The tabulated circumstances, when stitched together, form a complete chain of circumstantial evidence proving the appellant's guilt.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the CCTV footage was inadmissible due to the lack of a Section 65-B(4) certificate, that the 'last seen' testimonies were unreliable due to delays and media influence, and that the extra-judicial confession and recoveries were not credible or sufficiently corroborated. These arguments successfully demonstrated that the chain of circumstantial evidence was incomplete and did not exclude all other hypotheses of innocence.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal is allowed, the judgment of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay dated 20.12.2018 is set aside, and the appellant is acquitted with regard to the offences for which he was charged. The appellant shall be set at liberty forthwith, if not required in any other case.

judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court emphasized that the certificate required under Section 65-B(4) is a condition precedent to the admissibility of evidence by way of electronic record. It also highlighted the unreliability of identification parades conducted after significant delays and widespread media circulation of the accused's photographs.
