case_identification.petitioner_name: Chief Manager Of Rajasthan State Road Transport Corporation

bench_judges: HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE SATISH CHANDRA SHARMA

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the entitlement to back wages and continuity of service for an employee following termination, specifically challenging a High Court review order that granted full back wages after an initial order of 50% back wages.

judgements.case_summary: The case originated from a dispute regarding the termination of Haneef Khan's employment. The High Court, in D.B. Special Appeal Writ No.310/2018 and No.819/2018, initially ordered 50% back wages and continuity of service for the period 04.10.2001 to 30.11.2010 with 9% interest. The employer's appeal was dismissed. Subsequently, Haneef Khan filed D.B. Civil Review Petition No.263/2019, which was allowed on 11.07.2022, granting full back wages for the said period. The Chief Manager of Rajasthan State Road Transport Corporation appealed this review order to the Supreme Court. The appellant argued that the original rejection of permission under Section 33(2)(b) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, was contrary to law, and sought to set aside the review order and restore the 50% back wages. The respondent contended that the High Court was justified in granting full back wages. The Supreme Court found that while the Labour Court's rejection of termination permission implied continuity of service, granting full back wages for a period of nearly ten years during which no duties were performed was not just and proper. Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside the review petition order dated 11.07.2022 and restored the Division Bench's original order dated 12.02.2019, which awarded 50% back wages. The Corporation was directed to comply with this order and grant all monetary benefits due to the respondent's superannuation within one month.

petitioner_key_arguments: The order rejecting permission under Section 33(2)(b) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, by the Labour Court and sustained by the High Court is contrary to law.

Alternatively, the order of the Division Bench dated 12.02.2019 (granting 50% back wages) should be given effect, and the Review Petition order dated 11.07.2022 (granting full back wages) should be set aside.
respondent_key_arguments: There is no merit in the appeal.
The High Court was justified in allowing the Review Petition and granting full back wages.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's argument to set aside the review petition order granting full back wages and to restore the original order granting 50% back wages was accepted by the court.

outcome.relief_granted: The order passed in the Review Petition dated 11.07.2022, which granted full back wages, was set aside. The original order passed by the Division Bench dated 12.02.2019, granting 50% back wages and continuity of service, was sustained. The appellant-Corporation was directed to comply with the 12.02.2019 order and grant all monetary benefits the respondent is entitled to owing to his superannuation within one month.

precedents_cited: D.B. Special Appeal Writ No.310/2018
D.B. Special Appeal Writ No.819/2018
D.B. Civil Review Petition No.263/2019

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The court reasoned that while the Labour Court's rejection of permission for termination implied continuity of service, granting full back wages for a period of nearly ten years during which the respondent did not perform any duties was not just and proper. Therefore, the initial order of 50% back wages was deemed appropriate and restored.

special_directions.special_directions: The appellant-Corporation shall comply with the directions of the High Court in D.B. Special Appeal Writ No.310/2018 dated 12.02.2019 and grant all monetary benefits that the respondent is entitled to owing to his superannuation, if any, within a period of one month from today.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NOS.75-76 of 2025 (@Petitions for Special Leave to Appeal (C) Nos.18676-18677/2018)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the procedure for determining market value and demanding additional stamp duty under Section 47-A of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, specifically challenging the High Court's decision to quash undervaluation orders due to procedural non-compliance.

judgements.case_summary: The Supreme Court heard appeals filed by the Chief Revenue Controlling Officer and other revenue officers against a Madras High Court judgment. The High Court had quashed orders related to stamp valuation for two sale deeds, finding that the authorities failed to follow the correct procedure under the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, and the Tamil Nadu Stamp (Prevention of Undervaluation of Instruments) Rules, 1968. Specifically, the High Court noted that the Form-I notices issued did not provide reasons for believing the documents were undervalued, and the Special Deputy Collector (Stamps) did not issue a provisional order or Form II notice as required before passing the final valuation order. The Supreme Court affirmed the High Court's reasoning, emphasizing that the Registering Officer must have a reasoned belief for undervaluation, not a mechanical act, and that the Collector must strictly adhere to the prescribed procedural steps, including issuing provisional orders and Form II notices. Consequently, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, upholding the High Court's decision to set aside the undervaluation orders.

petitioner_key_arguments: It is not mandatory to assign reasons in the notice issued in Form I.
respondent_key_arguments: Form I notices must contain reasons for undervaluation.
The Registering Officer must record reasons for believing undervaluation.

The Collector must follow the procedure under Rules 4 and 6 of the Tamil Nadu Stamp (Prevention of Undervaluation of Instruments) Rules, 1968, including issuing a provisional order and Form II notice.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The respondent's arguments, as upheld by the High Court and affirmed by the Supreme Court, regarding the necessity of reasons in Form I and adherence to procedural rules (Rules 4 and 6) for stamp valuation.

outcome.relief_granted: The High Court's order quashing the stamp valuation orders is upheld, setting aside the original valuation by the authorities.

acts_cited: Tamil Nadu Stamp (Prevention of Undervaluation of Instruments) Rules, 1968, Rule 3
Tamil Nadu Stamp (Prevention of Undervaluation of Instruments) Rules, 1968, Rule 4
Tamil Nadu Stamp (Prevention of Undervaluation of Instruments) Rules, 1968, Rule 6
Tamil Nadu Stamp (Prevention of Undervaluation of Instruments) Rules, 1968, Rule 7
precedents_cited: Dawsons Ltd. v. Bonnin, 1922 (2) AC 413
Mohali Club, Mohali v. State of Punjab, reported in AIR 2011 P&H 23
G. Karmegnam v. The Joint Sub-Registrar, Madurai reported in 2007 (5) CTC 737

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The Registering Officer must have a "reason to believe" that an instrument is undervalued, and this belief must be based on material and recorded reasons, not a mechanical act or roving inquiry. The Collector must strictly follow the procedural rules (e.g., provisional order, Form II notice) under the Tamil Nadu Stamp (Prevention of Undervaluation of Instruments) Rules, 1968, before passing a final order on stamp valuation.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The expression 'reason to believe' is not synonymous with subjective satisfaction; it requires objective satisfaction based on material available on record.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO(S). 9694 OF 2024, CIVIL APPEAL NO(S). 9695 OF 2024

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the validity of the Chancellor's appointment for CMJ University, the State Government's order dissolving the University, and the High Court's decision to remand the matter for reconsideration on merits.

judgements.case_summary:
The case involves two Civil Appeals, No. 9694 of 2024 filed by CMJ Foundation and Others (appellants) and No. 9695 of 2024 filed by the State of Meghalaya (respondent), challenging a High Court Division Bench judgment dated May 6, 2021. The core issues revolve around the validity of the Chancellor's appointment for CMJ University and the subsequent dissolution order of the University by the State Government.

The appellants contended that the Chancellor's appointment was valid, arguing for "deemed approval" due to the Visitor's inaction, and that the State Government failed to follow proper procedure under Section 48 of the CMJ University Act, 2009, before dissolving the University. They argued that the Single Judge had correctly quashed the dissolution order.

The respondent-State countered that the Chancellor's appointment was invalid as it lacked the mandatory approval of the Visitor, and the "deemed approval" concept was not legally tenable. They asserted that the State Government had strictly adhered to the procedural requirements of Section 48 of the Act, including issuing show cause notices and providing opportunities for explanation, before passing the dissolution order. The State also challenged the Division Bench's decision to remand the matter to the Single Judge for reconsideration on merits, arguing that the issues were already conclusively determined.

The Supreme Court addressed three main issues: the adherence to procedure for the Chancellor's appointment, the adherence to procedure for the dissolution order, and the justification of the High Court's remand. The Court found that the Chancellor's appointment was "non est and void ab initio" due to the lack of mandatory Visitor approval, rejecting the "deemed approval" argument. It also held that the State Government had strictly followed the procedural requirements of Section 48 of the Act in dissolving the University. Consequently, the Court concluded that the Division Bench was not justified in remanding the matter for reconsideration on merits, as the issues had been exhaustively examined.

The Court dismissed Civil Appeal No. 9694 of 2024 (appellants) and allowed Civil Appeal No. 9695 of 2024 (State), affirming the State Government's dissolution order dated March 31, 2014, and setting aside the High Court's remand order. The State Government was permitted to take appropriate measures following the affirmation of the dissolution.

petitioner_key_arguments: CMJ University was established by an Act, UGC recognized, and had significant investment in infrastructure.
The Sponsor was entitled to appoint the Chancellor 'subject to approval', arguing that prior approval was not required or that 'deemed approval' occurred due to the Visitor's inaction.

The State Government failed to comply with the mandatory requirements of Sub-sections (2) and (3) of Section 48 of the CMJ University Act, 2009, which require issuing directions for rectification before dissolution.
The show cause notices lacked specific instances of mismanagement or maladministration.
The learned Single Judge rightly concluded that principles of natural justice and Section 48 of the Act were not followed before the dissolution order.
respondent_key_arguments: The Division Bench had upheld the procedure adopted by the State in passing the dissolution order, leaving no live issue for the Single Judge on remand.
The State Government complied with the Supreme Court's direction to pass a speaking order under Section 48 of the Act after giving notice and opportunity of hearing.
Section 14(1) of the Act makes the Chancellor's appointment 'subject to the approval' of the Visitor, making approval mandatory.
The concept of 'deemed approval' is a legal fiction not supported by statute.
CMJ University acted unilaterally, illegally admitting students and awarding degrees without a duly approved Chancellor.
Section 26 of the Act (regarding invalidity due to vacancy) does not apply as the initial appointment itself was flawed.
The CMJ University failed to comply with the directions issued by the Visitor vide letter dated 30th April, 2013, under Section 13(3)(b) of the Act.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the respondent's arguments that the Chancellor's appointment was invalid due to the lack of mandatory Visitor approval and that the State Government had followed due procedure under Section 48 of the CMJ University Act, 2009, in dissolving the University. The petitioner's argument for 'deemed approval' was rejected.

outcome.judgement_type: Dismissed for petitioner's appeal, Allowed for respondent's appeal
outcome.relief_granted: The dissolution order dated 31st March, 2014, is affirmed. The direction given by the Division Bench to remand the matter to the Single Bench is set aside.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The appointment of the Chancellor of CMJ University was invalid because it lacked the mandatory approval of the Visitor as required by Section 14(1) of the CMJ University Act, 2009, and the concept of 'deemed approval' is not supported by statute. The State Government followed due procedure under Section 48 of the Act in dissolving the University after giving notice and opportunity to be heard, and the High Court's remand for reconsideration on merits was unjustified as the issues were conclusively determined.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed that 'subject to' means 'conditional upon' and 'approval' means 'confirming, ratifying, assenting, sanctioning or consenting to'. It also reiterated that judicial review lies against a decision-making process, not the decision itself, and that remand orders should not be passed as a matter of course when evidence is sufficient for a decision on merits.

special_directions.special_directions: It would be open for the State Government to take appropriate measures pursuant to the affirmation of the decision to dissolve the CMJ University.
special_directions.interim_orders: This Court directed the parties to maintain status quo, as it existed on 1st June, 2021.

case_identification.petitioner_name: Constable 907 Surendra Singh & Anr. and Ashad Singh Negi
case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 355 OF 2013 WITH CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 788 OF 2013

case_details.subject_matter: The case challenges a High Court judgment that reversed the trial court's acquittal of police constables and convicted them for murder, focusing on the principles of common intention and the scope of appellate interference in acquittal cases.

judgements.case_summary: This case involves two criminal appeals challenging a judgment of the High Court of Uttarakhand which reversed the acquittal of the appellants (Constable 907 Surendra Singh, Constable Surat Singh, and Ashad Singh Negi) by the trial court and convicted them for an offense punishable under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, sentencing them to life imprisonment. The incident occurred on November 15, 2004, when police personnel, including the appellants and Head Constable Jagdish Singh, attempted to intercept a Maruti car suspected of smuggling illegal liquor. Head Constable Jagdish Singh fired a shot, killing a co-passenger in the Maruti car. The trial court had convicted Jagdish Singh but acquitted the appellants, finding no evidence of their mental involvement or common intention. The High Court, however, allowed the State's appeal, convicting the appellants on the ground that their mere presence in the vehicle with Jagdish Singh was sufficient to infer common intention. The petitioners argued that the High Court erred in convicting them under Section 34 IPC without proof of common intention and that interference with an acquittal judgment is warranted only if the trial court's view is perverse or impossible. The respondent-State contended that the High Court provided sound reasons for reversing the acquittal. The Supreme Court, reiterating principles for appellate interference in acquittal cases, found that the High Court's decision was unwarranted. It held that the prosecution failed to establish common intention among the appellants and Jagdish Singh, and the trial court's finding of acquittal was well-reasoned. Consequently, the appeals were allowed, the High Court's judgment was quashed, and the trial court's judgment of acquittal for the appellants was affirmed.

petitioner_key_arguments: The High Court grossly erred in convicting the appellants with the aid of Section 34 of the IPC.
There was no evidence to show that the appellants had shared a common intention with accused No.1-Jagdish Singh.
Allegations of assault made by Sanjeev Chauhan (PW-1) and Km. Bharti (PW-2) for the first time before the Court cannot be relied on.
Despite the incident taking place in public, no independent witness was examined by the prosecution.
Interference in an acquittal judgment is warranted only if the view taken by the trial judge was found to be perverse or impossible, which was not the case here.
respondent_key_arguments: The Division Bench of the High Court has given sound reasons for reversing the order of acquittal.
No interference is warranted in the present appeals.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the High Court erred in reversing the acquittal without sufficient evidence of common intention and by not adhering to the principles governing appellate interference in acquittal judgments.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeals are allowed. The judgment and order of the High Court of Uttarakhand at Nainital in Government Appeal No. 100 of 2008 is quashed and set aside. The judgment and order dated 6th September 2006 passed by the learned Sessions Judge, Dehradun in Sessions Trial No.50 of 2005 (acquitting the appellants) is affirmed. The appellants' bail bonds shall stand discharged.

precedents_cited: Gadadhar Chandra v. State of West Bengal5 (2022) 6 SCC 576
Babu Sahebagouda Rudragoudar and others v. State of Karnataka6 (2024) 8 SCC 149
Rajesh Prasad v. State of Bihar [Rajesh Prasad v. State of Bihar, (2022) 3 SCC 471 : (2022) 2 SCC (Cri) 31]
Chandrappa case [Chandrappa v. State of Karnataka, (2007) 4 SCC 415 : (2007) 2 SCC (Cri) 325]
Ezajhussain Sabdarhussain and another v. State of Gujarat7 (2019) 14 SCC 339
Jasdeep Singh alias Jassu v. State of Punjab8 (2022) 2 SCC 545
Madhusudan and others v. State of Madhya Pradesh9 2024 SCC OnLine SC 4035

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that interference with an acquittal judgment by an appellate court is warranted only if the judgment suffers from patent perversity, misreading/omission of material evidence, or if no two reasonable views are possible and only the view consistent with guilt is possible. The court found that the prosecution failed to prove common intention among the appellants and the main accused, and the High Court erred in reversing the trial court's well-reasoned acquittal based solely on the appellants' presence in the vehicle.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court reiterated that while an appellate court has full power to review and reappreciate evidence in an appeal against acquittal, it must bear in mind the double presumption of innocence in such cases. Expressions like 'substantial and compelling reasons' are flourishes of language to emphasize reluctance to interfere with acquittal, not to curtail the court's extensive powers.

special_directions.interim_orders: This Court by order dated 15th July 2013 admitted Criminal Appeal Nos. 355 of 2013 and 788 of 2013 and granted bail to the appellants in both the appeals.

case_identification.respondent_name: M/S Chemplast Cuddalore Vinyls Limited AND ANR
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NOS. 372-373 OF 2025 (@SLP (C) NOS. 1297-1298 OF 2025) (@ SLP(C) D. No.13548 of 2017)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the applicability of Order II Rule 2 of the Civil Procedure Code to a second suit for specific performance, where a previous suit for permanent injunction was filed, and whether the relief sought in the second suit was 'available' at the time of filing the first suit.

judgements.case_summary:
This case involves an appeal against a High Court judgment that restored a plaint in a second suit (O.S. No. 122 of 2008) for specific performance and declaration, which had been previously rejected by lower courts under Order II Rule 2 CPC. The original plaintiff (respondent no. 1) had initially filed a suit for permanent injunction (O.S. No. 28 of 2008) to protect possession of a property, following an agreement for sale and alleged interference. The appellant (original defendant no. 2) contended that the second suit was barred by Order II Rule 2 CPC, arguing that the relief of specific performance could have been sought in the first suit.

The Supreme Court meticulously analyzed the concept of 'cause of action' and the conditions for applying Order II Rule 2 CPC, emphasizing that for the bar to apply, the relief must not only be one the plaintiff is 'entitled to' but also 'available' at the time of filing the first suit. The Court noted that at the time the first suit was filed, a Government Order (GO) had imposed an absolute ban on registering sale deeds in the area, rendering specific performance impossible. This ban was subsequently quashed by the High Court, which the Supreme Court found created a new cause of action for specific performance.

Distinguishing the present facts from precedents where plaintiffs had prior knowledge of the defendant's refusal to perform the contract, the Court concluded that the non-availability of relief due to the GO ban meant the respondent could not have sought specific performance in the first suit. Therefore, the second suit was not barred by Order II Rule 2 CPC. The appeals filed by the appellant were dismissed, affirming the High Court's decision to restore the plaint.

petitioner_key_arguments: The second suit is barred by Order II Rule 2 CPC because the respondent no. 1 had knowledge of the refusal to perform the contract and the execution of the sale deed in favour of the appellant even before filing the first suit.
The omission to seek specific performance in the first suit amounts to a deliberate relinquishment of the claim.
Extraneous matters (like the GO ban) cannot be projected as a new cause for the second suit unless set forth in the original agreement.
The respondent no. 1 reserved its right to file a separate suit for specific performance but did not obtain leave of the court as required by Order II Rule 2(3) CPC.
respondent_key_arguments: The causes of action in the two suits are totally different, and the reliefs claimed in the second suit could not have been claimed in the first suit.
The first suit was for immediate protection against the threat of dispossession, while the second suit arose from the quashing of the GO ban which previously made specific performance impossible.
The relief of specific performance was not 'available' at the time of filing the first suit due to the absolute ban on registration of sale deeds imposed by the Government Order.
The High Court's decision to quash the GO created a new cause of action, making the relief of specific performance available.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The respondent's argument that the relief of specific performance was not 'available' at the time of filing the first suit due to a Government Order imposing a ban on registration of sale deeds, and that a new cause of action arose when this ban was quashed, was accepted by the Court.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeals filed by the appellant were dismissed, upholding the High Court's decision that the second suit (O.S. No. 122 of 2008) is not barred by Order II Rule 2 CPC and restoring its plaint.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that the bar under Order II Rule 2 CPC does not apply if the relief sought in a subsequent suit was not 'available' to the plaintiff at the time of filing the first suit, even if the plaintiff was 'entitled' to it. If external circumstances, such as a government ban, made obtaining such relief impossible, and these circumstances are later removed, a new cause of action arises, and the subsequent suit is not barred.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court emphasized the importance of reading plaints holistically to determine the true cause of action, rather than isolating specific paragraphs. It also reiterated that the object of Order II Rule 2 is to prevent multiplicity of suits and splitting of claims, but not to prevent suits based on genuinely different or newly available causes of action.

The Supreme Court did not issue new directions but upheld the High Court's decision.

case_identification.case_number: Special Leave Petition (C) No. 8687 of 2012

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the classification of land as 'Shamlat deh' and the applicability of an amendment to the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961, regarding land allotted on a quasi-permanent basis to displaced persons or transferred by sale.

judgements.case_summary:
This judgment addresses a batch of Special Leave Petitions, with Dalip Ram vs. State of Punjab (SLP (C) No. 8687 of 2012) serving as the lead case. The central issue revolves around the classification of land as "Shamlat deh" and the applicability of an amendment to the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961, specifically Section 2(g)(ii-a). This amendment provides protection to Shamlat deh land allotted on a quasi-permanent basis to a displaced person or transferred by sale or any other manner before July 9, 1985.

In the lead case, Dalip Ram challenged an eviction order, claiming his father was allotted/transferred the land as a landless Harijan. However, records showed the land was Shamlat deh, leased to his father for a 10-year period in 1961, and Dalip Ram continued unauthorized possession after the lease expired. The Court meticulously distinguished between "lease" and "allotment" and the meaning of "displaced person" and "quasi-permanent basis," drawing upon precedents like Amar Singh and Bakshish Singh. It found that Dalip Ram's father was a lessee, not an allottee on a quasi-permanent basis, nor a displaced person, thus not qualifying for the protection under the amended Act.

The Court upheld the High Court's decision, which had confirmed the concurrent findings of the authorities that the land vested with the Gram Panchayat and the petitioner was an unauthorized occupant. Similar arguments regarding land classification and the amendment's applicability were raised and dismissed in other connected Special Leave Petitions. The Court also addressed and rejected contentions about the non-framing of issues by the Collector, stating it does not vitiate proceedings if parties were aware and presented evidence. Ultimately, the Court found no reason to interfere with the High Court's findings, dismissing the lead petition and most other connected petitions.

petitioner_key_arguments: The subject land was allotted/transferred to his father (a landless Harijan) by the Government in 1961.
The petitioner is entitled to the benefit of the amendment brought to Section 2(g)(ii-a) of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961, which came into effect from 09.07.1985.
The land in question was evacuee property.
Non-framing of issues by the Collector was an illegality that prejudiced the petitioner.
The order is a nullity as no finding was recorded as to whether the subject land is Shamlat deh or not.
The land with 'Shamlat Deh' and 'Banjar Qadim' entries should not vest in Gram Panchayat or should be covered by the exclusion clause of Section 2(g) of the 1961 Act.
respondent_key_arguments: The land was Shamlat deh and vested with the Gram Panchayat.
The petitioner's father was a lessee, not an allottee on a quasi-permanent basis, and not a displaced person.
The petitioner was in unauthorized possession of the subject land after the expiry of the lease period.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court accepted the respondent's arguments that the land was Shamlat deh, the petitioner's father was a lessee, and the conditions for protection under the amended Section 2(g)(ii-a) of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961, were not met by the petitioner.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The protective benefits of the amended Section 2(g)(ii-a) of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961, apply only to Shamlat deh land allotted on a quasi-permanent basis to a displaced person or transferred by sale/other manner before 09.07.1985. A mere lease, even if long-standing, does not qualify for this protection, and unauthorized possession after lease expiry does not confer ownership.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court discussed the meaning of 'displaced person' and 'quasi' from Black's Law Dictionary. It also elaborated on the historical distinction between 'lease' and 'allotment' in the context of various East Punjab Ordinances and Central Acts. The Court observed that non-framing of issues by a lower authority does not vitiate proceedings if the parties were aware of the issues and adduced evidence.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 4359 OF 2024 (Arising out of Special Leave Petition (Crl.) No.12606/20

case_details.subject_matter: Whether a proclaimed offender status under Cr.P.C. Section 82 can subsist after acquittal in the main offense, and the independent nature of Section 174A IPC.

judgements.case_summary: This appeal challenges a High Court order dated 2nd June 2023, which refused to quash a complaint case, summoning order, and an order declaring the appellant a proclaimed offender under Section 82 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973. The appellant, Daljit Singh, was involved in a business dispute related to a contract for a National Highway project, leading to a complaint under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. Due to non-appearance, he was declared a proclaimed offender. Subsequently, an FIR under Section 174A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, was registered against him. A crucial development is that the appellant has since been acquitted in the germane proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The Supreme Court considered two main questions: whether a proclaimed offender status can subsist after acquittal in the main offense, and whether Section 174A IPC operates independently. The Court held that Section 174A IPC is an independent, substantive offense, meaning proceedings under it can continue even if the Section 82 proclamation is extinguished. However, given the appellant's acquittal in the original offense, the Court found it permissible to quash the proclamation and related proceedings. Consequently, the appeal was allowed, the High Court's order was set aside, and all criminal proceedings, including the FIR under Section 174A IPC, were closed, and the appellant's proclaimed offender status was quashed.

petitioner_key_arguments: The proclaimed offender status should not subsist once the appellant is acquitted in the main offense.
The High Court erred in dismissing the quashing petition.
respondent_key_arguments: The High Court's decision was correct, as a petition by a proclaimed offender is not maintainable.
Section 174A IPC is an independent offense and can proceed regardless of the outcome of the main case.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that, in the specific circumstances of this case (acquittal in the main offense and payment of the disputed amount), the proclaimed offender status and related proceedings should be quashed. While acknowledging the independent nature of Section 174A IPC, the court found it appropriate to close all proceedings against the appellant.

outcome.relief_granted: The judgment and order of the High Court dated 2nd June, 2023, are quashed and set aside. All criminal proceedings, inclusive of the FIR under Section 174A IPC, shall stand closed. The Appellant's status, as a 'proclaimed person', stands quashed.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: Section 174A IPC is an independent, substantive offense that can continue even if the proclamation under Section 82 Cr.P.C. is extinguished. However, if the accused is acquitted in the original offense that led to the proclamation, the court can quash the proclamation and related proceedings, especially when the original offense pertains to an old matter and the dispute has been settled.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court discussed the meaning of 'absconder' and the object and purpose of Section 82 Cr.P.C., emphasizing that its primary aim is to secure the presence of the accused. It also noted that the act of absconding, even if proved, is normally considered a somewhat weak link in the chain of circumstantial evidence.

special_directions.special_directions: The High Court's judgment and order dated 2nd June, 2023, are quashed and set aside. All criminal proceedings, inclusive of the FIR under Section 174A IPC, shall stand closed. The Appellant's status, as a 'proclaimed person', stands quashed.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS.2220-2221 OF 2022

case_details.subject_matter: The case involves an appeal against conviction for multiple murders and the confirmation of a death sentence, focusing on circumstantial evidence, reliability of witnesses, and the appropriateness of capital punishment.

judgements.case_summary:
The appellant, Deen Dayal Tiwari, was convicted for the brutal murder of his wife and four minor daughters in 2011. The Trial Court awarded the death penalty, which was confirmed by the High Court. The prosecution's case relied on circumstantial evidence, including the appellant's presence at the crime scene, his alleged possession of a blood-stained axe, and the recovery of incriminating weapons. Witnesses (PW-1, PW-2, PW-3) testified to hearing cries, seeing the appellant with an axe, and finding the bodies. Medical evidence corroborated the use of sharp-edged weapons. The appellant's defense was an alibi, claiming he was sleeping in a barn and unknown miscreants committed the crime, which he failed to substantiate.

The Supreme Court upheld the conviction, finding an unbroken chain of circumstantial evidence pointing to the appellant's guilt, especially given his failure to provide a satisfactory explanation under Section 106 of the Indian Evidence Act. The Court found minor discrepancies in witness testimonies non-fatal to the core prosecution story. However, regarding the sentence, the Court considered mitigating factors such as the appellant's lack of prior criminal antecedents and satisfactory prison conduct, suggesting a possibility of reformation. Weighing these against the aggravating factors of brutal multiple murders and vulnerability of victims, the Court concluded that the case, while heinous, did not meet the "rarest of rare" threshold for the death penalty. Consequently, the death sentence was commuted to life imprisonment until the appellant's natural lifespan.

petitioner_key_arguments: Entirely Circumstantial Evidence: No direct or ocular evidence linking the Appellant to the crime; chain of circumstances incomplete and cannot form basis for conviction.
Contradictions & Lacunae in Ocular Evidence: Material inconsistencies in testimonies of PW-1, PW-2, and PW-3 regarding events, arrivals, and police presence.
FIR Allegedly Ante-Timed: FIR lodged after Appellant's arrest, manipulated to suit prosecution's narrative.
Inadmissibility of Confessional Statement: Alleged confession to police inadmissible under Sections 25 and 26 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, and uncorroborated.
Unreliable Recovery of Weapons: Discrepancies in recovery, weapons allegedly planted, no disclosure memo bearing Appellant's signature.
Gaps in Forensic Evidence: No serological report confirming human blood match; injuries suggest broader instrument than axe/knives.
Possibility of Alibi: Appellant was sleeping in barn (khalihan) to guard paddy; unknown miscreants killed family; prosecution failed to disprove this defense.

Sentencing: Death Not Warranted: Violative of guidelines in Bachan Singh, Machhi Singh, and Manoj & Ors.; overlooked mitigating factors (age, no criminal antecedents, reformation possibility); death penalty is an exception.
respondent_key_arguments: Gravity and Heinous Nature of Offence: Extremely grave and heinous crime involving brutal murder of wife and four minor daughters with an axe.
Clear Evidence of Guilt: PW-1 and PW-2 heard cries, Appellant emerged with blood-stained axe, found inside locked room with axe, demonstrating guilt.
Recovery of Weapons & Medical Corroboration: Murder weapon (axe) recovered from Appellant at spot, two knives also found, corroborated by postmortem reports consistent with sharp-edged weapons.
Witness Credibility and Corroboration: Minor discrepancies are non-fatal; core prosecution story consistent and corroborated by medical and forensic evidence.
Concurrent Findings of Fact: Both Trial Court and High Court thoroughly examined evidence; findings are not perverse or contrary to law.
Case Falling Under ‘Rarest of Rare’: Brutality, sheer number of victims, diabolical manner of execution shock collective conscience of society.
Compliance with Manoj & Ors. v. State of Madhya Pradesh: Reports on prison conduct submitted, but these factors do not outweigh the magnitude, brutality, and impact of the crime.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the prosecution's arguments regarding the appellant's guilt based on an unbroken chain of circumstantial evidence and the reliability of witnesses, upholding the conviction. However, it accepted the petitioner's arguments regarding mitigating factors and the 'rarest of rare' doctrine, leading to the commutation of the death sentence.

outcome.relief_granted: The death sentence is modified to imprisonment for life until the end of the Appellant's natural lifespan.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The conviction was upheld based on an unbroken chain of circumstantial evidence, including the appellant's presence at the crime scene, possession of weapons, and failure to provide a satisfactory explanation under Section 106 of the Indian Evidence Act. The death sentence was commuted because, despite the heinous nature of the crime, mitigating factors such as the appellant's lack of criminal antecedents and satisfactory prison conduct indicated a possibility of reformation, thus not meeting the 'rarest of rare' threshold.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 1471 OF 2025

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns an appeal against the rejection of anticipatory bail for the appellant, who was accused of abduction, criminal intimidation, and offenses under the SC/ST Act, stemming from a dispute over temple lands with a Scheduled Caste complainant.

judgements.case_summary: The appellant, Deepak Kumar Tala, filed an appeal against the High Court's order dated 18.11.2024, which dismissed his application for anticipatory bail. The case originated from FIR No. 69 of 2024, lodged on 18.04.2024, alleging that the appellant, in a dispute over temple lands, abducted the complainant (a Scheduled Caste member), abused him with a caste slur, and threatened him to transfer the lands. The FIR included charges under various sections of the Indian Penal Code and the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. The Supreme Court examined the FIR and concluded that the essential ingredient for attracting the SC/ST Act sections, specifically the requirement of a caste slur being made within "public view," was prima facie not met. Furthermore, the court found the allegations regarding the appellant's involvement in the conspiracy for abduction and criminal intimidation to be inferential. Considering the long-standing association and subsequent disputes between the parties, the Court allowed the appeal, granting anticipatory bail to the appellant. The Court clarified that its observations were not an opinion on the merits of the case and would not influence the trial or final decision.

petitioner_key_arguments: The alleged caste slur was not made within "public view," which is a necessary ingredient for attracting Sections 2(1)(r) and 2(1)(s) of the SC/ST Act.
The allegations regarding the appellant's involvement in the alleged conspiracy for abduction and criminal intimidation are only inferential.
The parties had a long-standing association and subsequent civil disputes, indicating a different context for the allegations.
respondent_key_arguments: The appellant committed serious offenses including abduction, criminal intimidation, and offenses under the SC/ST Act.
The allegations in the FIR warrant denial of anticipatory bail.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the SC/ST Act provisions were not prima facie attracted due to the absence of "public view" for the caste slur, and that the conspiracy allegations were inferential.

outcome.relief_granted: Anticipatory bail granted to the appellant in connection with FIR No. 69 of 2024, subject to terms and conditions to be imposed by the Trial Court.

acts_cited: Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, Sections 3(1)(r), 3(1)(s), and 3(2)(va)
precedents_cited: Swaran Singh v. State, (2008) 8 SCC 435
Hitesh Verma v. State of Uttarakhand, (2020) 10 SCC 710

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The Court's decision to grant anticipatory bail was primarily based on the finding that the essential ingredient for attracting Sections 2(1)(r) and 2(1)(s) of the SC/ST Act, specifically the requirement of an insult/caste slur being made within "public view," was not prima facie established from the FIR. Additionally, the allegations of the appellant's involvement in the conspiracy for abduction and criminal intimidation were deemed inferential, not directly proven by the FIR.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court explicitly stated that it had not expressed any opinion on the merits of the matter and that the observations made in its order would have no bearing on the conduct of the trial or on the final decision in the criminal proceedings.

special_directions.special_directions: The appellant shall be released on bail, in the event of arrest, subject to such terms and conditions as the Trial Court may deem fit to impose.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (Arising out of SLP(C)No. 236/2024)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns an appeal for enhanced compensation in a motor accident claim, specifically regarding the calculation of notional income for an injured student.

judgements.case_summary: On October 12, 2012, the claimant-appellant, Deepak Singh, was grievously injured in a motor accident when the motorcycle he was riding collided with a Scorpio. The driver of the motorcycle succumbed to injuries. An FIR was registered under various sections of the Indian Penal Code. Deepak filed a claim petition on January 7, 2013, before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT), Gurgaon, which awarded Rs. 7,09,303/- with 7.5% interest. Dissatisfied with the compensation, Deepak appealed to the High Court of Punjab and Haryana, which enhanced the compensation to Rs. 23,90,719/-, maintaining the interest rate. Further aggrieved, Deepak appealed to the Supreme Court, primarily challenging the High Court's reliance on minimum wages for calculating his compensation. The Supreme Court, relying on its precedent in Harpreet Singh (supra), determined the notional income for an engineering student should be Rs. 10,000/- per month and recomputed the total compensation to Rs. 34,56,103/-, along with 7.5% interest from the date of filing the claim petition, excluding a 642-day delay in preferring the appeal to the Supreme Court. The appeal was allowed.

petitioner_key_arguments: The High Court erred by relying on minimum wages to calculate compensation for an injured student.
The notional income for an engineering student should be higher, as established in Harpreet Singh (supra), suggesting Rs. 10,000/- per month.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's argument that the notional income for an engineering student should not be equated with minimum wages and should be calculated based on precedents like Harpreet Singh (supra) was accepted by the court.

outcome.relief_granted: The total compensation was enhanced to Rs. 34,56,103/- with 7.5% interest per annum from the date of filing the claim petition, excluding a 642-day delay period in preferring the appeal before the Supreme Court.

precedents_cited: Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar
Harpreet Singh (supra)
Navjot Singh v. Harpreet Singh
constitutional_provisions: Article 142 of the Constitution of India

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that the notional income of a student undergoing a Degree course in Engineering from a premier institute should not be equated with the minimum wages of an unskilled worker for compensation calculation in motor accident claims. Instead, a higher notional income (e.g., Rs. 10,000/- per month in 2012) should be adopted, drawing guidance from previous Supreme Court judgments like Harpreet Singh (supra), to ensure fair and adequate compensation reflecting future prospects.

special_directions.special_directions: Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of accordingly.

case_identification.petitioner_name: Delhi Agricultural Marketing Board, through its Chairman
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 10757 OF 2017

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the legality of an agreement by the Delhi Agricultural Marketing Board to return a portion of compulsorily acquired land to the original owner, challenging an arbitral award and High Court judgments that upheld the agreement.

judgements.case_summary:
This appeal arises from a dispute concerning the acquisition of land by the Delhi Agricultural Marketing Board (the Board) for a grain market in Narela. In 1963-1969, 33 acres, including 6 bighas and 10 biswas owned by Bhagwan Devi, were acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. Possession was taken on 22.09.1986. Bhagwan Devi challenged this acquisition. Curiously, the Board, through its Chairman, entered into an agreement on 30.09.1988 to return half of Bhagwan Devi's acquired land (3 bighas and 5 biswas) to her. This agreement was made under suspicious circumstances, including its timing just before the Chairman's tenure ended and the purchase of stamp papers before the Board meeting.
The Board later questioned the agreement's validity, arguing it was void ab initio, against public policy, and beyond its powers, as the land had vested in the Government and could not be returned without the consent of the land acquisition authorities. Despite these objections, an Arbitrator upheld the agreement in 2007, directing the Board to comply. The Delhi High Court, both a single judge and a division bench, dismissed the Board's challenges under Sections 34 and 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, upholding the Arbitral Award.
The Supreme Court, in this appeal, analyzed whether the Board could reverse a compulsory acquisition through a private agreement. It held that once land is acquired and possession taken, it vests absolutely in the Government. The Board, as a beneficiary, lacked the power to return such land, especially without the involvement of the land acquisition authorities or a formal conveyance to the Board itself. The Court found the agreement to be in contravention of the fundamental policy of Indian law and patently illegal. Consequently, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court judgments and the Arbitral Award, thereby invalidating the agreement to return the land.

petitioner_key_arguments: The agreement dated 30.09.1988 was void ab initio and could not be implemented.
The land acquisition authorities were not party to the agreement.
The acquired land could not be returned without the consent of the Government.
The agreement was brought into existence with undue haste (stamp papers purchased on 26.09.1988, drafted on 27.09.1988, matter put up on 29.09.1988, Chairman signed on 30.09.1988, his last day).
The agreement was against public policy.
The Board did not have the power to return land that had vested absolutely in the Government.
respondent_key_arguments: The Board was competent to enter into the agreement dated 30.09.1988.
Sought implementation of the agreement dated 30.09.1988.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments that the agreement was void ab initio, against public policy, and beyond the Board's powers, and that the High Courts and Arbitrator erred in upholding it, were accepted by the Supreme Court.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal is allowed. The judgment dated 27.09.2013 of the Division Bench of the Delhi High Court in FAO (OS) No. 436 of 2013, along with the judgment dated 01.07.2013 delivered by the learned Judge of the Delhi High Court in OMP No. 561 of 2007 and the Arbitral Award dated 10.07.2007 are set aside.

acts_cited: Bombay Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1939, Section 16
Delhi Agricultural Produce Marketing (Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 5
Delhi Agricultural Produce Marketing (Regulation) Act, 1976, Section 5(3)
Delhi Agricultural Produce Marketing (Regulation) Act, 1998, Section 6
Delhi Agricultural Produce Marketing (Regulation) Act, 1998, Section 24(1)
Delhi Agricultural Produce Marketing (Regulation) Act, 1998, Section 24(2)
precedents_cited: Arb. P. No. 278 of 2004
OMP No. 561 of 2007
FAO (OS) No. 436 of 2013
SLP (C) No. 9491 of 2014

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: Once land is acquired under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and possession is taken, it vests absolutely in the Government, free from encumbrances. A statutory beneficiary (like the Board) cannot, through a private agreement, reverse the acquisition or return the land, especially when the land acquisition authorities are not party to it and the land has not been formally conveyed to the Board. Such an agreement is against public policy and the fundamental policy of Indian law.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that the preparation of the agreement dated 30.09.1988, by purchase of stamp papers and drafting even before the matter was considered by the Board in its meeting on 29.09.1988, clearly revealed something suspect about the transaction. The agreement was patently opposed to all tenets of law.

special_directions.special_directions: Pending applications shall stand closed in the light of this order. Parties shall bear their own costs.
special_directions.interim_orders: By order dated 28.03.2014, this Court directed status quo obtaining on that day to be maintained.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 1972 OF 2011

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the validity of a land sale and subsequent auction in liquidation proceedings, where the original lease deed was never executed, raising questions about the transfer of rights and payment of unearned income to the Delhi Development Authority.

judgements.case_summary: The Delhi Development Authority (DDA) executed an agreement to lease plot no.3 to M/s Mehta Constructions in 1957, but the lease deed was never executed. M/s Mehta Constructions subsequently entered into an agreement to sell the plot to M/s Pure Drinks Private Limited (second respondent) in 1972, and a sale deed was executed in 1985. The second respondent later went into liquidation, and the plot was sold in an auction to S.G.G. Towers (P) Ltd. (first respondent) in 2000. The appellant (DDA) contended that M/s Mehta Constructions never acquired any interest in the plot as the lease deed was not executed, and therefore, could not have sold it. DDA also argued that the plot is Nazul land, requiring DDA's prior consent for transfer, which was not obtained. The respondents argued that DDA had not challenged the transactions earlier. The Supreme Court noted that the lease was never executed, meaning M/s Mehta Constructions never acquired rights, title, or interest. Consequently, the first respondent, through the auction, could only acquire the rights that M/s Mehta Constructions possessed, which were none. The Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the lower court's confirmation of the auction sale but clarified that the first respondent did not acquire ownership or leasehold rights. The Court also stated that DDA is free to pursue remedies for possession and/or recovery of unearned income, and the first respondent can apply to DDA to regularize the transaction.

petitioner_key_arguments: The agreement executed in 1957 was only an agreement to lease, and the lease deed was never executed, thus M/s Mehta Constructions never acquired leasehold rights.
Clause 24 of the lease agreement stipulated that no right, title, or interest would be created until the lease was executed and registered.
The plot is Nazul land, and its transfer requires DDA's consent under Section 22 of the Delhi Development Act, 1957, and Rule 43 of the 1981 Rules, which was not obtained.
The sale in favour of the first respondent was illegal.
respondent_key_arguments: The appellant never filed any proceedings to challenge the transactions between M/s Mehta Constructions and the second respondent, nor the auction process, until the first respondent applied for confirmation of sale.
The auction sale was confirmed by the learned Single Judge and upheld by the Division Bench.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's premise that no leasehold rights were ever transferred to M/s Mehta Constructions due to the non-execution of the lease deed. However, the appeal was dismissed, affirming the lower court's confirmation of the auction sale, but with the clarification that the purchaser acquired only the rights the seller had (which were none) and DDA retained the right to pursue remedies.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal was dismissed. No direct relief was granted to the appellant. However, the court stated that it would be open for the appellant to adopt appropriate remedy for recovery of possession and/or recovery of unearned income against the first respondent. The first respondent was also given the option to apply to the appellant to accept unearned income or any other amount to regularize the transaction.

acts_cited: Delhi Development Authority (Disposal of Developed Nazul Land) Rules, 1981, Rule 43
precedents_cited: Delhi Development Authority v. Vijaya C. Gurshaney & Anr.,1 (2003) 7 SCC 301
Food Corporation of India & Ors. v. Babulal Agrawal2 (2004) 2 SCC 712
Delhi Development Authority v. Anant Raj Agencies Pvt.Ltd.3 (2016) 11 SCC 406
State of Rajasthan & Ors. v. Gotan Lime Stone Khanij Udyog Pvt. Ltd. and Anr.4 (2016) 4 SCC 469
Delhi Development Authority v. Nalwa Sons Investment Ltd. & Anr.5 (2020) 17 SCC 782

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: An agreement to lease does not confer rights, title, or interest if the lease deed itself is never executed. Consequently, any subsequent transfers by the party who only held an agreement to lease are invalid regarding the transfer of actual leasehold rights. While an auction sale confirmed by a court may proceed, the purchaser acquires only those rights that the original party possessed. The Delhi Development Authority retains the right to pursue remedies for recovery of possession and unearned income in such cases.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed that it could not direct funds available in liquidation proceedings for payment of unearned income due to a large number of other claims submitted by various creditors.

special_directions.special_directions: The appellant was permitted to implead Mr. Prashant Baliyan, Provisional Liquidator, as a party respondent. Mr. Prashant Baliyan was directed to make a statement about the availability and investment status of the amount deposited by the first respondent. The appellant was directed to communicate to the learned counsel for the first respondent the amount payable in respect of both transactions. It was clarified that the appellant is at liberty to adopt appropriate remedies for recovery of possession and/or recovery of unearned income against the first respondent. The first respondent may apply to the appellant to accept unearned income or any other amount to regularize the transaction.
special_directions.interim_orders: An order dated 4th October 2023 was passed, directing the impleadment of the Provisional Liquidator and seeking information regarding deposited amounts and their investment.

case_identification.case_number: PETITION FOR SPECIAL LEAVE TO APPEAL (CRL.) NO. 3247 OF 2025

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the denial of anticipatory bail to a public servant accused of demanding illegal gratification under the Prevention of Corruption Act and Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.

judgements.case_summary: The Supreme Court dismissed a Special Leave Petition filed by Devinder Kumar Bansal, an Audit Inspector, challenging the High Court's denial of anticipatory bail. Bansal was accused under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, and Section 61(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, for demanding illegal gratification related to an audit. It was alleged that a co-accused collected the bribe on his behalf, and an audio recording corroborated the demand. The petitioner argued for anticipatory bail, citing Article 21 of the Constitution and the lack of necessity for custodial interrogation. The respondent opposed, presenting evidence of the co-accused's apprehension, admission of bribe collection, and the audio recording. The Court, emphasizing the gravity of corruption, ruled that anticipatory bail is not a matter of right and is granted only in exceptional circumstances, which were not met in this case. It reiterated that the demand for a bribe itself constitutes an offense, making actual exchange non-essential. The Court dismissed the petition, affirming the High Court's decision, but clarified that any future regular bail application should be considered independently on its own merits.

petitioner_key_arguments: Anticipatory bail should be granted.
Custodial interrogation is not warranted in the facts and circumstances of the case.
Anticipatory bail is an integral part of Article 21 of the Constitution.
respondent_key_arguments: Co-accused Prithvi Singh was apprehended red-handed while accepting the bribe.
Co-accused admitted that the amount was received on behalf of the petitioner.
Audio recording dated 08.01.2025 corroborates the demand made by the petitioner and his instructions to transfer funds.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The respondent's arguments regarding the strong evidence against the petitioner (red-handed apprehension, admission, audio recording) and the legal principle that anticipatory bail is not a matter of right in corruption cases, especially when exceptional circumstances are not demonstrated, prevailed.

acts_cited: Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946, Section 6-A
precedents_cited: Ratan Moni Dey vs. Emperor, (1905) I.L.R. 32 Calcutta 292
Empress of India v. Baldeo Sahai, [(1879) I.L.R. 2 All 253]
Queen Empress v. Ramakha, [(1884) I.L.R. 8 Mad. 5]
Damodar Krishna Kamli vs. State, 1955 Cr.L.J. 181
State of M.P. and another v. Ram Kishna Balothia and another, AIR 1995 SC 1198
Siddharam Satlingappa Mhetre v. State of Maharashtra, AIR 2011 SC 312
Central Bureau of Investigation v. V. Vijay Sai Reddy, (2013) 7 Scale 15
Manoj Narula v. Union of India, (2014) 9 SCC 1
Niranjan Hemchandra Sashittal v. State of Maharashtra, (2013) 4 SCC 642
Subramanian Swamy v. Manmohan Singh, (2012) 3 SCC 64
K.C. Sareen v. C.B.I., Chandigarh, (2001) 6 SCC 584
Subramanian Swamy v. Director, Central Bureau of Investigation, (2014) 8 SCC 682
Neera Yadav v. Central Bureau of Investigation, (2017) 8 SCC 757
constitutional_provisions: Article 21 of the Constitution
Article 14 of the Constitution

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The Court held that anticipatory bail in serious corruption cases is not a matter of right and should only be granted in exceptional circumstances, which were not established by the petitioner. The demand for illegal gratification itself constitutes an offense under Section 7 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, making the actual exchange of bribe not an essential requirement for prosecution.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court extensively discussed the pervasive and destructive nature of corruption, citing various precedents that highlight its detrimental impact on society, governance, and the rule of law. It emphasized that the principles governing anticipatory bail are distinct from those for regular bail and that the presumption of innocence alone cannot be the sole consideration for granting anticipatory bail.

special_directions.special_directions: If the petitioner prays for regular bail, the same shall be considered on its own merits without being influenced by any observations made in this order, as this Court only considered whether the petitioner deserved anticipatory bail.

case_identification.case_number: CONTEMPT PETITION (C) OF 2025 [@DIARY NO. 20329 OF 2020] IN CIVIL APPEAL NO. 2703 OF 2017

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns contempt petitions alleging non-compliance with a Supreme Court order from 2017 regarding salary arrears and pension for university employees, following recommendations by the J. Sinha Commission.

judgements.case_summary: The Supreme Court addressed multiple contempt petitions alleging non-compliance with its order dated 31.08.2017 in Civil Appeal No. 2703 of 2017 (Krishna Nand Yadav & others Vs. Magadh University & others). This prior order had approved the J. Sinha Commission's directives concerning the payment of salary and pension to university employees, contingent on declarations of continuous work. Petitioners claimed they were denied arrears of salary and pension despite favorable recommendations and court orders. Respondents disputed these claims, asserting that arrears were not payable for periods when employees had not worked. The Court noted that the original Civil Appeal did not contain specific in personam directions for salary or arrears, and the issue of actual work required a fact-finding inquiry unsuitable for contempt proceedings. Given that the petitioners' absorption orders were passed after the J. Sinha Commission's orders, the Court directed that all related issues be adjudicated by the Registrar/Vice Chancellor of the University, guided by the precedent of State of Bihar & others vs Bihar Rajya M.S.E.S.K.K.M & others (2005). The contempt petitions were disposed of with specific directions for petitioners to submit claims, for university authorities to conduct discrete inquiries and pass reasoned orders on salary, arrears, and pension within stipulated timelines, and for recovery of any excess payments. The Court also clarified that pension claims should be decided uninfluenced by certain previous interim orders.

petitioner_key_arguments: Non-compliance with previous court orders regarding salary arrears and pension, despite J. Sinha Commission recommendations.
respondent_key_arguments: Arrears of salary not payable as petitioners did not work during absorption period.
Previous orders directed no further payment for periods not actually worked.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court directed a fresh adjudication process by university authorities, acknowledging the need for fact-finding on both sides' contentions regarding actual work and entitlement to salary/pension, while providing clear guidelines and timelines for this process.

outcome.relief_granted: The court directed individual petitioners to submit their claims for actual working, salary, and pension to the Registrar/Vice Chancellor of the University. The authorities are mandated to conduct a discrete inquiry, provide due opportunity, and pass a reasoned order regarding salary and arrears within three months. Pension claims are to be decided counting service from the date of absorption, uninfluenced by previous interim orders. Payment of adjudicated pension and arrears must be made within two months of the order, with provisions for adjusting already paid amounts and recovering any excess. Parties dissatisfied with the university's orders retain the liberty to approach the High Court.

precedents_cited: Krishna Nand Yadav & others Vs. Magadh University & others
Baidya Nath Choudhary Vs. Dr. Sree Surendra Kumar Singh
State of Bihar & others vs Bihar Rajya M.S.E.S.K.K.M & others (2005) 9 SCC 129

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core reasoning is that the original Civil Appeal did not contain specific in personam directions for salary/arrears, and the issue of actual working requires a fact-finding inquiry beyond the scope of contempt proceedings. Therefore, the matter should be adjudicated by the university authorities following established legal principles, uninfluenced by previous interim orders regarding pension.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed that previous orders (11.07.2019, 07.08.2019, 12.02.2021) did not address the issue of pension, and that pension claims should be decided notionally uninfluenced by these orders.

special_directions.special_directions:
1. Individual petitioner shall submit claim along with relevant documents setting up actual working in college in terms of absorption orders claiming salary and pension from absorption date up to February 28, 2025, before the Registrar/Vice Chancellor of the University.
2. On receiving the claim, a discrete enquiry be held affording due opportunity to the employee, college, and State representative, and a reasoned order be passed regarding payment of salary and arrears, if any, within three months.
3. The claim regarding pension of petitioner which has been withheld be decided counting the period of service, w.e.f. date of absorption notionally uninfluenced by the orders dated 11.07.2019, 07.08.2019 and 12.02.2021 passed in Contempt Petition (C) No. 1188 of 2018 in Baidya Nath Choudhary (supra).
4. After adjudicating the issue of pension and arrears, the same be paid adjusting the amount already paid as expeditiously as possible not later than two months from the date of such order.
5. Upon adjudication, if any excess amount has been paid either in salary or pension, it be quantified and the university/college/state shall have liberty to recover the same following prescribed procedure.
6. If employees have submitted joint claim of arrears of salary and pension, salary issue governed by direction (ii) and pension by direction (iii).
7. Parties dissatisfied by the orders of the Registrar/Vice Chancellor of the University shall be at liberty to take recourse as permissible before the High Court.

case_identification.petitioner_name: Dhirubhai Bhailalbhai Chauhan & Anr. and Kiritbhai Manibhai Patel & Ors.
case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL No.816 OF 2016 WITH CRL.A. NO.817 OF 2016

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns an appeal against a High Court judgment that reversed the acquittal of certain accused in a rioting case, examining whether mere presence at the scene of a large-scale riot is sufficient to establish membership in an unlawful assembly.

judgements.case_summary:
This case involves two criminal appeals challenging a common judgment of the High Court of Gujarat, which partly reversed a Trial Court's acquittal of 19 accused in a 2002 rioting incident. The High Court maintained the acquittal for 12 accused but convicted 7 appellants for offences under sections 143, 147, 153(A), 295, 436, and 332 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution alleged that a mob surrounded a graveyard and mosque, pelted stones at police, leading to tear gas and gunshots, and 7 persons were arrested on the spot. The Trial Court had acquitted all 19 due to benefit of doubt, citing stereotypical police depositions, inability to identify accused, and unreliable witness testimonies (PW-2, PW-4).

The appellants argued that their presence was natural as residents of the village during riots, no overt act was attributed, and key witnesses were unreliable. The State contended that in rioting cases, particularizing individual acts is difficult, and proven presence at the scene is sufficient for conviction. The Supreme Court analyzed that the rioting crowd was very large, no curfew was imposed, and police intervention caused a stampede. It noted the lack of specific evidence of incitement or violence by appellants, absence of weapon recovery, and the unreliability of PW-2 and PW-4. The Court held that mere presence of residents at a public place during a riot, especially when they could be bystanders, is not sufficient to infer membership in an unlawful assembly. Consequently, the Supreme Court allowed the appeals, setting aside the High Court's judgment and restoring the Trial Court's acquittal.

petitioner_key_arguments: The incident was an aftermath of events at Godhara.
Presence of villagers at a public street during rioting is natural and does not automatically imply membership in an unlawful assembly.
No reliable evidence attributes any overt act to the appellants.
The only witness (PW-2) was discarded by both the Trial Court and High Court.
The High Court erred in reversing an acquittal judgment.
respondent_key_arguments: In rioting cases, it is extremely difficult to particularize as to which person did what.
If the presence of the accused at the scene of the crime, as part of the mob, is proved, that alone is sufficient to record conviction.
The High Court found the presence of the appellants duly proved, and in absence of cogent explanation by the accused, the order convicting them cannot be faulted.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments that mere presence at the scene of a large-scale riot, especially for residents of the village, without specific overt acts or reliable evidence, is insufficient to prove membership in an unlawful assembly. The court also agreed that the High Court erred in reversing the acquittal based on such insufficient evidence.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned judgment and order of the High Court is set aside, and the order of the Trial Court is restored. If the appellants are on bail, they need not surrender. Their bail bonds, if any, are discharged. Pending application(s), if any, stand disposed of.

precedents_cited: Busi Koteswara Rao & others v. State of Andhra Pradesh, (2012) 12 SCC 711, paragraph 11
Nagarjit Ahir v. State of Bihar, (2005) 10 SCC 369, paragraph 14
Masalti v. State of U.P., AIR 1965 SC 202: 1964 SCC OnLine SC 30
State of U.P. v. Dan Singh, (1997) 3 SCC 747

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: Mere presence of individuals, who are residents of the village, at the scene of a large-scale public riot, particularly when no curfew is imposed and no specific overt act, incitement, or recovery of destructive instruments is proven against them, is insufficient to establish their membership in an unlawful assembly. The court must exercise caution to distinguish between innocent bystanders and actual participants, especially when primary witness testimonies are unreliable.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: In cases of group clashes involving a large number of persons, courts have an onerous duty to ensure no innocent bystander is convicted. A rule of caution, not law, suggests convicting only those against whom overt acts are alleged, or where a plurality test is met, especially when the scene is a public place.

special_directions.special_directions: If the appellants are on bail, they need not surrender. Their bail bonds, if any, are discharged. Pending application(s), if any, stand disposed of.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (@S.L.P (Crl.) No. of 2025 @ Diary No.46289 of 2024)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns a challenge to criminal proceedings initiated under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, against a former Minister for alleged irregularities in allotting fishing contracts, specifically focusing on the requirement of proving demand and acceptance of illegal gratification.

judgements.case_summary:
The appellant, Dileepbhai Nanubhai Sanghani, a former Minister in the Government of Gujarat, was proceeded against under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, following his resignation. The allegations pertained to the allotment of fishing contracts in reservoirs without following proper tender procedures, leading to alleged losses for the State. The High Court had refused to quash the criminal proceedings against him, prompting this appeal.

Shri Mukul Rohatgi, representing the appellant, argued that there was no material to suggest corruption by the appellant (accused No.2), and that the grants were intended to benefit tribal communities. He contended that a mere policy violation or peremptory grant without tender does not constitute corruption under the Act, citing the Supreme Court's decision in Neeraj Dutta v. State (NCT of Delhi) which mandates proof of demand and acceptance of illegal gratification. He also emphasized that a prima facie case cannot be based on mere suspicion.

Shri Iqbal Syed, for the complainant/respondent, argued for a statutory presumption under Section 20 of the Act, pointing to an alleged demand for a bribe by the Minister of State (accused No.1) and significant losses to the State due to policy deviation. Ms. Swati Ghildiyal, for the State, noted that while no clear acceptance of bribe by the investigation team was found, a demand by the 1st accused was recorded.

The Court, relying on Neeraj Dutta, held that proof of demand and acceptance of illegal gratification is a sine qua non for establishing guilt under Sections 7 and 13 of the Prevention of Corruption Act. It found no material in the investigation report or pre-charge statements indicating any allegation of demand or acceptance of bribe by the appellant (accused No.2). The Court concluded that misuse of authority alone, without evidence of demand and acceptance of bribe, does not fall under the Act. Consequently, the appeal was allowed, and the criminal proceedings against the appellant were dropped.

petitioner_key_arguments: There is no material to allege corruption by the appellant (accused No.2).
Grants were made to benefit the tribal community, not for illegal gratification.
Policy violation or peremptory grant without tender does not automatically lead to an allegation of corruption under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.
Suspicion must be premised on sufficient material, not mere suspicion, to form a prima facie opinion.
The presumption under Section 20 of the Act requires proof of demand and acceptance, which is absent for the appellant.
respondent_key_arguments: There is a statutory presumption against the accused under Section 20 of the Act.
A demand for a bribe by the Minister of State (accused No.1) is evident from the investigation report.
Inference of guilt can be drawn from circumstantial evidence even without direct oral or documentary evidence.
Policy deviation is a clear pointer to avaricious intent and resulted in huge losses to the State.
The High Court and Sessions Court have clearly found a prima facie case against the accused.
The illegal grants were cancelled by the High Court, which directed a proper tendering process.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's argument that proof of demand and acceptance of illegal gratification is a sine qua non for establishing guilt under Sections 7 and 13 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, and that such proof was absent for the appellant, was accepted by the court.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal is allowed, and the proceedings initiated against the second accused (appellant) are dropped.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. ____/2025 [@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO.1136/2023]

petitioner_advocates: Mr. Arvind Kumar Sharma, Aor, Adv.

bench_judges: HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE ABHAY S. OKA

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the legality of an arrest under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, and the subsequent grant of bail by the High Court due to the arrest being deemed illegal for violating constitutional and procedural safeguards.

judgements.case_summary: The Directorate of Enforcement (appellant) challenged a High Court order that granted bail to Subhash Sharma (respondent) in a case under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA). The High Court had concluded that the respondent's arrest was illegal, which formed the basis for granting bail. The appellant contended that the respondent was formally shown as arrested on March 6, 2022, and produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours from that recorded arrest time. However, the Supreme Court upheld the High Court's factual findings, which indicated that the respondent was initially detained by the Bureau of Immigration on behalf of the ED from March 4, 2022, and physical custody was taken by the ED at 11:00 AM on March 5, 2022. The Court found that the respondent was not produced before the nearest Magistrate within 24 hours from this actual time of detention/custody, thereby violating Article 22(2) of the Constitution of India and Section 57 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The Supreme Court affirmed that such an illegal or vitiated arrest necessitates the grant of bail, as it infringes upon fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 21 and 22, and in such circumstances, the stringent twin conditions for bail under Section 45 of the PMLA do not apply. Consequently, the appeal filed by the Directorate of Enforcement was dismissed, affirming the High Court's decision to grant bail.

petitioner_key_arguments: The respondent was shown as arrested at 01.15 hours on 6th March, 2022, by the Enforcement Directorate and was produced before the Court of the learned Magistrate within 24 hours from this recorded arrest time.
The High Court erred in granting bail.
respondent_key_arguments: The respondent was detained by the Bureau of Immigration on behalf of ED from 18.00 hours (6 pm) on 04.03.2022.
Physical custody was taken by ED at 11.00 hours (11 am) on 05.03.2022.
The respondent was not produced before the nearest learned Magistrate within 24 hours from 11.00 a.m. on 5th March, 2022, rendering the arrest completely illegal.
The illegal arrest violated clause 2 of Article 22 and Article 21 of the Constitution of India.
When an arrest is illegal or vitiated, bail cannot be denied on the grounds of non-fulfillment of twin tests under Section 45 of PMLA.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The High Court's finding that the respondent's arrest was illegal due to non-production before a Magistrate within 24 hours of actual detention/custody, thereby violating Article 22(2) and Article 21 of the Constitution of India, was accepted by the Supreme Court.

outcome.relief_granted: The High Court's order granting bail to the respondent was upheld.

acts_cited: Section 4 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002
Section 57 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
constitutional_provisions: Article 22 of the Constitution of India
clause 2 of Article 22 of the Constitution of India
