judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: An arrest that violates Article 22(2) of the Constitution of India and Section 57 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, is illegal and vitiated. In such cases, the accused is entitled to bail, and the conditions of Section 45 of the PMLA do not apply, as it is the Court's duty to uphold fundamental rights under Articles 21 and 22.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: It is the duty of every Court to uphold the fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 21 and 22 of the Constitution.

case_identification.case_number: ARBITRATION PETITION NO.48 OF 2023

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the appointment of an arbitral panel under Section 11(6) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, arising from disputes in an International Exclusive Distributor Agreement with conflicting clauses regarding governing law and jurisdiction.

judgements.case_summary: Disortho S.A.S, a company from Colombia, filed a petition under Section 11(6) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, seeking the appointment of an arbitral panel against Meril Life Sciences Private Limited, an Indian company. The dispute arose from an International Exclusive Distributor Agreement dated 16th May 2016. Meril opposed the petition, arguing that conflicting clauses (16.5 and 18) in the agreement did not grant Indian Courts jurisdiction to appoint arbitrators. Clause 16.5 stipulated that the agreement would be governed by Indian law and subject to the jurisdiction of courts in Gujarat, India. Clause 18 provided for arbitration in Bogota, Colombia, under the rules of the Chamber of Commerce of Bogota, with the award governed by Colombian law. The Court analyzed the interplay between lex contractus, lex arbitri, and lex fori, referring to various international and domestic precedents, including the three-step test from Enka Insaat. It concluded that Indian law governs the arbitration agreement, and Indian courts retain supervisory jurisdiction, interpreting Bogota as the venue for arbitration and not displacing the applicability of Indian law to the arbitration agreement itself. Based on a consensus reached during the hearing, the Court allowed the petition and appointed Mr. Justice S.P. Garg as the sole arbitrator, with the arbitration to be held in India under the rules of the Delhi International Arbitration Centre.

petitioner_key_arguments: Filed petition under Section 11(6) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, for appointment of an arbitral panel.
Impliedly argued for Indian courts' jurisdiction to appoint arbitrators based on the overall agreement and governing law clause.
respondent_key_arguments: Opposed the petition on jurisdictional grounds.
Contended that clauses 16.5 and 18 of the Distributor Agreement do not grant Indian Courts jurisdiction to appoint arbitrators, implying jurisdiction lies with Bogota/Colombian authorities.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's argument that Indian courts have jurisdiction to appoint arbitrators, as the court interpreted Indian law to govern the arbitration agreement, despite Bogota being the designated venue for arbitration.

outcome.relief_granted: Mr. Justice S.P. Garg, retired judge of the High Court of Delhi, is appointed as the sole arbitrator. The arbitration will be held in India, with the venue decided mutually by the parties and the learned arbitrator. The arbitration shall be governed by the rules applicable to the Delhi International Arbitration Centre attached to the High Court of Delhi. The fee schedule applicable to international arbitrations shall apply.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NOS.301-303 OF 2025 [ARISING OUT OF SLP (C) NOS.20360-20362 OF 2024]

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the selection and appointment of the Chairperson of the National Commission for Homeopathy, specifically challenging the eligibility of the third respondent based on statutory experience requirements.

judgements.case_summary: The case involves a challenge to the appointment of the Chairperson of the National Commission for Homeopathy (NCH) on the grounds that the third respondent, Dr. Anil Khurana, lacked the requisite experience of 10 years as a 'leader' (Head of Department/Organisation) as mandated by the NCH Act, 2020. The Single Judge of the High Court had quashed the appointment, finding the third respondent ineligible, but the Division Bench reversed this decision. The Supreme Court examined the third respondent's profile and various office orders, concluding that he did not possess the required 10 years of experience. The Court found the Secretary, GoI's determination of equivalence of experience to be an 'ipse dixit' lacking concrete evidence and suffering from 'gross perversity'. The Court emphasized that mandatory eligibility criteria cannot be waived and that judicial interference is justified in cases of statutory violations or 'malice in law', even if actual malice is not proven. The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, setting aside the Division Bench's judgment and restoring the Single Judge's order, thereby quashing the third respondent's appointment. The Court directed a fresh selection process to be initiated expeditiously, ensuring strict adherence to statutory requirements.

petitioner_key_arguments: The third respondent lacked the requisite experience of working for 10 (ten) years as a 'leader' in terms of the Explanation to Section 4 of the NCH Act.
The selection process was manifestly flawed and in violation of statutory requirements.
respondent_key_arguments: The third respondent was eligible and possessed the requisite experience.
The Search Committee, comprising experts, found the third respondent eligible, and judicial review in such matters is limited.
The Secretary, GoI, had verified the documents of experience and confirmed eligibility.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments that the third respondent lacked the mandatory 10 years of experience as a 'Head of Department' or 'Head of an Organisation' and that the selection process suffered from gross illegality and malice in law were accepted by the Court.

outcome.relief_granted: The appointment of the third respondent as Chairperson of the National Commission for Homeopathy is quashed. The third respondent shall step down from office within a week. A fresh selection process for the post is to be initiated expeditiously. Benefits already received by the third respondent are not touched, but no future benefit shall accrue from the quashed service.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that mandatory eligibility criteria for public appointments, especially those prescribed by statute, must be strictly adhered to. Any deviation or determination of equivalence without concrete evidence constitutes a 'manifestly flawed process' and 'malice in law,' justifying judicial interference even in expert selection processes. The Court held that the third respondent did not meet the statutory experience requirements, and the process leading to his selection was procedurally unfair and lacked proper justification.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 2643 OF 2025 (arising out of S.L.P. (Civil) No. 594 OF 2020)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the entitlement to interest on a refund of stamp duty paid for a lost e-stamp paper, which was initially denied by lower courts.

judgements.case_summary: The appellants, Dr. Poornima Advani & Anr., sought a refund of Rs. 28,10,000/- paid for an e-stamp paper dated 06.07.2016, which was subsequently lost. They purchased a fresh e-stamp paper and completed their property transaction. Their application for a refund of the lost e-stamp paper's value was rejected by the Collector of Stamps. A learned Single Judge of the High Court partly allowed their writ petition, ordering the refund of the principal amount but denying interest. Dissatisfied with the non-grant of interest, the appellants filed a Letters Patent Appeal, which was dismissed by the High Court on the grounds that the issue of interest was not argued before the Single Judge. The Supreme Court examined whether interest should be granted on the refunded amount. The Court emphasized that interest is a compensation for the deprivation of money and a normal accretion on capital. Citing Article 265 of the Constitution, it held that the State cannot retain money without the authority of law, and if it does, it is bound to pay interest. The Court found the High Court's reasoning for denying interest to be without merit. Consequently, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, directing the respondents to pay Rs. 4,35,968.58/- as interest within two months.

petitioner_key_arguments: Entitlement to interest on the refunded amount as compensation for the deprivation of money.
The State cannot retain money without the authority of law.
The issue of interest is a necessary corollary to the retention of money.
respondent_key_arguments: No specific statutory provision for payment of interest on refund of lost e-stamp paper.
The issue of interest was not raised before the learned Single Judge.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court accepted the petitioner's arguments that interest is a normal accretion on capital and compensation for the deprivation of money, and that the State cannot retain money without the authority of law.

outcome.relief_granted: Respondents are directed to pay an amount of Rs. 4,35,968.58/- towards interest within a period of two months.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 13422 OF 2024, CIVIL APPEAL NO. 13423 OF 2024

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns a dispute over promotion to the post of Assistant Professor in the Department of Neurosurgery, Medical Education Service, Kerala, specifically regarding the interpretation of experience criteria for promotion.

judgements.case_summary:
This judgment addresses two Civil Appeals, primarily focusing on Civil Appeal No. 13422 of 2024, filed by Dr. Sharmad. The appeal challenges a High Court judgment dated 20th January, 2017, which set aside a promotion granted to Dr. Sharmad to the post of Assistant Professor, Department of Neurosurgery. The High Court had allowed a writ petition by Dr. Jyothish, who contended that Dr. Sharmad lacked the requisite 5 years of physical teaching experience as an Assistant Professor after acquiring his M. Ch. degree. The Kerala Administrative Tribunal had initially dismissed Dr. Jyothish's application.

The core legal issue revolved around the interpretation of Government Order (G.O.) dated 07th April, 2008, which governed recruitment in the Medical Education Service. Dr. Jyothish argued that experience must be post-M.Ch. degree, relying on general service rules (KS & SSR). Dr. Sharmad and the official respondents argued that the G.O. dated 07th April, 2008, being a special rule, did not explicitly require post-M.Ch. experience for the Teaching Cadre (Branch-II), unlike the Administrative Cadre (Branch-I) where it was specified. The Supreme Court analyzed the G.O. and the KS & SSR, concluding that the absence of the 'after acquiring postgraduate degree' clause in the Teaching Cadre criteria was deliberate. The Court applied the maxim 'expressio unius est exclusio alterius' and found Rule 10(ab) of KS & SSR inapplicable due to the 'unless otherwise specified' clause. Consequently, the Supreme Court held that the High Court erred in interfering with Dr. Sharmad's promotion. The judgment also allowed Civil Appeal No. 13423 of 2024, which involved similar issues.

petitioner_key_arguments: The G.O. dated 07th April, 2008, which governs recruitment, does not explicitly require 5 years of physical teaching experience as an Assistant Professor after acquiring the M. Ch. degree for promotion to Associate Professor in the Teaching Cadre (Branch-II).

The absence of the 'after acquiring postgraduate degree' clause in the Teaching Cadre criteria, while present in the Administrative Cadre criteria, indicates a deliberate distinction by the rule framers.
G.O. dated 14th December, 2009, also supported Dr. Sharmad's eligibility for promotion.

General rules like Rule 10(ab) of the Kerala State and Subordinate Services Rules, 1958 (KS & SSR) are not applicable due to the specific nature of the G.O. dated 07th April, 2008, and the 'unless otherwise specified' clause in Rule 10(ab).
respondent_key_arguments: The 5 years of physical teaching experience as an Assistant Professor must be gained after acquiring the M. Ch. degree, even for the Teaching Cadre.
Rules 10 and 28 of the Kerala State and Subordinate Services Rules, 1958 (KS & SSR) mandate that experience should be post-qualification.
The G.O. dated 14th December, 2009, was misplaced and should not have been relied upon for promotion.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the G.O. dated 07th April, 2008, did not explicitly require post-M.Ch. degree experience for promotion in the Teaching Cadre. The court applied the maxim 'expressio unius est exclusio alterius' to interpret the G.O.'s deliberate omission of such a requirement for the Teaching Cadre, unlike the Administrative Cadre. It also found the general service rules (KS & SSR) inapplicable due to the specific nature of the G.O. and the 'unless otherwise specified' clause.

outcome.relief_granted: The judgment and order of the High Court dated 20th January, 2017 (and 4th April, 2017 for the connected appeal) were set aside. The judgment and order of the Kerala Administrative Tribunal, which dismissed Dr. Jyothish's original application, were restored. Dr. Sharmad's promotion stands.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that specific rules (G.O. dated 07th April, 2008) governing recruitment, which supersede general rules, must be interpreted literally. Where a specific qualification (post-M.Ch. experience) is explicitly required for one cadre (Administrative) but omitted for another (Teaching) within the same G.O., the omission is deemed deliberate, applying the maxim 'expressio unius est exclusio alterius'. General service rules (KS & SSR) are inapplicable when the specific G.O. provides otherwise, especially with clauses like 'unless otherwise specified'.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed that while experience is normally considered post-qualification, exceptions exist, and this case presented such an exception. It also noted that the requirement for physical teaching experience with a postgraduate degree would logically be more demanding for the Teaching Cadre than the Administrative Cadre, yet the G.O. explicitly omitted this requirement for the former.

case_identification.case_number: CONTEMPT PETITION (C) OF 2025 [@DIARY NO. 7955 OF 2022] IN CONTEMPT PETITION (C) NO. 1188 OF 2018 IN CIVIL APPEAL NO. 2703 OF 2017

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns a contempt petition filed by a lecturer whose absorption was confirmed by the Supreme Court, but whose arrears of salary and pension have not been finalized, allegedly in disobedience of previous court orders.

judgements.case_summary:
The petitioner, Dr. Yugeshwar Yadav, filed a contempt petition alleging non-finalization of his arrears of salary and pension, which he claimed amounted to disobedience of prior court orders. His absorption as a lecturer was confirmed by the Supreme Court in 2017, following the J. Sinha Commission's recommendations. The State of Bihar, in its counter-affidavit, contended that ascertainable arrears had been paid, an excess amount was recoverable, and an enquiry committee found the petitioner had not worked for certain periods, thus denying deliberate non-compliance.

The Supreme Court observed that the issues concerning the petitioner's actual working days, salary arrears, and pension required a detailed fact-finding enquiry, which was not suitable for adjudication within a contempt petition. The Court clarified that its previous interim orders did not prohibit the payment of pension. Consequently, the Court disposed of the contempt petition, directing the Registrar/Vice Chancellor of the University to adjudicate all pending issues.

Specific directions were issued: the petitioner must submit his claim with relevant documents for salary and pension up to February 28, 2025. A discrete enquiry must be conducted with due opportunity to all parties, and a reasoned order regarding salary and arrears must be passed within three months. The pension claim is to be decided by counting service from the absorption date, uninfluenced by prior interim orders. Any adjudicated arrears and pension are to be paid within two months of the order, with any excess payments quantified and recovered. Parties retain the liberty to approach the High Court if dissatisfied.

petitioner_key_arguments: Non-finalization of arrears of salary and pension amounts to disobedience of court orders.
respondent_key_arguments: Ascertainable arrears of salary have been paid.
Excess amount is recoverable.
An enquiry committee found the petitioner did not work for certain durations.
No case of deliberate or willful non-compliance can be made out.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court did not rule on the merits of either party's arguments but directed an adjudication process by the competent authorities.

outcome.relief_granted: The contempt petition is disposed of with directions for the Registrar/Vice Chancellor of the University to adjudicate the petitioner's claims for salary arrears and pension, conduct an enquiry, and ensure payment or recovery of amounts as per the adjudication.

precedents_cited: Baidya Nath Choudhary Vs. Dr. Sree Surendra Kumar Singh
Krishna Nand Yadav & others Vs. Magadh University & others
State of Bihar & others vs Bihar Rajya M.S.E.S.K.K.M & others (2005) 9 SCC 129

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that complex issues requiring detailed fact-finding, such as actual working days, salary arrears, and pension entitlements, are not suitable for adjudication in a contempt petition. Instead, such matters should be referred to the competent administrative authorities for a thorough enquiry and reasoned decision.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that the issue regarding payment of pension was not part of the previous orders dated 11.07.2019, 07.08.2019, and 12.02.2021, and these orders did not direct the stoppage of pension.

special_directions.special_directions:
1. The petitioner shall submit his claim along with relevant documents setting up his actual working in college in terms of the orders of absorption claiming salary, and also for pension from the date of absorption upto February 28, 2025, before the Registrar/Vice Chancellor of the University.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 118 OF 2013

case_details.subject_matter: This criminal appeal challenges a High Court of Kerala judgment concerning the acquittal and conviction of accused persons in a murder case involving political clashes and the use of explosive substances, where two individuals lost their lives.

judgements.case_summary: This criminal appeal arises from a High Court of Kerala judgment dated 12th April 2011, which acquitted some accused (A4-A10, A13-A15) and confirmed the conviction of others (A1-A3, A11-A12) in a 2002 murder case. The incident occurred during a hartal, leading to violent clashes between members of the Communist Party of India (M) and RSS, resulting in the deaths of Sunil and Sujeesh. The appellants (convicted accused) argued that the FIR was ante-timed, contained interpolations, the bodies were moved to the scene, and witness testimonies had material contradictions. They also questioned the credibility of evidence recovery and alleged defective investigation. The State of Kerala contended that the High Court's judgment was well-reasoned and based on proper appreciation of evidence. The Supreme Court analyzed the arguments, holding that minor inconsistencies in witness testimonies do not necessarily impair their credit, and the maxim 'falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus' is not a rule of law in India. The Court also stated that defective investigation does not automatically benefit the accused if other clinching evidence exists. Finding the eyewitness testimonies (PW1, PW2, PW4) honest and trustworthy, and upholding the conviction of A3 under the Explosive Substances Act, the Court dismissed the appeal.

petitioner_key_arguments: FIR is ante-timed and the prosecution story is not palpable.
FIR recorded Sunil's death at 3 am, but knowledge of death was only at 7:30 am.
Major interpolations in the FIR, including insertion of names (A14, A15) and date correction.
Prosecution attempted to implicate innocent persons, as evidenced by witness statements about Ashraf.
Violation of Section 154 Cr.P.C. due to belated FIR.
Sunil was murdered elsewhere, and his body was brought to the scene to implicate appellants.
Recovery made under Section 27 of IEA is not credible (e.g., no mahazar for blood stains in jeep).
Eyewitnesses could not have seen the incident due to obstacles (coconut husk, mangrove, shed).
Inquest report was not made properly, and eyewitnesses gave 'parrot like statements' due to political enmity.
It is improbable human conduct for eyewitnesses to stay during a bomb attack instead of fleeing.
Recovery of bomb was not made in a proper manner.
respondent_key_arguments: The judgment passed by the High Court is a very well-reasoned judgment.
The High Court rightly convicted the accused persons based on a proper appreciation of evidence.
The appeal of the appellants should be dismissed.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the respondent's arguments, finding that minor contradictions do not discredit witnesses, the principle of 'falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus' is not applicable in Indian law, and defective investigation does not automatically benefit the accused. The court found the eyewitness testimonies reliable and upheld the convictions.

acts_cited: The Indian Evidence Act, 1872, Section 27, Section 145, Section 155
precedents_cited: Rammi vs State of MP
Birbal Nath vs State of Rajasthan2
Tehshildar Singh v State of UP3
Rammi (Supra)
Ram Vijay Singh vs State of UP4
IIangovan vs State of T.N.

Paras Yadav & ors. vs. State of Bihar5
Ram Bihari Yadav v. State of Bihar
Raju alias Balachandran and ors. vs. State of Tamil Nadu6
Dalip Singh
Sarwan Singh

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that minor inconsistencies in witness testimonies do not necessarily impair their credit or discredit them, and the maxim 'falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus' is not a mandatory rule of evidence in Indian criminal jurisprudence. Furthermore, defective investigation alone does not entitle the accused to acquittal if other clinching evidence, such as reliable eyewitness accounts and medical evidence, supports the prosecution's case.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed that crime creates societal fear and affects societal conscience, and the purpose of the criminal administrative system is to protect individual dignity and restore societal stability and order. It also noted that the courts balance the interests of the accused and the state/society.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.257 OF 2013

case_details.subject_matter: Criminal appeal challenging a conviction for murder under Section 302 IPC and seeking reconsideration of the appellant's premature release based on applicable remission policies.

judgements.case_summary: The appellant, Firoz Khan Akbarkhan (accused no.1), along with two co-accused, was prosecuted for murder under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. The prosecution alleged that on 19.04.2005, following a quarrel, the appellant stabbed the deceased with a knife, leading to his death. The Trial Court convicted the appellant and accused no.2, sentencing them to life imprisonment, which was upheld by the High Court. The appellant argued false implication, manipulated witnesses, delay in recording statements, inconsistencies, lack of clear motive, and that the incident should be classified as culpable homicide not amounting to murder (Section 304-I IPC). The respondent-State contended that the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt, supported by concurrent findings of lower courts, and that minor discrepancies were immaterial. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on merits, upholding the conviction under Section 302 IPC. The Court found consistent eye-witness accounts and noted that the appellant being armed indicated a prior intention to cause bodily injury, thus ruling out Section 304-I. The delay in recording witness statements was adequately explained by the prevailing communal riots. However, regarding the appellant's plea for premature release, the Court directed the State Government to reconsider his case afresh, applying the remission policy in vogue at the time of his conviction or a more beneficial policy, within three months.

petitioner_key_arguments: Falsely implicated due to community rivalry.
Eyewitness statements were recorded after 2/3 days, indicating manipulation.
No cogent and reliable evidence against the appellant.
Inconsistencies in witness testimonies and lack of clear motive.
Incident was not pre-planned and occurred in the heat of the moment, warranting conviction under Section 304-I IPC instead of Section 302 IPC.
Entitled to premature release based on the remission policy applicable at the time of conviction or a more beneficial policy.
respondent_key_arguments: Prosecution proved the case beyond reasonable doubt.
Concurrent findings of the Trial Court and High Court should not be interfered with.
Minor discrepancies in witness statements do not affect the core of the prosecution's case.
Delay in recording witness statements was justified due to prevailing communal riots.
Appellant's flight from the crime scene indicates complicity.
The State had already rejected the premature release application based on existing policy requiring 24 years inclusive of remission.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The respondent's arguments for upholding the conviction under Section 302 IPC prevailed. However, the petitioner's arguments regarding the applicable remission policy led to a specific direction for reconsideration of premature release.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal on merits was dismissed. However, the appellant was granted liberty to apply afresh for premature release, and the State Government was directed to pass a reasoned order within three months, considering the remission policy applicable at the time of conviction or a more beneficial policy.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The Court upheld the conviction under Section 302 IPC, finding that the prosecution proved its case beyond reasonable doubt through consistent eye-witness testimony. The appellant being armed with a knife indicated a prior intention to cause bodily injury, thus ruling out Section 304-I IPC. Minor discrepancies and explained delays in recording statements were deemed not fatal to the prosecution's case.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that minor variations in witness accounts are often the hallmark of truth, and normal discrepancies due to observation errors or memory lapse should not discredit testimony. It also reiterated the principle that the remission policy applicable at the time of conviction, or a more beneficial one, should be considered for premature release.
