case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS. 2814-2815 OF 2024

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the procedure for granting bail to foreigners, specifically addressing whether a Foreign Registration Officer or Civil Authority needs to be impleaded in bail applications and the communication of bail orders to these authorities.

judgements.case_summary: This Supreme Court judgment, following a previous decision on bail conditions, addresses the specific issue of whether a Foreign Registration Officer (FRO) appointed under the Registration of Foreigners Rules, 1992, or a Civil Authority, needs to be impleaded in bail applications filed by foreigners. The court examined the powers vested in the Central Government and Civil Authorities under the Foreigners Act, 1946, and the Foreigners Order, 1948, particularly concerning the departure and detention of foreigners. While acknowledging the Civil Authority's power to prohibit departure if a foreigner's presence is required for a criminal charge, the court found no propriety in directing the impleadment of these authorities in every bail application. The court reasoned that such a requirement would lead to unnecessary delays and that these authorities generally lack the locus to oppose bail unless the allegation pertains to an offense punishable under Section 14 of the Act. Instead, the court directed that when bail is granted to a foreigner, the investigating agency or the State must immediately inform the concerned FRO, who will then communicate the order to all relevant Civil Authorities. This mechanism ensures that authorities under the Foreigners Act, Rules, and Order can take appropriate steps in accordance with the law without being a party to the bail proceedings. The court also directed that a copy of this order be circulated to all High Courts and criminal courts.

legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the argument that impleading the Civil Authority or Registration Officer in every bail application for a foreigner is not proper and would cause unnecessary delay. Instead, a system of communication of bail orders to these authorities was deemed appropriate.

outcome.relief_granted: Directions issued for communication of bail orders for foreigners to relevant authorities, and for circulation of the order to all criminal courts.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The court held that impleading the Civil Authority or Registration Officer in every bail application filed by a foreigner is not proper as it would cause unnecessary delay and these authorities generally lack the locus to oppose bail. The appropriate course is to direct the investigating agency or the State to immediately inform the concerned Registration Officer about the grant of bail, who will then communicate it to the Civil Authorities for necessary action under the Foreigners Act and Order.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court appreciated the valuable assistance rendered by Shri Vinay Navare, learned senior counsel appointed as Amicus Curiae, and Shri Vikramjeet Banerjee, learned Additional Solicitor General of India.

special_directions.special_directions: (i) While granting bail to a foreigner, the concerned court shall direct the State or prosecuting agency to immediately communicate the order granting bail to the concerned Registration Officer appointed under Rule 3 of the Rules, who, in turn, shall communicate the order to all concerned authorities including the Civil Authorities. (ii) A copy of this order shall be forwarded to Registrar Generals of all the High Courts, who in turn will forward the copies of the order to all the criminal courts in the respective States.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.1759 OF 2025

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the necessity of prior sanction for prosecuting police officers for alleged illegal activities, including assault, false cases, and defamation, committed while acting or purporting to act in discharge of official duty.

judgements.case_summary: The case originated from a private complaint filed by Seetaram (respondent) against G.C. Manjunath and others (appellants/accused police officers) alleging illegal activities, physical assault, false cases, and defamation. The complainant claimed that police officers, in retaliation for his prosecution of other officers, assaulted him, lodged false complaints, and defamed him. The Magistrate took cognizance and issued summons, which was affirmed by the Sessions Judge. The High Court refused to quash the summoning order, holding that the acts were not done in discharge of official duty and thus prior sanction under Section 197 CrPC and Section 170 Karnataka Police Act was not required. The appellants argued that there was an inordinate delay in filing the complaint, it was retaliatory, and prior sanction was mandatory as their actions, even if excessive, were connected to their official duties. The Supreme Court, citing precedents, held that the allegations, though grave, fell within the ambit of acts done 'under colour of, or in excess of, such duty or authority' and had a reasonable nexus to official functions, especially since the complainant was a 'rowdy sheeter' and the allegations arose during the investigation of cases against him. Therefore, prior sanction was necessary. Given that accused Nos. 1, 3, and 4 had passed away, and accused Nos. 2 and 5 had superannuated, the Court found no meaningful purpose in prolonging the criminal prosecution. The appeal was allowed, and the High Court's order, along with the summoning and affirming orders, was quashed.

petitioner_key_arguments: Inordinate and unexplained delay in filing the complaint.
Complaint is a retaliatory measure filed vindictively after complainant's acquittal in other cases.
Lack of requisite prior sanction under Section 197 of the CrPC and Section 170 of the Karnataka Police Act.
High Court erroneously concluded that prior sanction was not necessary, misinterpreting D. Devaraja judgment.
Alleged offences fall within 'under colour or in excess of any such duty' as per Section 170 of the Police Act, requiring sanction.
respondent_key_arguments: Complainant was subjected to physical assault and grievous injuries by accused persons.
Medical documents (wound certificate, X-ray report) corroborate injuries.
Complainant made consistent efforts from 2002-2006 to obtain sanction for prosecution.
Police officers exceeded their limits; brutal conduct cannot be termed as an act done in discharge of official duty.
Acts were not reasonably connected to official duties and were beyond the scope of official duty.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that prior sanction under Section 197 CrPC and Section 170 Karnataka Police Act was mandatory because the alleged acts, even if in excess of authority, had a reasonable nexus to the official duties of the police officers and were done 'under colour of, or in excess of, such duty or authority'.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned order dated 17.03.2021 passed by the High Court in Criminal Petition No.4512 of 2020 was set aside. The summoning order dated 07.05.2016 and the affirming order dated 11.06.2020 were quashed. Criminal proceedings against accused Nos.2 and 5 were quashed.

precedents_cited: D. Devaraja vs. Owais Sabeer Hussain, (2020) 7 SCC 695
Virupaxappa Veerappa Kadampur vs. State of Mysore, AIR 1963 SC 849
Bakhshish Singh Brar vs. Gurmej Kaur, (1987) 4 SCC 663
B. Saha vs. M.S. Kochar, (1979) 4 SCC 177
Baijnath vs. State of Madhya Pradesh, (AIR 1966 SC 220)
Amod Kumar Kanth vs. Association of Victim of Uphaar Tragedy, (2023) 16 SCC 239
Gurmeet Kaur vs. Devender Gupta, 2024 SCC OnLine SC 3761

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that prior sanction under Section 197 of the CrPC and Section 170 of the Karnataka Police Act is mandatory for prosecuting public servants if the alleged acts, even if in excess of authority or improper, have a reasonable nexus to their official duties or are done 'under colour of, or in excess of, such duty or authority'. The statutory protection is not displaced merely because the public servant exceeded the scope of their powers.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that the complainant was declared a 'rowdy sheeter' and the allegations arose during the investigation of criminal cases against him, which supports the reasonable nexus to official duty. It also noted that with some accused having passed away and others superannuated, no meaningful purpose would be served by prolonging the criminal prosecution against the remaining accused.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S). OF 2025 (ARISING FROM SLP(Crl.) No. 12249 OF 2023)

case_details.subject_matter: The case involves an appeal by the husband seeking dissolution of marriage on grounds of irretrievable breakdown and a one-time settlement for permanent alimony, challenging previous maintenance orders under CrPC and DV Act.

judgements.case_summary: The appellant-husband and respondent-wife were married in October 2006 and separated in December 2007. The respondent initiated maintenance proceedings under Section 125 CrPC, being awarded Rs. 5,000/- per month in 2010. Subsequently, in 2015, she filed a complaint under the DV Act, leading to an order in 2016 for an additional Rs. 15,000/- per month and accommodation. The husband's revision petition seeking adjustment of maintenance amounts was dismissed by the High Court in 2022. The husband had also filed for divorce, which was rejected by the Family Court, while the wife's prayer for restitution of conjugal rights was allowed; an appeal against this is pending. The Supreme Court noted that the parties have been living separately for over 17 years, with no issue, and their relations have grown irreconcilably sour, leading to an irretrievable breakdown of marriage. Exercising its power under Article 142, the Court granted a decree of divorce. Considering the financial status (wife unemployed, husband a lecturer), the Court awarded Rs. 40 lakhs as a one-time permanent alimony to the respondent-wife, covering all pending and future monetary claims. This amount is to be paid in four equal monthly installments of Rs. 10 lakhs each, with the first installment due within one month.

petitioner_key_arguments: The marriage has irretrievably broken down, as parties have lived separately for over 17 years with no issue.
Sought divorce under Article 142 of the Constitution of India.
Offered Rs. 25,00,000/- as permanent alimony.
Sought adjustment of Rs. 5,000/- paid under CrPC against Rs. 15,000/- awarded under DV Act.
Claimed arrears of maintenance up to February 2023 amounted to Rs. 8,00,000/-.
Submitted current net salary is Rs. 91,030/- and no additional source of income.
Claimed to have provided accommodation to the respondent in his father's property.
respondent_key_arguments: Initially prayed for restitution of conjugal rights.
Claimed arrears of maintenance amounted to Rs. 10,01,152/-.
Claimed appellant was drawing a salary of around Rs. 65,000/- per month in 2016 and Rs. 1,34,544/- per month as of November 2023.
Claimed appellant has additional income of around Rs. 1,15,000/- per month from ancillary sources.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that the marriage had irretrievably broken down and granted a divorce under Article 142 of the Constitution of India. While the alimony amount was determined by the court, the primary relief of divorce sought by the petitioner was granted.

outcome.relief_granted: The marriage between the parties is dissolved, and a decree of divorce is granted. The respondent-wife is awarded Rs. 40 lakhs as a one-time permanent alimony, covering all pending and future monetary claims.

acts_cited: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, Section 23
precedents_cited: Shilpa Sailesh v. Varun Sreenivasang, 2023 SCC OnLine SC 544
constitutional_provisions: Article 142 of the Constitution of India

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The marriage has irretrievably broken down, as the parties have lived separately for over 17 years with no issue, and their relations have grown sour beyond reconciliation. Insisting on continuing a dead marital relationship serves no purpose, justifying the exercise of power under Article 142 to dissolve the marriage.

special_directions.special_directions: The appellant is directed to pay Rs. 40 lakhs as permanent alimony to the respondent within a period of four months in four equal monthly installments of Rs. 10 lakhs each, with the first installment due within one month from the date of judgment. The Registry is directed to draw the decree only after proof of payment of the full Rs. 40,00,000/-.
special_directions.interim_orders: On 15.09.2023, the appellant deposited Rs. 4,00,000/- towards 50% of the arrears of maintenance, which was invested in an interest-bearing fixed deposit account. On 18.03.2024, this amount with accrued interest was directed to be paid to the respondent-wife. The counsel for the appellant also stated that the pending monthly maintenance for the four months preceding the date of hearing would be paid directly to the respondent-wife on or before 31.03.2024.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S). 850-851 OF 2019

case_details.subject_matter: Criminal appeal against conviction and death sentence for murder, where the prosecution relied on circumstantial evidence (motive, last seen theory, and recoveries) to prove guilt.

judgements.case_summary: Gambhir Singh was convicted and sentenced to death for the gruesome murder of his brother, sister-in-law, and their four children in village Turkiya on the intervening night of 8th and 9th May, 2012. The prosecution's case was based on circumstantial evidence, primarily focusing on motive (a land dispute), the 'last seen' theory, and the recovery of blood-stained weapons and clothes at the instance of the accused. The trial court found him guilty, and the High Court affirmed both the conviction and the death sentence. The appellant-accused challenged this, arguing that the prosecution failed to prove any of the incriminating circumstances beyond reasonable doubt, asserting the case was fabricated. The respondent State maintained that the prosecution had successfully established all circumstances. The Supreme Court meticulously analyzed the evidence and found significant infirmities. It concluded that the alleged motive was a 'bald aspersion' lacking plausible evidence, the 'last seen' witnesses were 'cooked-up' and unreliable, and the recoveries were discredited due to the Investigating Officer's procedural lapses, including failure to prove disclosure statements or properly attest recovery memos. Furthermore, the FSL report did not specify blood grouping. The Court criticized the 'utter lackadaisical approach' of the investigation and the 'casual and lackadaisical manner' of the trial. Consequently, the Supreme Court quashed the impugned judgments, set aside the conviction and death sentence, and acquitted Gambhir Singh, ordering his immediate release.

petitioner_key_arguments: The entire case of the prosecution is false and fabricated.
The prosecution failed to prove even one of the so-called incriminating circumstances (last seen, motive, recoveries) beyond reasonable doubt.
No credible evidence was presented to connect the appellant-accused with the crime.
respondent_key_arguments: The prosecution proved the charges against the appellant-accused beyond all manner of doubt.
The appellant-accused committed the murders due to a long-standing land dispute and a vow for revenge.
The circumstances of motive, last seen theory, and recovery of incriminating blood-stained weapons and clothes were proved by cogent evidence.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments that the prosecution failed to prove the incriminating circumstances (motive, last seen, and recoveries) beyond reasonable doubt, and that the chain of circumstantial evidence was not complete.

outcome.relief_granted: The appellant-Gambhir Singh is acquitted of the charges. He is in custody and shall be released from prison forthwith, if not wanted in any other case.

precedents_cited: Sharad Birdhichand Sharda v. State of Maharashtra (1984) 4 SCC 116
Shivaji Sahabrao Bobade v. State of Maharashtra (1973) 2 SCC 793

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The prosecution failed to establish the chain of circumstantial evidence beyond reasonable doubt, as the alleged motive was unproven, the 'last seen' evidence was unreliable, and the recoveries were legally flawed due to investigative deficiencies. In a case based purely on circumstantial evidence, the onus is upon the prosecution to prove the chain of circumstances beyond all manner of doubt, which was not met.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed an 'utter lackadaisical approach' on the part of the Investigating Agency and prosecution, and criticized the 'casual and lackadaisical manner' in which the trial was conducted by the Public Prosecutor and the Presiding Officer, without adhering to mandatory procedural requirements.

special_directions.special_directions: The appellant-Gambhir Singh is acquitted of the charges and shall be released from prison forthwith, if not wanted in any other case.

case_identification.respondent_name: THE STATE OF TAMILNADU REP. BY INSPECTOR OF POLICE
case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 860 OF 2023 (@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRL.) NO.11560 OF 2022)

case_details.subject_matter: The case involves an appellant who, after losing his job, attacked his mother-in-law with a billhook and injured his wife, leading to convictions under various sections of the Indian Penal Code. The appeal primarily concerns the quantum of sentence imposed.

judgements.case_summary: The appellant, Ganesan, after losing his employment abroad, returned home and began harassing his wife and children. His wife moved to live with her mother. Enraged, the appellant, with premeditation, attacked his mother-in-law with a billhook, also injuring his wife who tried to intervene. He was convicted by the trial court under Sections 498A, 294(b), 307, 506(II), and 324 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and sentenced to life imprisonment for Section 307, among other sentences. The High Court reduced the sentence for Section 307 to 12 years rigorous imprisonment and acquitted him under Section 506(II), while confirming other convictions. The Supreme Court, in this appeal, considered only the quantum of sentence. The Court noted that the maximum sentence under Section 307 IPC, if life imprisonment is avoided, cannot exceed 10 years. Citing precedents, it held that an Appellate Court cannot impose a punishment higher than the maximum permissible by the Trial Court for that specific part of the section. Consequently, the Supreme Court modified the sentence for Section 307 IPC from 12 years RI to 7 years RI, with all sentences running concurrently, thereby partly allowing the appeal.

petitioner_key_arguments: The quantum of sentence imposed by the Appellate Court for Section 307 IPC was excessive and beyond the maximum permissible limit if life imprisonment is avoided.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's argument regarding the excessive quantum of sentence for Section 307 IPC, specifically that it exceeded the statutory maximum of 10 years when life imprisonment is not imposed, was accepted by the court.

outcome.relief_granted: The sentence under Section 307 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, was modified from 12 years Rigorous Imprisonment (RI) to 7 years RI. Other sentences were confirmed and directed to run concurrently.

precedents_cited: Jagat Bahadur Vs. State of Madhya Pradesh1
Amit Rana @ Koka Vs. State of Haryana2

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that the maximum sentence under Section 307 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, if life imprisonment is avoided, cannot exceed 10 years. An Appellate Court is not competent to impose a punishment higher than the maximum that could have been imposed by the Trial Court for that specific part of the section.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The unshaking testimony of injured witnesses has to be accorded a special status in law.

special_directions.special_directions: The sentences handed over under the other penal provisions of the I.P.C. stand confirmed and shall run concurrently as directed by the Appellate Court.

case_identification.respondent_name: Gangaram Sakharam Dhuri (D) Thr. LRs And Ors.
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO.3183 OF 2009

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns a property dispute involving the validity of a sale deed executed by a co-owner, the administration of a deceased's estate, and the partition of inherited property, with a focus on the necessity of proper parties in such suits.

judgements.case_summary:
The case originated from a property dispute concerning C.T.S. No.1048 and the 'Sai Niwas' building. The original owner, Gangaram Thakoji Shelar, passed away in 1967, leaving behind his widow, son Vishnu, and four daughters, including the Plaintiff. Vishnu, the son, allegedly sold half of the property to the second defendant based on a Relinquishment Deed, which the Plaintiff claimed was obtained fraudulently. The Plaintiff filed Suit No.2060 of 1970 seeking administration of the deceased's estate and a declaration that the sale deed was null and void.

The Trial Court decreed the suit, declaring the Sale Deed of 10.01.1969 null and void and directing the second defendant to hand over possession of 1/2 portion of the suit property. However, it also found the suit for administration of property not maintainable due to the non-joinder of Vishnu's children.

The High Court reversed the Trial Court's decision, holding that Vishnu had a 1/5th undivided share in the property (after his mother's demise) and that the sale deed was valid to that extent. It also noted that a decree for possession against the second defendant was improper as other co-owners had not sought their shares, and that consequential relief could not be granted if the main administration suit was not maintainable.

The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's reasoning, affirming that the sale deed was valid to the extent of Vishnu's 1/5th share. The Court emphasized the importance of impleading all necessary parties in property disputes and clarified that relief must align with the prayers made and the proper legal framework. The Civil Appeal was disposed of with directions to maintain the Plaintiff's possession until a partition suit is filed and decided, and to continue the status quo regarding the property's alienation.

petitioner_key_arguments: Vishnu could not have sold more than his actual share (1/6th initially, then 1/5th after his mother's demise) in the suit property.
The second defendant, as a purchaser, should have availed the remedy for partition to demarcate his separate share.
The second defendant/vendee was not a bonafide purchaser without notice.
respondent_key_arguments: An undivided share in a Hindu Undivided Family property can be transferred for valuable consideration by way of sale.
The Plaintiff cannot seek relief for a separate share in an estate administration suit; such relief can only be granted in a properly-instituted partition suit.
The second defendant's LRs were ready and willing to pay reasonable compensation or a lump-sum amount.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the respondent's argument that Vishnu could transfer his undivided share and that the sale deed was valid to the extent of his share. It also agreed with the High Court's reasoning that the administration suit was not the proper forum for partition without all necessary parties and that relief must align with prayers and proper parties.

outcome.relief_granted: The Plaintiff's possession shall not be disturbed until the suit property is partitioned. The second defendant is recognized to have a 1/5th share in the suit property. The Trial Court is directed to endeavor to decide any partition suit, if filed, within three months from its filing date. The interim order maintaining status quo regarding non-alienation of the property is continued. Applications for bringing Legal Representatives on record were allowed.

precedents_cited: Chief Conservator of Forests, Government of Andhra Pradesh v Collector, (2003) 3 SCC 472
Bachhaj Nahar v Nilima Mandal, (2008) 17 SCC 491

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: A sale deed executed by a co-owner for their undivided share is valid to the extent of their actual share, even if they purported to sell a larger portion. A suit for administration of an estate cannot be converted into a partition suit without impleading all necessary parties, and relief granted in a civil suit must be strictly circumscribed by the pleadings, prayers, and proper parties. Non-joinder of necessary parties can be fatal to a suit.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed the distinction between misdescription and misjoinder/non-joinder of parties, emphasizing that while misdescription is not fatal, non-joinder of a necessary party can cause a suit to fail. It also remarked that the scope of relief in civil suits is limited by factors such as court fees, limitation, and the specific prayers made.

special_directions.special_directions: The Trial Court concerned shall positively endeavour to decide any partition suit, if so filed, within three months from the date of filing thereof. The status quo order regarding non-alienation of the property shall continue till the property is partitioned as per law.
special_directions.interim_orders: An interim order dated 01.05.2009, directing that the subject matter of dispute shall not be alienated by any of the parties, was continued.

case_identification.petitioner_name: GARDEN REACH SHIPBUILDERS AND ENGINEERS LIMITED
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 3243 OF 2025 [arising out of SLP (C) No. 28399/2024]

case_details.subject_matter: The appeal concerns the High Court's jurisdiction and judicial discipline in hearing a writ petition regarding compassionate appointment, which was not assigned to it by the Chief Justice.

judgements.case_summary: The Supreme Court heard an appeal against a High Court Division Bench's judgment which allowed a writ petition concerning compassionate appointments. The writ petition had initially been de-listed by a Single Judge awaiting a reference decision. Despite this, a predecessor Division Bench, and subsequently the impugned Division Bench, proceeded to hear and decide the writ petition, reportedly based on an agreement between the parties. The Supreme Court found that the High Court's Division Bench lacked jurisdiction to hear the writ petition. It emphasized that consent does not confer jurisdiction, and a bench cannot hear a matter not assigned by the Chief Justice, who is the master of the roster. The Court held that the High Court's order was without jurisdiction and therefore a nullity. Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside the impugned order, allowed the appeal, and remanded the writ petition back to the High Court. It requested the Chief Justice of the High Court to assign the writ petition to an appropriate bench for consideration and disposal within six months. The Court also recorded an undertaking from GRSE Ltd. that no appointments would be made to render the writ petition infructuous until its disposal by the High Court.

petitioner_key_arguments: The High Court's Division Bench lacked jurisdiction to hear the writ petition as it was not assigned by the Chief Justice.
Consent of parties cannot confer jurisdiction where none exists.
respondent_key_arguments: GRSE Ltd. had agreed to the consideration and disposal of the writ petition by the appellate court.
The Supreme Court should not take a 'too technical view of the matter' and should decide the appeal on its merits.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that the High Court's Division Bench lacked jurisdiction because the matter was not assigned by the Chief Justice, and consent does not confer jurisdiction.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned order of the High Court was set aside. The writ petition was remanded to the High Court for fresh consideration by an appropriate bench assigned by the Chief Justice, preferably within six months. An undertaking from GRSE Ltd. regarding no appointments until disposal was recorded.

acts_cited: Rule 26 of the Rules framed by the High Court at Calcutta
precedents_cited: State Bank of India v. Sheo Shankar Tewari
N.C. Santhosh v. State of Karnataka
Shah Babulal Khimji v. Jayaben D. Kania
Sohan Lal Baid v. State of West Bengal
State of Rajasthan v. Prakash Chand
Campaign for Judicial Accountability and Reforms v. Union of India
constitutional_provisions: Article 225 of the Constitution of India
Article 226

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: A judicial order passed by a bench without proper assignment from the Chief Justice (master of the roster) is without jurisdiction and a nullity, as consent of parties cannot confer jurisdiction. The Chief Justice's determination for hearing cases is final and binding on all benches.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed that the Single Judge was not entirely right in de-listing the writ petition on the stated ground and ought to have proceeded with consideration of the writ petition finally, giving due regard to the law then prevailing.

special_directions.special_directions: The Chief Justice of the High Court is requested to assign the writ petition to an appropriate bench for consideration and disposal, as early as possible, but preferably within six months.
special_directions.interim_orders: The court recorded an undertaking from GRSE Ltd. that no appointment shall be made until the writ petition is disposed of by the appropriate Bench of the High Court. The court refrained from making any interim order to be operative during the pendency of the writ petition or to extend the ad-interim order dated August 1, 2016.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CIVIL) NO. 6470 OF 2022)

case_details.subject_matter: The issue involved in this batch of appeals is, whether, the imported goods is to be treated as Base Oil as claimed by the appellants or High Speed Diesel (HSD) as determined by the Customs Authorities, which is contested by the appellants.

judgements.case_summary:
The case concerns a batch of appeals challenging a High Court decision that classified imported goods as High Speed Diesel (HSD) rather than Base Oil, as claimed by the appellants (Gastrade International, M/s Rajkamal Industrial Pvt Ltd, and M/s Divinity Impex). The Customs Authorities had determined the goods to be HSD, a prohibited item for private import, leading to confiscation and penalties. The Commissioner of Customs initially upheld this, but the CESTAT reversed it, deeming the goods Base Oil. The High Court then overturned CESTAT's decision, relying on partial test reports and expert testimony, applying a "preponderance of probability" standard.

The Supreme Court examined the three laboratory test reports and the cross-examination of the expert, Dr. Gobind Singh. It found the test reports inconclusive, as not all 21/22 parameters of the Indian Standard IS 1460:2005 for HSD were tested, and the flash point of the samples was significantly higher than the minimum for HSD. The expert's testimony was deemed evasive and failed to definitively state that the samples *were* HSD, only that they *conformed to certain specifications*.

The Court held that for classification disputes with confiscatory and penal consequences, the standard of proof required from the Revenue is higher than mere "preponderance of probability." It emphasized that either full compliance with all statutory parameters or a clear expert opinion establishing the goods as "most akin" to the specified product is necessary. As the evidence was inconclusive and the expert's opinion non-committal, the Court granted the benefit of doubt to the appellants. The High Court's judgment was set aside, and the appeals were allowed. The Court also directed the Customs Authorities to ensure adequate testing facilities for all relevant parameters within six months to prevent similar disputes.

petitioner_key_arguments: Imported goods are Base Oil, not HSD.
Customs failed to conclusively prove HSD classification.
Not all 21/22 parameters of IS 1460:2005 were tested, making the classification unreliable.
The flash point of the samples (above 93°C) was too high for HSD, which has a minimum flash point of 66°C.
Expert opinion and test reports were inconclusive and evasive.
respondent_key_arguments: Imported goods are High Speed Diesel (HSD).
Test reports from three laboratories confirmed characteristics of HSD for the tested parameters (14 out of 21).
The expert (Dr. Gobind Singh) confirmed the samples showed HSD characteristics.
Classification can be established based on "preponderance of probability".
The burden shifted to the appellants to prove the goods were not HSD, which they failed to do.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court accepted the appellants' arguments that the evidence presented by the Customs Authorities was inconclusive and did not meet the required standard of proof for classification, especially given the penal consequences. The Court found the test reports incomplete and the expert's testimony evasive, particularly regarding the flash point.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeals were allowed, setting aside the impugned common judgment and order dated 20.01.2022 passed in Revenue Tax Appeal No. 297 of 2021, Revenue Tax Appeal No. 298 of 2021 and Revenue Tax Appeal No. 299 of 2021. The benefit of doubt was given to the appellants. Specific directions were issued to the respondents regarding testing facilities.

precedents_cited: Collector of Customs, Madras and others Vs. D Bhoormall, AIR 1974 SC 859
A.N. Guha & Co Vs. Collector [1996 (86) ELT 333]
R.V.E Venkatachala Gounder Vs. Arulmigu Viswesaraswami & V.P. [Order dated 08.10.2003 in Civil Appeal number 10585 of 1996]
State of H.P. v. Jai Lal, (1999) 7 SCC 280
Dayal Singh v. State of Uttaranchal, (2012) 8 SCC 263
M. Siddiq (Ram Janmabhumi Temple-5 J) v. Suresh Das, (2020) 1 SCC 1
Bater v. Bater [Bater v. Bater, [1951] P. 35 (CA).]
Miller v. Minister of Pensions [Miller v. Minister of Pensions, (1947) 2 All ER 372.]
N.G. Dastane v. S. Dastane [N.G. Dastane v. S. Dastane, (1975) 2 SCC 326.]
State of U.P. v. Krishna Gopal [State of U.P. v. Krishna Gopal, (1988) 4 SCC 302]
Durga Oil Company Vs State of U.P., (1998) 6 SCC 299

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The Court ruled that for classification of goods under the Customs Tariff Act, especially when it leads to confiscatory and penal consequences, the standard of proof required from the Revenue is higher than mere "preponderance of probability." When specific scientific criteria (like IS 1460:2005 for HSD) are laid down, either full compliance with all parameters must be demonstrated, or a clear expert opinion establishing the goods as "most akin" to the specified product is necessary. In this case, the test reports were incomplete (not all parameters tested) and the expert's opinion was evasive and inconclusive, particularly regarding the critical flash point, thus failing to definitively prove the goods were HSD.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that the non-availability of adequate facilities for testing all parameters leads to uncertainty and prolonged litigation. It directed the respondents to ensure proper testing facilities are made available for all parameters, or at least those of essential character, within six months to avoid such difficulties in the future.

special_directions.special_directions: The respondents are directed to ensure that proper facilities are made available in the appropriate laboratories for undertaking tests for all these parameters or at least for those parameters which the Authorities consider are of essential character to satisfy the “most akin” test without which the article in issue cannot be properly classified. Accordingly, we direct the respondents to take necessary steps in this regard within a period of six months for proper testing in all the parameters in future.
special_directions.interim_orders: The High Court passed an interim order on 30.07.2018 directing the Department to send requisite quantity of samples to the Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. (IOCL), Mumbai which is one of the notified laboratories as per the Department's circular dated 16.11.2017.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(s). OF 2025 (Arising out of Special Leave Petition (Criminal) No.9556) and CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(s). OF 2025 (Arising out of Special Leave Petition (Criminal) No.428)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the quashing of criminal proceedings related to dowry demand, harassment, and domestic violence allegations against the appellants, citing vague and generalized accusations without specific overt acts.

judgements.case_summary: This common order addresses two Criminal Appeals arising from Special Leave Petitions (Criminal) No. 9556 of 2022 and No. 428 of 2024. The appellants, Geddam Jhansi and Geddam Sathyakama Jabali, sought to quash criminal proceedings initiated against them under various sections of the IPC, Dowry Prohibition Act, and DV Act, following complaints filed by Premlata, the wife of Samuel Suresh. The High Court had previously declined to quash these proceedings, finding prima facie triable issues. The appellants argued that the allegations against them were vague, generalized, and lacked specific overt acts. The Supreme Court examined the complaints, charge-sheet, and witness statements, noting that the evidence against the appellants, including statements from the complainant's parents and panchayat elders, was largely based on hearsay or was generalized without specific details. The Court emphasized that criminal proceedings, especially in domestic disputes, require specific allegations and credible material, not just generalized accusations, to avoid misuse of the legal process. It also noted that the appellants did not reside with the principal accused (complainant's husband and mother-in-law) and that one appellant (Geddam Jhansi) was even stated to have attempted mediation. Finding no prima facie case against the appellants based on the available evidence, the Supreme Court allowed the appeals, quashing the criminal proceedings against Geddam Jhansi and Geddam Sathyakama Jabali in C.C. No. 46 of 2022 and against Geddam Jhansi in DVC No. 25 of 2021.

petitioner_key_arguments: Allegations against them are vague and of a generalised nature without any specific overt act attributed to them.
The allegations are incapable of being fastened with criminal liability.
The High Court failed to appreciate the lack of specific evidence.
respondent_key_arguments: Prima facie, there are certain allegations against the appellants.
The issues are triable and need to be decided only after enquiry.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments that the allegations were vague, generalized, and lacked specific overt acts, and that the evidence against them was largely hearsay or non-specific, were accepted by the court.

outcome.relief_granted: The criminal proceedings in C.C. No. 46 of 2022 pending before the Court of the Judicial Magistrate, First Class, Bhongir, were quashed qua the two appellants, Geddam Jhansi and Geddam Sathyakama Jabali. The criminal proceedings in DVC No. 25 of 2021 pending before the Court of the Additional Judicial Magistrate, First Class, Bhongir, were quashed qua the appellant, Geddam Jhansi.

acts_cited: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (DV Act)
precedents_cited: State of Haryana and Ors. vs. Bhajan Lal and Ors., 1992 Supp (1) SCC 335
Anand Kumar Mohatta v. State (NCT of Delhi), (2019) 11 SCC 706
Joseph Salvaraj A. v. State of Gujarat, (2011) 7 SCC 59 : (2011) 3 SCC (Cri) 23
State of Gujarat, 2007 SCC OnLine Guj 365
G. Sagar Suri v. State of U.P., (2000) 2 SCC 636
Umesh Kumar v. State of A.P., (2013) 10 SCC 591
constitutional_provisions: Article 226 of the Constitution of India
Article 142 of the Constitution of India

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: Criminal proceedings, particularly in domestic disputes, cannot be sustained on vague, generalized allegations without specific overt acts attributed to the accused. Hearsay evidence and identical statements from witnesses are insufficient to establish a prima facie case, especially when the accused do not reside with the complainant and their involvement is not clearly defined. The court must be circumspect in allowing criminal process when allegations lack specificity and credible material.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed that invoking criminal process is a serious matter with penal consequences, and in matrimonial disputes, emotions run high, leading to a tendency to implicate other family members. It emphasized the importance of the institution of family and the need for a balance between bringing perpetrators to book and not indiscriminately involving all family members in criminal nets. The court also noted that genuine cases of cruelty and violence in the domestic sphere should be handled with utmost sensitivity, but mere general allegations of harassment without specific details are insufficient.

special_directions.special_directions: The observations and findings recorded in this judgment are specific to the present appellants and will have no bearing on the criminal proceedings against other accused persons. The trial courts are expected to proceed with the criminal proceedings pending against the other accused persons after proper appreciation of evidence and in accordance with law.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NOS. 3994-3997 OF 2024

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns an inter-se seniority dispute between original employees of the Directorate of Medical Education (DME) and employees absorbed from the Directorate of Health Services (DHS) following a State policy decision to abolish a dual control system.

judgements.case_summary: The present appeals challenge an order of the High Court of Kerala concerning the inter-se seniority of employees absorbed from the Directorate of Health Services (DHS) into the Directorate of Medical Education (DME). This absorption was a result of a State policy decision to abolish a dual control system, requiring DHS staff working in medical colleges to transfer to DME. The absorbed employees (appellants) argued they were entitled to retain their seniority from their original DHS service, citing Rule 8 of Appendix I of G.O. (P) No. 548/2008/H&FWD and Rules 27(a) and 27(c) of the Kerala State and Subordinate Service Rules (KS&SS Rules). The Single Judge upheld their claim, but the Division Bench reversed this, treating the transfer as a 'request' transfer, thereby applying the proviso to Rule 27(a) of KS&SS Rules, which would fix seniority from the date of joining DME. The Supreme Court, allowing the appeals, held that the transfer was an absorption based on a policy decision and administrative exigency, not a voluntary 'request' transfer. Consequently, the proviso to Rule 27(a) was deemed inapplicable, and the absorbed employees were entitled to retain their seniority from their initial appointment date in DHS. The Court directed the State of Kerala to draw the seniority list accordingly.

petitioner_key_arguments: The transfer was an absorption based on a State policy decision to abolish a dual control system, not a 'request' transfer.
Rule 27(a) of KS&SS Rules and its proviso, which applies to 'request' transfers, is not applicable in this case.
Seniority of absorbed employees should be maintained from their past service rendered in DHS as per Rule 8 of Appendix I of G.O. (P) No. 548/2008/H&FWD and Rules 27(a) and 27(c) of KS&SS Rules.
The lien of the employees was shifted, and their service was specifically protected.
respondent_key_arguments: Absorbed employees exercised an 'option' to join DME, which constitutes an inter-departmental transfer on 'request'.
The proviso to Rule 27(a) of KS&SS Rules is attracted, meaning seniority should be reckoned from the date of joining duty in the new department (DME).
Past service in DHS should be foregone upon such transfer.
If seniority is reckoned from initial appointment in DHS, it would cause grave prejudice to original DME employees who were never given an option.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court accepted the arguments of the absorbed employees (appellants) that their transfer was an absorption due to a policy decision and administrative exigency, not a 'request' transfer. Therefore, the proviso to Rule 27(a) of KS&SS Rules did not apply, and their seniority from DHS service should be maintained.

outcome.relief_granted: The State of Kerala is directed to draw the seniority list of DME employees, including original and absorbed employees, reckoning the seniority of the absorbed employees as directed in paragraph 52 of the judgment.

acts_cited: Kerala State and Subordinate Service Rules, 1958 (KS&SS Rules) Rule 27(a)
Kerala State and Subordinate Service Rules, 1958 (KS&SS Rules) Rule 27(c)
precedents_cited: K.P. Sudhakaran and Another Vs. State of Kerala and Others1 (2006) 5 SCC 386
Kartar Singh v. State of Punjab, 1989 SCC OnLine P&H 482

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The transfer of DHS employees to DME was an absorption based on a State policy decision to abolish a dual control system, driven by administrative exigency and public interest, rather than a voluntary 'request' transfer. Consequently, the proviso to Rule 27(a) of the KS&SS Rules, which applies specifically to 'request' transfers and mandates seniority from the date of joining the new department, is not applicable. The seniority of the absorbed employees must therefore be maintained from their original date of appointment in DHS as per Rule 27(a) and 27(c) of KS&SS Rules.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court elaborated on the distinct meanings of 'absorption', 'option', and 'request', emphasizing that an absorption due to policy decision cannot be equated with a transfer on 'request'. It also noted that the Government's intention, as reflected in G.O. (P) No. 548/2008/H&FWD, was to maintain the seniority of absorbed employees.

special_directions.special_directions: The State of Kerala is directed to draw the seniority list of DME employees, including original and absorbed employees, reckoning the seniority of the absorbed employees as directed in paragraph 52 of the judgment.
special_directions.interim_orders: Pending interlocutory applications (if any) stand disposed- of.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 3334 OF 2023

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the cancellation of an apartment booking by consumers and the forfeiture of earnest money by the developer, specifically challenging the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission's decision to reduce the forfeiture amount and award interest.

judgements.case_summary: The case involves an appeal filed by Godrej Projects Development Limited against an order of the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC). The respondents (complainants) had booked an apartment in 2014, paid Rs. 51,12,310/-, but later sought cancellation in 2017 due to a recession in the market. The NCDRC directed the appellant to deduct only 10% of the Basic Sale Price (BSP) as cancellation charges and refund the balance with 6% interest. The appellant argued that the NCDRC erred in interfering with contractual terms, which allowed for forfeiture of 20% of the BSP as earnest money, citing precedents like Satish Batra v. Sudhir Rawal. The respondents contended that the 20% forfeiture was unreasonable and that the agreement was one-sided, citing NCDRC's consistent view and Supreme Court judgments like Pioneer Urban Land and Ireo Grace Realtech, which deemed such clauses unfair trade practices. The Supreme Court found the builder-buyer agreement to be one-sided, disproportionately favoring the developer, and upheld the NCDRC's decision to reduce the forfeiture to 10% of the BSP, aligning with the principle that forfeiture must be reasonable. However, the Court set aside the award of interest, noting that the cancellation was initiated by the buyers due to market conditions, implying they might have utilized the funds elsewhere. The appeal was partly allowed, directing the appellant to pay the remaining balance of Rs. 12,02,955/- without interest.

petitioner_key_arguments: NCDRC grossly erred in interfering with contractual terms, specifically the forfeiture clause.
The agreement specifically provided for forfeiture of the entire earnest money (20% of BSP).
Respondents cancelled the deal due to market recession, justifying forfeiture of earnest money.
Relied on judgments in Satish Batra v. Sudhir Rawal and Desh Raj and others v. Rohtash Singh.
respondent_key_arguments: NCDRC consistently held that 20% forfeiture of BSP was unreasonable and reduced it to 10%.
The condition of forfeiture of 20% of BSP was one-sided and unconscionable, hence not enforceable.
Relied on judgments in Ireo Grace Realtech Private Limited and Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Limited.

Cited 'The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016' and 'The Haryana Real Estate Regulatory Authority Gurugram (Forfeiture of earnest money by the builder) Regulations, 2018', limiting forfeiture to 10% of BSP.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the respondent's argument that the 20% forfeiture clause was unreasonable and one-sided, upholding the NCDRC's reduction to 10% of the BSP. However, it sided with the petitioner by setting aside the award of interest, reasoning that the buyers initiated cancellation due to market conditions.

outcome.relief_granted: The appellant is directed to pay the balance amount of Rs. 12,02,955/- to the respondents within a period of six weeks. The forfeiture of 10% of the Basic Sale Price was upheld, but the award of interest on the refunded amount was set aside.

acts_cited: The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016
The Haryana Real Estate Regulatory Authority Gurugram (Forfeiture of earnest money by the builder) Regulations, 2018
precedents_cited: Satish Batra v. Sudhir Rawal
Desh Raj and others v. Rohtash Singh
Komal Aggarwal v. Godrej Projects Development Ltd.
DLF Ltd. v. Bhagwanti Narula
Ramesh Malhotra and Another v. Emaar Mgf Land Limited and Another
Ireo Grace Realtech Private Limited v. Abhishek Khanna and others
Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Limited v. Govindan Raghavan
Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Limited and Another v. Brojo Nath Ganguly and Another (1986) 3 SCC 156
Wing Commander Arifur Rahman Khan and Aleya Sultana and others v. DLF Southern Homes Private Limited (Now Known as Begur OMR Homes Private Limited) (2020) 16 SCC 512
Maula Bux v. Union of India
Chiranjit Singh v. Har Swarup
Roshan Lal v. Delhi Cloth and General Mills Company Ltd. Delhi [1910 SCC OnLine All 98 : ILR (1911) 33 All 166]
Mohd Habibullah v. Mohd Shafi [1919 SCC OnLine All 87 : ILR 41 All 324]
Bishan Chand v. Radhakishan Das [1897 SCC OnLine All 52 : ILR (1897) 19 All 490]
constitutional_provisions: Article 14 of the Constitution of India

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The court held that while a forfeiture clause for earnest money is permissible, it must be reasonable and not amount to a penalty. Builder-buyer agreements with one-sided clauses that disproportionately favor the developer are unconscionable and constitute an unfair trade practice. Therefore, a 20% forfeiture of BSP was deemed unreasonable, and 10% was upheld as a reasonable deduction. However, interest on the refunded amount was disallowed because the buyers initiated cancellation due to market recession, not due to the developer's fault.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court discussed the evolution of the concept of 'unfair trade practice' under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, and 'unfair contract' under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. It reiterated the principle that courts will not enforce unfair and unreasonable contracts entered into between parties with unequal bargaining power, as per Article 14 of the Constitution.

special_directions.special_directions: The Appellant is directed to pay the balance amount of Rs. 12,02,955/- to the respondents within a period of six weeks from the date of the judgment.
special_directions.interim_orders: By an order dated 24th April, 2023, this Court had granted stay of the impugned order on the condition that the Appellant refunds the amount deposited by the Complainants after deducting 20% (earnest money deposit) along with interest @ 6% per annum from the date of cancellation of the contract.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO(S) 13192 OF 2024 (Arising out of Special Leave Petition (Civil) No.25645 of

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the validity of a Will executed by Sanjhi Ram and the interpretation of Section 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, specifically the meaning of "by the direction of the testator" in relation to attestation.

judgements.case_summary: This appeal concerns the validity of a Will executed by Sanjhi Ram on November 7, 2005, who passed away the following day. The Will was challenged by the respondents as forged and fabricated. The Civil Court initially found the Will suspicious and invalid, but the Lower Appellate Court reversed this, upholding its validity. The High Court, however, reinstated the Civil Court's finding, concluding the Will was not proved due to alleged improper attestation and suspicious circumstances, including narrow spacing in the document. The Supreme Court examined the interpretation of Section 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, specifically the phrase "by the direction of the testator." The Court clarified that the word "OR" in the section is disjunctive, meaning an attesting witness seeing the testator sign or affix their mark is sufficient, and the "direction" clause only applies if another person signs on the testator's behalf. Finding that the attesting witness had seen the deceased affix his mark, the Supreme Court held that the High Court erred in its strict interpretation. Consequently, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's judgment and restoring the Lower Appellate Court's decision, thereby validating Sanjhi Ram's Will and the subsequent sale deeds.

petitioner_key_arguments: The Will of Sanjhi Ram was validly executed and duly attested.
The High Court erred in its interpretation of Section 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, particularly regarding the phrase "by the direction of the testator."
The testimony of the attesting witness (DW-1, Janak Raj) confirmed he saw the deceased affix his mark, which satisfies the requirements of Section 63(c).
The "direction of the testator" clause is only applicable when another person signs on behalf of the testator, not when the testator affixes their own mark.
The Lower Appellate Court's judgment, which upheld the Will's validity, should be restored.
respondent_key_arguments: The Will was not proved due to suspicious circumstances, including the testator's illness, his death shortly after execution, and narrow spacing in the document.

The attestation of the Will was not in accordance with Section 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, as the attesting witness did not explicitly state that the thumb impression was affixed "by the direction of the testator."
The High Court correctly identified the flaws in the Will's execution and attestation.
The Civil Court's initial finding that the Will was suspicious and invalid should be upheld.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court accepted the petitioner's argument that the High Court had misconstrued Section 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925. The Court clarified that the word "OR" in Section 63(c) is disjunctive, and the requirement for an attesting witness to have seen the testator sign or affix his mark is a distinct and sufficient condition for valid attestation, separate from the requirement concerning another person signing by the testator's direction. The testimony of DW-1, who saw the deceased affix his mark, was deemed sufficient to satisfy the attestation requirements.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal is allowed. The impugned judgment of the High Court is set aside. The judgment of the First Appellant Court (Lower Appellate Court) is restored. Consequently, the Will of Sanjhi Ram is valid, and so are the subsequent Sale Deeds executed by Gopal Krishan.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is the interpretation of Section 63(c) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925. The Court held that the word 'OR' in Section 63(c) is disjunctive, meaning that the requirement for an attesting witness to have seen the testator sign or affix his mark is a distinct and sufficient condition for valid attestation, separate from the requirement concerning another person signing by the testator's direction. The High Court erred by strictly applying the 'direction of the testator' clause even when the testator himself affixed his mark.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that suspicious circumstances must be 'real, germane and valid' and not merely 'the fantasy of the doubting mind'. It also referenced Justice G.P Singh's treatise on statutory interpretation regarding the normal disjunctive nature of 'or' and conjunctive nature of 'and'.

case_identification.case_number: CONTEMPT PETITION (C) NO. 372 OF 2019 IN CIVIL APPEAL NO. 2703 OF 2017

case_details.subject_matter: Alleged non-compliance of a previous order regarding absorption, payment of salary arrears, and pension for petitioners by Magadh University.

judgements.case_summary: The petitioners filed contempt petitions alleging non-compliance with an order dated 31.08.2017 in Civil Appeal No. 2703 of 2017, which confirmed their absorption by Magadh University based on the J. Sinha Commission's recommendations. The petitioners claimed that despite absorption, their arrears of salary and pension had not been paid. The State of Bihar, in its counter-affidavit, contended that ascertainable arrears had been paid, and for some petitioners, attendance records were either missing or showed periods of non-work, making it difficult to ascertain actual working periods and thus precluding a finding of willful non-compliance. The Supreme Court observed that the issues regarding actual working days, salary, and pension arrears required a fact-finding inquiry, which was not suitable for contempt proceedings. Consequently, the Court disposed of the contempt petitions, directing the Registrar/Vice Chancellor of the University to conduct a discrete inquiry into the petitioners' claims for salary, arrears, and pension within three months. The Court also directed that pension claims be decided notionally from the date of absorption, uninfluenced by previous orders. Any excess payments found could be recovered, and dissatisfied parties were granted liberty to approach the High Court.

petitioner_key_arguments: Alleged non-compliance with the order dated 31.08.2017 regarding absorption.
Non-payment of arrears of salary and pension despite absorption by the university.
respondent_key_arguments: Ascertainable arrears of salary for actual working days have been paid.
For some petitioners, attendance records were incomplete or showed periods of non-work, making actual working periods unascertainable.
No case of willful non-compliance can be made out.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court did not definitively rule on the merits of either party's arguments but directed a fact-finding inquiry by the university authorities to resolve the factual disputes regarding actual working days, salary arrears, and pension claims.

outcome.relief_granted: The contempt petitions were disposed of with directions for the Registrar/Vice Chancellor of the University to conduct a discrete inquiry into the petitioners' claims for salary, arrears, and pension within three months, and to decide pension claims notionally from the date of absorption. Any excess payments found could be recovered.

precedents_cited: Krishna Nand Yadav & others Vs. Magadh University & others
Baidya Nath Choudhary Vs. Dr. Sree Surendra Kumar Singh (Contempt Petition (C) No. 1188 of 2018)
State of Bihar & others vs Bihar Rajya M.S.E.S.K.K.M & others (2005) 9 SCC 129

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core reasoning was that the factual disputes concerning actual working days, salary arrears, and pension claims required a detailed fact-finding inquiry, which is beyond the scope of contempt proceedings. Therefore, the court deemed it appropriate to refer these matters to the university authorities for adjudication.

special_directions.special_directions: 1. Individual petitioners shall submit claims with relevant documents to the Registrar/Vice Chancellor of the University by February 28, 2025. 2. A discrete inquiry shall be held, affording due opportunity, and a reasoned order passed within three months regarding salary and arrears. 3. Pension claims shall be decided counting service from the date of absorption notionally. 4. After adjudication, pension and arrears shall be paid within two months. 5. Any excess amount paid shall be quantified and recovered. 6. Joint claims for arrears of salary and pension will be governed by directions (ii) and (iii) respectively. 7. Dissatisfied parties may approach the High Court.

case_identification.case_number: Criminal Appeal No.1408/2014, 2025 INSC 263

bench_judges: HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE ABHAY S. OKA

case_details.subject_matter: Criminal appeal challenging conviction for offences under the Indian Penal Code, specifically concerning the establishment of the accused's identity by prosecution witnesses.

judgements.case_summary: This criminal appeal was filed by two appellants, Gopal Singh (accused no.4) and Avtar Singh (accused no.5), challenging their conviction. Initially, they were convicted by the Sessions Court for offences under Sections 302 and 323 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and sentenced to life imprisonment. The High Court subsequently reduced the conviction to Section 304 Part II of the IPC. The prosecution's case stemmed from an incident on November 21, 1997, where PW-1 (Soban Singh) and the deceased (Gaje Singh) were allegedly assaulted by the accused. The prosecution relied on the testimony of two alleged eyewitnesses, PW-1 and PW-3, and four court witnesses. The Supreme Court meticulously examined the evidence and found that neither PW-1 nor PW-3 identified the appellants in court, primarily because the appellants were not present when their evidence was recorded. The Court also noted that the testimony of the court witnesses was largely hearsay or lacked specific identification of the appellants. Emphasizing the fundamental requirement for the prosecution to establish the identity of the accused, the Court concluded that there was no evidence against the present appellants. Consequently, the impugned judgments were quashed, and the appellants were acquitted of all charges.

petitioner_key_arguments: The identity of the appellants as the accused was not established by prosecution witnesses (PW-1 and PW-3) in court.
Appellants were not present in court when PW-1 and PW-3 recorded their evidence, preventing in-court identification.
Evidence from Court Witnesses (CW-1, CW-2, CW-3) was either hearsay or lacked specific identification of the appellants.
respondent_key_arguments: The prosecution relied on the depositions of alleged eyewitnesses PW-1 and PW-3.
The prosecution also relied on the depositions of Court Witnesses no.1 to 4 to establish the case against the appellants.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that the prosecution failed to establish the identity of the appellants as the perpetrators of the crime, as the key witnesses did not identify them in court.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned judgments against the appellants were quashed and set aside. The appellants were acquitted of the alleged offences, and their bail bonds were cancelled.

acts_cited: Indian Penal Code, 1860, Section 304 Part II

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that the prosecution bears the fundamental duty to establish the identity of the accused as the person who committed the offence. Failure of key eyewitnesses to identify the accused in court, especially when the accused were not present during testimony, constitutes a fatal flaw in the prosecution's case, leading to acquittal.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 116 OF 2011

case_details.subject_matter: Appeal against conviction and sentence under Section 302 IPC, later converted to Section 304 Part I IPC, involving the assault and death of Suraj.

judgements.case_summary:
The present appeal challenges a 30.11.2009 High Court judgment that upheld the conviction and sentence of two appellants (Goverdhan and Rajendra) under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), while acquitting a third accused, Chintaram. The prosecution's case was based on an incident on 23.09.2001 where the deceased, Suraj, was assaulted with an axe and iron pipe, leading to his death on 25.09.2001. The initial FIR was lodged by Santosh (PW-6), who later turned hostile. The primary eyewitness was Lata Bai (PW-10), the mother of the deceased.

The appellants argued for acquittal based on parity with the acquitted third accused, uncorroborated and unreliable testimony of the sole eyewitness (PW-10) due to delay in recording her statement and inconsistencies, and hostile non-official witnesses. The prosecution contended that the conviction was based on admissible evidence and lacked perversity.

The Supreme Court, after cautious review, found that the FIR was duly proved and the eyewitness testimony of PW-10, despite minor discrepancies and delay in recording, was credible and corroborated by medical evidence and the circumstances. The court noted the unreliability of hostile witnesses who appeared to be influenced. While upholding the conviction of the two appellants, the Court observed that the death was not instantaneous, the motive was not clearly established, and the injuries, though grievous, were not individually fatal but cumulative. Therefore, the conviction was converted from Section 302 IPC to Part I of Section 304 IPC. The appellants were sentenced to the period already undergone (10 years 3 months) and a fine of Rs. 50,000/- each, with additional simple imprisonment for non-payment.

petitioner_key_arguments: Acquittal of the third accused (Chintaram) on the same evidence should lead to acquittal of the appellants on grounds of parity.
Conviction cannot be sustained on uncorroborated testimony of a sole, interested eyewitness (Lata Bai, PW-10).
Lata Bai (PW-10) could not have been an eyewitness as the FIR stated Santosh informed the parents.
Delay of 5 days in recording Lata Bai's (PW-10) statement under Section 161 CrPC makes her testimony unreliable.
Lata Bai (PW-10) and the father (PW-5) did not intervene, making their eyewitness claims doubtful.
Improvements and embellishments in Lata Bai's (PW-10) testimony render it unreliable.
Almost all non-official prosecution witnesses, including the informant (Santosh, PW-6) and seizure witnesses, turned hostile.
respondent_key_arguments: The conclusion drawn by the Trial Court and High Court is based on admissible and relevant evidence.
The conviction does not suffer from any illegality or perversity.
The testimony of Lata Bai (PW-10) should be believed despite delayed recording, as her name was in the FIR and there were corroborating evidences.
Delay in examination of witnesses is not fatal if plausible explanations are offered.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the prosecution's arguments regarding the credibility of the eyewitness (PW-10) and the corroborative value of the FIR and medical evidence, leading to the upholding of conviction. However, the court partially accepted the petitioner's implicit argument regarding the intent and nature of the crime by converting the conviction from Section 302 to Section 304 Part I IPC and reducing the sentence.

outcome.relief_granted: Conviction converted from Section 302 IPC to Part I of Section 304 IPC. Appellants sentenced to the period already undergone (10 years 3 months) and a fine of Rs. 50,000/- each to be paid to the deceased's mother (Lata Bai, PW-10). In case of non-payment, additional 6 months simple imprisonment. Bail bonds to stand discharged upon payment of fine or completion of default sentence.

However, considering the non-instantaneous death, lack of clear motive, and the cumulative nature of injuries rather than a single fatal one, the court concluded that the act amounted to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The judgment extensively discusses the principles of proof beyond reasonable doubt, the treatment of minor discrepancies versus material contradictions in witness testimonies, the approach to hostile witnesses, and the distinction between "interested" and "related" witnesses. case_identification.case_number: 2025 INSC 195, CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS. OF 2025 (@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRL.) NOS. 6954-6955 of 2023), CIVIL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (C) NO. 1555 of 2024)
case_identification.case_type: Criminal Appeal, Civil Appeal, Special Leave Petition

case_details.subject_matter: Matrimonial dispute involving divorce on grounds of irretrievable breakdown, maintenance, and related appeals concerning the validity of marriage and grounds for divorce.

judgements.case_summary:
This case involves a long-standing matrimonial dispute between Gudivada Seshagiri Rao (husband/appellant) and Gudiavada Ashalatha (wife/respondent). Married in 1999, the couple separated after just four months, leading to extensive litigation over divorce and maintenance. The husband sought divorce on grounds of desertion and cruelty and challenged maintenance awarded to the wife. The wife sought enhanced maintenance. The High Court had previously remanded the divorce petition, citing errors in the trial court's assessment of divorce grounds and the nature of the marriage (Hindu vs. Christian rites).

The Supreme Court, observing the marriage as "unworkable, emotionally dead and beyond salvation" and recognizing the parties' advanced age and prolonged acrimony, exercised its powers under Article 142 of the Constitution. Citing the precedent of Shilpa Sailesh Vs. Varun Sreenivasan, the Court granted divorce on the grounds of irretrievable breakdown of marriage. To ensure complete justice, particularly for the wife who is a post-graduate but unemployed and unable to establish a career at her age, the Court directed the husband to pay Rs. 25,00,000 as alimony, in addition to Rs. 2,00,000 already deposited. The Court ordered that all pending criminal and civil proceedings related to the marriage be closed upon proof of this payment. The appeals were disposed of with these directions, and the case will be monitored for compliance.

petitioner_key_arguments: Sought divorce on grounds of desertion and cruelty.
Challenged the grant of maintenance of Rs. 10,000/- to the wife.
respondent_key_arguments: Sought enhancement of maintenance to double the amount.
Opposed the husband's prayer for divorce on the ground of desertion and cruelty (implicitly, as the High Court remanded the rejection of divorce).
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the principle of irretrievable breakdown of marriage as a ground for divorce under Article 142 of the Constitution, leading to the dissolution of the marriage, while also ensuring the financial security of the respondent-wife.

outcome.relief_granted: Divorce granted on grounds of irretrievable breakdown of marriage. Husband directed to pay Rs. 25,00,000 (Rupees Twenty Five lacs only) as alimony, in addition to Rs. 2,00,000 already deposited. All pending criminal and civil proceedings related to the marriage to be closed upon payment.

acts_cited: Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, sub-section (2) to Section 13-B
precedents_cited: Shilpa Sailesh Vs. Varun Sreenivasanı
constitutional_provisions: Article 142 of the Constitution of India

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The court can grant divorce on the ground of irretrievable breakdown of marriage, even if not explicitly pleaded, by exercising powers under Article 142 of the Constitution, especially when the marriage is "totally unworkable, emotionally dead and beyond salvation," and ensuring complete justice, including adequate alimony for the financially weaker spouse.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The legislative intent behind Section 13-B(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, was to enable parties to introspect before a second motion for divorce by mutual consent. The court also observed that the powers under Article 142 should be invoked with great care and caution, ensuring 'complete justice' to both parties.

The amount of Rs. 2,00,000/- (Rupees Two lacs only) deposited before this Court shall be over and above Rs. 25,00,000. Upon further payment, a divorce shall be effective. Either spouse is entitled to produce the judgment with proof of payment before any court where criminal or civil proceedings related to the marriage are pending, for closure of such proceedings. The matters shall be placed before the Court after six months to ensure compliance.

case_identification.case_number: WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO. 1018 OF 2022

respondent_advocates: Mr. Sanjay Kapur (for State Bank of India)

case_details.subject_matter: This writ petition seeks a writ of mandamus directing respondents to provide facilities like a scribe and compensatory time to the petitioner and other persons with disabilities for upcoming examinations, challenging the restriction of such facilities to only persons with benchmark disabilities.

judgements.case_summary: Gulshan Kumar, diagnosed with Focal Hand Dystonia (25% permanent disability), filed a Public Interest Litigation seeking facilities like a scribe and compensatory time for examinations. He argued that these were denied to him and other Persons with Disabilities (PwD) because such facilities were restricted only to Persons with Benchmark Disabilities (PwBD), contrary to the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (RPwD Act). The petitioner contended that the application forms lacked provisions for PwD candidates and that the Office Memorandum (OM) dated 10.08.2022 was defective, granting selective facilities and lacking a grievance redressal mechanism. The respondents, particularly IBPS, initially argued they were not a 'State' under Article 12, while SBI and Bihar Staff Selection Commission stated they complied with court orders or provided benefits to PwBD candidates. The Supreme Court emphasized the principle of 'reasonable accommodation' as central to ensuring equality for all PwD, not just PwBD. It reiterated that denying scribe or compensatory time constitutes discrimination under the RPwD Act, 2016, and clarified that fundamental rights are enforceable against private entities. The Court allowed the petition, directing Respondent No.5 to revisit and re-notify the OM dated 10.08.2022 within two months, removing restrictions and extending relaxations to all PwD candidates. Specific directions were issued for uniform implementation, sensitization, grievance redressal, extended scribe certificate validity, incentives for scribes, pre-exam interaction with scribes, diverse examination modes, and penal action for non-compliant officials.

petitioner_key_arguments: Petitioner is a PwD as defined under Section 2(s) of the RPwD Act, 2016.
Application forms lacked provisions for PwD candidates to seek scribe, compensatory time, etc., restricting these facilities to PwBD candidates.

Restriction of facilities to PwBD candidates is discriminatory and contrary to judgments in Vikas Kumar v. Union Public Service Commission and Others and Avni Prakash v. National Testing Agency (NTA) & Others.

The Office Memorandum dated 10.08.2022 is defective as it grants selective facilities, does not provide for other examination modes (Braille, large print, audio recording), and lacks a grievance redressal mechanism.
respondent_key_arguments: Respondent No.1 (IBPS) is not a 'State' under Article 12 of the Constitution of India and is a Public Trust/Society, hence not amenable to writ jurisdiction.

Respondent No.1 has been acting in accordance with judgments in Vikas Kumar and Avni Prakash, and the Office Memorandum dated 10.08.2022, and will incorporate scribe/compensatory time options in future application forms.
Respondent No.2 (SBI) complied with the court's order dated 15.12.2022, providing the petitioner with a scribe and compensatory time.

Respondent No.4 (Bihar Staff Selection Commission) provides scribe and extra time facilities to PwBD candidates (40% or more disability) as per approved procedure, and the petitioner did not approach them for a scribe.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the principle of 'reasonable accommodation' under the RPwD Act, 2016, mandates facilities like scribes and compensatory time for all Persons with Disabilities, not just those with benchmark disabilities. It also affirmed that fundamental rights can be enforced against private entities in this context, and that the existing Office Memorandum needed revision to remove discriminatory restrictions and ensure comprehensive accessibility.

outcome.relief_granted: The writ petition was disposed of with directions to Respondent No.5 to revisit and re-notify the Office Memorandum dated 10.08.2022 within two months, removing restrictions and granting relaxations to all PwD candidates. Specific directions were issued for uniform implementation, sensitization, grievance redressal, extended scribe certificate validity, incentives for scribes, pre-exam interaction, diverse examination modes, and penal action for non-compliance.
