Fundamental rights under Articles 19 and 21 are enforceable even against private entities in this context.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed the urgent need for a uniform memorandum for examinations applicable to all PwD candidates, the importance of periodic sensitization drives at educational institutions, and the necessity of a robust grievance redressal mechanism to address instances where relaxations are denied to PwD candidates.

special_directions.special_directions: The Court directed Respondent No.5 to revisit and re-notify the Office Memorandum dated 10.08.2022 within two months, incorporating the following: uniform adherence to guidelines by all authorities, periodic sensitization drives, establishment of a grievance redressal portal, inspection and re-notification of existing guidelines, extension of scribe certificate validity, incentive programs for scribes, provision for pre-examination interaction with scribes, offering choice of examination modes (scribe, Braille, large print, audio recording), penal action against non-compliant officials, sensitization and training of respondent authorities' staff, and strict compliance with judgments and the RPwD Act, 2016 focusing on reasonable accommodation.
special_directions.interim_orders: On 15.12.2022, the court clarified that Respondent No.2 should not insist on a benchmark disability for the facility of a scribe, having regard to the judgment in Vikas Kumar v. Union Public Service Commission and Others.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S). OF 2025 (Diary No. 36334 of 2024)

respondent_advocates: learned counsel appearing for the respondent-State

case_details.subject_matter: Appeal against conviction and sentence for sexual assault on a minor, involving the interpretation of sentencing provisions under the Indian Penal Code and the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, and the High Court's power to enhance sentence.

judgements.case_summary:
This appeal was preferred by Gyanendra Singh @ Raja Singh, challenging the judgment of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad which dismissed his Jail Appeal and affirmed his conviction and sentence. The appellant was convicted for offences under Sections 376(2)(f) and 376(2)(i) of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and Sections 3/4 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, for sexually assaulting his minor daughter. The trial court had awarded life imprisonment and a fine. The High Court, while affirming the conviction, clarified that the life imprisonment would mean for the remainder of the appellant's natural life, which the appellant contended was an enhancement of sentence without due process.

The petitioner's counsel argued that the conviction under both IPC and POCSO Act was erroneous as the special law (POCSO Act) should prevail, and that the High Court erred in enhancing the rigor of the sentence. The respondent-State argued that the High Court was justified given the heinous nature of the crime. The Supreme Court upheld the conviction under both IPC and POCSO Act, clarifying that Section 42 of the POCSO Act mandates applying the law with the greater punishment. However, the Court found that the High Court erred in directing that life imprisonment would mean for the remainder of the natural life, as this amounted to an enhancement without an appeal for it. The Court restored the trial court's sentence of life imprisonment for POCSO Act offences and for IPC offences, but without the stipulation of 'remainder of natural life', along with a fine of Rs. 5,00,000/-. The appeal was partially allowed.

petitioner_key_arguments: The trial Court ought not to have convicted the appellant for the offences punishable under Sections 376(2)(f) and 376(2)(i) IPC because the acts alleged are defined as offences in both categories of laws (IPC and POCSO Act), and the special law (POCSO Act) should prevail over the general law (IPC).
Conviction of the appellant could not have been recorded by the trial Court for both offences, and should have been only under the POCSO Act.

Section 42A of the POCSO Act provides that where there is an inconsistency between the provisions of the POCSO Act and any other law, the provisions of the special law would have an overriding effect.

The High Court, in an appeal against conviction, ought not to have enhanced the rigor of the punishment (by directing life imprisonment for the remainder of natural life) without there being an appeal for enhancement of sentence.
respondent_key_arguments: The appellant has been convicted for a reprehensible act and the heinous offence of subjecting his own minor daughter to forcible sexual assault.
The High Court was fully justified in awarding the enhanced punishment to the appellant under Sections 376(2)(f) and 376(2)(i) of IPC.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that the High Court erred in enhancing the rigor of the sentence by stipulating that life imprisonment would mean for the remainder of the natural life, as this was done without an appeal for enhancement. The court rejected the petitioner's argument that the POCSO Act should exclusively prevail over the IPC for conviction, affirming that Section 42 of POCSO Act allows for the application of the law providing a greater degree of punishment.

outcome.relief_granted: The judgment of the trial Court is restored. The sentence of life imprisonment awarded by the trial Court for the offences under Sections 3/4 of the POCSO Act shall stand revived. For the offences punishable under Sections 376(2)(f) and 376(2)(i) of IPC, the accused is sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life, without the stipulation that the life term will enure till the natural life of the appellant, and a fine of Rs. 5,00,000/-. In default of fine, two years additional imprisonment. Both sentences shall run concurrently. The fine, upon being deposited, shall be paid to the victim.

acts_cited: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, Sections 3
Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, Sections 4
Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, Sections 5
Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, Section 42A
Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012, Section 42
precedents_cited: Shiva Kumar @ Shiva @ Shivamurthy v. State of Karnataka
Navas @ Mulanavas v. State of Kerala
Swamy Shraddhananda v. State of Karnataka, (2008) 13 SCC 767
Union of India v. V. Sriharan alias Murugan, (2016) 7 SCC 1
Veerendra v. State of Madhya Pradesh

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that when an act constitutes an offence under both the POCSO Act and the IPC, Section 42 of the POCSO Act mandates that the offender shall be liable to punishment under the Act or law that provides for punishment which is greater in degree. Section 42A of the POCSO Act, dealing with procedural aspects and overriding effect in case of inconsistency, does not override the substantive provision of Section 42. Furthermore, while life imprisonment is a possible sentence under IPC Section 376(2), the High Court erred in unilaterally enhancing the rigor of the sentence to mean 'for the remainder of natural life' without an appeal for enhancement, as the courts retain discretion in fixing the term of life imprisonment.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that there is no mandate of law that under Sections 376(2)(f) and 376(2)(i) of IPC, the convict must be awarded life imprisonment for the remainder of that person's natural life. It also reiterated the principle from previous judgments that Constitutional Courts can exercise the power of imposing a modified or fixed-term sentence for life imprisonment, beyond 14 years, to ensure proportionality.

special_directions.special_directions: The fine of Rs. 5,00,000/- imposed on the appellant, upon being deposited, shall be paid to the victim.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NOS. 1180-1181 OF 2025 (arising out of S.L.P. (Civil) Nos. 5785-5786 of 2023) WITH CIVIL APPEAL NOS. 1182-1183 OF 2025 (arising out of S.L.P. (Civil) Nos. 6724-6725 of 2023)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the High Court's decision to condone a significant delay and grant leave to appeal to subsequent purchasers (transferees pendente lite) in a specific performance suit, which the Supreme Court found erroneous.

judgements.case_summary: The appeals challenge a High Court order that condoned a 586-day delay and granted leave to appeal to subsequent purchasers (Respondent Nos. 1 & 2) in a specific performance suit. The original suit (O.S. No. 458/2006) was for specific performance of an agreement to sell land, where the Defendant No.1 had agreed to sell land to the plaintiffs (appellants). During the pendency of the suit and despite an injunction, Defendant No.3 (who had purchased from Defendant No.1) sold portions of the land to Respondent Nos. 1 & 2. An earlier application by Respondent Nos. 1 & 2 to be impleaded in the suit was rejected and attained finality. After the Trial Court decreed specific performance, and Defendant No.3's appeal was dismissed, Respondent Nos. 1 & 2 filed an appeal before the High Court with a significant delay, which the High Court condoned, and granted them leave to appeal. The petitioners argued that the delay was inexcusable, the respondents were not bona fide purchasers, and their earlier impleadment rejection was final. The respondents contended they had a substantial interest, alleged collusion between the vendor and plaintiffs, and cited their status as senior citizens. The Supreme Court found that the High Court committed an egregious error in condoning the delay without sufficient cause. While acknowledging that non-parties prejudicially affected by a judgment can seek leave to appeal, the Court concluded that Respondent Nos. 1 & 2, having purchased pendente lite and despite an injunction, did not make a good case for such leave. The appeals were allowed, and the High Court's order was set aside.

petitioner_key_arguments: The High Court committed a serious error in condoning the unexplained and inordinate delay of 586 days in preferring the regular first appeal.
The Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 were not vigilant of their rights and do not deserve indulgence, especially as they purchased the property pendente lite and in contravention of a temporary injunction.
The earlier rejection of the impleadment application by Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 attained finality, precluding them from seeking leave to appeal.
Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 cannot be said to be bona fide purchasers of the suit property for value without notice.
respondent_key_arguments: Respondent Nos. 1 and 2, as subsequent purchasers, have a substantial interest in the suit property and its final outcome.
There was collusion between the vendor (Defendant No. 3) and the plaintiffs, and Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act does not apply to collusive proceedings.
The High Court was justified in granting permission to prefer an appeal to defend their rights, especially since their vendor colluded with the plaintiffs.
A subsequent purchaser should ordinarily be allowed to implead himself in pending proceedings to protect his interests.
The condonation of delay is justified under Section 17 of the Limitation Act, 1963 read with Section 5.
Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 are senior citizens residing in Scotland and were assured by Defendant No. 3 that he would protect their interest.
Lis pendens purchasers, though not arrayed as parties, can claim under Section 146 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments that the High Court erred in condoning the significant delay without sufficient cause and that the respondents, as transferees pendente lite who purchased despite an injunction and whose impleadment was previously rejected, did not make a good case for leave to appeal, were accepted by the Supreme Court.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned order passed by the High Court, which condoned the delay and granted leave to appeal, is set aside. Respondent Nos. 1 & 2 are granted liberty to avail appropriate legal remedy against Respondent No. 7/Defendant No. 3 for recovery of the amount towards sale consideration.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The High Court committed an egregious error in condoning a significant delay of 586 days in filing a regular first appeal on mere asking, as the assigned cause was insufficient. While a person prejudicially affected by a judgment, though not a party, can seek leave to appeal, the transferees pendente lite in this case, who purchased property despite an injunction and whose impleadment application was previously rejected, did not establish a good case for such leave.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court discussed the principles governing the grant of leave to appeal to non-parties, emphasizing that such leave should be granted to persons who would be bound by the decree and precluded from attacking its correctness. It also reiterated that a transfer pendente lite is not void ab initio but remains subservient to the pending litigation, and transferees pendente lite can seek to be brought on record under Order XXII Rule 10 CPC or Section 146 CPC, though not as a matter of right.

special_directions.special_directions: If Respondent Nos. 1 & 2 feel that they have been duped or cheated by Respondent No. 7/Defendant No. 3, they are at liberty to avail appropriate legal remedy before the appropriate forum for recovery of the amount towards sale consideration paid at the time of execution of the sale deed.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 317 OF 2025 (@Petition for Special Leave to Appeal (C) No.9719/2020)

case_details.subject_matter: This case concerns an appeal against a High Court order that condoned a significant delay in filing an application for recall, thereby reviving a very old civil suit, and the application of limitation laws.

judgements.case_summary:
This appeal challenges a High Court of Karnataka order dated 30.01.2020, which set aside a Trial Court's dismissal of a recall application and condoned a significant delay of approximately 2200 days. The original suit (O.S. No. 1833/1980), filed in 1977, had a complex history: it was dismissed for default in 1983, restored in 1984, and subsequently abated in 2000 due to the respondents' failure to bring legal heirs on record despite multiple opportunities. The respondents then filed a recall application in 2006, six years after the abatement, which the Trial Court dismissed in 2014, citing inordinate delay, lack of sufficient cause, and res judicata. The High Court, however, allowed the writ petition, condoning the delay.

The petitioners (appellants) argued that the High Court erred by overlooking the Trial Court's detailed reasons, reviving a 48-year-old suit, and ignoring the respondents' repeated negligence and the 6-year delay in filing the recall application itself. The respondents contended that the High Court's decision aimed at substantial justice.

The Supreme Court critically reviewed the case, highlighting the suit's protracted history, the respondents' repeated failures, and the substantial delay. It emphasized that concepts like "liberal approach" or "substantial justice" cannot override the law of limitation, which serves public policy by ensuring prompt remedies and preventing indefinite litigation. The Court found the High Court's approach to be a "complete absence of judicial conscience and restraints."

Consequently, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's order and restoring the Trial Court's order dated 05.08.2014, effectively dismissing the recall application. The decision underscores the importance of adhering to limitation periods and the need for litigants to act diligently.

petitioner_key_arguments: The High Court erred in condoning a delay of about 2200 days without considering the reasons assigned by the Trial Court.
The High Court proceeded to revive a suit that was instituted 48 years ago and is still at the stage of leading evidence.
There was a delay of six years in filing the application for recall itself.
This is the second instance that the suit came to be dismissed due to negligence and callous attitude on the part of the respondents.
respondent_key_arguments: No error was committed by the High Court in passing the impugned order.
The High Court condoned the delay with a view to do substantial justice between the parties.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments, emphasizing the long delay, the respondent's negligence, and the misapplication of "substantial justice" to override limitation laws. The court found that the High Court erred by condoning an inordinate delay without sufficient cause and by overlooking the principles of limitation.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned order passed by the High Court is set aside and that of the Trial Court dated 05.08.2014 passed in Misc. No. 223 of 2006 is hereby restored.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The High Court erred by condoning an inordinate delay of 2200 days (and an initial 6-year delay) in filing a recall application, thereby reviving a 48-year-old suit, without sufficient cause. The principles of "liberal approach" or "substantial justice" cannot be used to jettison the substantial law of limitation, which is based on sound public policy and equity, and prevents indefinite litigation. The court must ascertain the bona fides of the explanation for delay, and the merits of the main matter should not be considered when deciding on condonation of delay unless the explanation is equally balanced.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed that the High Court exhibited a "complete absence of judicial conscience and restraints" and that rules of limitation are not meant to destroy rights but to ensure prompt remedy and prevent dilatory tactics. It also noted that the question of limitation is not merely a technical consideration.

case_identification.case_number: MISCELLANEOUS APPLICATION NO. 2667 OF 2024 IN SLP(CRL.) NO. 895 OF 2024

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns a Miscellaneous Application seeking to compound an offense under Section 326 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, based on a compromise reached between the parties, after the dismissal of a Special Leave Petition.

judgements.case_summary:
The applicant, H.N. Pandakumar (Accused No. 3), filed a Miscellaneous Application seeking to compound an offense under Section 326 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. This application was filed after his Special Leave Petition (Criminal) No. 895/2024, challenging his conviction, was dismissed by the Supreme Court on 19.01.2024. The original complaint, FIR No. 198/2008, was lodged by Puttaraju, alleging assault and grievous injuries. The Trial Court convicted Accused Nos. 3 and 4 under Section 326 read with Section 34 IPC, sentencing them to two years rigorous imprisonment. The High Court reduced the sentence to one year and enhanced the fine.
The applicant and the complainant reached an amicable settlement, with the applicant agreeing to pay Rs. 5,80,000/- as compensation. The complainant filed an Interlocutory Application supporting the compounding, emphasizing the need for peace due to their close proximity and distant relation, and the settlement also covered related property disputes.
Despite Section 326 IPC being a non-compoundable offense, the Court, exercising its inherent powers, allowed the Miscellaneous Application due to the exceptional circumstances, including the voluntary settlement and the complainant's unequivocal consent. The order dismissing the SLP in limine was recalled, the conviction was confirmed, but the sentence of one year rigorous imprisonment was reduced to the period already undergone.

petitioner_key_arguments: A compromise has been reached between the parties.
The applicant has agreed to pay Rs. 5,80,000/- as compensation.
The complainant has filed an Interlocutory Application supporting the compromise and seeking closure.
The parties reside in close proximity and are distantly related, necessitating a peaceful relationship.
The compromise covers not only the criminal case but also related property disputes.
The settlement reflects a genuine effort to end discord and uphold the terms of the settlement.
Exceptional circumstances warrant the exercise of the Court's inherent powers to give effect to the compromise, even for a non-compoundable offense.
respondent_key_arguments: The complainant (part of the respondent side) supported the compromise and sought closure, effectively aligning with the petitioner's request for compounding.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court accepted the petitioner's arguments regarding the amicable settlement, the complainant's unequivocal consent, and the exceptional circumstances justifying the exercise of inherent powers to allow compounding and reduce the sentence.

outcome.relief_granted: The Miscellaneous Application is allowed. The order dated 19.01.2024 dismissing the SLP in limine is recalled. The conviction recorded by the courts below is confirmed, but the sentence of one year rigorous imprisonment is reduced to the period already undergone.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The Supreme Court, in exceptional circumstances, can exercise its inherent powers to allow the compounding of a non-compoundable offense (like Section 326 IPC) when there is a voluntary and amicable settlement between the parties, supported by the complainant, to ensure peace and harmony, especially when the parties are closely related or reside in close proximity.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court noted that the parties reside in close proximity with only a road separating their houses, are distantly related, and any lingering hostility could disturb the social fabric. The compromise also covered related property disputes, including the right of way, which had been a point of contention for years.

special_directions.special_directions: The I.A. for impleadment stands disposed of. All pending applications, if any, are also disposed of.

case_identification.case_number: MISC. APPLICATION NO. OF 2025 [@ DIARY NO. 38122 OF 2024] in CONTEMPT PETITION (C) NO. 110 OF 2019 in CIVIL APPEAL NO. 2703 OF 2017

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns a miscellaneous application seeking directions for the release of arrears of salary, pension, and other benefits for a petitioner whose absorption was previously ordered, following alleged non-compliance with a contempt petition order.

judgements.case_summary: The petitioner, Haldhar Prasad Gupta, filed a miscellaneous application seeking directions for the release of arrears of salary, pension, and other benefits. His absorption as Lab In-charge was allowed by the J. Sinha Commission and confirmed by the Supreme Court in 2017, and he superannuated in 2016. Previously, a Contempt Petition (C) No. 110 of 2019 was filed for non-compliance, which was disposed of on 27.02.2019 with a direction to pay remaining arrears after verification. The current application arises from continued non-compliance. The core issues are the payment of salary arrears, requiring verification of absence periods and actual working days, and the stoppage of pension. The Court noted that the petitioner's absorption was notified in 2018. It clarified that previous orders in the 'Baidya Nath Choudhary' case, which put pension on hold for employees who received salaries without actually working, were not intended to stop pension payments entirely but addressed payments for non-working periods. The Court declined to conduct a fact-finding inquiry itself. Instead, it directed the Registrar/Vice Chancellor of the University to adjudicate all issues. The petitioner is to submit claims with relevant documents for salary and pension. A discrete inquiry must be held for salary claims, with a reasoned order issued within three months. The pension claim is to be decided by counting service from the absorption date, uninfluenced by the 'Baidya Nath Choudhary' orders. Adjudicated amounts are to be paid within two months, with provisions for recovering any excess payments. Parties dissatisfied with the University's orders may approach the High Court. The miscellaneous application was disposed of with these directions.

petitioner_key_arguments: The petitioner sought directions against contemnors to release arrears of salary, pension, and other benefits as directed by the Court's order dated 27.02.2019 in Contempt Petition (C) No. 110 of 2019, implying non-compliance with the previous order.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's need for a formal adjudication process for his claims of salary arrears and pension, directing the university authorities to conduct a detailed inquiry and pass reasoned orders.

outcome.relief_granted: The Court directed the Registrar/Vice Chancellor of the University to adjudicate the petitioner's claims for arrears of salary and pension through a discrete inquiry within specified timelines. It also provided for payment of adjudicated amounts, adjustment of already paid sums, recovery of excess payments, and recourse to the High Court for dissatisfied parties.

precedents_cited: Krishna Nand Yadav & others Vs. Magadh University & others
Baidya Nath Choudhary Vs. Dr. Sree Surendra Kumar Singh
State of Bihar & others vs Bihar Rajya M.S.E.S.K.K.M & others (2005) 9 SCC 129

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that complex factual issues concerning the calculation of salary arrears (requiring verification of actual working days) and pension entitlements (requiring service period calculation) are best adjudicated by the concerned administrative authorities through a detailed inquiry, rather than by the Supreme Court in a miscellaneous application. This ensures due process, fact-finding, and a reasoned decision at the appropriate level.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that previous orders in the 'Baidya Nath Choudhary' case, which dealt with payment of salaries for periods not actually worked, should not influence the decision on the petitioner's pension claim, implying that the stoppage of pension was not the direct intent of those orders.

special_directions.special_directions:
1. The petitioner shall submit his claim along with relevant documents to the Registrar/Vice Chancellor of the University for salary and pension (from absorption date up to 28.02.2025).
2. A discrete inquiry shall be held for salary claims, affording due opportunity, and a reasoned order passed within three months.
3. The pension claim shall be decided by counting service from the date of absorption, uninfluenced by orders dated 11.07.2019, 07.08.2019 and 12.02.2021 in Contempt Petition (C) No. 1188 of 2018 in Baidya Nath Choudhary.
4. After adjudication, pension and arrears shall be paid within two months, adjusting any amounts already paid.
5. Any excess amount paid (salary or pension) shall be quantified and recovered by the university/college/state.
6. If joint claims are submitted, salary will be governed by direction (ii) and pension by direction (iii).
7. Parties dissatisfied with the Registrar/Vice Chancellor's orders may approach the High Court.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 1387 OF 2012

case_details.subject_matter: Appeal against conviction for murder under Section 302 IPC, where the prosecution's case was based solely on circumstantial evidence.

judgements.case_summary: The appellant, Hansraj, was convicted under Section 302 IPC for the murder of Ramlal and sentenced to life imprisonment, a decision upheld by the High Court. The Supreme Court heard the appeal, noting a delay in filing the Special Leave Petition, and had previously directed the appellant's release on bail. The prosecution's case relied entirely on circumstantial evidence, with no eyewitnesses. The appellant's counsel argued that the case was false, the circumstances were not conclusively proven, and there were significant contradictions in the prosecution witnesses' testimonies. The prosecution asserted that the appellant was last seen with the deceased, the weapon (farsi) was recovered at his instance, and the injuries were consistent with the weapon. The Court meticulously applied the 'five golden principles' for cases based on circumstantial evidence, which require the circumstances to be fully established, consistent with guilt, conclusive, exclude all other hypotheses, and form a complete chain of evidence. The Court found the alleged motive trivial, the 'last seen' theory doubtful due to lack of independent corroboration, the recovery of the weapon questionable, and the evidence of the appellant fleeing contradictory and lacking conclusive identification. Crucially, no forensic reports were produced to match bloodstains on the weapon or the appellant's clothes to the deceased. Concluding that the prosecution failed to establish the appellant's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, the Court granted the benefit of doubt.

petitioner_key_arguments: The case is completely false.
The circumstances have not been proved conclusively to hold the appellant guilty.
There are stark contradictions in the testimonies of the prosecution witnesses.
respondent_key_arguments: The appellant was the person last seen in the company of the deceased.
The weapon of recovery (farsi) was recovered at the appellant's pointing out.
The injuries sustained by the deceased were opined to have been caused by the recovered weapon.
The evidence on record proves beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant alone committed the offence.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that the circumstantial evidence presented by the prosecution was not conclusive, contained contradictions, and failed to establish guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, thus not meeting the 'five golden principles' for such cases.

outcome.relief_granted: The appellant is acquitted from the offence charged with. His sureties and bail bonds are discharged.

precedents_cited: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda vs State of Maharashtra2

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: In cases based solely on circumstantial evidence, the prosecution must establish a complete and unbroken chain of events that conclusively points to the guilt of the accused and excludes every other possible hypothesis of innocence. If the circumstances are not fully established, are inconsistent, or leave room for reasonable doubt, the benefit of doubt must be given to the accused.

special_directions.special_directions: The appellant's sureties and bail bonds are discharged.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 2204 OF 2025 (Arising out of SLP(C)No.5541/2023)

case_details.subject_matter: The case is an appeal seeking enhancement of compensation under the Motor Vehicle Act, 1988, for injuries sustained in a road accident.

judgements.case_summary: The case involves an appeal for enhanced compensation under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, following a road accident on December 6, 2016. The Claimant-Appellant, a 51-year-old Primary School Teacher, suffered serious injuries when his motorcycle was hit by an offending vehicle. The Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT) initially awarded Rs. 6,17,515, considering 10% permanent disability. The High Court subsequently enhanced this by an additional consolidated sum of Rs. 60,000. Dissatisfied with the awarded amount, the Claimant-Appellant appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that the Tribunal had incorrectly assessed the injury and that his permanent disability was 40%. The Supreme Court, reiterating the principle of ensuring "just compensation" even if it exceeds the claimed amount, re-evaluated the compensation. Based on a detailed calculation of various heads including income, future prospects, permanent disability, medical expenses, attendant charges, special diet & transportation, pain and suffering, and loss of income during treatment, the Court modified the total compensation to Rs. 17,82,825, with interest as originally awarded by the Tribunal. The appeal was allowed.

petitioner_key_arguments: The Tribunal had incorrectly appreciated the nature of the injury.
Claimed permanent disability to the extent of 40%.
Sought enhancement of compensation.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that the compensation awarded by the lower courts was insufficient and required enhancement based on a comprehensive re-evaluation of all compensation heads, aligning with the principle of "just compensation" under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988.

outcome.relief_granted: The Civil Appeal is allowed, and the compensation is enhanced to Rs. 17,82,825/-. Interest is to be paid as awarded by the Tribunal.

precedents_cited: Meena Devi v. Nunu Chand Mahto1, (2023) 1 SCC 204
Pranay Sethi (2017) 16 SCC 680 Para 42 & 59
Kajal v. Jagdish Chand (2020) 4 SCC 413 Para 19 and 25
Sidram v. Divisional Manager, United India Insurance Ltd. (2023) 3 SCC 439 Para 89
K.S. Muralidhar v. R. Subbulakshmi and Anr. 2024 SCC Online SC 3385 Para 13 and 14
Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar (2011) 1 SCC 343 Para 6

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core reasoning is that the objective of granting compensation under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, is to ensure "just and fair compensation" to the aggrieved party. This principle dictates that the Tribunal/Court ought to award just compensation based on the evidence, and a lower valuation in the claim petition should not impede awarding a higher, just compensation. The court re-calculated the compensation based on established legal principles and precedents for various heads of damages.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The observation that "less valuation, if any, made in the claim petition would not be impediment to award just compensation exceeding the claimed amount."

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL No. Of 2025 (Arising out of SLP (Crl.) No.452 of 2024)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the quashing of criminal proceedings against the appellant for alleged offences under Sections 353, 298, and 504 of the Indian Penal Code, arising from an incident during the delivery of official information.

judgements.case_summary:
The case involves an appeal against an order of the High Court which sustained criminal proceedings against the appellant, Hari Nandan Singh. An FIR (Bokaro Sector-IV P.S. Case No. 140 of 2020) was registered against Singh for allegedly abusing a public servant (informant) who was delivering information, using religiously offensive terms ("Miyan-Tiyan" and "Pakistani"), and manipulating documents. The charges included offences under IPC Sections 298, 504, 506, 353, and 323. The Magistrate took cognizance and framed charges under Sections 353, 298, and 504, dismissing the application for discharge. Subsequent revision and High Court petitions by the appellant were dismissed.

The appellant argued that the essential ingredients for Sections 353 (assault/criminal force), 298 (wounding religious feelings), and 504 (intentional insult to provoke breach of peace) were not met. He contended there was no assault, and while his words were in "poor taste," they did not constitute hurting religious sentiments or provoking a breach of peace. The respondent maintained that the offences were rightly alleged.

Applying principles from Sajjan Kumar v. CBI, the Supreme Court analyzed the FIR's contents. It found no evidence of assault or criminal force for Section 353. For Section 298, it ruled that the appellant's statements, though inappropriate, did not amount to wounding religious feelings. Similarly, for Section 504, no act was found that could have provoked a breach of peace. Consequently, the Court concluded that the essential ingredients for these offences were not made out. The High Court's order was set aside, and the appellant was discharged from all charges under Sections 353, 298, and 504 IPC, allowing his appeal.

petitioner_key_arguments: The ingredients of Sections 353, 298, and 504 of the IPC are not made out against the appellant.
There was no assault or use of force by the appellant to attract Section 353 IPC.
Calling names like "Miyan-Tiyan" and "Pakistani" does not amount to hurting religious sentiments under Section 298 IPC.
There was no act on the appellant's part that could have provoked a breach of peace, thus Section 504 IPC is not applicable.
The appellant is presently aged about 80 years and should not be forced to face criminal proceedings.
respondent_key_arguments: There is no merit in the appeal.
The offences have been rightly alleged against the appellant.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments that the essential ingredients of Sections 353, 298, and 504 of the IPC were not made out based on the facts of the case prevailed.

outcome.relief_granted: The order of the High Court sustaining the order of the Trial Court is set aside, and the application filed by the appellant is allowed. The appellant is discharged from all three offences alleged against him (Sections 353, 298, and 504 IPC).

precedents_cited: Sajjan Kumar v. CBI, (2010) 9 SCC 368

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that for charges to be framed against an accused, the essential ingredients of the alleged offences must be prima facie made out from the material on record. The Court found that the facts stated in the FIR did not disclose the necessary ingredients for Sections 353 (no assault/force), 298 (statements in poor taste but not wounding religious feelings), and 504 (no act to provoke breach of peace) of the IPC, thus warranting the discharge of the appellant.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that while the statements made by the appellant were in "poor taste," they did not amount to hurting the religious sentiments of the informant as required by Section 298 IPC.

special_directions.special_directions: Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (Arising out of SLP (C) No.21778 of 2024)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the rejection of the Appellants' claim for refund of stamp duty under the Maharashtra Stamp Act, 1958, specifically regarding the applicable limitation period for refund and the power of a quasi-judicial authority to review its own orders.

judgements.case_summary:
The Appellants, Harshit Harish Jain & Anr., sought a refund of stamp duty paid on an Agreement to Sell for a residential flat in Mumbai, which was subsequently cancelled due to the developer's inability to deliver possession. The Agreement to Sell was executed on 30.08.2014, and stamp duty of ₹27,34,500 was paid. A Deed of Cancellation was executed on 17.03.2015 but registered on 28.04.2015. An amendment to Section 48(1) of the Maharashtra Stamp Act, 1958, on 24.04.2015, curtailed the refund limitation period from two years to six months. The Appellants applied for a refund on 06.08.2016, arguing the unamended two-year period should apply as the cancellation deed was executed before the amendment. The Chief Controlling Revenue Authority (CCRA) initially allowed the refund on 08.01.2018 but later recalled its decision on 03.03.2018, deeming the claim time-barred under the amended six-month period. The High Court dismissed the Appellants' writ petition, holding that the registration date triggered the amended limitation.

The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, holding that the Appellants' right to claim a refund accrued upon the execution of the Cancellation Deed (17.03.2015), prior to the amendment. The Court emphasized that a shorter limitation period cannot retroactively extinguish a vested right of action. It also ruled that the CCRA lacked statutory power to review or recall its own orders, making its subsequent recall orders invalid. The Court directed the refund of stamp duty with 6% simple interest from 08.01.2018, with an additional 12% p.a. interest for any further delay in disbursement.

petitioner_key_arguments: The right to seek refund accrued on the date of execution of the Cancellation Deed (17.03.2015), thus invoking the unamended two-year limitation window.
The CCRA had no statutory power of review to recall its initial order granting the refund.
A mere technical delay in registration should not extinguish an otherwise valid claim, especially when the cancellation was due to the developer's fault.
The State should not rely on technicalities to deny a legitimate refund.
respondent_key_arguments: The date of registration (28.04.2015) triggered the Appellants' claim, which fell under the amended provision stipulating a six-month limitation.
The CCRA's recall of the initial order was valid, and the Appellants had submitted themselves to the review process.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the right to refund accrued on the date of execution of the cancellation deed, making the unamended two-year limitation applicable, and that the CCRA lacked statutory power to review its own orders.

outcome.relief_granted: The Appellants are entitled to the refund of stamp duty of ₹27,34,500 with simple interest at 6% per annum from 08.01.2018 till the date of payment. Any further delay will entail additional interest at 12% per annum. The subsequent orders of the CCRA recalling the refund are quashed, and the initial order allowing refund is restored.

precedents_cited: M.P. Steel Corporation v. Commissioner of Central Excise
New India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Shanti Misra [(1975) 2 SCC 840 : (1976) 2 SCR 266]
Vinod Gurudas Raikar v. National Insurance Co. Ltd. [(1991) 4 SCC 333]
Union of India v. Harnam Singh [(1993) 2 SCC 162 : 1993 SCC (L&S) 375: (1993) 24 ATC 92]
Bano Saiyed Parwaz v. Chief Controlling Revenue Authority & Inspector General of Registration & Controller of Stamps
Committee-GFIL v. Libra Buildtech Private Limited
Firm Kaluram Sitaram v. Dominion of India [1953 SCC OnLine Bom 39: AIR 1954 Bom 50]

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The Court held that a vested right to claim a refund, accrued upon the execution of a cancellation deed, cannot be retroactively curtailed by a subsequent amendment introducing a shorter limitation period. Furthermore, a quasi-judicial authority lacks inherent power to review or recall its own final orders unless explicitly conferred by statute.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that the State should not ordinarily rely on technicalities to deny a legitimate claim, especially when the applicant is not blameworthy and the underlying transaction was rescinded for bona fide reasons.

special_directions.special_directions: The Respondents are directed to process and disburse the refund of stamp duty along with accrued interest within a period of four weeks from the date of the judgment. Any further delay will entail further interest component at 12% p.a.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(s). 579-580 OF 2012, CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(s). 581-583 OF 2012, CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(s). 584 OF 2012

case_details.subject_matter: The case involves a bank fraud through fake Telegraphic Transfers and subsequent withdrawals, leading to criminal charges and a dispute over the return of seized gold bars.

judgements.case_summary:
This judgment addresses multiple criminal appeals arising from a common order of the Bombay High Court concerning a bank fraud. The fraud involved fake Telegraphic Transfers (TTs) and subsequent withdrawals totaling Rs. 6,70,00,000/- from Vijaya Bank, Nasik Branch. The account was opened using forged documents by a fictitious firm, Globe International. The investigation led to charges against bank officials (accused nos. 1 and 2) and Nandkumar Babulal Soni (accused no. 3) under various sections of the IPC and Prevention of Corruption Act. The Trial Court convicted all three, but the High Court acquitted the bank officials while upholding Nandkumar Babulal Soni's conviction for criminal conspiracy (Section 120B IPC) and receiving stolen property (Section 411 IPC). The High Court also allowed CBI's appeal to confiscate 205 seized gold bars, which the Trial Court had ordered to be returned to Nandkumar.

Nandkumar Babulal Soni appealed his conviction, arguing insufficient evidence and reliance on suspicion. Hiralal Babulal Soni and Vijaya Bank also appealed, seeking the return of the gold bars. The respondent (CBI) argued for upholding the conviction and confiscation.

The Supreme Court analyzed the Trial Court's finding that the seized gold bars were not definitively proven to be the same stolen property. The Court emphasized that for a conviction under Section 411 IPC, the prosecution must establish the identity of the stolen property beyond reasonable doubt. It held that the prosecution failed to bridge the gap between "may" and "must" regarding the identity of the gold bars. The Court also clarified that Section 106 of the Evidence Act cannot be invoked if the prosecution fails to establish the initial facts. Consequently, the Supreme Court allowed Nandkumar Babulal Soni's appeals, setting aside his conviction and sentence, and directed the return of the 205 gold bars to him. The appeals by Hiralal Babulal Soni and Vijaya Bank for the return of gold bars were dismissed, as the identity of the property as stolen was not established.

petitioner_key_arguments: Appellant (Nandkumar Babulal Soni) was wrongly convicted for the offence under Section 411 of the IPC without there being any evidence against him.
Incomplete chain of circumstantial evidence was relied upon for conviction, making it legally unsustainable and based only on suspicion.
Hiralal Babulal Soni and Vijaya Bank sought return of gold bars, arguing they were entitled to possession.
respondent_key_arguments: There is independent evidence on record to link the appellant (Accused No. 3) with Mukesh Shah @ Mayur Desai and the fraudulent transactions.
The conviction of Accused No. 3 and the High Court's order regarding the custody of the gold bars should be upheld.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted Nandkumar Babulal Soni's arguments that the prosecution failed to prove the identity of the seized gold bars as stolen property beyond reasonable doubt and that the chain of circumstantial evidence was incomplete, thus his conviction could not be sustained.

outcome.judgement_type: Allowed for Nandkumar Babulal Soni's appeals, Dismissed for Hiralal Babulal Soni's and Vijaya Bank's appeals
outcome.relief_granted: Nandkumar Babulal Soni's conviction and sentence under Sections 120B and 411 of the IPC are set aside. The 205 seized gold bars (Article 2) are to be handed over to Nandkumar Babulal Soni.

precedents_cited: Kamal vs. State (NCT of Delhi)5
Trimbak vs. State of M.P'- AIR 1954 SC 39
Mohan Lal vs. State of Maharashtra”6
Shiv Kumar vs. State of M.P."7
Nagendra Sah vs. State of Bihar”8

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: For a conviction under Section 411 IPC, the prosecution must prove that the seized property is indeed the stolen property beyond reasonable doubt. If the identity of the seized property as the stolen property is not established, the conviction cannot be sustained. Furthermore, Section 106 of the Evidence Act cannot be invoked if the prosecution fails to establish the initial facts from which a reasonable inference can be drawn.

special_directions.special_directions: The 205 seized gold bars (Article 2) are to be handed over to the appellant- Nandkumar Babulal Soni.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NOS. 4560-4563 OF 2025 (Arising out of SLP (C) Nos. 11779 - 11782 of 2022)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the appropriate rate of interest to be awarded for the delayed payment of enhanced valuation of shares in a long-standing dispute involving a commercial transaction between private parties and the State Government.

judgements.case_summary:
The case involves a five-decade-long dispute concerning the valuation of shares of Bikaner Gypsums Ltd. (later Rajasthan State Mines and Mineral Ltd.) sold by I.K. Merchants Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. (appellants) to the State of Rajasthan (respondent) in 1973. The High Court initially awarded 6% simple interest on the enhanced share valuation, later correcting it to 5%. The appellants sought a higher interest rate, arguing they were deprived of fair value for over 50 years, and the transaction was commercial, warranting interest as compensation for the time value of money, citing Section 34(1) of the Civil Procedure Code. They requested 15% or 18% interest with monthly/quarterly rests.
The respondents contended that the amount was not a debt or damages, the company was mismanaged, and the acquisition was not compulsory. They argued the State infused capital to keep the company afloat, and the transaction was not commercial, thus Section 34 CPC's 6% limit should apply, and appellate courts should not interfere with the High Court's discretion.
The Supreme Court acknowledged the prolonged delay and affirmed that the transaction, involving the sale and purchase of shares, was commercial. While noting the absence of an agreement on interest, the Court applied Section 34 CPC. It discussed principles of unconscionable contracts and inequality of bargaining power. Balancing the need for fair compensation for the appellants' "loss of use" of money against the financial burden on the State, the Court rejected the appellants' request for excessively high interest rates.
The Court modified the High Court's order, awarding simple interest at 6% per annum from 08/07/1975 (date of sale) until the date of the decree, and 9% per annum from the date of the decree until the date of realization. The payment, after adjusting amounts already paid, is to be made within two months.

petitioner_key_arguments: Payment of interest for delayed remittance of fair value of shares is a recognized right.
Interest is compensation for the time value of money, for funds withheld when due.
The transaction was a "commercial transaction" as per Section 34(1) of the Civil Procedure Code, allowing for interest rates higher than 6%.
Appellants were deprived of fair value for over 50 years due to faulty valuation by the State.
The State, being a profit-making entity (Respondent No.2), is not entitled to sympathy for lower interest rates.
Previous court decisions support higher interest rates (e.g., 15%).
The High Court's reduction of interest from 6% to 5% was arbitrary and whimsical.
The respondents breached the contract and caused delays at every stage.
respondent_key_arguments: The amount was neither a debt nor for damages, which normally entails interest.
The company was mismanaged, and the State intervened to keep it afloat, not for compulsory acquisition.
Appellants initially claimed a much lower share value (Rs.70.50) and sought amendment much later (23 years).
The transaction was not a "commercial transaction" as the State was not engaged in industry, trade, or business for profit in this context.
Section 34 of CPC limits interest to 6% per annum for non-commercial transactions.
Appellate Courts should not interfere with the discretion of lower courts in awarding interest unless arbitrary or capricious.
The High Court's order of 5% interest was reasonable and should not be interfered with.
Appellants already received Rs.11.50 per share and are only entitled to the difference.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that the transaction was commercial and that a higher interest rate than awarded by the High Court was warranted due to the prolonged delay and the time value of money. However, it rejected the petitioner's request for excessively high interest rates (15-18% with rests) as unreasonable and beyond the scope of Section 34.

outcome.relief_granted: Simple interest at 6% per annum on the enhanced valuation of shares from 08/07/1975 till the date of decree, and 9% per annum from the date of decree till the date of realization. Payment to be made within two months after adjusting amounts already paid.

precedents_cited: Union of India v. Tata Chemicals Ltd3
Fertilizer Corporation of India Ltd and others v. Coromandal Sacks Private Ltd4
Bernard Francis Joseph Vaz and others v. Government of Karnataka and others (Civil Appeal No.17 of 2025 in SLP(C) No.10338 of 2023)

Photo Production Ltd. v. Securicor Transport Ltd. 1980 A.C. 827
Central Bank of India v. Ravindra & Ors.; (2002) 1 SCC 367
Clariant International Limited and another v. Securities & Exchange Board of India8
Thazhathe Thazhathe Purayil Sarabi v. Union of India9
Rampur Fertiliser Limited v. Vigyan Chemicals Industries10

Kaushnuma Begum v. New India Assurance Co. Ltd. [(2001) 2 SCC 9 : 2001 SCC (Cri) 268]

United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. PatriciaJean Mahajan [(2002) 6 SCC 281 : 2002 SCC (Cri) 1294]

constitutional_provisions: Article 14 of the Constitution
Article 38 of the Constitution
Article 39 of the Constitution

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core reasoning is that in a commercial transaction involving delayed payment for shares, where no contractual interest rate exists, Section 34 of the Civil Procedure Code applies. The court must balance fair compensation for the time value of money (considering the prolonged delay) with the financial impact on the judgment debtor (the State), leading to an award of reasonable simple interest that is higher than the High Court's initial award but not punitive.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court extensively discussed the concepts of unconscionable contracts, inequality of bargaining power, distributive justice, and the evolution of contract law, citing various English and American legal principles and cases to emphasize the judiciary's role in ensuring fairness in transactions, especially when one party has significantly weaker bargaining power.

special_directions.special_directions: The interest shall be paid along with the amount due towards the enhanced value of the shares, after adjusting the amount already paid, to the appellants, within a period of two months from today.

case_identification.petitioner_name: ICICI Lombard General Insurance Co. Ltd.
case_identification.case_number: Civil Appeal No. of 2025 (@ SLP (C) No. 29302 of 2019)

case_details.subject_matter: The case involves an appeal by an insurance company against a Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal award, upheld by the High Court, for compensation due to a fatal motor vehicle accident, primarily disputing the finding of negligence based on police records.

judgements.case_summary: ICICI Lombard General Insurance Co. Ltd. appealed against a judgment by the High Court of Orissa, which dismissed its appeal against an award passed by the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal. The Tribunal had awarded compensation to the legal heirs of Udayanath Sahoo, who died in a motor vehicle accident involving a motorcycle and a truck insured by the appellant. The appellant contended that the accident was solely due to the deceased's negligence and that the lower courts erred in relying on a 'fraudulent' chargesheet. The respondents argued that there was no illegality in relying on police records. The Supreme Court, referencing precedents like Mangla Ram v. Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. and Dulcina Fernandes v. Joaquim Xavier Cruz, affirmed that negligence in motor accident cases can be established on the 'preponderance of probabilities' and that police records (FIR, final form, chargesheet) are admissible and can be relied upon for this purpose. The Court noted that even an acquittal in a criminal case does not affect the assessment of liability in motor accident cases. Finding no perversity in the concurrent findings of the Tribunal and the High Court, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, thereby upholding the compensation award.

petitioner_key_arguments: The accident occurred solely due to the rash and negligent driving of the deceased, not the driver of the truck insured with the appellant.
The Tribunal erred in relying on the FIR and other records.
The chargesheet was fraudulent, prepared by the respondents in connivance with the police.
The vehicle insured with the appellant was not involved in the accident, and the accident occurred solely due to the rash and negligent driving on the part of the deceased.
respondent_key_arguments: There is no illegality in relying on police records (FIR and final report) for considering the question of negligence in a motor vehicle accident case.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted that negligence in motor vehicle accident claims can be established on the preponderance of probabilities, and that police records such as FIRs, final reports, and chargesheets are admissible and can be relied upon for this purpose. The court found no perversity in the concurrent findings of the Tribunal and the High Court, thereby upholding the lower court's decision.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal was dismissed, meaning the award of compensation passed by the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal and upheld by the High Court stands.

precedents_cited: Mangla Ram v. Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. and Ors.1
Dulcina Fernandes v. Joaquim Xavier Cruz, (2013) 10 SCC 646
Mathew Alexander v. Mohammed Shafi & Anr.2
Bimla Devi

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: In motor vehicle accident claims, negligence can be established based on the preponderance of probabilities, and police records such as FIRs, final reports, and chargesheets are admissible and can be relied upon for this purpose. The concurrent findings of lower courts based on such evidence, when not perverse, should not be interfered with.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: Even if the accused were to be acquitted in a criminal case, the same may be of no effect on the assessment of liability required in respect of motor accident cases by the Tribunal.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.1545 OF 2025

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the quashing of an FIR registered against a Member of Parliament for posting a video with a poem on social media, alleged to incite enmity and hurt religious sentiments. The court examined the applicability of various penal provisions and the scope of freedom of speech.

judgements.case_summary: The case involves an appeal against the High Court's refusal to quash an FIR registered against Imran Pratapgadhi, a Member of Parliament, for posting a video on social media containing a poem. The FIR alleged that the poem incited people of one community against another, hurt religious sentiments, and created enmity, thereby violating Sections 196, 197(1), 302, 299, 57, and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. The appellant argued that the poem, on a plain reading, did not promote disharmony or hatred but rather conveyed a message of love, non-violence, and fighting injustice with resilience, thus falling within the ambit of freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. The Solicitor General, representing the State, maintained that the police were obligated to register the FIR. The Supreme Court meticulously analyzed the poem's text and its English translation, concluding that it had no connection to religion, community, or race, and did not promote enmity or jeopardize national unity. The Court found it "ridiculous" and "not applicable on its face" that the poem could outrage religious feelings or wound them deliberately. It emphasized that the effect of words must be judged by the standards of "reasonable, strong-minded, firm and courageous men," not by "weak and vacillating minds." The Court highlighted the significant departure in Section 173(3) of the BNSS from Section 154 of the CrPC, allowing a preliminary inquiry for cognizable offenses punishable between 3 and 7 years, even if a prima facie case exists. It stressed that police officers must uphold constitutional ideals, particularly freedom of speech, and conduct preliminary inquiries in such cases to protect fundamental rights. The Court criticized the High Court for failing to recognize that no offense was made out and for mechanically upholding the FIR. Ultimately, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, quashing the impugned order and the FIR, reaffirming the paramount importance of freedom of speech and expression in a democracy and the duty of courts to protect these fundamental rights against mechanical application of penal laws.

petitioner_key_arguments: None of the ingredients of the alleged offences are made out on a plain reading of the complaint and the poem.
The poem does not promote disharmony or feelings of enmity, hatred or ill-will between religious, racial, language or regional groups and castes or communities.
The poem is about sacrificing oneself to fight for rights and truth, promotes non-violence, and preaches suffering injustice with love.
Registering the FIR based on the said poem violates the appellant's fundamental right guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.
The police have shown insensitivity, and the High Court failed to appreciate the message conveyed by the poem.
respondent_key_arguments: The Learned Solicitor General of India left the decision to the Court.
The appellant's claim on oath that the poem's author can be either Faiz Ahmed Faiz or Habib Jalib is entirely wrong and has no basis.
It is the obligation of the police to register an FIR.
The High Court followed the law while rejecting the appellant's petition.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments that the poem did not constitute an offense under the cited sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and that the FIR violated his fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution, were accepted by the Court.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned order of the High Court was set aside. FIR No. 11202008250014 of 2025, registered with City A-Division Police Station, Jamnagar, and further proceedings based thereon, were quashed.

precedents_cited: Neeharika Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. v State of Maharashtra, 2021 SCC Online SC 315
Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of U.P., (2014) 2 SCC 1
Bhagwati Charan Shukla v. Provincial Government, C.P. & Berar
Manzar Sayeed Khan v. State of Maharashtra
Ramesh v. Union of India
Javed Ahmad Hajam v. State of Maharashtra, (2024) 4 SCC 156
Patricia Mukhim v. State of Meghalaya
State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
Anand Chintamani Dighe and anr. Vs. State of Maharashtra and ors., 2001 SCC OnLine Bom 891
Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) SCC 1
constitutional_provisions: Article 19 (1)(a) of the Constitution of India
Article 226 of the Constitution of India
Article 12 of the Constitution of India
Article 51-A (a) of the Constitution of India
Article 19(2) of the Constitution of India
Article 21 of the Constitution of India
Preamble to the Constitution of India

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that freedom of speech and expression, guaranteed by Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution, is a fundamental right that must be zealously protected by courts. Penal provisions like Section 196 of the BNS, which deal with promoting enmity, must be interpreted strictly, requiring proof of mens rea and judging the effect of words by the standards of 'reasonable, strong-minded, firm and courageous men,' not by 'weak and vacillating minds.' A preliminary inquiry under Section 173(3) of the BNSS is appropriate for offenses based on spoken/written words punishable up to seven years to ascertain a prima facie case and protect fundamental rights.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that police officers ought to be educated and sensitized about their duty to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals, including freedom of speech, suggesting massive training programs. It also noted that 75 years into the republic, the state should not be so shaky on its fundamentals that mere recital of a poem or any form of art can be alleged to lead to animosity, as such a view would stifle legitimate expressions in a free society.

special_directions.special_directions: The State must ensure that police officers are educated and sensitized about their duty of abiding by the Constitution and respecting its ideals, by starting massive training programs.

case_identification.petitioner_name: In Re Recruitment Of Visually Impaired ...
case_identification.respondent_name: The Registrar General The High Court Of ...
case_identification.case_number: SUO MOTU WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO. 2 OF 2024, SUO MOTU WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO. 6 OF 2024, CIVIL APPEAL NO. 3496 OF 2025 (Arising out of SLP (C) No.7683 of 2024), CIVIL APPEAL NO. 3497 OF 2025 (Arising out of SLP (C) No.12179 of 2024), WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO. 484 OF 2024, WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO. 494 OF 2024

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the recruitment of visually impaired and Persons with Disabilities (PwD) candidates in judicial services, challenging rules that exclude them or impose discriminatory eligibility criteria, and seeking appropriate reservations and relaxations.

judgements.case_summary:
This consolidated judgment addresses multiple petitions and appeals challenging recruitment rules for judicial services in Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan, specifically concerning visually impaired and Persons with Disabilities (PwD) candidates. The core issue revolves around the exclusion of visually impaired persons from judicial service (Madhya Pradesh Judicial Service Rules, 1994, Rule 6A) and discriminatory eligibility criteria (Rule 7, requiring 3-year practice or 70% marks in first attempt). Additionally, the non-publication of separate cut-off marks for PwD candidates in Rajasthan Judicial Service Examinations was challenged.
Petitioners argued that these rules violate Articles 14, 16, and 21 of the Constitution and the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (RPwD Act), which mandates reasonable accommodation and non-discrimination. They contended that visually impaired individuals can effectively perform judicial duties with appropriate support and that the medical model of disability is outdated. Respondents, including the High Courts, defended the rules, citing medical opinions on suitability and the necessity of minimum qualifying marks.
The Court, adopting a rights-based approach and recognizing the RPwD Act as a 'super statute', emphasized the principle of reasonable accommodation. It rejected the notion that visual impairment inherently renders candidates unsuitable for judicial service, citing numerous examples of successful visually impaired legal professionals. The Court found that the impugned rules constituted direct and indirect discrimination.
The Supreme Court struck down Rule 6A of the Madhya Pradesh Judicial Service Rules, 1994, to the extent it excludes visually impaired and low vision candidates. It also struck down the proviso to Rule 7 regarding additional requirements (3-year practice or 70% marks in first attempt) as it applies to PwD candidates. The Court mandated separate cut-off marks and merit lists for PwD candidates in judicial service examinations. The orders of the High Courts dismissing the challenges were set aside, and specific appellants were directed to be considered for selection with applicable relaxations. The Court directed the authorities to complete the selection process within three months.

petitioner_key_arguments: Madhya Pradesh Judicial Service Rules, 1994, Rule 6A, which excludes visually impaired and low vision candidates, violates Articles 14, 15, 16, and 21 of the Constitution of India.
The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (RPwD Act) mandates reasonable accommodation and non-discrimination for PwD, treating it as a 'super statute'.
Visually impaired persons can effectively discharge judicial duties with appropriate support and technological aids, as evidenced by successful legal professionals.
The medical expert opinion used to justify exclusion is outdated and reflects a biased, medical model of disability, rather than a social model.
The proviso to Rule 7 of the Madhya Pradesh Judicial Service Rules, requiring a 3-year practice period or 70% marks in the first attempt, constitutes indirect discrimination against PwD candidates.
The non-publication of separate cut-off marks and merit lists for PwD candidates in Rajasthan Judicial Service Examinations is discriminatory and violates their right to equal opportunity.
respondent_key_arguments: The exclusion of visually impaired persons under Rule 6A of the Madhya Pradesh Judicial Service Rules, 1994, is based on a medical expert's opinion that such persons cannot perform the duties of a judge.
An exemption for the establishment of District Judiciary was granted by the State Government, aligning with the RPwD Act, 2016.
There is no restriction on visually impaired persons to participate in recruitment examinations for judicial service.
The appellant (Alok Singh) failed to secure the minimum qualifying marks in the interview, which is a necessary criterion for selection.
The Office Memorandum dated 15.01.2018 regarding relaxation of standards applies only to Central Government posts, not state judicial services.
For Rajasthan, PwD candidates compete within their respective vertical categories, and non-fixation of separate cut-off marks for PwD is not arbitrary or violative of fundamental rights.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments regarding the unconstitutionality of exclusionary rules, the necessity of reasonable accommodation under the RPwD Act, 2016, and the requirement for separate cut-offs and merit lists for Persons with Disabilities prevailed.

outcome.relief_granted: Rule 6A of the Madhya Pradesh Judicial Service (Recruitment and Conditions of Service) Rules, 1994, is struck down insofar as it excludes visually impaired and low vision candidates for appointment. The proviso to Rule 7 of the same rules is struck down as it applies to PwD candidates. The impugned orders of the High Courts are set aside. Visually impaired candidates are declared eligible, and separate cut-offs and merit lists for PwD candidates are mandated. Specific appellants (Ayush Yardi and Alok Singh) and petitioners (Manvendra Singh Rathore & Ors., Alisha Khan) are entitled to be considered for selection with applicable relaxations.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 6071 OF 2023

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns statutory appeals challenging NCLAT judgments regarding the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of Hindustan National Glass and Industries Ltd., specifically focusing on the mandatory nature and timing of Competition Commission of India (CCI) approval for combinations within a resolution plan under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016.

judgements.case_summary:
The case involves appeals against NCLAT judgments concerning the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of Hindustan National Glass and Industries Ltd. (HNGIL). The core dispute revolves around whether the Competition Commission of India (CCI) approval for a combination, as stipulated in the proviso to Section 31(4) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), must mandatorily precede the approval of the resolution plan by the Committee of Creditors (CoC). The NCLAT had ruled that while CCI approval is mandatory, its timing (prior to CoC approval) is merely directory.

The appellant, Independent Sugar Corporation Limited (INSCO), argued that the proviso's language is clear and unambiguous, requiring a literal interpretation that mandates prior CCI approval before CoC consideration. They highlighted procedural lapses by the Resolution Professional (RP) and CCI, including the RP's unauthorized relaxation of the approval timeline and the CCI's failure to issue a show cause notice to all "parties to the combination," specifically HNGIL. INSCO also pointed out discrepancies in data provided by the successful resolution applicant, AGI Greenpac Ltd., which could affect competitive assessment.

The respondents, including AGI Greenpac, the CoC, and the RP, contended that the proviso should be interpreted purposively as directory to avoid disrupting the time-bound CIRP. They argued that the NCLAT's view was consistent with previous judgments and that the CCI, as an expert body, had adequately reviewed the combination.

Justice Hrishikesh Roy, writing for the majority (concurred by Justice Sudhanshu Dhulia), held that the proviso to Section 31(4) IBC is mandatory, requiring CCI approval prior to CoC approval for resolution plans involving combinations. The court emphasized literal interpretation of the clear statutory language and rejected the argument that the timing was merely directory. It found significant procedural lapses by the CCI and RP, rendering AGI Greenpac's resolution plan unsustainable. Consequently, the CoC's approval of AGI's plan was set aside, and the CoC was directed to reconsider other resolution plans that had requisite CCI approval as of the relevant date. Justice S.V.N. Bhatti delivered a separate, dissenting opinion, affirming the NCLAT's view that the proviso's timing was directory and dismissing the appeals.

petitioner_key_arguments: The entire resolution process from AGI's plan submission to CoC approval was riddled with irregularities and should be nullified.
The RP violated Section 31(4) IBC, the RFRP, and its own email clarification by submitting AGI's plan without the required prior CCI approval.
AGI Greenpac's undertaking before the NCLT (Clause 5.5) stated that CCI approval would be secured prior to CoC approval and NCLT submission.
The proviso to Section 31(4) IBC, specifically for combinations under Section 5 of the Competition Act, requires stricter compliance and mandatory prior CCI approval.
The NCLAT judgment failed to recognize that there is no inconsistency between IBC and Competition Act timelines, as CCI's process is typically swift.
The CCI bypassed mandatory procedures under Section 29(1) of the Competition Act, such as issuing a Show Cause Notice (SCN) to the Corporate Debtor and inviting public objections.
The CCI's approval was based on incorrect and misleading data provided by AGI Greenpac, and the modifications were suggested by AGI, not proposed by CCI post-SCN as legally required.
The RP lacked authority to divest assets without CoC permission under Section 28(1) IBC.
AGI's resolution plan was conditional, violating the IBC framework, and created unfeasible complications regarding divestment.
respondent_key_arguments: The IBC aims to facilitate time-bound resolution and maximize asset value, with the CoC playing a pivotal role in assessing feasibility and viability.
Adherence to IBC timelines is sacrosanct, and the proviso to Section 31(4) should be interpreted purposively as 'directory' rather than 'mandatory' to avoid disrupting the CIRP.
NCLAT judgments, which have not been overturned by the Supreme Court, have consistently held the proviso to be directory.
The Green Channel approval mechanism, which INSCO utilized, gave it an unfair advantage over established industry players.
The CoC fully complied with the IBC and Competition Act, and CCI's approval terms did not necessitate specific CoC approval.
The RP's role is procedural, and he adhered to the legal position in force at the relevant time.
The term 'CoC' in the proviso was a drafting error, and the intended reference was to the 'Adjudicating Authority'.
If the proviso were interpreted as mandatory, IBC timelines would become unworkable, compromising the objective of stressed businesses surviving as going concerns.
The legislature prescribed no consequences for non-compliance with the proviso, indicating its directory nature.
Unsuccessful resolution applicants lack vested rights and thus locus standi to challenge the plan.

The CCI is an expert body, and its examination of the combination, including the acceptance of AGI's modifications, was appropriate and did not warrant further investigation under Section 29(2) of the Competition Act.

The NCLAT's findings, including on the directory nature of the proviso and the sufficiency of notice, are sustainable and have been affirmed by the Supreme Court in previous cases (e.g., Makalu Trading Ltd.).
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's (Independent Sugar Corporation Limited) key arguments regarding the mandatory nature of prior CCI approval and the procedural lapses by the CCI and RP prevailed in the majority judgment.

outcome.judgement_type: Allowed in part and Dismissed in part
outcome.relief_granted: AGI Greenpac's Resolution Plan, approved by the CoC on 28.10.2022, was set aside and quashed. All actions taken pursuant to the Resolution Plan were nullified, and the rights of all stakeholders were restored to status quo ante. The CoC was directed to reconsider the Appellant's Resolution Plan and any other Resolution Plans which possessed the requisite CCI approval as on 28.10.2022. Costs of Rs. 25,00,000, Rs. 10,00,000, Rs. 10,00,000, Rs. 10,00,000, and Rs. 50,000 were awarded against various dismissed appeals, to be credited to the RP's account.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The proviso to Section 31(4) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, which mandates obtaining Competition Commission of India (CCI) approval for a combination "prior to the approval of such resolution plan by the committee of creditors," is mandatory and not merely directory. This interpretation is based on the plain and unambiguous language of the statute, the legislative intent to create an exception for combinations, and the principle that a statutory requirement for a specific action in a specific manner must be strictly followed.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed that the RP's role is administrative and he lacked authority to relax statutory requirements. It also noted that discrepancies in data and procedural lapses by the CCI, such as failing to issue a show cause notice to all parties to the combination, vitiated the approval process. The court emphasized that the "spirit of the law" cannot override the plain language of the statute.
judicial_reasoning.dissenting_opinion: Justice S.V.N. Bhatti dissented, arguing that the proviso to Section 31(4) IBC, particularly the timing of CCI approval, should be considered directory to align with the time-bound objectives of the IBC and to avoid precluding resolution applicants. He maintained that previous NCLAT judgments, affirmed by the Supreme Court, supported this directory interpretation and that the CCI, as an expert body, had adequately addressed the combination.
