Basawaraj v. Special Land Acquisition Officer11
Kusha Duruka v The State of Odisha12
constitutional_provisions: Article 309 of the Constitution of India
Article 16 of the Constitution
Article 14 of the Constitution

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: Recruitment to a public post must strictly adhere to statutory rules. If rules mandate direct recruitment for a post, it cannot be filled by promotion, especially if the candidate does not meet the prescribed qualifications or the proper recruitment procedure (like public advertisement) is not followed. The principle of negative equality does not allow perpetuation of illegalities.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court strongly criticized the casual approach of the State authorities in handling litigation, failing to present correct statutory rules, and generating unnecessary litigation. It also emphasized the importance of public advertisement for public posts to ensure fairness and transparency.

special_directions.special_directions: A copy of this order be sent to the Chief Secretary, State of Odisha for perusal and taking appropriate corrective steps to streamline proceedings and avoid anomalies.

case_identification.respondent_name: THE DEPUTY COMMISSIONER OF INCOME TAX
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 2411 OF 2025

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the levy of penalty under Section 271AAA of the Income Tax Act, 1961, related to undisclosed income found during a search and the interpretation of conditions for exemption from such penalty.

judgements.case_summary: The present appeal challenges a High Court judgment upholding a penalty under Section 271AAA of the Income Tax Act, 1961. Following a search and seizure operation, the appellant initially disclosed Rs. 2,27,65,580/- as income and later filed a return showing a total income of Rs. 4,77,11,330/-. Penalties were imposed for Assessment Years 2010-11 and 2011-12. The key legal issues revolved around whether the conditions under Section 271AAA(2) for penalty exemption are mandatory, the definition of 'undisclosed income,' and the scope of 'found in the course of search.' The petitioner argued that penalty is not mandatory, the AO failed to prove 'undisclosed income' as defined, and the declaration was voluntary. The respondent contended that the appellant failed to meet the mandatory conditions of Section 271AAA(2). The Supreme Court clarified that the AO's power to levy penalty under Section 271AAA(1) is discretionary, not mandatory, and the conditions for exemption under sub-section (2) are crucial. It emphasized that 'undisclosed income' must be strictly construed, with the onus on the AO to prove it was found during the search. The Court ruled that no penalty is attracted to the Rs. 2,27,65,580/- amount as the appellant met the conditions of Section 271AAA(2) for this portion. However, a 10% penalty was levied on Rs. 2,49,90,000/-, which was not admitted during the search but disclosed during assessment proceedings, as the conditions for exemption were not met for this amount. The appeal was disposed of with these directions.

petitioner_key_arguments: The levy of penalty under Section 271AAA(1) of the Act 1961 is not automatic and the only exception thereto was sub-clause (2) of Section 271AAA.
The Revenue Authorities levied penalty without satisfying themselves as to the satisfaction of 'undisclosed income' as stipulated in Section 271AAA(1).
The imposition of penalty is not mandatory, as held in Dilip N. Shroff vs. CIT.
Unless there is 'undisclosed income' in terms of the definition in Section 271AAA, an order of levy of penalty cannot be issued.
The MOU dated 19th January, 2009, could not have formed the basis for the Penalty Order dated 30th September, 2013.
The declaration before the DDIT(Inv.) during search proceedings was made voluntarily and had no direct co-relation with the MOU or sale deeds.
The sum of Rs.4,78,02,616/- was not the undisclosed income of the Appellant for FY 2010-2011.
Penalty could not have been imposed on the entire returned income for FY 2010-2011; at most, it should be on the alleged undisclosed income of Rs.2,27,65,580/-.
respondent_key_arguments: There were concurrent findings of all authorities below against the Appellant upholding the Penalty amount on the entire income returned.
The Appellant failed to meet the conditions of Section 271AAA(2) of the Act 1961.
The assessee never admitted to any undisclosed income, and the income was detected only after a search.
The assessee never disclosed or explained the manner in which the income was derived/earned.
The assessee did not pay the tax and interest thereon until 2016, three years after the assessment order.
To claim the benefit of Section 271AAA(2), the assessee has to satisfy its requirements/conditions, as held by the Delhi High Court in PCIT vs. Amul Gabrani.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that penalty under Section 271AAA(1) is discretionary and not leviable on the amount of Rs. 2,27,65,580/- for which the conditions of Section 271AAA(2) were met. However, it sided with the respondent regarding the amount of Rs. 2,49,90,000/-, holding that penalty is leviable as this amount was not admitted during the search and the conditions for exemption under Section 271AAA(2) were not satisfied for it.

outcome.relief_granted: Penalty under Section 271AAA(1) is not attracted on Rs. 2,27,65,580/-. Penalty at the rate of 10% is leviable on Rs. 2,49,90,000/-.

acts_cited: Section 260A of the Income Tax Act, 1961
precedents_cited: Dilip N. Shroff vs. CIT [(2007) 6 SCC 329]
DCIT vs. Aryan Mining & Trading Corporation Ltd. [2019 SCC OnLine ITAT 4649]
Ajay Kumar Sood Engineers And Contractors K N Kandla & Co. vs. DCIT [MANU/IG/0095/2024]
Som Raj and Others vs. State of Haryana and Others, (1990) 2 SCC 653
PCIT vs. Amul Gabrani (ITA No.1251 of 2018 dated 24th July, 2024)
Amul Gabrani (supra)

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The court held that the power to levy penalty under Section 271AAA(1) is discretionary, not mandatory, and must be exercised with sound discretion. Exemption from penalty under Section 271AAA(2) requires strict compliance with all three conditions: admission of undisclosed income, substantiation of its derivation, and timely payment of tax and interest. The expression 'undisclosed income' must be strictly construed, and the onus is on the Assessing Officer to demonstrate that such income was found during the search.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The expression 'found in the course of search' has a wide amplitude, encompassing not just documents found in the assessee's premises but also those collected as a result of the search, including through further investigation or interrogation of third parties.

special_directions.special_directions: The Appellant is directed to pay penalty at the rate of 10% on Rs. 2,49,90,000/-.

case_identification.respondent_name: M/S MORGAN SECURITIES AND CREDITS PVT. LTD.
case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 [Arising out of SLP (Criminal) No. 4774 of 2024]

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the quashing of criminal proceedings initiated against non-executive directors under Section 138 read with Section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, for the dishonor of cheques issued by a company.

judgements.case_summary: K.S. Mehta and Basant Kumar Goswami, non-executive directors of M/s Blue Coast Hotels & Resorts Ltd., were implicated in criminal proceedings after two post-dated cheques issued by the company for an Inter-Corporate Deposit (ICD) were dishonored due to insufficient funds. The appellants were not signatories to the cheques, nor were they present at the board meeting approving the ICD agreement. Their role was limited to governance oversight without executive or financial decision-making power. The petitioners argued their non-executive status negated vicarious liability under Section 141 of the NI Act, citing lack of involvement in financial transactions and non-signatory status to the cheques. They relied on CGRs and ROC records confirming their non-executive roles. The respondents contended that the appellants' names appeared as directors at the relevant time, implying involvement, and that resignation doesn't automatically absolve liability. They argued that the question of non-executive status should be determined at trial, not at the quashing stage, and that attendance at board meetings indicated knowledge of financial dealings. The Court reiterated that non-executive directors cannot be held liable under Section 138/141 NI Act unless specific allegations demonstrate direct involvement. Mere designation as a director or attendance at board meetings is insufficient. Vicarious liability requires clear averments on how the director was in charge of and responsible for the business conduct at the time of the offence. The Court found a lack of specific allegations and direct involvement, setting aside the High Court's judgment and quashing the criminal proceedings against the appellants.

petitioner_key_arguments: Appellants had no role in the company's financial transactions and no responsibility for its financial affairs.
Appellants were not signatories to the dishonored cheques and did not authorize their issuance.
Appellants' directorship was non-executive and limited to corporate governance oversight, negating vicarious liability under Section 141 of the NI Act.
CGRs and ROC records consistently reflected appellants' non-executive roles, reinforcing lack of involvement in operational or financial matters.
Absence of specific allegations linking appellants to the issuance or dishonor of cheques makes proceedings legally untenable.
respondent_key_arguments: Appellants' names appeared as directors in the company at the relevant time, presuming their involvement in the company's affairs.
Mere resignation does not automatically absolve a director from liability under Section 141 NI Act; onus is on them to establish non-involvement.
Status as independent/non-executive director should be determined during trial, not at the quashing stage.
Appellants' attendance at board meetings indicated knowledge of financial dealings, including cheque issuance.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court accepted the petitioners' arguments that non-executive directors cannot be held vicariously liable under Section 141 of the NI Act without specific allegations demonstrating their direct involvement in the company's financial affairs or being signatories to the dishonored cheques. The Court found a lack of such specific allegations against the appellants.

outcome.relief_granted: The Impugned Judgment and Order dated 28.11.2023 of the High Court is set aside, and the criminal proceedings against the Appellant(s) in Complaint No(s). 15858 and 15857 of 2017 pending before the Court of Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, New Delhi are hereby quashed.

precedents_cited: Kamalkishor Shrigopal Taparia v. India Ener-Gen Private Limited & Anr., 2025 SCC Online SC 321
S.M.S. Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Neeta Bhalla & Anr., (2005) 8 SCC 89
Pooja Ravinder Devidasani v. State of Maharashtra & Anr., (2014) 16 SCC 1
Ashutosh Ashok Parasrampuriya & Anr. v. Gharrkul Industries Pvt. Ltd. & Ors., (2023) 14 SCC 770
National Small Industries Corpn. Ltd. v. Harmeet Singh Paintal & Anr., (2010) 3 SCC 330
N. K. Wahi v. Shekhar Singh & Ors., (2007) 9 SCC 481
Ashok Shewakramani & Ors. v. State of Andhra Pradesh & Anr., (2023) 8 SCC 473
Hitesh Verma v. M/s Health Care At Home India Pvt. Ltd. & Ors., Crl. Appeal No. 462 of 2025

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that non-executive directors cannot be held vicariously liable under Section 138 read with Section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, unless there are specific allegations demonstrating their direct involvement in the company's financial affairs or that they were in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the business at the time of the offence. Mere designation as a director or attendance at board meetings is insufficient to establish such liability.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that Section 141, being a penal provision creating vicarious liability, must be strictly construed, and a bald cursory statement in a complaint is insufficient; the complaint must spell out how and in what manner a director was in charge of or responsible for the conduct of the business.

special_directions.special_directions: No order as to costs.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. of 2025 (@ Special Leave Petition (Civil) No. 10245 of 2024)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the correctness of a High Court order dismissing a contempt petition, specifically regarding the grant of retrospective promotion and monetary benefits to an employee after disciplinary proceedings were set aside due to bias.

judgements.case_summary: The appellant, K. Samba Moorthy, a former Probationary Officer at Bank of Baroda, faced disciplinary proceedings in 1999-2000, resulting in a minor penalty and the cancellation of his promotion from Scale-II to Scale-III, which had been held in abeyance. In 2017, the High Court set aside these disciplinary proceedings due to a finding of bias by the Enquiry Officer and directed the grant of "consequential benefits." The Bank's subsequent appeal was disposed of in 2022, affirming the Single Judge's order. The appellant then filed a contempt petition seeking compliance, including retrospective promotion and monetary benefits. The High Court dismissed the contempt petition, holding that the orders were complied with by paying a reduced pay amount and that promotion up to Scale-V was not adjudicated. The Supreme Court, in this judgment, found that merely paying Rs. 19,446/- did not constitute full compliance. It held that the term "consequential benefits" encompassed retrospective promotion from 28.07.2001 with all monetary benefits, as the disciplinary proceedings were set aside due to a fundamental defect not attributable to the appellant, and the employer did not contest this finding. The Court partly allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's judgment, and directed the respondents to grant the appellant promotion from Manager Scale-II to Scale-III from 28.07.2001 with 6% interest on monetary benefits within four weeks. It also granted liberty to the appellant to pursue claims for further promotions without being barred by limitation or laches.

petitioner_key_arguments: Upon exoneration from penalty proceedings, the employee is entitled to retrospective promotion by opening the sealed cover and monetary benefits.
The appellant was entitled to promotion from Scale-II to Scale-III from July 2001.
Subsequent promotion in 2012 and inability to secure higher promotions are irrelevant to the claim for 2001 promotion.
The promotion granted in 2012 was without any pay hike in benefits.
The promotion should be effective from July 2001 until superannuation with all consequential benefits.
The term 'consequential benefits' granted by the Single Judge's order includes retrospective promotion.
respondent_key_arguments: The promotion cancellation letter dated 30.08.2002 was not challenged by the appellant.
No relief can be granted in the absence of pleadings regarding the cancellation order.
The Single Judge's order only granted consequential benefits, not promotions or notional promotion up to Scale-V.
Consequential benefits only meant arrears in salary due to the minor penalty being set aside, not promotion.
The appellant accepted the subsequent promotion in 2012 and appeared in further promotion exercises, thereby forfeiting his right to challenge the cancellation.
A court in contempt cannot go behind the main order or decide questions not dealt with in the original judgment.
No contempt is made out as two interpretations of the order were possible.
Promotion becomes effective on assumption of duties; since the appellant superannuated, he is not entitled to retrospective financial benefits.
The judgment in K.V. Jankiraman (supra) is not applicable due to the lack of challenge to the cancellation order.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court accepted the petitioner's argument that 'consequential benefits' included retrospective promotion and monetary benefits, especially since the disciplinary proceedings were set aside due to a fundamental defect (bias) not attributable to the employee, and the employer did not contest this finding. The Court rejected the respondent's arguments regarding the non-challenge of the cancellation order and the limited scope of 'consequential benefits' as hyper-technical.

outcome.relief_granted: Promotion to the appellant from Manager Scale-II to Scale-III from 28.07.2001 with all monetary benefits and interest at the rate of 6% per annum from the respective due dates. The impugned judgment of the High Court dated 24.08.2023 is set aside.

precedents_cited: C.O. Arumugam & Ors. v. State of T.N. & Ors., 1991 Supp (2) SCC 199
Union of India & Ors. v. K.V. Jankiraman & Ors., (1991) 4 SCC 109
Bachhaj Nahar v. Nilima Mandal & Anr., (2008) 17 SCC 491
Chaduranga Kanthraj URS and Anr. V. P. Ravi Kumar & Ors. (2024 INSC 957)
Govt. of West Bengal & Ors. vs. Dr. Amal Satpathi & Ors., (2024 INSC 906)

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: When disciplinary proceedings are set aside due to a fundamental defect (e.g., bias of the enquiry officer) not attributable to the employee, and the employer does not challenge this finding, the employee is entitled to all consequential benefits, which include retrospective promotion and monetary benefits. The term 'consequential benefits' is broad enough to cover such promotion, and a hyper-technical interpretation limiting it to only salary arrears is not permissible.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that merely paying a 'princely sum' of Rs. 19,446/- after a long legal battle amounted to a 'pyrrhic victory' for the appellant. It also stated that it would not put its imprimatur on unfair interpretations and reserved liberty for the appellant to pursue claims for further promotions without being barred by limitation or laches.

special_directions.special_directions: The respondents are directed to pass orders within four weeks from the date of this judgment, granting promotion to the appellant from Manager Scale-II to Scale-III from 28.07.2001 and granting him all monetary benefits with interest at the rate of 6% per annum from the respective dates the monetary benefits fell due. Liberty is reserved for the appellant to resort to remedies for denial of further promotions, and such proceedings should not be rejected on grounds of limitation or laches.
special_directions.interim_orders: The Division Bench suspended the order of the learned Single Judge on 13.09.2017 during the pendency of the Writ Appeal.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S). OF 2025 [Arising out of SLP (Crl.) Nos. 4051-4054 of 2020]

case_details.subject_matter: The case involves the quashing of criminal proceedings initiated against an independent non-executive director under Section 138 read with Section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, for dishonoured cheques.

judgements.case_summary: The case pertains to an appeal filed by Kamalkishor Shrigopal Taparia, an independent non-executive director, against a High Court order that dismissed his plea to quash criminal proceedings under Sections 138 and 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The Appellant was accused in complaints related to dishonoured cheques issued by M/s D.S. Kulkarni Developers Ltd. He contended that he had no involvement in the company's financial operations, did not sign or authorize the cheques, and had resigned from his directorship before the cheques were issued. The High Court had previously ruled that the director's role was a matter for trial. The Supreme Court, referencing established precedents such as National Small Industries Corporation Limited and Pooja Ravinder Devidasani, emphasized that mere designation as a director is insufficient to establish liability under the NI Act. It held that specific averments demonstrating active involvement and responsibility for the company's business at the relevant time are mandatory. Given that the Appellant was a non-executive director, not a signatory to the cheques, and had resigned prior to the alleged offence, and the complaints lacked specific allegations of his active involvement, the Supreme Court concluded that he could not be held vicariously liable. Consequently, the High Court's order was set aside, and the criminal proceedings against the Appellant were quashed.

petitioner_key_arguments: The Appellant was a non-executive director and had no involvement in the financial affairs of the company; the complaints lacked specific averments detailing his role in the dishonoured cheques.
The Appellant had resigned from the company well before the offence occurred, and making him liable post-resignation was a misuse of the legal process.
Section 141 of the NI Act establishes vicarious liability only upon directors who were in-charge of and responsible for the conduct of the business of the company at the relevant time.
respondent_key_arguments: The High Court rightly observed that the role of the Appellant was a matter to be examined during the trial.
Vicarious liability under Section 141 of the NI Act could extend to directors, regardless of their executive or non-executive status.
The Appellant, by virtue of his directorship, was part of the decision-making apparatus of the company and could not escape liability at the pre-trial stage.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments that a non-executive director cannot be held vicariously liable under Section 141 of the NI Act without specific averments of active involvement and responsibility for the company's business at the relevant time. The court noted that the appellant was not a signatory to the cheques and had resigned before the offence, and the complaints lacked specific averments of his active involvement.

outcome.relief_granted: The Impugned Judgment and Order dated 06.08.2019 of the High Court is set aside, and the criminal proceedings against the Appellant in Complaint Nos. 66/SS, 645/SS, 697/SS, 1595/SS (all) of 2017 pending against the present Applicant before the Learned Metropolitan Magistrate 28th Court, Esplanade, Mumbai are hereby quashed.

precedents_cited: National Small Industries Corporation Limited v. Harmeet Singh Paintal and Another, (2010) 3 SCC 330
N.K. Wahi v. Shekhar Singh, (2007) 9 SCC 481
S.M.S. Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Neeta Bhalla and Another, (2005) 8 SCC 89
Pooja Ravinder Devidasani v. State of Maharashtra, (2014) 16 SCC 1

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that vicarious liability under Section 138 read with Section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, cannot be automatically fastened upon a director merely by virtue of their designation. For a director, especially an independent non-executive director, to be held liable, the complaint must contain specific averments demonstrating their active involvement and responsibility for the conduct of the company's business at the time the offence was committed. Without such specific allegations and evidence of active participation or signing of the cheques, a non-executive director cannot be held vicariously liable.

special_directions.special_directions: No order as to costs.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (Arising out of SLP (C) No. 21965 OF 2022)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns an eviction suit filed by a landlord against a tenant on grounds of default in rent payment, refusal to vacate, and bona fide personal need to establish an ultrasound machine for his unemployed sons.

judgements.case_summary:
Kanahaiya Lal Arya (landlord) initiated Eviction Suit No.25/2001 against Md. Ehshan & Ors. (tenants) seeking eviction from premises in Chatra Municipality. The grounds for eviction included default in rent, refusal to vacate, and a bona fide personal need to establish an ultrasound machine for his two unemployed sons. The court of first instance decreed the suit on 15.07.2006, recognizing the landlord's bona fide need. However, this decision was subsequently reversed by the First Appellate Court and affirmed by the High Court in Second Appeal No.317/20061 on 18.08.2022. The landlord then appealed to the Supreme Court.

The appellant-landlord argued that the lower courts erred in denying his bona fide need, emphasizing his financial capability to purchase the machine, his annual income, and the strategic location of the premises near a medical clinic. He also contended that his sons' lack of expertise was irrelevant, as technicians typically operate such equipment, and a previous partial eviction for a different family member's need did not negate the current bona fide requirement. The respondents-tenant countered, citing an earlier compromise in Eviction Suit No.11/1981 that allegedly granted them perpetual tenancy for three rooms, rendering the current suit non-maintainable. They also claimed the landlord had alternative accommodation and had misused a prior eviction by re-letting the vacated space.

The Supreme Court, in its analysis, affirmed that the landlord is the ultimate judge of his bona fide need, which cannot be dictated by the tenant. It found the landlord's need established, noting the suitability of the premises and the irrelevance of the sons' direct expertise. The Court clarified that the prior compromise decree did not bar subsequent eviction proceedings for a new, distinct bona fide need, and the need should be assessed at the time of filing the suit (28.11.2001). Consequently, the appeal was allowed, setting aside the judgments of the High Court and First Appellate Court, and decreeing the landlord's eviction suit.

petitioner_key_arguments: The First Appellate Court and High Court manifestly erred in law by not recognizing the appellant's bona fide need.
The appellant proved his capability to purchase an ultrasound machine and his annual income.
The suit premises are the most appropriate place for the ultrasound machine due to proximity to a medical clinic and pathology center.
The sons' lack of expertise is irrelevant as technicians usually operate ultrasound machines.
A previous partial eviction for a different need (brother-in-law) does not affect the current bona fide need for his sons.
respondent_key_arguments: An earlier compromise in Eviction Suit No.11/1981 allowed them to occupy the premises as perpetual tenants, making the current suit non-maintainable.
The appellant has sufficient alternative accommodation for any new business.
The appellant misused a previous partial eviction by re-letting the vacated premises at a higher rent instead of using it for the stated purpose.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the landlord's bona fide need was established, that the sons' lack of expertise was not a bar, and that a previous compromise did not preclude the current eviction suit for a different bona fide need.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal is allowed, and the impugned judgment and order dated 18.08.2022 and 25.09.2006 of the High Court and the First Appellate Court respectively are set aside. The suit of the appellant-landlord stands decreed, leading to the eviction of the respondents-tenant.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The landlord is the best judge of his bona fide need for his property, and the tenant cannot dictate which property the landlord should use. The lack of specific expertise by the landlord's sons to operate an ultrasound machine does not negate the bona fide need, as such machines are typically operated by technicians. A prior compromise decree for eviction based on a different need does not bar a subsequent eviction suit for a new, established bona fide need.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The law with regard to eviction of a tenant from the suit premises on the ground of bona fide need of the landlord is well settled. The need has to be a real one rather than a mere desire to get the premises vacated.

special_directions.special_directions: The suit of the appellant-landlord stands decreed, implying the eviction of the respondents-tenant from the premises in dispute.

case_identification.respondent_name: THE STATE OF WEST BENGAL & ANOTHER
case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS. (@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NOS.8609-8614 OF 2024) OF 2025

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the retrospective application of the Supreme Court's ruling in Priyanka Srivastava vs. State of Uttar Pradesh, which mandated affidavits for applications under Section 156(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code, in the context of criminal proceedings involving charges of forgery and criminal conspiracy.

judgements.case_summary: Kanishk Sinha & Another, a married couple, appealed against a Calcutta High Court order dismissing their criminal revisions. They faced two FIRs (2010 and 2011) for offenses including forgery, cheating, and criminal conspiracy under the IPC and IT Act. The second FIR originated from a complaint under Section 156(3) CrPC, which lacked an accompanying affidavit. The appellants argued that this violated the Supreme Court's directive in Priyanka Srivastava (2015), which required affidavits for such applications, and contended that this ruling should apply retrospectively. The High Court had ruled that the Priyanka Srivastava directive was prospective. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, clarifying that while judicial pronouncements are generally retrospective, the specific direction in Priyanka Srivastava was intended to be prospective to avoid unsettling past actions and undue hardship, as indicated by the phrase "a stage has come in this country...". Consequently, the appeals were dismissed. The Court noted that if charges had not yet been framed, the appellants retained the liberty to apply for discharge. Interim orders, if any, were vacated.

petitioner_key_arguments: The FIRs are motivated and false, and thus liable to be quashed.
The second FIR was registered on a complaint filed under Section 156(3) CrPC without an accompanying affidavit, violating the law laid down in Priyanka Srivastava vs. State of Uttar Pradesh.
All judgments of the Supreme Court are retrospective in nature unless specifically stated otherwise, and Priyanka Srivastava (supra) did not state it would operate prospectively.
respondent_key_arguments: The direction in Priyanka Srivastava (supra) regarding affidavits for Section 156(3) CrPC applications is prospective in nature and does not apply retrospectively to complaints filed in 2010-2011.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The respondent's argument that the direction in Priyanka Srivastava (supra) requiring affidavits for Section 156(3) CrPC applications is prospective in nature, as upheld by the High Court and affirmed by the Supreme Court.

outcome.relief_granted: No relief granted to the appellants; appeals dismissed. Appellants have liberty to move an application for their discharge if charges have not been framed.

precedents_cited: Priyanka Srivastava vs. State of Uttar Pradesh (2015) 6 SCC 287
constitutional_provisions: Article 226 of the Constitution of India

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that while judgments of Constitutional Courts are generally retrospective, the specific direction in Priyanka Srivastava (supra) mandating affidavits for Section 156(3) CrPC applications was intended to be prospective. This is inferred from the language used ("a stage has come in this country...") and the purpose of avoiding undue hardship and unsettling matters that were bona fidely done under the previous understanding of the law.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The general observation that a law made by the legislature is always prospective unless stated otherwise, whereas a law laid down or interpreted by a Constitutional Court is always retrospective unless the judgment itself specifically states it will operate prospectively. Prospective operation is normally done to avoid unnecessary burden or undue hardships.

special_directions.special_directions: If charges have not been framed by the Court, the appellants would be at liberty to move an application for their discharge, which shall be considered in accordance with law. A copy of the judgment is to be sent to all Chief Justices of the High Courts, who in turn will circulate it to all Magistrates for increased vigilance and diligence while exercising power under Section 156(3) CrPC.
special_directions.interim_orders: Interim order(s), if any, stand(s) vacated.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 1076 OF 2014

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns an appeal against conviction for dowry death (Section 304-B IPC) and cruelty (Section 498-A IPC) following the suicide of the appellant's wife, focusing on the sufficiency of evidence for dowry demand and cruelty 'soon before death'.

judgements.case_summary: The appellant, Karan Singh, was convicted by the Sessions Court and High Court for offences under Sections 304-B (dowry death) and 498-A (cruelty) of the Indian Penal Code, while his parents were acquitted. The deceased, Asha Rani, married the appellant on 25th June 1996 and committed suicide on 2nd April 1998, with the cause of death being asphyxia due to hanging. The appellant's counsel argued that allegations of dowry demand and cruelty by prosecution witnesses (PW-6 and PW-7) were omissions in their prior statements, thus lacking legal evidence, and that there was no proof of cruelty 'soon before her death'. Conversely, the State's counsel contended that there was sufficient evidence from PW-6 and PW-7 regarding a demand of Rs.60,000/- for a jeep made 9-10 days before the incident, which should invoke the presumption under Section 113-B of the Indian Evidence Act. The Supreme Court meticulously examined the testimonies of PW-6 and PW-7, finding significant omissions and contradictions in their statements regarding dowry demands and specific acts of cruelty. Many allegations were found to be belated or not present in initial police reports, appearing as afterthoughts. The Court concluded that the prosecution failed to establish the essential ingredients of Sections 304-B and 498-A, particularly the crucial element of cruelty or harassment 'soon before death' for dowry. Consequently, the presumption under Section 113-B of the Evidence Act could not be invoked. The Court quashed the impugned judgments, acquitted the appellant, and cancelled his bail bonds, also noting repeated errors by trial courts in such cases.

petitioner_key_arguments: All allegations regarding demand of dowry made by witnesses are omissions in prior statements, thus lacking legal evidence.
There is no evidence that the appellant subjected the deceased to cruelty.
There is no evidence to show that soon before her death, the deceased was subjected to cruelty or harassment by the appellant for or in connection with demand for dowry.
In the absence of legal evidence, the Courts ought to have acquitted the appellant.
respondent_key_arguments: There is more than sufficient evidence on record from PW-6 and PW-7 to establish the demand for dowry.
The deceased had met PW-6 and PW-7 9-10 days before the incident and stated about the demand of Rs.60,000/- by the appellant for purchasing a jeep.
The appellant himself made the said demand to the witnesses.
Presumption under Section 113-B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, will apply, and the Court must presume the appellant caused the dowry death.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments prevailed, as the court found that the prosecution failed to prove the essential ingredients of the offences beyond a reasonable doubt due to significant omissions and contradictions in witness testimonies regarding dowry demands and cruelty 'soon before death'.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned judgments dated 9th November 2010 and 24th January 2002 are hereby quashed and set aside. The appellant is acquitted of the offences alleged against him, and his bail bonds are cancelled.

precedents_cited: Charan Singh alias Charanjit Singh v. State of Uttarakhand

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that for a conviction under Sections 304-B and 498-A IPC, the prosecution must establish the essential ingredients, particularly cruelty or harassment 'soon before death' for dowry. Significant omissions and contradictions in the testimonies of key witnesses regarding dowry demands and specific acts of cruelty render their evidence unreliable, preventing the invocation of the presumption under Section 113-B of the Evidence Act.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Trial Courts are committing the same mistakes repeatedly. It is for the State Judicial Academies to step in. Perhaps this is a case of moral conviction.

special_directions.special_directions: The Court observed that Trial Courts are repeatedly making mistakes in such cases and suggested that State Judicial Academies should intervene.

case_identification.respondent_name: STATE REP. BY THE DEPUTY SUPERINTENDENT OF POLICE, LALGUDI TRICHY & ORS.
case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS. OF 2025 [Arising out of Special Leave Petition (Criminal) No.8778-8779 of 2024]

case_details.subject_matter: The case challenges a High Court judgment that dismissed petitions to quash criminal proceedings against the Appellant under the Indian Penal Code and the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, specifically concerning whether the alleged offence occurred 'within public view'.

judgements.case_summary: The present appeals challenge a High Court judgment dated 28th February 2024, which dismissed petitions filed by the Appellant under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, seeking to quash criminal proceedings. The Appellant was accused of offences under Sections 294(b) and 353 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and Sections 3(1)(r) and 3(1)(s) of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, for allegedly abusing a Revenue Inspector by his caste name within his office. The High Court had held that no prejudice would be caused to the Appellant by subjecting him to trial. The Supreme Court, after hearing arguments, focused on the interpretation of 'in any place within public view' as required by the SC-ST Act. Citing precedents like Swaran Singh and Bhajan Lal, the Court determined that an incident occurring within the private chambers of an office does not satisfy this criterion. The Court found that even if the allegations in the FIR were taken at face value, they did not prima facie constitute an offence under the relevant sections of the SC-ST Act. Consequently, the Supreme Court allowed the appeals, quashed the High Court's judgment, and set aside the charge-sheet and all subsequent proceedings in the trial court.

petitioner_key_arguments: The learned Single Judge of the High Court grossly erred in rejecting the petition of the Appellant.
Even taking the allegations in the FIR at its face value, the ingredients to constitute an offence under Sections 3(1)(r) and 3(1)(s) of the SC-ST Act are not made out.
The learned Single Judge of the High Court ought to have exercised its jurisdiction under Section 482 of the CrPC and quashed the proceedings.
The incident did not take place in a place which can be termed to be a place within public view.
respondent_key_arguments: Upon detailed investigation, a charge-sheet was filed by the Investigating Officer.
The learned Single Judge of the High Court, on a perusal of the charge-sheet, found that no case for quashing of the proceedings was made out.
No interference is warranted in the facts and circumstances of the present case.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments prevailed. The Court accepted that the allegations, even if taken at face value, did not prima facie constitute an offence under the SC-ST Act because the incident did not occur 'within public view'.

outcome.relief_granted: The judgment and final order dated 28th February 2024 in Criminal Original Petition (MD) No. 6676 of 2022 and Criminal Miscellaneous Petition (MD) No.4621 of 2022 passed by the learned Single Judge of the High Court of Madras at Madurai is quashed and set aside. The charge-sheet in Special S.C. No. 7 of 2022 on the file of I Additional District and Sessions Judge (PCR), Tiruchirappalli and all proceedings pursuant thereto shall stand quashed and set aside.

acts_cited: Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
Sections 294(b) and 353 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860
Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
Sections 3(1)(r) and 3(1)(s) of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
precedents_cited: Swaran Singh and others v. State through Standing Counsel and another
Hitesh Verma v. State of Uttarakhand and another
Swaran Singh v. State, (2008) 8 SCC 435 : (2008) 3 SCC (Cri) 527
State of Haryana and others v. Bhajan Lal and others4. This 1992 Supp (1) SCC 335 Court
constitutional_provisions: Article 226

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: For an offence under Sections 3(1)(r) and 3(1)(s) of the SC-ST Act to be constituted, the act of intentionally insulting or intimidating, or abusing by caste name, must occur 'in any place within public view'. An incident occurring within the private chambers of an office, even if witnessed by colleagues who arrive later, does not satisfy this 'public view' requirement, and therefore, no prima facie offence under these sections is made out.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The power under Section 482 of the CrPC is required to be exercised sparingly and with circumspection and that too in the rarest of rare cases. The court will not be justified in embarking upon an enquiry as to the reliability or genuineness of allegations, but can exercise discretion if the case falls under categories where allegations do not prima facie constitute an offence.

special_directions.special_directions: The judgment and final order dated 28th February 2024 in Criminal Original Petition (MD) No. 6676 of 2022 and Criminal Miscellaneous Petition (MD) No.4621 of 2022 passed by the learned Single Judge of the High Court of Madras at Madurai is quashed and set aside. The charge-sheet in Special S.C. No. 7 of 2022 on the file of I Additional District and Sessions Judge (PCR), Tiruchirappalli and all proceedings pursuant thereto shall stand quashed and set aside.
special_directions.interim_orders: Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

case_identification.case_number: Criminal Appeal No. of 2025 (@ SLP (Crl.) No.4849 of 2020)

case_details.subject_matter: This case involves an appeal against a High Court judgment that refused to quash an FIR registered under various sections of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, concerning allegations of criminal conspiracy, cheating, fraud, and misappropriation of funds related to a construction project.

judgements.case_summary: The appellant, Kim Wansoo, Project Manager of HEC India LLP, filed a special leave appeal against a High Court judgment dated 26.08.2020, which refused to quash FIR No.64/2020 registered at Police Station, Sadar Bazar, District Meerut. The FIR alleged criminal conspiracy, cheating, fraud, and misappropriation of Rs.9 Crores against multiple accused, including the appellant, stemming from a sub-contracted construction project where payments were allegedly defaulted by M/s. YSSS India Construction. The appellant contended that no specific allegations were made against him or his company, and the High Court erred in not exercising its power to quash the FIR. The Supreme Court, after examining the FIR and relevant precedents, found that the allegations of payment default were not made against the appellant or HEC India LLP, but against different companies. The Court concluded that the FIR did not disclose the commission of any offense against the appellant, and allowing him to stand trial would be an abuse of the process of law. Consequently, the appeal was allowed, and the FIR and all subsequent proceedings against the appellant were quashed.

petitioner_key_arguments: The appellant approached the High Court seeking quashment of the FIR.
No specific allegation could be seen made against the appellant herein or against the company by name ‘HEC India LLP' wherein he was the Project Manager.

The allegations of committing default in payment of an amount around Rs.9 Crores was not made against the appellant herein or against the company in which he was the Project Manager, but against a different company/different companies.

The FIR did not disclose commission of offence(s) as alleged without anything being added to the recitals thereof, and even if taken as true, would not disclose the commission of any offence and make out a case against the appellant.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court accepted the petitioner's argument that the FIR did not disclose any specific offense against him or his company, and the allegations of payment default were directed at other entities, making the continuation of proceedings against him an abuse of the legal process.

outcome.relief_granted: The judgment dated 26.08.2020 in Criminal Misc. Writ Petition No.8063 of 2020 is set aside. The subject FIR No.64/2020 registered at Police Station, Sadar Bazar, District Meerut and all further proceedings pursuant thereto, qua the appellant stand quashed and set aside.

acts_cited: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, Chapter XIV
precedents_cited: Joginder Kumar v. State of U.P. 1994, Cr.L.J. 1981
State of Haryana and Ors. v. Bhajan Lal and Ors.1
AIR 1992 SC 604

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core reasoning is that a perusal of the subject FIR, even when taken at face value, did not disclose the commission of any offense against the appellant, Kim Wansoo. The allegations of payment default were found to be against different companies, not the appellant or his employer HEC India LLP. Therefore, allowing the appellant to stand trial would constitute an abuse of the process of law, warranting the quashing of the FIR.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court reiterated the established principles for quashing criminal proceedings, emphasizing that High Courts can exercise extraordinary powers under Article 226 or inherent powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to prevent abuse of process or secure justice, especially when the FIR does not disclose a cognizable offense or when allegations are vague and do not make out a case against the accused.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CIVIL) NO.7261 OF 2024)

case_details.subject_matter: This case concerns an appeal against a High Court order remanding a child custody and visitation rights matter to the Family Court. It involves the implementation and modification of a divorce decree regarding the custody of a minor child.

judgements.case_summary:
The case involves Kiran Raju Penumacha (Appellant-father) and Tejuswini Chowdhury (Respondent-mother) who divorced by mutual consent in 2021. The mother was granted permanent custody of their minor son, with the father having interim weekend custody. The father alleged the mother obstructed contact and filed an Execution Petition (E.P. No.7 of 2023) to implement the decree. The mother subsequently filed an application (I.A. No.865 of 2023) to modify the decree regarding interim custody. The Family Court allowed the father's E.P., but the High Court, in an appeal by the mother, remanded the matter back to the Family Court to decide both the E.P. and I.A. afresh.

The Appellant-father argued that a minor child needs the love of both parents, the High Court erred, and the mother's 'tutoring' caused the child's animosity. The Respondent-mother contended that the child was unhappy with the father's lack of interest and that custody issues could not be raised in an execution petition. The Supreme Court, while noting the child's disinclination to meet the father and the mother's attempts to stall, emphasized that the paramount consideration is the child's welfare. The Court decided not to 'interdict' the High Court's remand but issued interim directions for the father's visitation rights every Sunday from 4:00 PM to 6:00 PM, with a caretaker, at the father's residence in the child's city. The Family Court was directed to conclude the matter within three months. The appeal was disposed of accordingly.

petitioner_key_arguments: A minor child requires the love and affection of both parents, and divorce should not deprive the child of care from both parents.
The High Court ought to have considered that the minor child used to enjoy his father's company.
The child's animosity towards the Appellant is due to the Respondent's tutoring.
The child became increasingly agitated during Court visits.
respondent_key_arguments: The child was unhappy with the Appellant for not spending enough time during visitations.
The Appellant's lack of interest is evident in video calls where he blamed the child, causing trauma.
The Appellant cannot raise issues regarding custody in an execution petition.
The mechanism for custody-related rights is prescribed in The Guardians and Wards Act, 1890.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court's reasoning centered on the paramount consideration of the child's welfare and well-being, leading to the decision to uphold the remand for a fresh consideration of both the execution and modification petitions, while simultaneously granting interim visitation rights to the father to ensure the child's contact with both parents.

outcome.relief_granted: The matter is remanded back to the Family Court with a direction to conclude the matter expeditiously within three months. Interim visitation rights are granted to the Appellant-father every Sunday from 04:00 PM to 06:00 PM, with the son accompanied by a caretaker to the father's house in the child's city. The caretaker must remain present but not in the immediate company of the father or his family members. The son is to return to the mother at 06:00 PM with the caretaker.

precedents_cited: Amyra Dwivedi (Minor) through her mother, Pooja Sharma Dwivedi v Abhinav Dwivedi, (2021) 4 SCC 698
Nil Ratan Kundu v Abhijit Kundu, 2008 (9) SCC 413
Nithya Anand Raghavan v State (NCT of Delhi), (2017) 8 SCC 454
Yashita Sahu v State of Rajasthan, (2020) 3 SCC 67

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that in child custody matters, the paramount consideration is the welfare and well-being of the minor child. Courts exercise parens patriae jurisdiction, requiring a human touch and consideration of the child's comfort, health, education, and moral/ethical values. While execution of a decree might typically proceed, the potential negative impact on a child's tender mind necessitates a fresh, combined consideration of both execution and modification petitions.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed the Respondent-mother's conduct in attempting to obstruct the visitation rights granted to the Appellant-father. It also noted the minor son's consistent stand of being disturbed by visits to his father. The Court warned that obstruction of the interim arrangement by the Respondent-mother would lead to necessary consequences in law, including coercive measures.

special_directions.special_directions: The Family Court is directed to conclude the matter expeditiously and latest within three months from the date of communication of the judgment. The parties are directed to cooperate. If the Respondent-mother obstructs the implementation of the interim arrangement, the Appellant-father may apprise the Supreme Court, and necessary consequences, including coercive measures, will follow.
special_directions.interim_orders: Till the Family Court decides the modification and execution petitions, the Appellant-father shall have visitation rights every Sunday from 04:00 PM to 06:00 PM. The minor son will go with his caretaker to the father's house, where the caretaker must remain present (not in immediate company of the father or his family). The son will return to the mother at 06:00 PM with the caretaker. These visitation rights shall be at the place/city where the minor son resides. If the father lacks permanent accommodation, he must intimate the mother of his hotel for visitation.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 8968 OF 2013

case_details.subject_matter: Challenge to the High Court's dismissal of a writ petition seeking release of land from acquisition and impugning the State's rejection of the release request.

judgements.case_summary: The appellant, Kishore Chhabra, challenged an order passed by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana, which dismissed his writ petition against the State's rejection of his representation for the release of his land from acquisition. The land, measuring 386 sq. yards and 3078 sq. yards at Sultanpur, Sonipat, Haryana, was purchased by the appellant in 1986 and was part of a larger acquisition initiated by the State of Haryana in 1992 for residential and commercial development. The appellant claimed continuous physical possession and operation of a factory on the land since 1970, arguing discrimination as other similarly situated lands were released, and that his case fell under the State's release policies. The respondent State contended that the appellant's request suffered from delay and laches, possession had already been taken, and the appellant lacked a valid Change of Land Use (CLU) certificate, which was a statutory prerequisite. The State also highlighted significant development expenditure incurred in the acquired area. The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's plea for release of land on grounds of discrimination, finding that the appellant did not possess a valid CLU and that other released lands were distinguishable. However, acknowledging the appellant's continuous physical possession and the operation of a factory, the Court, exercising its power under Article 142, directed that compensation be calculated for the appellant under the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, as a special case not to be treated as a precedent.

petitioner_key_arguments: Discrimination, as other similarly situated lands from the same notification and village were released.
Continuous operation of a factory on the subject land since 1970, falling within the parameters of State Government's policy dated 26.10.2007 for land release.
The rejection order dated 17.08.2010 is unsustainable as it was passed without assigning any reason.
respondent_key_arguments: The writ petition suffers from huge delay and laches.
Possession of the land having already been taken, its release is not legally permissible.
The appellant does not possess a valid Change of Land Use (CLU) certificate, which is a fundamental prerequisite for land release.
The land falls within a designated green belt, and substantial government expenditure has already been incurred on development.
The appellant did not prefer objections under Section 5-A of the Act.
The appellant claimed compensation, not release, in response to the Section 9 notice.
Previous writ petitions bar the current one on principles of res judicata.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court largely accepted the respondent's arguments against the release of land, particularly regarding the lack of a valid CLU and the distinction from other released lands. However, the court, exercising its power under Article 142, granted the petitioner relief in the form of compensation due to continuous physical possession, which was a partial win for the petitioner on a different ground.

outcome.relief_granted: Compensation payable to the appellant should be calculated under the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, as on the date of commencement of the said Act.

acts_cited: Punjab Scheduled Roads & Controlled Areas Restrictions of ‘CLU’ Unregulated Development Act, 1963
Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013
precedents_cited: Sube Singh vs. State of Haryana
Hari Ram Vs. State of Haryana
Sham Lal vs State of Punjab
Haryana State Industrial Development Corporation vs. Shakuntla
Raghbir Singh Sehrawat vs. State of Haryana
Patasi Devi vs. State of Haryana
Usha Stud & Agricultural Farms (P) Ltd. vs. State of Haryana
Women's Education Trust vs. State of Haryana
Siemens Engg. & Mfg. Co. of India Ltd. vs. Union of India
State of Punjab vs. Bandeep Singh
constitutional_provisions: Article 142

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The court rejected the appellant's prayer for release of land primarily because the appellant did not possess a valid Change of Land Use (CLU) certificate, which is a statutory mandate, and the plea of discrimination was not sustained as other cases were distinguishable. However, recognizing the appellant's continuous physical possession and operation of a factory, the court exercised its power under Article 142 to direct compensation under the 2013 Act as a special case.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The order for compensation is made on the peculiar facts of this case and is not to be treated as a precedent to be relied upon in other cases.

special_directions.special_directions: Compensation payable to the appellant should be calculated under the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, as on the date of commencement of the said Act. This order is made on the peculiar facts of the case and is not to be treated as a precedent to be relied upon in other cases.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (Arising out of SLP(C) No. 19139 of 2024)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the validity of the 18-month Diploma in Elementary Education (D. El. Ed.) obtained through the National Institute of Open Schooling (NIOS) for in-service teachers, in light of previous Supreme Court judgments, for the purpose of appointment as teachers.

judgements.case_summary: This case addresses the validity of the 18-month D. El. Ed. (ODL) program from NIOS for in-service teachers. The appellants, who completed this program, challenged a High Court decision that deemed it invalid for recruitment to the post of Assistant Teachers. The Supreme Court, referencing its previous judgments in Jaiveer Singh and Viswanath, clarified that the 18-month D. El. Ed. was a specific, one-time provision by NCTE and MHRD to allow in-service untrained teachers employed as of August 10, 2017, to acquire minimum qualifications by March 31, 2019. The Court held that teachers meeting these specific criteria are valid diploma holders for the purpose of continuing in service, promotional avenues, and for applying to other institutions. Consequently, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, quashed the High Court's orders, and directed the respondent-authorities to consider the candidature of eligible appellants who were in-service as on 10th August 2017 and completed the 18 months D. El. Ed. (ODL) programme through NIOS before 1st April 2019, within three months. The ruling emphasizes the specific context and limited applicability of the 18-month NIOS D. El. Ed. program.

petitioner_key_arguments: All appellants were in-service as on 10th August 2017 and completed the 18 months D. El. Ed. programme through NIOS before 31st March 2019.
The judgment of Jaiveer Singh does not oust them as it covers only teachers who failed to fulfill the requirements.
The order in Viswanath clarified that such teachers (in employment as on 10th August 2017 and completed 18 months diploma) would be treated as valid diploma holders.
NCTE relaxed certain provisions of the 2014 NCTE Regulations, reducing the course duration to 18 months for in-service teachers.
respondent_key_arguments: The 18 months D. El. Ed. programme through NIOS was only to bring in-service untrained teachers at par with eligibility requirements, not for fresh appointments.
Appellants who completed the 18 months D. El. Ed. programme after the cut-off date of 31st March 2019 cannot be treated at par with the 2 years D. El. Ed. programme.
Other requirements like clearing the Teacher Eligibility Test (TET) must also be fulfilled for appointment.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that in-service teachers as of 10th August 2017 who completed the 18-month D. El. Ed. through NIOS before 1st April 2019 are valid diploma holders for the purpose of applying in other institutions or for promotional avenues, and their candidature for appointment should be considered.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal is allowed. The judgment and order dated 29th February 2024 passed by the learned Single Judge of the High Court is quashed and set aside. The judgment and order dated 24th July 2024 passed by the Division Bench of the High Court is quashed and set aside. The Writ Petition being W.P.A. No. 16118 of 2023 is dismissed. It is clarified that such of the teachers who were in employment as on 10th August 2017 and who completed the 18 months D. El. Ed. (ODL) programme through NIOS before 1st April 2019 shall be considered as valid diploma holders for the purpose of applying in other institutions and/or for promotional avenues. The respondent-authorities are directed to consider the candidature of such of the appellants who were in-service as on 10th August 2017 and who, on verification, are found to satisfy the eligibility criteria, within a period of three months from today.

acts_cited: The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009
precedents_cited: Jaiveer Singh & Ors. vs. The State of Uttarakhand & Ors.
Viswanath & Ors. vs. The State of Uttarakhand & Ors.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that the 18-month D. El. Ed. (ODL) program through NIOS was a specific, one-time relaxation and window provided by the NCTE, under the MHRD's directive, exclusively for in-service untrained elementary teachers who were employed as of 10th August 2017, to acquire minimum qualifications by 31st March 2019. Therefore, teachers who met these precise conditions are deemed valid diploma holders, distinguishing their qualification from the standard 2-year D. El. Ed. program for general recruitment.

special_directions.special_directions: The respondent-authorities are directed to consider the candidature of such of the appellants who were in-service as on 10th August 2017 and who, on verification, are found to satisfy the eligibility criteria, within a period of three months from today.

case_identification.petitioner_name: KRISHNA DEVI @ SABITRI DEVI (RANI) M/S S.R. ENGINEERING CONSTRUCTION
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 47 OF 2025 Arising out of SLP (C) No. 10621/2024

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the interpretation of "notice of filing the award" under the Arbitration Act, 1940, to determine the commencement of the limitation period for filing objections to an arbitral award.

judgements.case_summary:
This case addresses the crucial question of when the limitation period for filing objections to an arbitral award commences under the Arbitration Act, 1940, specifically concerning the interpretation of "notice of filing the award." The appellant's husband secured an arbitration award on 31.05.2022. An application under Section 17 of the Act to pronounce judgment according to the award was dismissed by lower courts as premature, holding that the limitation period for objections began only upon formal notice on 18.11.2022.

The appellant argued that the limitation period commenced on 21.09.2022, when the District Judge ordered the respondents to clear the arbitrator's fees, making them aware of the award's existence. Therefore, the Section 17 application filed on 10.11.2022 was not premature, as the objection period (30 days from 21.09.2022) had already expired on 20.10.2022. The respondents contended that formal notice on 18.11.2022 was required to trigger the limitation.

The Supreme Court, relying on precedents, held that "notice of filing the award" does not necessitate a formal written notice but rather sufficient awareness or knowledge of the award's existence and accessibility. The court found that the respondents were aware of the award's filing on 21.09.2022. Consequently, the limitation period for filing objections expired on 20.10.2022, making the appellant's Section 17 application on 10.11.2022 valid and not premature. The Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the lower court orders, and directed the District Judge to expeditiously dispose of the appellant's application.

petitioner_key_arguments: The limitation for filing objections to an award began on 21.09.2022, when the District Judge directed respondents to pay the arbitrator's fees, making them aware of the award's existence.
The 30-day limitation period for objections expired on 20.10.2022, so the Section 17 application filed on 10.11.2022 was not premature but filed after the limitation had run out.
The essential requirement of Section 14(2) of the 1940 Act is that the award-debtor merely has to have information that the award has been filed; formal notice is not strictly required.
The respondents were fully aware of the making of the Award by 21.09.2022, and the law does not require a formal notice of the making of the Award, as against knowledge/notice of the Award.
respondent_key_arguments: The limitation period for filing objections commenced on 18.11.2022, when the respondents received a formal notice of the award from the District Court.
The appellant's application filed on 10.11.2022 was premature as it was made before the expiry of the 30-day period reckoned from 18.11.2022.
Section 14(2) of the 1940 Act requires a formal notice of the award's filing, and mere communication or awareness is insufficient.
The order dated 21.09.2022 merely stated that fees needed to be cleared for the award to be published, and did not constitute a formal notice of filing.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the limitation period for filing objections to an arbitral award commences from the date of awareness or knowledge of the award's existence, rather than requiring a formal notice of filing. The court found that the respondents were sufficiently aware of the award's filing on 21.09.2022, making the appellant's subsequent application valid.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal is allowed, and the order dated 27.03.2024 passed by the High Court in Civil Revision Petition No. 138/2022 is set aside. The District Judge, Sonitpur, Tezpur, is directed to take up and dispose of Misc. (J) 61 of 2022 as expeditiously as possible, preferably within a period of five months from the date of receipt of this judgment.

acts_cited: Article 119 of the Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1963
Article 119(b), Schedule I of the Limitation Act, 1963
precedents_cited: Nilkantha Sidramappa Ningashetti v. Kashinath Somanna Ningashetti, 2 1961 SCC OnLine SC 75
Deo Narain Choudhury v. Shree Narain Choudhury. 3 (2000) 8 SCC 626
Ch. Ramalinga Reddy v. Superintending Engineer, 4 (1999) 9 SCC 610
Food Corporation of India v. E. Kuttappan, 5 (1993) 3 SCC 445
Indian Rayon Corporation Ltd. v. Raunaq and Co. (P) Ltd. 6 (1988) 4 SCC 31
Bharat Coking Coal Ltd. v C.K. Ahuja 7 1995 Supp (1) SCC 744

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle established is that for the purpose of Section 14(2) of the Arbitration Act, 1940, and the commencement of the limitation period under Article 119(b) of the Limitation Act, 1963, "notice of filing the award" does not necessarily require a formal written notice from the court. Instead, mere awareness or knowledge of the award's existence and its accessibility by the parties is sufficient to trigger the limitation period for filing objections.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed that a contrary interpretation, insisting on formal notice despite actual awareness, would allow award-debtors to delay arbitration by insisting on procedural nuances, thereby undermining the speedy intent of the Arbitration Act, 1940.

special_directions.special_directions: The District Judge, Sonitpur, Tezpur, is directed to take up and dispose of the Misc. (J) 61 of 2022 as expeditiously as possible, preferably within a period of five months from the date of receipt of this judgment.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO(S). 4806 OF 2011

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the validity of appointments made for the post of school teachers (Shiksha Karmi Grade III) in 1998, focusing on the conflict between the principles of natural justice: rule against bias and the right to a fair hearing.

judgements.case_summary:
This Supreme Court case, Krishnadatt Awasthy vs State Of M.P, addresses the validity of appointments of school teachers (Shiksha Karmi Grade III) made in 1998. The appointments were challenged by an unsuccessful candidate, Archana Mishra, alleging nepotism, corruption, and bias due to relatives of selection committee members being selected. The Collector initially quashed the select list without providing a hearing to the appointees, a decision upheld by the Commissioner and the High Court. The matter reached the Supreme Court due to a split verdict between Justice JK Maheshwari, who upheld the cancellation based on bias, and Justice KV Vishwanathan, who found a breach of the right to a fair hearing.

The appellants (appointees) argued that their appointments were cancelled without a hearing, they were not made parties to the initial challenge, and no relatives influenced the selection. The respondents contended that the presence of close relatives vitiated the process and that any lack of hearing was cured at the revisional stage. The Court, endorsing Justice KV Vishwanathan's view, found a gross violation of the principle of audi alteram partem, emphasizing that procedural fairness is inherently valuable and a constitutional requirement. It held that a fundamental breach of natural justice at the initial stage cannot generally be cured at the appellate stage. Considering the 25-year time lag and the appointees having served under interim orders, the Court deemed a fresh inquiry impractical and unjust. Consequently, the appeals were allowed, and the Division Bench's judgment was set aside.

petitioner_key_arguments: Appointments were cancelled without affording them any hearing.
Appellants were not arrayed as parties in the initial challenge.
No relatives of candidates participated or awarded marks to influence the selection.
The selection was fair, and intervention was unmerited.
respondent_key_arguments: Section 40(c) of the Adhiniyam, 1993, prohibits office bearers from causing financial gain to relatives.
Presence of close relatives in the selection process vitiated it.
Non-adherence to audi alteram partem was cured by proceedings before the Commissioner, where appellants had full opportunity.
Reasonable likelihood of bias was established by the close relationship between Committee members and selected candidates who received high marks.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioners' arguments that there was a gross violation of the principle of audi alteram partem due to the lack of notice and opportunity to be heard at the initial stage, and that such a fundamental breach could not be cured at the appellate stage. The court also implicitly accepted that the selection should not be set aside given the long passage of time and service under interim orders.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal(s) were allowed, and the judgment of the Division Bench was set aside, effectively upholding the appointments of the appellants.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle established is that a gross violation of the principle of audi alteram partem, specifically the denial of notice and opportunity to be heard at the initial stage, renders a decision invalid. Such a fundamental breach of procedural fairness, which holds inherent value and is a constitutional requirement, cannot generally be cured at the appellate stage.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that remanding the matter for a fresh inquiry after 25 years, during which the appointees had continuously held office and performed their duties under interim orders, would be an impractical exercise and would result in an injustice to the appointees, especially since one had already superannuated.
judicial_reasoning.dissenting_opinion: Justice JK Maheshwari's opinion, which upheld the cancellation of appointments based on the rule against bias and considered non-impleadment a useless formality, was not endorsed by the majority of the bench.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (Arising out of SLP(Crl.)No.13277 of 2023)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns an appeal seeking to quash an FIR lodged under Sections 366, 376, and 506 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, against the appellant, who claims to be legally married to the alleged victim, arguing that no offense of rape can be sustained under Exception 2 of Section 375 IPC.

judgements.case_summary: This case involves an appeal against an order of the High Court of Punjab and Haryana, which dismissed a petition to quash FIR No. 148 of 2022. The FIR was initially lodged by Respondent No. 2, the cousin of Respondent No. 3 (the victim), alleging abduction of the victim by the appellant. The appellant contended that he and Respondent No. 3 had married on 15.06.2022 with mutual consent and had even obtained a protection order from the High Court. Subsequently, Respondent No. 3 recorded a statement under Section 164 Cr.P.C., alleging rape and forced marriage, leading to the addition of Sections 363, 120B, and 376 IPC against the appellant and his family. A Special Investigation Team (SIT) found that the victim had solemnized the marriage with consent, resulting in the deletion of Section 366 IPC, leaving only Sections 376 and 506 IPC against the appellant. The Supreme Court noted the non-appearance of Respondent No. 2 and 3 despite notice. The appellant argued that as the legally wedded husband, Exception 2 to Section 375 IPC applied, meaning sexual intercourse with his wife could not be termed as rape. The Court concurred, finding no prima facie case for rape given the consensual marriage and the victim's subsequent conduct. Consequently, the appeal was allowed, and the FIR and all consequential proceedings were quashed.

petitioner_key_arguments: He is the legally wedded husband of Respondent No. 3.
No offence under Section 376 IPC is made out against him due to Exception No. 2 appended to Section 375 IPC.
Respondent No. 3's written statement in the restitution of conjugal rights case did not contain any allegations pertaining to rape.
A protection petition was jointly filed by him and Respondent No. 3, seeking protection as they had married of their own free will.
The SIT investigation found that the victim solemnized the marriage with consent, leading to the deletion of Section 366 IPC.
The non-appearance of Respondent No. 2 and 3 despite sufficient notice indicates that it is a 'dead case'.
respondent_key_arguments: The High Court dismissed the quashing petition, holding that it lacked merit and required evaluation of evidence and adjudication by the Trial Court.
Respondent No. 3 recorded a statement under Section 164 Cr.P.C. alleging rape and forced marriage.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments that he was the legally wedded husband of the victim, and therefore, under Exception 2 of Section 375 IPC, no charge of rape could be sustained. The court also noted the consensual nature of the marriage as found by the SIT and the non-appearance of the respondents, indicating a lack of a prima facie case.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned order of the High Court was set aside. FIR No. 148 of 2022 dated 14.06.2022 and all consequential proceedings arising therefrom were quashed.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that sexual intercourse by a man with his own wife, where the marriage is valid and consensual, does not constitute rape under Exception 2 of Section 375 of the Indian Penal Code. The court found that the victim had solemnized the marriage with the appellant with her own consent, and thus, no prima facie case for rape could be made out against the legally wedded husband.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed that the conduct of Respondent No. 2 and 3 in failing to enter appearance despite sufficient notice was reflective of the fact that it is a dead case where no purpose shall be served in continuing the criminal proceedings alleging charges of rape against the appellant.
