case_identification.petitioner_name: M/S C And C Constructions Ltd
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 6657 OF 2023

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns an appeal against a High Court judgment upholding an arbitral award that rejected claims for damages due to construction delays, based on a contractual clause (49.5 GCC) barring such claims, and the scope of interference under Section 37 of the Arbitration Act.

judgements.case_summary: This appeal arises from a judgment of the High Court of Delhi which upheld an arbitral award rejecting claims for damages made by M/s C And C Constructions Ltd (appellant) against Ircon International Ltd (respondent). The dispute originated from an agreement for the construction of five Road Over Bridges (ROBs) in Rajasthan, where delays occurred, attributed by the appellant to the respondent. The appellant sought extensions of time and later claimed Rs. 44.11 crores in damages. The Arbitral Tribunal, and subsequently the Single Judge and Division Bench of the High Court, rejected these claims based on clause 49.5 of the General Conditions of Contract (GCC), which bars claims for damages or compensation due to employer-caused delays, allowing only for extensions of time. The appellant argued that clause 49.5 was contrary to public policy and the Indian Contract Act, 1872, and that the respondent had waived this clause. The respondent contended that clause 49.5 and clause 12 of the Special Conditions of Contract were valid limitation of liability clauses, and the appellant, by seeking extensions under clause 49.5 and providing undertakings not to claim damages beyond escalation, had made an irreversible election. The Supreme Court, in its 'OUR VIEW' section, affirmed that the appellant had acted upon clause 49.5, sought extensions, and given undertakings. It rejected the argument of waiver and noted that the contentions regarding Sections 23 and 28 of the Contract Act were raised for the first time in appeal. Emphasizing the limited scope of interference under Section 37 of the Arbitration Act, the Court found no merit in the appeal.

petitioner_key_arguments: The award of the Arbitral Tribunal was contrary to public policy and suffered from patent illegality.
A clause prohibiting the payment of damages, like clause 49.5, could not be enforced.
The Arbitral Tribunal and the learned Single Judge failed to appreciate crucial aspects.
Parties to the contract cannot contract against the Indian Contract Act, 1872.
The finding that clause 49.5 aims to protect the interests of PSUs and the Government is illegal.
The respondent had waived clause 49.5.
The validity of clause 49.5 ought to have been examined in the light of Sections 23 and 28 of the Contract Act.
respondent_key_arguments: Clause 49.5 of GCC read with clause 12 of the Special Conditions of Contract (SCC) are limitation of liability clauses.
These clauses are not in conflict with either Section 23 or Section 28 of the Contract Act.
The appellant made an irreversible election to accept the extension of time in terms of the agreed scheme without payment of liquidated damages.
The appellant gave undertakings not to make any additional claim for compensation and/or damages beyond escalation.
The appellant lost its right to challenge clause 49.5.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the respondent's arguments that clause 49.5 was a valid limitation of liability clause, that the appellant was estopped from claiming damages due to its prior actions (seeking extensions under the clause and giving undertakings), and that the scope of interference in an appeal under Section 37 of the Arbitration Act is limited.

precedents_cited: Pam Developments Pvt. Ltd. v. State of West Bengal1 (2019) 8 SCC 112
ONGC v. Wig Brothers Builders and Engineers Private Limited2 (2010) 13 SCC 377
Larsen Air Conditioning and Refrigeration Company v. Union of India and Ors.3 (2023) 15 SCC 472
Associate Builders [Associate Builders v. DDA, (2015) 3 SCC 49 : (2015) 2 SCC (Civ) 204]
Konkan Railway Corporation Limited v. Chenab Bridge Project Undertaking4 (2023) 9 SCC 85
MMTC Ltd. v. Vedanta Ltd. [MMTC Ltd. v. Vedanta Ltd., (2019) 4 SCC 163 : (2019) 2 SCC (Civ) 293]
MANU/SC/1620/2009, Asian Techs Ltd. v. Union of India

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The court held that the appellant, by repeatedly invoking clause 49.5 for extensions of time and providing solemn undertakings not to claim damages beyond escalation, was estopped from challenging the validity of the clause or claiming damages. The court also reiterated the limited scope of interference in an appeal under Section 37 of the Arbitration Act, which cannot go beyond the restrictions laid down under Section 34.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed that the contentions regarding the validity of clause 49.5 in light of Sections 23 and 28 of the Contract Act, and the argument of waiver of clause 49.5, were raised for the first time in appeal and thus could not be entertained.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO.14157 OF 2024

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns an appeal against an NCDRC order directing a finance company to refund money to a complainant in a housing loan dispute, primarily examining whether the complainant qualifies as a 'consumer' and the existence of a Tripartite Agreement.

judgements.case_summary:
The appeal was filed by M/S Citicorp Finance (India) Limited against an NCDRC order directing them to refund Rs. 13,20,000/- with interest and litigation costs to Snehasis Nanda. The dispute arose from a housing loan transaction where Nanda sold a flat, and a borrower (Mr. Mubarak Vahid Patel) took a loan from Citicorp to purchase it. Nanda claimed a balance payment was due under an alleged Tripartite Agreement involving himself, the borrower, and Citicorp. The NCDRC had allowed Nanda's complaint, finding Citicorp liable.
Citicorp argued that Nanda was not a 'consumer' under the Consumer Protection Act, as there was no privity of contract between them. They denied the existence of a signed Tripartite Agreement involving them and stated their contract was solely with the borrower. They also raised objections regarding the complaint being time-barred and the non-joinder of the borrower as a necessary party.
The Supreme Court analyzed two main issues: whether Nanda was a 'consumer' and whether Citicorp was liable to disburse the entire sale consideration. The Court found that the NCDRC had erred in presuming the existence of a Tripartite Agreement without sufficient proof and that the onus was on Nanda to prove it. It reiterated that without privity of contract, a party cannot be termed a 'consumer' under the Act. The Court also noted the NCDRC's failure to address the limitation period and the non-joinder of the borrower.
Ultimately, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the NCDRC's Impugned Order. It concluded that Nanda was not a 'consumer' of Citicorp, and there was no basis to hold Citicorp liable for the claimed amount.

petitioner_key_arguments: Respondent is not a 'consumer' under Section 2(1)(d) of the Act, as there was no service provided by the appellant to the respondent.
The NCDRC wrongly concluded the existence of a Tripartite Agreement without evidence; no such agreement signed by the appellant was filed.
The appellant only had privity of contract with the borrower, and the payment to ICICI Bank was on the borrower's instruction, not evidence of a relationship with the respondent.
The borrower was a necessary and proper party to the complaint, and the NCDRC failed to adjudicate on this objection.
The complaint was barred by limitation, and the NCDRC failed to provide reasoning for condoning delay.
respondent_key_arguments: The Impugned Order correctly noted evidence and materials, finding the appellant guilty of deficiency in service and unfair trade practices.
The Home Loan was approved based on the Tripartite Agreement and Agreement for Sale, implying the appellant's knowledge and involvement.
The Supreme Court's previous order (06.09.2019) held the respondent to be a 'consumer' prima facie.
The appellant deliberately misled all fora to hide the Tripartite Agreement and escape liability.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the respondent was not a 'consumer' due to lack of privity of contract, the non-existence of a proven Tripartite Agreement involving the appellant, the complaint being time-barred, and the non-joinder of a necessary party (the borrower).

outcome.relief_granted: The Impugned Order dated 19.01.2023 passed by the learned National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, New Delhi is set aside.

precedents_cited: Indian Oil Corporation v Consumer Protection Council, Kerala, (1994) 1 SCC 397
Janpriya Buildestate Pvt. Ltd. v Amit Soni, 2021 SCC OnLine SC 1269
Tata Motors Limited v Antonio Paulo Vaz, (2021) 18 SCC 545
Udit Narain Singh Malpaharia v Additional Member Board of Revenue, Bihar, 1963 Supp (1) SCR 676
King v. Electricity Commissioners [(1924) 1 KB 171]
King v. London County Council [(1931) 2 KB 215, 243]
M Hemalatha Devi v B Udayasri, (2024) 4 SCC 255
Emaar-3 [Emaar MGF Land Ltd. v. Aftab Singh, (2019) 12 SCC 751: (2018) 5 SCC (Civ) 652]
National Seeds Corpn. [National Seeds Corpn. Ltd. v M. Madhusudhan Reddy, (2012) 2 SCC 506: (2012) 1 SCC (Civ) 908]
constitutional_provisions: Article 226 of the Constitution

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The Court held that for a complainant to be considered a 'consumer' under the Consumer Protection Act, there must be privity of contract with the opposite party. In this case, the respondent failed to prove the existence of a Tripartite Agreement involving the appellant, and thus, no contractual relationship or deficiency of service could be established. Additionally, the complaint was found to be time-barred, and a necessary party (the borrower) was not joined.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that while the Consumer Protection Act is a welfare legislation, the existence of an obligation under a contract is a sine qua non for a consumer to successfully prosecute a case. It also discussed the arbitrability of disputes under welfare legislation, noting that the consumer has the choice to opt for public fora over arbitration.

special_directions.special_directions: Parties to bear their own costs. The judgment shall not impact proceedings, if any, inter-se borrower and respondent, and shall not relax/extend any period of limitation for resort to lawful remedies.

case_identification.respondent_name: DISTRICT DEPUTY REGISTRAR, CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETIES (3), MUMBAI & ORS.
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (@ SLP(CIVIL) NO.26654 OF 2023)

respondent_advocates: learned counsel appearing for respondent No.2- Society

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the validity of an order by the Competent Authority granting unilateral assignment of leasehold rights to a Co-operative Housing Society, specifically regarding the Competent Authority's jurisdiction and the principle of res judicata.

judgements.case_summary: This case involves an appeal against a Bombay High Court judgment that dismissed a writ petition filed by M/S Faime Makers Pvt. Ltd. The writ petition challenged an order dated 05.10.2021 by the District Deputy Registrar, Co-operative Societies (Competent Authority), which granted unilateral assignment of leasehold rights to Prakash Apartment Co-operative Housing Society Limited (respondent No.2-Society). Previously, the Competent Authority had dismissed the Society's first application (No.53 of 2020) on 22.02.2021, finding the issues complicated and directing the Society to resolve them in a Civil Court before re-applying. Despite this, the Society filed a second application (No.101 of 2021) for the same relief, which the Competent Authority allowed. The appellant argued that the second application was barred by res judicata, that the Competent Authority lacked the power to review its own order, and that the High Court misinterpreted the first order as granting unconditional liberty. The respondent contended that the High Court's interpretation was correct and the second application was distinct. The Supreme Court held that the first order did not grant unconditional liberty and required prior resolution of issues in a Civil Court. It emphasized that quasi-judicial authorities are bound by their final orders and the principle of res judicata. The Competent Authority, lacking review powers, erred in entertaining the second application. The Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment, and quashed the Competent Authority's order dated 05.10.2021, while clarifying that the Society could still re-apply after fulfilling the conditions of the first order.

petitioner_key_arguments: The Competent Authority dismissed the first application (No.53 of 2020) on 22.02.2021, directing the Society to approach a Civil Court for complicated issues; thus, the second application (No.101 of 2021) was not maintainable and barred by res judicata.
The Competent Authority, as a quasi-judicial body, lacked the power of review, and its order dated 05.10.2021 allowing the second application amounted to an unauthorized review of the first order.
On merits, the Competent Authority erred in granting relief as constructions were unauthorized, and no commencement certificate was obtained, precluding benefits under Section 11 of the 1963 Act.
Granting assignment for 1,361 sq.m. was unjustified when the building occupied only 870 sq.m.

The High Court committed a manifest error by incorrectly interpreting the first order (22.02.2021) as granting unconditional liberty, when it clearly required resolution of complications by a Civil Court first.
respondent_key_arguments: The High Court correctly appreciated and interpreted the first order dated 22.02.2021 as granting unconditional liberty to file a fresh application for the assignment of leasehold rights.

The second order dated 05.10.2021 did not amount to a review, as it dealt with an application seeking a distinct relief from the first application, and was filed under the liberty granted, to be dealt with on its own merits.
The issue relating to the demarcation of boundary (870 sq.m. vs 1361 sq.m.) was unsubstantiated before the High Court, and a subsequent City Survey Officer report cannot be relied upon.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments regarding the Competent Authority's lack of jurisdiction to review its own order, the applicability of res judicata to quasi-judicial bodies, and the High Court's incorrect interpretation of the first order were accepted by the Supreme Court.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal is allowed. The impugned order of the High Court is set aside. The writ petition is allowed. The order dated 05.10.2021 passed by the Competent Authority is quashed. The liberty granted in the first order dated 22.02.2021 to re-apply after resolving complications before the appropriate Court/Forum remains available to respondent No.2-Society.

acts_cited: Maharashtra Ownership of Flats (Regulation of the Promotion of Construction, Sale, Management and Transfer) Act, 1963
Section 5/11 of the Maharashtra Ownership of Flats (Regulation of the Promotion of Construction, Sale, Management and Transfer) Act, 1963
precedents_cited: Ujjam Bai vs. State of U.P.
Abdul Kuddus vs. Union of India and others

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: A quasi-judicial authority is bound by its previous orders once they attain finality and cannot review them without specific statutory power. The principle of res judicata applies to quasi-judicial bodies. An application dismissed with a specific direction to resolve issues in a civil court before re-applying cannot be re-entertained by the same authority without those conditions being met.

special_directions.special_directions: The liberty granted in the first order of the Competent Authority dated 22.02.2021, while rejecting Application No. 53 of 2020, would still be available to the respondent No.2-Society but only after getting the complications resolved/sorted out before the appropriate Court/Forum.

case_identification.petitioner_name: M/S FERRO CONCRETE CONSTRUCTION (INDIA) PVT. LTD.
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 ARISING OUT OF SLP (C) No. 7851 OF 2023

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns whether a contractual clause barring a contractor from claiming interest on payments or arrears constitutes an express bar on an arbitrator's power to grant pendente lite interest under the Arbitration Act, 1940.

judgements.case_summary: M/S Ferro Concrete Construction (appellant) was awarded a works contract by the State of Rajasthan (respondent) in 1988, which included Clause 22 stating the contractor was not entitled to claim interest on any payments or arrears. A dispute led to arbitration, resulting in an award dated 07.03.1995 for the appellant, including 15% pendente lite interest. The District Judge subsequently set aside the 15% interest, granting 9% simple interest instead, a decision upheld by the High Court on 06.01.2023, leading to this appeal. The core issue before the Supreme Court was whether Clause 22 constituted an express bar on the arbitrator's power to grant pendente lite interest under the Arbitration Act, 1940. The appellant argued that the clause did not explicitly exclude this power, relying on precedents advocating for strict construction of such clauses. The respondent contended that ouster clauses are interpreted similarly under both the 1940 and 1996 Arbitration Acts, and that narrower clauses could bar interest. The Supreme Court distinguished the interpretative approaches, emphasizing that under the 1940 Act, a "clear and express bar" is required to curtail an arbitrator's power to grant interest. It found that Clause 22, being a general bar on the contractor claiming interest, was insufficient to expressly bar the arbitrator's power. Consequently, the Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's judgment and granting 9% pendente lite interest to the appellant from 18.12.1991 to 07.03.1995, to be paid within 60 days.

petitioner_key_arguments: Clause 22 of the agreement does not specifically exclude the power of the arbitrator to grant pendente lite interest.
Relied on Reliance Cellulose Products Ltd Vs Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Limited and Pam (2018) 9 SCC 266 for the principle of strict construction of interest-barring clauses.
respondent_key_arguments: The interpretation of an ouster clause is the same under the 1940 Act and the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
Narrower contractual clauses have been treated as ouster clauses that bar pendente lite interest.
Reliance Cellulose (supra), relied upon by the appellant, was based on Engineers-De-Space-Age, which has been doubted in several cases.
The respondent has already paid a sum of Rs. 4.65 crores, of which Rs. 2.83 crores is the interest component, implying further pendente lite interest is not warranted.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that Clause 22 did not constitute an express, specific bar against the arbitrator's power to grant pendente lite interest under the Arbitration Act, 1940, applying the principle of strict construction.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned judgment of the High Court dated 06.01.2023 was set aside. 9% pendente lite interest was granted to the appellant from 18.12.1991 till 07.03.1995 (date of the arbitral award), to be paid within 60 days.

precedents_cited: Reliance Cellulose Products Ltd Vs Oil and Natural Gas Corporation Limited
Developments Private Limited v. State of West Bengal 3
Secretary, Irrigation Department, Government of Orissa v. G.C. Roy, (1992) 1 SCC 508
M.B. Patel & Co. v. ONGC, (2008) 8 SCC 251
Union of India v. Krafters Engg. & Leasing (P) Ltd., (2011) 7 SCC 279
Board of Trustees For The Port of Calcutta v. Engineers-De-Space-Age 7
Union of India v. Ambica Construction 8 (First Ambica case)
Executive Engineer, Dhenkanal Minor Irrigation Division v. N.C. Budharaj, (2001) 2 SCC 721
Sayeed Ahmed & Co. v. State of U.P., (2009) 12 SCC 26
Sree Kamatchi Amman Constructions v. Railways, (2010) 8 SCC 767
Union of India v. Bright Power Projects (India) (P) Ltd., (2015) 9 SCC 695
Chittaranjan Maity v. Union of India, (2017) 9 SCC 611
Garg Builders v. BHEL, (2022) 11 SCC 697
Madnani Construction Corpn. (P) Ltd. v. Union of India, (2010) 1 SCC 549
Tehri Hydro Development Corpn. Ltd. v. Jai Prakash Associates Ltd.15

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle established is that under the Arbitration Act, 1940, a contractual clause must contain a clear and express bar against the arbitrator's power to grant pendente lite interest for such power to be curtailed. A general clause merely stating that the contractor is not entitled to claim interest is insufficient to constitute an express bar on the arbitrator's jurisdiction.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed a significant difference in the interpretative approach to interest-barring clauses between the 1940 Act and the 1996 Act, noting that Section 31(7)(a) of the 1996 Act more readily sanctifies party autonomy in this regard. It also emphasized the importance of judicial precedents.

special_directions.special_directions: The Court directed the payment of 9% pendente lite interest from 18.12.1991 till 07.03.1995 (date of the arbitral award) within a period of 60 days.
special_directions.interim_orders: On 24.04.2023, while issuing notice in the special leave petition, the Court passed an order noting the petitioner's reliance on Reliance Cellulose Products Ltd and the argument that Clause 22 did not specifically exclude the arbitrator's power to grant pendente lite interest.

case_identification.respondent_name: STATE OF ANDHRA PRADESH AND ANOTHER
case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (Arising out of SLP (Crl.) No. 5067 of 2024)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns an appeal against the High Court's dismissal of a petition to quash criminal proceedings initiated under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, specifically challenging a summoning order issued by a Magistrate without providing reasons.

judgements.case_summary: The appeal arises from a complaint filed by the Drugs Inspector, Kurnool, against M/s. J.M. Laboratories and others, alleging the manufacture and sale of "Not of Standard Quality" drugs, in violation of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940. The trial court summoned the appellants, which was challenged in the High Court under Section 482 CrPC, but the petition was dismissed. The appellants argued violations of statutory provisions, that the case was barred by limitation under CrPC Section 468(2), non-compliance with CrPC Section 202, and crucially, that the Magistrate's summoning order was non-speaking and lacked reasons. The Supreme Court, relying on established precedents (e.g., Pepsi Foods Ltd., Sunil Bharti Mittal), emphasized that summoning an accused is a serious matter requiring the Magistrate to apply their mind and record reasons. Finding that the summoning order in this case was entirely non-speaking, the Court allowed the appeal, quashing both the High Court's judgment and the original summoning order and the proceedings arising therefrom. The decision reinforces the procedural requirement for reasoned orders in criminal proceedings.

petitioner_key_arguments: Violations of various statutory provisions.
Case barred by limitation in view of the provisions contained in Section 468(2) of the Cr.P.C. (complaint filed beyond three years from analytical report date).
Non-compliance of the provisions of Section 202 of Cr.P.C.
The learned Magistrate has issued the process without assigning any reasons.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that the Magistrate issued the process without assigning any reasons, making the summoning order a non-speaking one and thus unsustainable in law.

outcome.relief_granted: The present appeal is allowed. The impugned judgment and order dated 4th October 2023 passed by the High Court of Andhra Pradesh at Amravati in Criminal Petition No. 5766 of 2023 is quashed and set aside. The summoning order dated 19th July 2023 passed by the Trial Court in C.C. No. 1051 of 2023 and the proceedings arising therefrom are also quashed and set aside.

precedents_cited: Pepsi Foods Ltd. and Another v. Special Judicial Magistrate and Others (1998) 5 SCC 749
Sunil Bharti Mittal v. Central Bureau of Investigation (2015) 4 SCC 609
Mehmood Ul Rehman v. Khazir Mohammad Tunda and Others (2015) 12 SCC 420
Krishna Lal Chawla and Others v. State of Uttar Pradesh and Another (2021) 5 SCC 435
Lalankumar Singh and Others v. State of Maharashtra 2022 SCC OnLine SC 1383
INOX Air Products Limited Now Known as INOX Air Products Private Limited and Another v. The State of Andhra Pradesh (SLP (Crl.) No. 2345 of 2024)
Ashoke Mal Bafna (supra)

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that a Magistrate's order summoning an accused must reflect the application of mind and provide reasons, even if brief, for finding a prima facie case. A non-speaking summoning order, without any recorded reasons, is unsustainable in law and warrants being set aside.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: Summoning of an accused in a criminal case is a serious matter, and criminal law cannot be set into motion as a matter of course. The Magistrate must carefully scrutinize the evidence and determine if any offence is prima facie committed by the accused.

special_directions.special_directions: Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

case_identification.petitioner_name: M/S Jsw Ispat Special Products Limited
case_identification.case_number: CONTEMPT PETITION (CIVIL) NO. 629 OF 2023

case_details.subject_matter: This Contempt Petition concerns the alleged willful disobedience of a Supreme Court judgment regarding the extinguishment of pre-resolution plan claims under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, specifically concerning demand notices for taxes issued by state authorities.

judgements.case_summary: This Contempt Petition was filed by M/s JSW Ispat Special Products Limited (now M/s JSW Steel Limited) against Pratishtha Thakur Haritwal & Ors., alleging willful disobedience of the Supreme Court's judgment in 'Ghanshyam Mishra and Sons Private Limited v. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Limited and others'. The petitioner, having acquired Monnet Ispat and Energy Ltd. through an IBC resolution plan, faced demand notices from state tax authorities for sales tax, entry tax, and other dues pertaining to a period prior to the resolution plan's approval. The petitioner argued that these claims were extinguished by the approved resolution plan and the Ghanshyam Mishra judgment, which explicitly covered their case. The respondents contended that the Ghanshyam Mishra judgment was not applicable as the State of Chhattisgarh was not a party to the NCLT proceedings, and their claims were justified, while also tendering an unconditional apology. The Court reiterated its clear pronouncement in Ghanshyam Mishra that all claims, including statutory dues of Central/State/local authorities, not part of the resolution plan, stand extinguished upon approval. It noted that the petitioner's case was part of the batch considered in Ghanshyam Mishra and distinguished the 'Rainbow Papers Limited' case. The Court found the actions of the respondents contemptuous but accepted their unconditional apology, deciding not to take stern action. Consequently, the demand notices and all proceedings pursuant thereto were declared illegal, quashed, and set aside.

petitioner_key_arguments: The respondents' actions in initiating proceedings for dues not part of the Resolution Plan are contemptuous and violate the law laid down in Ghanshyam Mishra (supra).
Once a Resolution Plan is approved, all claims not included are frozen and binding on all stakeholders, including Central, State, and local authorities.
Respondents proceeded with recovery despite being informed of the Ghanshyam Mishra judgment and its specific applicability to the Petitioner Company.
Respondents failed to file claims during the resolution process despite public announcement, making their demands belated and raised after Resolution Plan approval.
The approval of a Resolution Plan leads to a 'clean slate' for the Successful Resolution Applicant.
respondent_key_arguments: The demand notices were issued in good faith and not to undermine the dignity of the Court.
The judgment in Ghanshyam Mishra (supra) was not applicable as neither the State of Chhattisgarh nor any of its authorities were made parties in the insolvency proceedings before the NCLT.
The learned NCLT could not have passed an order ignoring all government dues, including indirect taxes.
The State was entitled to its dues for the period between 1st April 2017 and 30th June 2017.
The Petitioner Company's Miscellaneous Application seeking clarification of the Ghanshyam Mishra judgment was rejected, making the present Contempt Petition untenable.
Unconditional apology tendered for the actions.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments prevailed. The Court found the actions of the respondents contemptuous, reiterating that claims not part of an approved resolution plan, including statutory dues, stand extinguished. The demand notices issued by the respondents were quashed and set aside.

outcome.relief_granted: The demand notices issued by the contemnors on the Petitioner Company and all proceedings pursuant thereto are held to be illegal and the same are quashed and set aside. The contempt petition is disposed of by accepting the unconditional apology of the contemnors.

acts_cited: Gujarat Value Added Tax Act, 2003, Section 48
precedents_cited: Ghanshyam Mishra and Sons Private Limited v. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Limited and others
State Tax Officer v. Rainbow Papers Limited (2023) 9 SCC 545
Dena Bank vs. Bhikhabhai Prabhudas Parekh and Co. & Ors. (2000) 5 SCC 694
Committee of Creditors of Essar Steel India Limited through Authorised Signatory v. Satish Kumar Gupta and others
Innoventive Industries Ltd. vs. ICICI Bank & Anr. (2018) 1 SCC 407
K. Shashidhar v. Indian Overseas Bank and Others (2019) 12 SCC 150
Maharashtra Seamless Limited v. Padmanabhan Venkatesh and others (2020) 11 SCC 467
Karad Urban Cooperative Bank Ltd. vs. Swwapnil Bhingardevay & Ors. (2020) 9 SCC 729
Kalpraj Dharamshi and Another vs. Kotak Investment Advisors Limited and Another (2021) SCC OnLine SC 204
K.N. Rajakumar v. V. Nagarajan and others (2022) 4 SCC 617
Ruchi Soya Industries Limited and others v. Union of India and others (2022) 6 SCC 343
Ajay Kumar Radheyshyam Goenka v. Tourism Finance Corporation of India Limited (2023) 10 SCC 545 = 2023 SCC OnLine SC 266
Standard Chartered Bank v. Satish Kumar Gupta, 2019 SCC OnLine NCLAT 388
constitutional_provisions: Article 129 of the Constitution of India
Article 142 of the Constitution of India

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that once a resolution plan is duly approved by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 31 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, all claims, including statutory dues owed to the Central Government, any State Government, or any local authority, which are not part of the resolution plan, shall stand extinguished. Any proceedings initiated for such pre-resolution plan claims, especially after a clear Supreme Court pronouncement, are illegal and contemptuous.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: A successful resolution applicant cannot suddenly be faced with “undecided” claims after the resolution plan submitted by him has been accepted, as this would amount to a hydra head popping up which would throw into uncertainty amounts payable by a prospective resolution applicant. Even if a stakeholder is not a party to the proceedings before the NCLT, if they do not raise their claim before the Interim Resolution Professional/Resolution Professional, the approved Resolution Plan would still be binding on them.

special_directions.special_directions: The demand notices issued by the contemnors on the Petitioner Company and all proceedings pursuant thereto are held to be illegal and the same are quashed and set aside. The contempt petition is disposed of by accepting the unconditional apology of the contemnors.
special_directions.interim_orders: Notice was issued in the Contempt Petition on 20th February 2023, returnable in four weeks, and the personal presence of the alleged contemnors was dispensed with until specific orders were passed.

case_identification.petitioner_name: M/S Maxim India Integrated Circuit Design (P) Ltd.
case_identification.case_number: Civil Appeal Nos. 3650-3655 of 2018, Civil Appeal No. 3656 of 2018

case_details.subject_matter: The case involves appeals against a common judgment of the High Court of Karnataka concerning land disputes, specifically challenging the condonation of a 1378-day delay in filing a writ appeal, and the merits of land claims, mutation orders, and tenancy rights under the Karnataka Land Reforms Act, 1961.

judgements.case_summary:
This judgment addresses a set of seven Civil Appeals (Nos. 3650-3655 of 2018 and 3656 of 2018) filed by M/s Maxim India Integrated Circuit Design (P) Ltd. against a common judgment and order of the High Court of Karnataka dated 26.02.2010. The core dispute revolves around land in Sy. No.49/3 of Jakkasandra village, which the appellant purchased from Sh. Basant Kumar Patil. The respondent, Andappa, had filed a writ appeal (WA No.206 of 2007) against an order directing mutation in favor of Basant Kumar Patil, with a significant delay of 1378 days being condoned by the High Court.

The appellant argued that the condonation of such an inordinate delay was erroneous and that the underlying tenancy petition (LRF No.835/74-75) had attained finality as early as 1981. They further contended that the respondent had failed to disclose crucial facts and consequential orders, and had engaged in manipulation, including changing names. The respondent, conversely, argued that the non-disclosure was inconsequential due to the pendency of another appeal.

The Supreme Court found the respondent's arguments untenable, emphasizing that a litigant must approach the court with clean hands. It noted the respondent's manipulation and failure to disclose material facts, and concluded that the High Court erred in not appreciating the finality of the LRF proceedings and in condoning the delay. Consequently, the Supreme Court allowed the appeals, setting aside the High Court's common judgment and restoring the judgments in the original Writ Petitions.

petitioner_key_arguments: The condonation of 1378 days delay in filing Writ Appeal No.206/2007 was erroneous and convoluted the matters.
The tenancy petition LRF No.835/74-75 had attained finality as early as 1981.
Respondent No.1 (Andappa) failed to disclose crucial consequential orders and the dismissal of his appeal against the Tehsildar's order.
Respondent No.1 engaged in manipulation, including changing names.
The High Court's common judgment failed to appreciate the finality of LRF No.835/74-75.
respondent_key_arguments: Non-disclosure of facts was inconsequential due to the pendency of an appeal against the judgment dated 25.03.2003.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments regarding the finality of LRF No.835/74-75, the erroneous condonation of delay, and the respondent's manipulation and non-disclosure of facts were accepted by the court.

outcome.relief_granted: The common judgment and order dated 26.02.2010 passed by the High Court of Karnataka in Writ Appeal Nos. 1708, 1705, 1707, 1709, 1738 of 2006 and 206 of 2007 is set aside. The judgment in the Writ Petitions from which the corresponding appeals arose are restored.

precedents_cited: Ramjas Foundation v. Union of India

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The court held that a litigant who does not come to court with clean hands is not entitled to relief. It found that the respondent had engaged in manipulation and failed to disclose crucial facts, and that the High Court erred in not appreciating the finality of earlier orders (LRF No.835/74-75) and in condoning an inordinate delay without proper justification.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed that a 'fact being inconsequential' and 'non-disclosure of the said fact' are different and distinct, emphasizing the respondent's manipulation of names and facts.

special_directions.special_directions: The judgment in the Writ Petitions from which the corresponding appeals arose are restored, implying that the outcomes and directions of those original Writ Petitions are now in effect.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S). OF 2025 (ARISING OUT OF SLP(CRL.) NO(S). 11002-11009 OF 2024)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the dishonour of post-dated cheques issued as a security deposit refund for a lease agreement, and whether these cheques constituted a legally enforceable debt under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, given the respondent-complainant's continued occupation of the leased property.

judgements.case_summary:
This case is an appeal against a High Court judgment that upheld a conviction under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The dispute originated from a lease agreement where the respondent-complainant deposited Rs. 9,00,000/- as a security deposit. Upon the lease's completion, the appellant-accused issued four post-dated cheques totaling Rs. 9,00,000/- for the security deposit refund, which were subsequently dishonoured due to 'funds insufficient.' The trial court initially convicted the appellant, imposing a fine of Rs. 3,00,000/-. This compensation was later enhanced to Rs. 9,00,000/- by the appellate court and the High Court.

The appellant argued that the respondent continued to occupy the leased flat for nearly five years without paying rent or maintenance, even after a suit for ejectment was partly decreed in the appellant's favor. Consequently, the appellant contended that the cheques did not represent a legally enforceable debt for the full amount, as he was entitled to deduct arrears. The respondent maintained that the cheques were for a security deposit refund, and their dishonour justified the conviction.

The Supreme Court found merit in the appellant's argument, concluding that the respondent's prolonged occupation without payment negated the appellant's full liability to refund the entire security deposit. Thus, the cheques did not constitute a fully legally enforceable debt under Section 138 of the NI Act. The Court quashed the High Court and appellate court judgments, restoring the trial court's original award of Rs. 3,00,000/- compensation to the respondent. Any amount paid exceeding Rs. 3,00,000/- is to be reimbursed to the appellant.

petitioner_key_arguments: The respondent-complainant continued to occupy the subject flat for nearly 5 years without paying any rent or maintenance charges, even after a suit for ejectment was partly decreed.
The appellant-accused was not liable to refund the entire security deposit amount of Rs. 9,00,000/- as he was entitled to deduct due rent and maintenance.
The post-dated cheques were misused by the respondent-complainant.
The case set up by the respondent-complainant does not satisfy the parameters of a legally enforceable debt against the appellant-accused under Section 138 of the NI Act.
respondent_key_arguments: The cheques were issued by the appellant-accused for the refund of the security deposit of Rs. 9,00,000/-.
The cheques were dishonoured due to insufficient funds.
The appellate Court and High Court were justified in confirming the conviction and enhancing the compensation amount.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's argument that the respondent's continued occupation of the flat without paying rent negated the appellant's full liability to refund the entire security deposit, thus making the cheques not fully representative of a legally enforceable debt under Section 138 of the NI Act, was accepted.

outcome.relief_granted: The judgments of the High Court and the appellate Court are quashed and set aside. The judgment of the trial Court, awarding Rs. 3,00,000/- as compensation to the respondent-complainant, is restored. Any amount paid over and above Rs. 3,00,000/- is to be reimbursed to the appellant-accused.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: For a cheque to attract liability under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, it must be issued for a 'legally enforceable debt or other liability.' If the payee (respondent-complainant) continues to occupy the payer's (appellant-accused's) property without paying rent, thereby creating a counter-claim for the payer, the payer's liability to refund the full security deposit (for which the cheques were issued) is diminished, and thus the cheques may not represent a fully legally enforceable debt.

special_directions.special_directions: The trial Court shall reimburse the amount in the above terms to ensure compliance of this judgment within a period of two months from today. The Registry was previously directed to transmit demand drafts of Rs. 4,20,000/- to the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court, Bangalore, for investment in an interest-bearing fixed deposit.
special_directions.interim_orders: The appellant-accused had previously deposited two demand drafts of Rs. 2,10,000/- each, totaling Rs. 4,20,000/-, which were directed to be deposited with the Secretary General of the Court and later transmitted to the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Court for investment in an interest-bearing fixed deposit.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (Arising out of SLP (Crl.) No. 8659 of 2023)

petitioner_advocates: Mr. Navin Pahwa, learned Senior Counsel

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the quashing of a summoning order in a complaint filed under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, by the High Court, specifically regarding the competence and personal knowledge of the power of attorney holder who filed the complaint on behalf of a firm.

judgements.case_summary:
This appeal challenges a High Court judgment dated 12th April 2023, which quashed a summoning order and the entire proceedings in a complaint case filed by M/s Naresh Potteries (appellant) under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, against M/s Aarti Industries (respondent). The appellant had supplied goods to the respondent, and a cheque issued by the respondent for Rs. 1,70,46,314/- was dishonoured. Following a legal notice, the appellant's manager, Sh. Neeraj Kumar, filed the complaint based on a Letter of Authority. The High Court quashed the proceedings, finding that the power of attorney holder lacked personal knowledge of the facts, relying on the precedent of A.C. Narayanan (supra).

The petitioner argued that the High Court's decision was based on an incorrect assumption of fact and misinterpretation of law, particularly regarding the distinction between individual and company complainants. They asserted that the manager, Sh. Neeraj Kumar, was well-conversant with the transactions and duly authorized. The respondent (No.2) adopted the appellant's submissions. The Supreme Court analyzed the requirements of Section 142 of the NI Act and Section 200 of the Cr.P.C., clarifying that for a company, an authorized employee with knowledge can represent it. The Court found that the Letter of Authority and affidavits clearly indicated Sh. Neeraj Kumar's personal knowledge and authorization. The Court held that the High Court's quashing was unwarranted and based on an incorrect factual basis, and that such issues are for trial. The appeal was allowed, the High Court's order was set aside, and the original complaint case was restored for hearing on its merits.

petitioner_key_arguments: The High Court quashed the complaint on an incorrect assumption of fact and misinterpretation of law, particularly regarding TRL Krosaki Refractories Limited v. SMS Asia Private Limited.
The power of attorney holder (Sh. Neeraj Kumar) had personal knowledge of the facts and circumstances of the case, as explicitly stated in the Letter of Authority and affidavits.
The purpose of a sworn statement is to satisfy the prima facie existence of an offence, and further examination can occur later.
Relied on precedents like Shankar Finance, Praveen, A.C. Narayanan, and Vinita S. Rao.
respondent_key_arguments: Respondent No.2 adopted the submissions of the appellant, stating the matter is essentially a dispute between private parties and praying for the appeal to be allowed.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the power of attorney holder (Sh. Neeraj Kumar) had sufficient personal knowledge and authorization to file the complaint on behalf of the firm, distinguishing the case from precedents where such knowledge was lacking or not explicitly averred. The Court found the High Court's quashing order to be based on incorrect factual assumptions and unwarranted interference.

outcome.relief_granted: The final judgment and order dated 12th April 2023 passed by the learned Single Judge of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad in Criminal Miscellaneous Application No. 29906 of 2022 is quashed and set aside. The Complaint No. 701 of 2021 is restored to the file of the Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Khurja, Bulandshahar to be heard and decided on its own merits.

acts_cited: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (2 of 1974), Section 200
precedents_cited: TRL Krosaki Refractories Limited v. SMS Asia Private Limited and Another4
Shankar Finance and Investments v. State of Andhra Pradesh and Ors.5
Praveen v. Mohd. Tajuddin6
A.C. Narayanan v. State of Maharashtra and Another7
Vinita S. Rao v. Essen Corporate Services Private Limited and Another8
National Small Industries Corporation Limited v. State (NCT of Delhi) and Others9
M.M.T.C. Ltd. and Another v. Medchl Chemicals & Pharma P. Limited and Another10
Janki Vashdeo Bhojwani and Another v. IndusInd Bank Limited and Others11
M.M.T.C. [M.M.T.C. Ltd. v. Medchl Chemicals and Pharma (P) Ltd., (2002) 1 SCC 234 : 2002 SCC (Cri) 121]
Janki Vashdeo Bhojwani [Janki Vashdeo Bhojwani v. IndusInd Bank Ltd., (2005) 2 SCC 217]
Vinita S. Rao v. Essen Corporate Services (P) Ltd. [Vinita S. Rao v. Essen Corporate Services (P) Ltd., (2015) 1 SCC 527 : (2015) 1 SCC (Civ) 558 : (2015) 1 SCC (Cri) 726]
A.C. Narayanan [A.C. Narayanan v. State of Maharashtra, (2014) 11 SCC 790 : (2014) 4 SCC (Civ) 343]
Samrat Shipping Co. (P) Ltd. v. Dolly George [Samrat Shipping Co. (P) Ltd. v. Dolly George, (2002) 9 SCC 455 : 2003 SCC (Cri) 1224]

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: For a complaint under Section 138 of the NI Act filed by a company, the authorized representative (power of attorney holder) must have personal knowledge of the transactions. This knowledge can be gathered from the overall circumstances, the Letter of Authority, and supporting affidavits, and does not require a specific 'straightjacket' averment. Quashing such a complaint at the threshold based on perceived lack of explicit averment of personal knowledge, especially when the representative is involved in day-to-day affairs, is unwarranted and such issues are matters for trial.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court reiterated that inherent powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. should be exercised sparingly and with great caution, and not to interfere with lower court jurisdiction or scuttle fair investigation/prosecution.

special_directions.special_directions: The Complaint No. 701 of 2021 is restored to the file of the Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Khurja, Bulandshahar to be heard and decided on its own merits. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 4763 OF 2025 ARISING OUT OF SLP (C) No. 26489 OF 2024

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the calculation of the limitation period for filing an application to set aside an arbitral award under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, specifically the applicability of Sections 4 and 12 of the Limitation Act, 1963 when the limitation period expires on a court holiday.

judgements.case_summary: This appeal challenges an order of the Chhattisgarh High Court dated 27.09.2024, which allowed the respondent's appeal under Section 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, holding that its application under Section 34 was filed within the limitation period. An arbitral award was passed on 09.04.2022 in favor of the appellant, and the respondent filed a Section 34 application on 11.07.2022. The Trial Court initially found the application within limitation but later, after a recall, held it time-barred, stating the 3-month period expired on 08.07.2022. The High Court reversed this, applying Section 12 of the Limitation Act to exclude 09.04.2022, making the limitation expire on 09.07.2022, which was a court holiday. Consequently, Section 4 of the Limitation Act applied, deeming the 11.07.2022 filing timely. The Supreme Court affirmed the High Court's decision, reiterating that Section 12(1) of the Limitation Act applies to Section 34 proceedings, and if the limitation period ends on a court holiday, Section 4 allows filing on the next working day. The appeal was dismissed, and the High Court's interim direction regarding the stay of execution was not interfered with.

petitioner_key_arguments: The limitation period must be calculated from 09.04.2022, expiring on 08.07.2022.
The Limitation Act, including Section 12, does not apply to proceedings under Section 34 of the ACA.
Since the court was working on 08.07.2022, Section 4 of the Limitation Act does not apply.
There was a 3-day delay in filing the Section 34 application, and the respondent did not file an application for condonation of delay.
The respondent should be required to deposit 100% of the arbitral sum, not 50%.
respondent_key_arguments: Section 12 of the Limitation Act applies, and the date of award receipt (09.04.2022) must be excluded while calculating the limitation.
The limitation period expired on 09.07.2022, which was a court holiday.
Section 4 of the Limitation Act applies, making the application filed on the next working day (11.07.2022) within time.
Relied on the judgment in Himachal Techno Engineers (supra).
The appellant had previously sought deposit of 60% and a bank guarantee for 40%, and thus cannot demand 100% deposit now.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The respondent's arguments regarding the applicability of Section 12 and Section 4 of the Limitation Act to Section 34 proceedings, leading to the conclusion that the application was filed within the limitation period, were accepted by the Court.

outcome.relief_granted: The respondent's application under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, is considered to have been filed within the limitation period. The High Court's direction to stay the execution of pending recovery till the matter is adjudicated on merits was not interfered with.

precedents_cited: State of Himachal Pradesh v. Himachal Techno Engineers (2023) 8 SCC 453
Bhimashankar Sahakari Sakkare Karkhane Niyamita v. Walchandnagar Industries Limited (2010) 12 SCC 210
My Preferred Transformation & Hospitality Pvt Ltd v. Faridabad Implements Pvt Ltd
State of West Bengal v. Rajpath Contractors and Engineers Ltd (2024) 7 SCC 257
constitutional_provisions: Article 227 of the Constitution

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that Section 12(1) of the Limitation Act, 1963, applies to proceedings under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, requiring the exclusion of the day on which the arbitral award was received. Furthermore, if the three-month limitation period, calculated after such exclusion, expires on a court holiday, Section 4 of the Limitation Act, 1963, allows the application to be filed on the next working day, deeming it within the limitation period.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court clarified that the limitation period under Section 34(3) is 'three months' (calendar months) and not 'ninety days,' emphasizing the legislative intent behind the distinct language for the initial and condonable periods. It also noted that the High Court's interim direction regarding the deposit of 50% of the arbitral sum would not be interfered with, especially since the appellant had already withdrawn the amount.

special_directions.interim_orders: The High Court's direction that the interim order in respect of execution of pending recovery shall continue till the application is decided on merits.

case_identification.petitioner_name: M/S S.R.S. TRAVELS BY ITS PROPRIETOR K.T. RAJASHEKAR
case_identification.respondent_name: THE KARNATAKA STATE ROAD TRANSPORT CORPORATION WORKERS & ORS.
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NOS OF 2025 @ SLP(CIVIL) NOS.27833-27834 OF 2011

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the constitutional validity of the Karnataka Motor Vehicles Taxation and Certain Other Law (Amendment) Act, 2003, which repealed the Karnataka Contract Carriages (Acquisition) Act, 1976, and the power of the State Transport Authority to delegate permit-granting functions to its Secretary.

judgements.case_summary: This case involves appeals challenging a High Court judgment regarding two primary issues: the constitutional validity of the Karnataka Motor Vehicles Taxation and Certain Other Law (Amendment) Act, 2003 (2003 Repeal Act), and the permissibility of delegating permit-granting powers by the State Transport Authority (STA) to its Secretary. The 2003 Repeal Act repealed the Karnataka Contract Carriages (Acquisition) Act, 1976 (KCCA Act), which had previously vested private contract carriages in state-owned corporations like KSRTC. The private bus operators and the Karnataka STA (appellants) argued for the validity of the 2003 Repeal Act and the legality of delegation for non-stage carriage permits, citing administrative efficiency and statutory provisions (Section 68(5) of MV Act and Rule 56(1)(d) of KMV Rules). Conversely, the KSRTC (respondent) contended that the 2003 Repeal Act was unconstitutional, effectively overruling Supreme Court precedents and requiring Presidential assent for repeal. KSRTC also argued that permit-granting is a quasi-judicial function that cannot be delegated to a single officer. The Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of the 2003 Repeal Act, stating that the power to repeal is coextensive with the power to enact and that prior judicial affirmations do not bind future legislative policy changes. The Court also affirmed that delegation of non-stage carriage permit-granting powers to the Secretary is legally permissible and necessary for administrative efficiency, even for quasi-judicial functions, when explicitly provided by statute. Consequently, the appeals filed by KSRTC were dismissed, while those by the private bus operators and Karnataka STA were allowed.

petitioner_key_arguments: The 2003 Repeal Act is constitutionally valid as the Legislature has plenary power to repeal a statute within its domain, and previous Supreme Court decisions only affirmed the 1976 Act's validity at the time of enactment, not precluding future repeal.
Fresh Presidential assent was not required for the repeal of the 1976 Act, as the repeal falls within the legislative competence of the State.

Section 68(5) of the MV Act and Rule 56(1)(d) of the KMV Rules expressly permit the STA to delegate its power to grant permits (other than stage carriage permits) to the Chairman, Secretary, or other officers.
Delegation of routine permit issuance to the Secretary ensures administrative efficiency and timely service, which is vital for the smooth functioning of the transport regulatory system.

Even quasi-judicial functions can be delegated if the enabling statute expressly provides for it, as supported by precedents like Newtech Promoters & Developers Private Limited v. State of Uttar Pradesh & Others.
respondent_key_arguments: The 2003 Repeal Act is unconstitutional because it effectively overrules Supreme Court decisions (Ranganatha Reddy and Vijayakumar Sharma) that upheld the 1976 Act.

The repeal of the 1976 Act, which was enacted under Entry 42 (Concurrent List) with Presidential assent, should also have required Presidential assent for its repeal, and attempting to repeal it via a taxation measure (Entry 57 of List II) is ultra vires.
The power to grant Contract Carriage Permits is a quasi-judicial function expressly vested in the STA or RTA as composite bodies, requiring deliberation by multiple high-ranking officials.

Delegation of permit-granting power to a single officer (Secretary) is inadmissible and contrary to the statutory scheme, undermining the multi-member decision-making process mandated by Section 68(2) of the MV Act.
Excessive delegation through amended Rules amounts to a de facto rewriting of Sections 68 and 96 of the MV Act and is inconsistent with the General Clauses Act, 1897.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court accepted the arguments that the 2003 Repeal Act is constitutionally valid and that the State Transport Authority (STA) possesses the power to delegate non-stage carriage permit-granting functions to its Secretary, as expressly provided by the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, and the Karnataka Motor Vehicle Rules, 1989.

outcome.relief_granted: The 2003 Repeal Act is declared constitutional. The impugned orders of the High Court denying the delegation power of the STA are set aside. The Secretary of the STA is empowered to grant non-stage carriage permits (including contract carriage, special, tourist, and temporary permits) in accordance with Section 68(5) of the MV Act and Rule 56(1)(d) of the KMV Rules, subject to prescribed limitations and conditions.

acts_cited: Karnataka Motor Vehicles Taxation and Certain Other Law (Amendment) Act, 2003
precedents_cited: State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy
Vijayakumar Sharma v. State of Karnataka
Newtech Promoters & Developers Private Limited v. State of Uttar Pradesh & Others
Ramakrishna v. Janpad Sabha
Attorney-General for Ontario v. Attorney-General for the Dominion
constitutional_provisions: Article 39(b) and (c) of the Constitution
Entry 42 of the Concurrent List in the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution
Entry 57 of List II

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The power to repeal a law is coextensive with the power to enact, and a legislature's power to modify or repeal a statute remains unimpaired even if its constitutional validity was previously affirmed by the Supreme Court, provided it falls within legislative competence and does not violate fundamental rights. Delegation of quasi-judicial functions is permissible if expressly authorized by statute and rules, especially for routine administrative tasks, to ensure efficiency without undermining statutory oversight.

special_directions.special_directions: The appropriate authorities are directed to take all necessary measures to implement the findings and ensure that the delegation of permit-granting power is exercised in a manner consistent with the statutory provisions and the objectives of efficient public transport administration. All pending applications are disposed of.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO.1188/2025 (@Petition for Special Leave to Appeal (C) No.26695/2019)

case_details.subject_matter: This case concerns the legality of an auction sale conducted by a bank under the SARFAESI Act, challenged by a guarantor on grounds of procedural irregularities, specifically regarding the notice period.

judgements.case_summary: The case originates from an auction sale conducted by Indian Bank on 31-7-2007, where M.S. Sanjay (appellant) was the successful bidder. The property was mortgaged by M/s. Arihant Sarees (Respondent No.2) and the loan was guaranteed by Respondent No.4. The borrower defaulted, leading the bank to proceed under the SARFAESI Act. The auction purchaser deposited Rs.24,00,000/-, and a Sale Certificate was issued on 30-11-2007. The guarantor (Respondent No.4) challenged the auction proceedings before the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT) in 2008, which set aside the auction on 23-1-2009, citing non-compliance with the 30-day notice period and other formalities. The Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal (DRAT) reversed the DRT's order on 11-4-2017, affirming the sale and stating that the bank could not be held guilty for technicalities, especially given the initial 30-day gap and the guarantor's negligence. The High Court of Karnataka, in a Writ Petition filed by the guarantor, set aside the DRAT's order on 15-6-2019, reinstating the DRT's decision. The High Court focused on the 15-day clear notice requirement, concluding it was not met. The Supreme Court, hearing the appeal from the auction purchaser, observed that the High Court took a strict view on the notice period. The Supreme Court emphasized that interference by a Writ Court for mere statutory infraction not resulting in injustice is not a matter of course. It held that legal formulations should be tempered with equity, especially when the auction had attained finality in 2007, and the appellant had developed the property. The Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's judgment and affirming the auction sale.

petitioner_key_arguments: The auction purchaser (appellant) was the successful bidder in 2007, deposited the amount, and received a sale certificate.
The appellant has been in possession and developed the property.
The guarantor initiated frivolous litigation on technical grounds after a significant delay.
The High Court erred by taking an overly strict view on procedural technicalities (notice period) without considering the practical implications and the finality of the auction.
Mere infraction of statutory provisions, if not resulting in injustice, should not lead to setting aside proceedings, especially after a long time.
respondent_key_arguments: The bank did not follow the mandatory 30-day clear notice period as required by the SARFAESI Act for the auction sale.
The bank failed to provide proper valuation reports and other documents as per legal requirements.
The sale was conducted without due compliance with all formalities, making it illegal and invalid.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Supreme Court accepted the appellant's arguments, emphasizing that the High Court should have taken a practical view and that mere technical infractions not resulting in injustice should not lead to setting aside an auction that had attained finality and where rights had accrued.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal was allowed, and the impugned Judgment and Order passed by the High Court were set aside. The order of the DRAT dated 11.04.2017 was effectively reinstated, and the auction sale dated 31.7.2007 was affirmed.

precedents_cited: Shiv Shanker Dal Mills v. State of Haryana reported in (1980) 2 SCC 437
Kewal Krishna Puri v. State of Punjab reported in (1980) 1 SCC 416
constitutional_provisions: Article 32 of the Constitution
Article 226 of the Constitution of India

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that while exercising extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 226, courts should adopt a practical and equitable approach. Mere technical infractions of statutory provisions that do not result in actual injustice should not be a ground to set aside proceedings, especially when significant time has passed, and third-party rights (like an auction purchaser's) have accrued and been acted upon. The law must be tempered with equity, and the final order should reflect equitable considerations.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that the Respondent No.4 (guarantor) was wholly responsible for dragging the appellant into frivolous litigation on a technical point. It also refrained from imposing costs on the respondent despite the frivolous litigation.

special_directions.interim_orders: An interim order dated 8.11.2019 stayed the impugned order of the High Court until further orders from the Supreme Court.

case_identification.petitioner_name: M/S Shri Sendhuragro And Oil Industries
case_identification.case_number: TRANSFER PETITION (CRL.) NO. 608 OF 2024 WITH T.P.(CRL) NO. 670 OF 2024 T.P.(CRL) NO. 761 OF 2024 T.P.(CRL) NO. 662 OF 2024 T.P.(CRL) NO. 977 OF 2024 T.P.(CRL) NO. 850 OF 2024

respondent_advocates: The learned counsel appearing for the Respondent - Bank

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the transfer of criminal complaints filed under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, from Chandigarh to Coimbatore, primarily on grounds of territorial jurisdiction and convenience.

judgements.case_summary:
The petitioner, M/s Shri Sendhuragro And Oil Industries, sought the transfer of criminal complaints filed by Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, from the Judicial Magistrate Ist Class, Chandigarh, to the Metropolitan Magistrate, Coimbatore. The petitioner argued that all transactions, including loan processing and EMI deductions, occurred in Coimbatore, making Chandigarh an inappropriate forum chosen by the bank to harass the petitioner, citing language barriers and pending SARFAESI proceedings in Coimbatore. The respondent bank contended that the complaints were filed in Chandigarh because the routing/collection account for the dishonoured cheque was located there, which is permissible under Section 142(2)(a) of the NI Act. They argued that the petitioner was not disputing jurisdiction but merely seeking transfer on general grounds of inconvenience, which is not sufficient for transfer under Section 406 CrPC.

The Supreme Court analyzed Sections 138, 142, and 142A of the NI Act, and Section 406 of the CrPC, along with various precedents. The Court reiterated that Section 142(2)(a) of the NI Act clearly establishes jurisdiction where the payee's bank account for collection is situated. It emphasized that the power to transfer under Section 406 CrPC is discretionary and should be exercised sparingly, requiring a reasonable apprehension that justice will not be done, rather than mere inconvenience. The Court clarified that issues of territorial jurisdiction should primarily be raised before the trial court. Ultimately, the Court found that the petitioner failed to make out a case for transfer under Section 406 CrPC, as the bank had jurisdiction in Chandigarh as per the NI Act, and inconvenience alone is not a sufficient ground. The transfer petitions were dismissed.

petitioner_key_arguments: All transactions between the Petitioner and the Respondent wholly happened in Coimbatore, and Coimbatore Courts alone have jurisdiction.
The Petitioner holds a savings Account in the Respondent's Coimbatore Branch and the loan was also processed in the same branch.
The Court in Chandigarh will have no jurisdiction to entertain the present Criminal Complaint.
The present Complaint does not satisfy any of the conditions under Sec.142.
Already pending proceedings between the Petitioner and the Respondent in Coimbatore.
Respondent has purposefully filed the present proceedings in Ahmedabad only to harass the Petitioner with multiple proceedings in different States.
The Petitioner fears his safety to travel alone to Chandigarh to attend the proceedings.
The Petitioner doesn't Know anyone in Chandigarh and does not even know the local language to effectively defend himself.
Respondent Bank has already initiated Sarfaesi proceedings for the recovery of entire loan amount in Coimbatore.
The invocation of power of transfer presupposes the existence of jurisdiction.
The expression 'expedient for the ends of justice' should be invoked.
Section 142A contemplates that cases against the same drawer ought to be filed in the same Court where the first case pertaining to dishonor of cheque is filed or 'transferred'.
The legislative intent of Section 142A also contemplates that holder in due course is not allowed to misuse the availability of multiple jurisdictions.
respondent_key_arguments: The Cheque was presented at Respondent's Chandigarh Branch for the reason that the routing/collection account in respect of the subject cheque (in a NPA account) was located at Chandigarh.
The petitioner has in its written submissions clarified that it is not disputing the jurisdiction of the court where the complaint was filed.

Section 142 A of the Negotiable Instrument Act stipulates the conditions when the Complaint filed under Section 138 may be transferred. The object of the provision is that all the complaint cases arising out of one transaction should be tried at one place. In the present cases as well as the connected cases, the Respondent has filed cases at Chandigarh only; thus, no ground under Section 142 A to seek transfer arises.
The transfer petitions are not supported by any sufficient grounds. Petitioner has sought transfer only on the general grounds viz the distance and the difference in language.
Virtual Facility is available in courts in Chandigarh and the option to attend the hearing virtually is always available to the Petitioner.
The cheque bouncing cases filed by the respondent in Chandigarh were prior in time to the original application filed before the DRT, Coimbatore.
Complaint case Under Section 138 of the NI Act cannot be transferred at the convenience of the accused.
Under Section 142 (2) (a) of the NI Act, the court within whose jurisdiction the branch of the bank where the payee maintains the account is situated, will have jurisdiction to try the offence.
Mere language factor/convenience of a party is not enough ground to seek transfer.
Jurisdiction under the Section 406 of the CrPC ought to be sparingly used.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the respondent's arguments that jurisdiction for Section 138 NI Act cases is determined by Section 142(2)(a) based on where the payee's bank account for collection is situated, and that mere inconvenience or alleged lack of territorial jurisdiction is not a sufficient ground for transfer under Section 406 CrPC.

case_details.subject_matter: The seminal issue is whether a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution would be maintainable against an order passed by the Micro and Small Enterprises Facilitation Council under Section 18 of the MSMED Act, and under what circumstances, particularly in light of conflicting precedents regarding the MSEFC's power and the availability of alternative remedies.

judgements.case_summary: This case involves M/s Tamil Nadu Cements Corporation Ltd (TANCEM) challenging an order by the Micro and Small Enterprises Facilitation Council (MSEFC) under Section 18 of the MSMED Act, 2006. TANCEM had a dispute with Unicon Engineers regarding a work order, leading to an MSEFC order for payment. TANCEM subsequently filed various challenges, including a writ petition questioning the maintainability of such petitions against MSEFC orders and the vires of Sections 16-19 of the MSMED Act. The Supreme Court identified a direct conflict between two of its earlier two-judge bench judgments: Jharkhand Urja Vikas Nigam Limited (which distinguished conciliation and arbitration) and Gujarat State Civil Supplies Corporation Limited (which allowed MSEFC to act as both). The Court also expressed reservations about M/s India Glycols Limited, which held that writ petitions are not maintainable against MSEFC orders, with recourse only through Section 34 of the A&C Act, subject to a pre-deposit. Given these conflicting precedents and the significant legal questions regarding the scope of writ jurisdiction, the applicability of alternative remedies, the onerous pre-deposit conditions, and the MSEFC's dual role, the Court deemed it appropriate to refer these issues to a larger bench of five Judges for a definitive resolution.

petitioner_key_arguments: The MSEFC order was a nullity and contrary to the MSMED Act and A&C Act.
A writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution is maintainable against an order passed by the MSEFC, especially given the onerous pre-deposit requirement under Section 19 of the MSMED Act.
The vires of Sections 16 to 19 of the MSMED Act are challenged.
respondent_key_arguments: The MSEFC order should be enforced.
Objections raised by TANCEM were barred by limitation.
TANCEM failed to furnish the 75% pre-deposit as mandated by Section 19 of the MSMED Act.

outcome.relief_granted: No final relief granted to either party. The case is referred to a larger bench for determination of key legal questions.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (Arising out of SLP(C) No.10042/2023) / 2025 INSC 236

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns a challenge to a show cause notice issued by the Chhattisgarh Textbook Corporation to M/S Techno Prints, proposing blacklisting for three years and forfeiture of EMD due to alleged breach of a textbook printing contract.

judgements.case_summary:
This appeal arises from a challenge by M/S Techno Prints (appellant) against a show cause notice issued by the Chhattisgarh Textbook Corporation (respondent). The respondent proposed blacklisting the appellant for three years and forfeiting an Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) of Rs. 5,00,000/- due to alleged breach of a textbook printing contract. Previously, an earlier blacklisting order against the appellant was quashed by the High Court for exceeding the scope of its show cause notice, though the High Court did not prevent fresh proceedings. The appellant subsequently challenged the fresh show cause notice (dated 14.12.2022) in a writ petition, which was dismissed by both the Single Judge and the Appellate Court, on the grounds that a show cause notice should not ordinarily be challenged at an initial stage.

Before the Supreme Court, the appellant argued that blacklisting, a drastic measure, should only be invoked for deliberate default or intent to cheat, which was absent, and that their inability to complete the work was due to the COVID-19 pandemic. They contended the show cause notice was an empty formality. The respondent maintained that blacklisting was warranted due to contractual breaches, irrespective of intent.

The Supreme Court, while acknowledging that show cause notices are generally not challenged, treated the notice in this peculiar case as a final order to assess its validity. Citing precedents, the Court emphasized that blacklisting is a severe punishment reserved for "deviant or aberrant" conduct, not mere contractual breaches, especially when other legal remedies exist. The Court found the show cause notice for blacklisting to be an empty formality issued with a pre-determined mind.

Consequently, the Supreme Court quashed and set aside the show cause notice for blacklisting. However, it permitted the Chhattisgarh Textbook Corporation to forfeit the EMD of Rs. 5,00,000/-. This decision highlights the principle that blacklisting requires a higher threshold of misconduct beyond simple breach of contract.

petitioner_key_arguments: One cannot be blacklisted or called upon to show cause for blacklisting unless there is an intent to cheat or take undue advantage, which is not present in this case.
There is nothing to indicate that the appellant deliberately defaulted.
The obligation in terms of the contract could not be discharged due to circumstances beyond its control (COVID-19 pandemic).
The show cause notice is an empty formality and the authority has a pre-determined mind, making it suitable for challenge.
respondent_key_arguments: The action of blacklisting does not depend on whether default was deliberate or if there was an intention to take undue advantage or to cheat, but on the contravention of the contract and the damage caused.
The petitioner violated clauses 13.3, 16.1, 16.3, and 16.9 of the terms of the Agreement.
A writ application does not ordinarily lie against a charge-sheet or show-cause notice as it does not give rise to any cause of action at an initial stage.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's argument that blacklisting is a drastic measure not warranted for a mere breach of contract without intent to cheat or aberrant conduct, and that the show cause notice in this specific case was an empty formality, prevailed.

outcome.relief_granted: The show cause notice calling upon the appellant as to why it should not be blacklisted is quashed and set aside. The respondent Corporation is permitted to forfeit the EMD of Rs. 5,00,000/-.

precedents_cited: STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH V. BRAHM DATT SHARMA & ANR.” (1987) 2 SCC 179
SECRETARY, MINISTRY OF DEFENCE & ORS. V. PRABHASH CHANDRA MIRDHA” (2012) 11 SCC 565

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: Blacklisting is a punitive measure that should only be invoked for conduct that is "deviant or aberrant" and warrants such a punitive measure, not for a mere allegation of breach of contractual obligations without anything more. A show cause notice, if it is an empty formality or issued with a pre-determined mind, can be challenged, especially when blacklisting is a drastic step with severe consequences.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that authorities are expected to be very careful before issuing a show cause notice, understanding the facts well and ascertaining the nature of the violation. It used an analogy of police power to arrest, stating that while the power exists, it is not necessary to effect arrest in all cases and discretion should be exercised.
