case_details.subject_matter: Dispute over the cancellation of an allotment for a 5-star hotel site and car park, involving breach of contractual obligations, forfeiture of deposited amount, and entitlement to refund and interest.

judgements.case_summary:
M/s. Tomorrowland Limited (Appellant) was the highest bidder for a 5-star hotel site and car park allotted by Housing and Urban Development Corporation Limited (HUDCO/Respondent No. 1). The Appellant paid the first installment. A dispute arose when Respondent No. 1 failed to fulfill reciprocal obligations, such as executing a sub-lease and obtaining statutory approvals, leading to the cancellation of the allotment and forfeiture of the deposited amount. The Appellant filed a suit seeking a declaration that the cancellation was null and void.

The Appellant contended that Respondent No. 1's failure to execute necessary documents and obtain approvals constituted a breach of contract and misrepresentation, and that the forfeiture was unjustified. They also alleged discriminatory treatment compared to other bidders (Ansals). Respondent No. 1 argued that the Appellant defaulted on payments, engaged in forum shopping, and approached the court with "unclean hands," thus not being entitled to discretionary relief, including interest.

The Supreme Court found Respondent No. 1 in breach of its obligations, particularly regarding securing approvals and executing the sub-lease, which disentitled it from forfeiting the amount. Consequently, Respondent No. 1 was held liable to refund the principal amount. However, the Court also noted the Appellant's "unclean hands," including abandoning relief to avoid court fees, forum shopping, and non-compliance with court orders, which justified denying discretionary interest.

The appeal was partly allowed. Respondent No. 1 was directed to refund Rs. 28,11,31,939 to the Appellant within three months, but without interest. A 6% p.a. interest would apply only if the refund was delayed beyond three months. The Court clarified that these directions pertained only to the hotel and car park property.

petitioner_key_arguments: Respondent No. 1 failed to disclose it had no subsisting lease to execute a sub-lease, constituting misrepresentation.
Respondent No. 1 was obligated to execute the 'agreement to sub-lease' and obtain statutory approvals after the first installment, but failed to do so.
The High Court erroneously held the Second Suit suffered from a fatal defect for not claiming possession, as possession could only be sought after sub-lease execution.
The Appellant deserved to be treated at par with Leela, who received a refund with interest due to Respondent No. 1's failure to disclose revised layout plan issues.
The Appellant received discriminatory treatment compared to Ansals, who were granted interest-free extensions for payments.
Forfeiture of the amount was based on misconstruction of mutual obligations, not actual loss by Respondent No. 1.
respondent_key_arguments: The Appellant defaulted on the payment schedule, breaching contractual obligations, justifying cancellation and forfeiture as per Clause 5(iii) of the Allotment Letter.
The Second Suit was barred under Order II Rule 2 of the CPC, as the cause of action was the same as the First Suit and the Appellant relinquished a portion of the claim.
The Second Suit was barred under Order XXIII Rule 1 of the CPC, as the First Suit was unconditionally withdrawn without liberty to institute a fresh suit.
The Appellant abandoned the consequential relief of possession in the Second Suit to avoid paying court fees, defying the proviso to Section 34 of the SR Act.
The Appellant engaged in forum shopping and overreached the judicial process by dishonoring court directions, withdrawing the First Suit, and crafting the Second Suit to change forum.
Unlike the Appellant, Ansals secured Income Tax approvals, so no parity can be claimed.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that the respondent was in breach of contractual obligations, leading to the refund of the principal amount. However, it accepted the respondent's argument regarding the petitioner's conduct ("unclean hands") to deny interest.

outcome.relief_granted: Respondent No. 1/HUDCO is directed to refund the amount of Rs. 28,11,31,939 to the Appellant within three (3) months from the date of this order. If Respondent No. 1 fails to refund the amount within the stipulated time, the Appellant shall be entitled to interest at the rate of 6% per annum till the date of realisation.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that Respondent No. 1 was in breach of its reciprocal contractual obligations, specifically failing to secure statutory approvals and execute a sub-lease, which disentitled it from forfeiting the Appellant's deposited amount. However, the Appellant's conduct, characterized by forum shopping and a lack of 'clean hands', justified the denial of discretionary interest on the refunded principal amount under Section 34 of the CPC.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO(S).215 OF 2025 (ARISING OUT OF S.L.P (CIVIL) NO(S).6053/2021)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the validity of an arbitration award challenged on grounds of the sole arbitrator's jurisdiction, specifically whether a party can object to jurisdiction after agreeing to the appointment and submitting a statement of defence.

judgements.case_summary:
This case concerns an arbitration dispute arising from a building construction contract between M/S Vidyawati Construction Company (petitioner) and Union of India (respondent). The original contract stipulated a three-arbitrator tribunal. Following the resignation of an initially appointed Umpire, the Chief Justice appointed a retired Chief Justice as the sole arbitrator. The respondent subsequently challenged the sole arbitrator's jurisdiction, arguing that the contract mandated three arbitrators.

The Supreme Court examined whether the respondent could raise this jurisdictional objection after having explicitly agreed to the sole arbitrator's appointment on December 5, 2003, and subsequently filing a statement of defence on February 14, 2004. The petitioner contended that Section 16(2) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, bars such objections once a statement of defence is submitted. The respondent argued that the initial appointment was administrative and their statement of defence was prepared for a different tribunal, justifying their later objection.

The Court found that the respondent's conduct, including their express agreement to the sole arbitrator and failure to modify their statement of defence despite opportunities, precluded them from challenging jurisdiction under Section 16(2). The Court held that the High Court and District Judge erred in upholding the respondent's objection.

Consequently, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the impugned judgments. Arbitration Case No.25/2008 was restored to the District Judge, Allahabad, for a decision on merits, with a clear directive that the issue of the sole arbitrator's jurisdiction is now concluded and cannot be re-agitated. The District Judge was instructed to prioritize the disposal of the case and transfer it to the Commercial Court if jurisdiction required.

petitioner_key_arguments: The respondent agreed to and accepted the order appointing the sole Arbitrator on 05/12/2003.
The respondent filed the statement of defence on 14/02/2004.
Under Section 16(2) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, it was impermissible to raise a plea of lack of jurisdiction after filing the statement of defence.
The Sections 34 and 37 Courts erred in upholding the respondent's objection to jurisdiction.
respondent_key_arguments: The order appointing the sole Arbitrator on 26/09/2003 was an administrative order.
The statement of defence filed was originally for the three-arbitrator tribunal, so the objection to the sole arbitrator's jurisdiction could not have been incorporated at that stage.
The respondent was within its rights to raise the objection under Section 16 of the Arbitration Act on 24/04/2004.
The arbitration clause in the contract mandated three arbitrators, so a sole arbitrator could not have been appointed.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the respondent had agreed to the sole arbitrator's appointment and, under Section 16(2) of the Arbitration Act, could not subsequently challenge jurisdiction after submitting a statement of defence.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned judgments dated 17th November, 2020 (High Court) and 9th September, 2013 (District Judge) are set aside. Arbitration Case No.25/2008 is restored to the file of the learned District Judge, Allahabad, for decision on merits. The issue of the sole Arbitrator's jurisdiction is concluded and cannot be re-agitated by the respondent.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: A party cannot challenge the jurisdiction of an arbitral tribunal after having expressly agreed to the appointment of the arbitrator and subsequently submitting a statement of defence, as per the mandate of Section 16(2) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The conduct of the party in agreeing to the appointment and participating in proceedings without timely objection is crucial.

special_directions.special_directions: The learned District Judge, Allahabad, shall hear and decide Arbitration Case No.25/2008 on merits, giving necessary priority. If the Principal District Judge finds that the jurisdiction to decide the petition under Section 34 of the Arbitration Act vests in the Commercial Court, he shall transfer the restored Petition to the appropriate Commercial Court. The issue of the sole Arbitrator's jurisdiction stands concluded and cannot be agitated.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (@ SLP Criminal No. 9885 of 2023)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns an appeal against conviction under Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code and Section 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, stemming from allegations of dowry demand and harassment in a marriage that lasted only three days.

judgements.case_summary: The Supreme Court heard an appeal challenging the conviction and sentence of M. Venkateswaran under Section 498A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and Section 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961. The marriage between the appellant and the de facto complainant (PW-4) was solemnized on 31.03.2006 and lasted only three days. A complaint was lodged on 23.08.2007 alleging dowry demand (100 sovereigns of gold) and harassment. The trial court convicted the appellant, which was upheld by the High Court, though the sentence was modified from three years to two years imprisonment under Section 498A IPC and one year under Section 4 DP Act, to run concurrently. The Supreme Court, after reviewing the evidence of witnesses (PW-1, PW-2, PW-4, PW-7, PW-11), found the ingredients of Section 498A IPC and Section 4 of the DP Act to be fully satisfied, confirming the conviction. However, considering the long pendency of the case (nearly 19 years), the short duration of the marriage, and the fact that the complainant had moved on, the Court modified the sentence to the period already undergone. Additionally, the appellant was directed to pay a compensation of Rs. 3,00,000/- to the complainant (PW-4 Sridevi) within four weeks. The bail bonds were discharged upon deposit of this amount, failing which the appeal would be dismissed and the appellant would have to surrender to undergo the remaining sentence.

petitioner_key_arguments: Challenged the correctness of the judgment and order dated 21.06.2022 passed by the High Court of Judicature at Madras.
Sought modification or reduction of the sentence imposed.
respondent_key_arguments: Argued for upholding the conviction and sentence as confirmed by the High Court.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the respondent's arguments regarding the conviction under Section 498A IPC and Section 4 of the DP Act, finding the ingredients fully satisfied. However, the court partially accepted the appellant's implied argument for sentence reduction, modifying it to the period already undergone due to the long pendency of the case, short marriage duration, and the complainant having moved on, while imposing a compensation.

outcome.relief_granted: The conviction under Section 498A IPC and Section 4 of the DP Act is sustained. The sentence imposed is set aside and substituted with that of the period already undergone. The appellant is directed to pay a sum of Rs. 3,00,000/- (Three Lakhs) within a period of four weeks as compensation to PW-4 Sridevi.

precedents_cited: Samaul Sk. vs. The State of Jharkhand & Anr. (2021 INSC 429)

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The court found that the overwhelming evidence presented by the prosecution witnesses (PW-1, PW-2, PW-4, PW-7, PW-11) clearly established that the appellant subjected the complainant (PW-4) to harassment with a view to coercing her and her mother to meet unlawful demands for gold sovereigns, thereby satisfying the ingredients of Section 498A IPC and Section 4 of the DP Act. The modification of sentence was based on humanitarian grounds, considering the nearly 19-year pendency of the case, the extremely short duration of the marriage (three days), and the fact that both parties had moved on in life, coupled with a compensatory payment to the victim.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court noted an observation from a previous order (11.08.2023) regarding exploring the possibility of utilizing the appellant's experience as an I.T. professional for community service, such as coaching in colleges or schools, as a factor worth noticing while applying the proviso to Section 4 of the DP Act for a sentence of less than six months.

special_directions.special_directions: The appellant shall deposit Rs. 3,00,000/- (Three Lakhs) in the 4th Metropolitan Magistrate Court, Saidapet, Chennai, within four weeks. This amount shall be paid as compensation to PW-4 Sridevi after due identification. The Trial Court shall ensure disbursement and send a compliance report to the Supreme Court within six months. If the compliance report is not received, the appeal will be posted for further directions. The bail bonds of the appellant shall stand discharged upon the deposit of the amount; otherwise, the appeal will be treated as dismissed, and the appellant shall surrender to undergo the remaining sentence.
special_directions.interim_orders: The appellant was enlarged on bail by an order of this Court dated 11.08.2023.

case_identification.petitioner_name: MAATR SPARSH AN INITIATIVE BY AVYAAN FOUNDATION
case_identification.case_number: WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.950/2022

case_details.subject_matter: The petition seeks directions for the construction of feeding rooms and child care rooms at public places to protect the fundamental rights of nursing mothers and infants.

judgements.case_summary: The non-Governmental organization, Maatr Sparsh An Initiative By Avyaan Foundation, filed a public interest writ petition seeking reliefs for the establishment of feeding rooms, child care rooms, and other facilities for infants and mothers at public places. The petitioner argued that the lack of such facilities infringes upon the fundamental rights of children and nursing mothers, and that despite legal provisions, concrete steps were lacking. The Union of India, respondent no.1, highlighted that it had already acknowledged the need for such services and had issued an advisory dated 27.02.2024 to all States and Union Territories, requesting them to set up gender-friendly spaces, including feeding and child-care rooms. The Supreme Court emphasized the importance of breast-feeding for a child's right to life and a mother's health and well-being, linking these to fundamental rights under Articles 14, 15(3), 21, 39(f), 47, and international conventions. Finding that the Union of India's advisory addressed the petitioner's prayers, the Court directed the Union of India to re-issue this advisory as a reminder, along with a copy of the present order, to all States/UTs within two weeks to ensure compliance. The Court also directed that existing public places should implement these directions, new public buildings should reserve space for such facilities, and further advisories should be issued to Public Sector Undertakings. The writ petition was disposed of in these terms.

petitioner_key_arguments: Depriving any child of mother's milk due to lack of basic facilities at public places infringes the fundamental right of a child and the mother.
Child-care facilities are imperative in public spaces as women are equally participating in the growth of the nation.
No concrete steps have been taken by governments to provide such basic facilities despite legal provisions for crèche facilities.
Nursing a child in an environment conducive to a mother's dignity and privacy is a fundamental right.
Specific guidelines and/or directions should be issued for the construction of baby feeding rooms and child-care rooms at public places throughout the country.
respondent_key_arguments: The Union of India had previously informed the Delhi High Court that feeding rooms and child-care rooms are essential services.
The Union of India had already written a letter dated 27.08.2018 to all States and Union Territories requesting them to set up feeding rooms and child-care rooms.

A recent communication/advisory dated 27.02.2024 was issued by the Ministry of Women and Child Development to all States/Union Territories regarding gender-friendly spaces, including feeding rooms and child-care facilities.
Compliance with the advisory issued on 27.02.2024 would fulfill the purpose of filing this writ petition.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court largely accepted the petitioner's arguments regarding the fundamental rights of nursing mothers and infants and the need for facilities, and directed the Union of India to ensure compliance with its own advisories, thereby addressing the petitioner's core demands.

outcome.relief_granted: The Union of India is directed to issue a reminder communication incorporating the advisory dated 27.02.2024 to all States/Union Territories along with a copy of the order within two weeks. States/Union Territories are to ensure implementation of directions in existing public places and reserve space in new constructions. Union of India may issue further advisories to Public Sector Undertakings.

acts_cited: Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015
precedents_cited: Master Avyaan Rastogi through Guardian Neha Rastogi vs. Union of India, WP (C) No.7356 of 2018
constitutional_provisions: Article 14 of the Constitution of India
Article 15(3) of the Constitution of India
Article 21 of the Constitution of India
Article 39(f) of the Constitution of India
Article 47 of the Constitution of India
Article 51A(e) of the Constitution of India

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The fundamental right of a child to mother's milk and the right of a mother to breastfeed are integral to life, survival, and dignity, emanating from Articles 14, 15(3), 21, 39(f), 47 of the Constitution and international conventions. The State has an obligation to ensure adequate facilities for this, and existing advisories from the Union of India must be complied with by States/UTs to facilitate nursing mothers and infants.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: Citizens have a duty to “renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women” as enshrined in Article 51A(e) of the Constitution of India, and must ensure that the practice of breast-feeding in public places and at workplaces is not stigmatized.

special_directions.special_directions: The Union of India is directed to incorporate the advisory dated 27.02.2024 in a reminder communication to the Chief Secretaries/Administrators of all States/Union Territories along with a copy of this order, within two weeks. States/Union Territories should ensure that the aforesaid directions are given effect to in existing public places as far as practicable. Public buildings which are at the stage of planning and construction must ensure that sufficient space is reserved for child-care/nursing rooms. The Union of India may issue further advisories to the State Governments/Union Territories to communicate to all Public Sector Undertakings to set apart separate rooms/accommodation for child care/feeding & nursing of infants by mothers.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (@Special Leave Petition (Crl.) No. (@D. No.18552 of 2022)) WITH CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (@Special Leave Petition (Crl.) No.6895 of 2022)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the prosecution and conviction of an Enforcement Inspector and Office Assistant for demand and acceptance of bribe under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, following a trap operation.

judgements.case_summary:
This case involves two criminal appeals challenging the conviction of an Enforcement Inspector (Madan Lal, 2nd accused) and an Office Assistant (Narendra Kumar, 1st accused) under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. The prosecution stemmed from a trap laid by the Anti Corruption Bureau following a complaint by PW 5, who alleged demand and acceptance of a bribe for issuing a license. The Trial Court and High Court had convicted both accused, sentencing them to rigorous imprisonment and fines.

Before the Supreme Court, the appellants argued that the prosecution failed to prove the demand for a bribe, citing glaring inconsistencies in the complainant's (PW 5) testimony and significant deviations from his initial complaint. They further contended that independent witnesses (PW 1, PW 2, PW 6) either turned hostile or did not corroborate the physical transaction of the bribe, with some suggesting the money was thrust upon the accused or scattered. The State, conversely, asserted that the trap successfully caught the accused red-handed, supported by official witnesses and the positive reaction of the test solution on the accused's hands and clothes, arguing that the accused failed to rebut the presumption under Section 20 of the Act.

The Supreme Court meticulously examined the evidence, noting the substantial inconsistencies in PW 5's statements regarding the demanded amount. Crucially, the Court found that the independent witnesses did not support the prosecution's narrative of bribe acceptance, with their testimonies raising doubts about the actual transaction. The Court concluded that the prosecution had failed to establish the demand and acceptance of the bribe beyond all reasonable doubt. Consequently, the Court held that the presumption under Section 20 of the Prevention of Corruption Act could not be invoked. The appeals were allowed, and the convictions and sentences of both accused were set aside, leading to their acquittal. The bail bonds executed by the accused were also cancelled.

petitioner_key_arguments: The demand for bribe was not proven due to inconsistencies in PW 5's statement and differences from the complaint.
Independent witnesses (PW 1, 2, 6) turned hostile or did not witness the physical transaction of bribe.
The money was thrust upon the accused, and currency notes were scattered, not accepted.
No reliance can be placed on the test solution results as there was no demand or acceptance.
respondent_key_arguments: The trap proceedings successfully caught the accused red-handed.
The demand was spoken of by the complainant.
Official witnesses spoke of the receipt of money, validated by the test solution turning pink.
The accused failed to rebut the presumption under Section 20 of the Prevention of Corruption Act.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the prosecution failed to establish the demand and acceptance of bribe beyond all reasonable doubt, leading to the setting aside of the conviction.

outcome.relief_granted: The conviction and sentence of the accused are set aside. The bail bonds, if any executed by the accused, shall stand cancelled. The accused are acquitted.

acts_cited: Section 13(i)(d) of Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988
Section 13(2) of Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988
Section 7(2) of Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988
Section 20 of Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988
Section 164 of Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The prosecution failed to establish the demand and acceptance of bribe beyond all reasonable doubt. Inconsistencies in the complainant's testimony and the lack of corroboration from independent witnesses created reasonable doubt, thereby negating the presumption under Section 20 of the Prevention of Corruption Act.

special_directions.special_directions: The bail bonds, if any executed by the accused, in these cases, shall stand cancelled.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 3998 OF 2024

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the applicability of the “theory of deduction” for determining compensation payable under The Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, specifically regarding the market value of acquired land.

judgements.case_summary: The appellant, Madhya Pradesh Road Development Corporation, acquired land for road widening. Compensation was determined by the Competent Authority based on the Collector's Guidelines. Dissatisfied landowners, including Vincent Daniel, appealed to the Commissioner, who enhanced the compensation. The Corporation's objections were dismissed by the District Judge and subsequently by the High Court. The core issue before the Supreme Court was whether the 'theory of deduction,' traditionally applied under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, should be applied to determine compensation under the newer Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013. The Court analyzed Section 26 of the 2013 Act, which outlines methods for determining market value, including reliance on Stamp Act values (circle rates). It noted that while the Collector has discretion under Explanation 4 to Section 26(1) to adjust values, this discretion must be supported by recorded reasons. In this specific case, the Court found that the compensation was correctly calculated based on the Collector's Guidelines (circle rates) as per Section 26(1)(a) of the 2013 Act, and no opinion was formed by the Competent Authority or Commissioner to apply any deduction. The Court emphasized that circle rates should be scientifically fixed and reflect true market value. Ultimately, the Supreme Court upheld the compensation awarded by the Commissioner, dismissing the appeals filed by the Madhya Pradesh Road Development Corporation.

petitioner_key_arguments: The compensation awarded was disproportionately high for an undeveloped piece of land.
A significant portion of the land would be required for development (roads, drainage, electricity poles, etc.), incurring substantial expense.
Principles of compensation for developed lands should not apply to undeveloped land.
The 'theory of deduction' should be applied to reduce the compensation.
The circle rate used was not the baseline or floor rate and was considered too high.
respondent_key_arguments: The compensation was calculated in accordance with the mandate of the Acquisition Act, 2013.
The market value was determined based on the Collector's Guidelines (circle rates) as specified under the Stamp Act, which is permissible under Section 26(1)(a) of the 2013 Act.

The 'theory of deduction' as applied under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, does not automatically apply under the Acquisition Act, 2013, unless the Collector exercises discretion under Explanation 4 with recorded reasons, which was not done here.
The land in question was situated within municipal areas where the Collector's Guidelines were applicable.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the respondent's argument that the compensation was correctly calculated based on the Collector's Guidelines (circle rates) as per Section 26(1)(a) of the Acquisition Act, 2013. It ruled that the 'theory of deduction' was not applicable in this specific case because the Collector had not formed an opinion, with recorded reasons, to apply it under Explanation 4 to Section 26(1).

outcome.relief_granted: The compensation awarded by the Commissioner, based on the circle rate and Collector's Guidelines, is upheld. The appeals filed by the Madhya Pradesh Road Development Corporation are dismissed.

acts_cited: The Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (Acquisition Act, 2013) - Sections 2, 11, 15, 19, 20, 21, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 31, 105(3), First Schedule, Second Schedule, Third Schedule, Fourth Schedule

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that under the Acquisition Act, 2013, compensation for acquired land is determined by the market value as per Section 26. While the 'theory of deduction' was relevant under the 1894 Act, its application under the 2013 Act is contingent on the Collector's discretion under Explanation 4 to Section 26(1), supported by recorded reasons. In this case, the compensation was correctly based on the Stamp Act/Collector's Guidelines (circle rates) as per Section 26(1)(a), and no such discretionary opinion to apply deduction was formed.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that circle rates should be fixed scientifically by expert committees, reflect the true market value, and be made public to ensure predictability and reduce litigation. It also noted that public authorities, including state development corporations, cannot complain about high circle rates if they are responsible for fixing them, and it is their duty to ensure rates are neither inflated nor disproportionately low.

special_directions.special_directions: The Court advised that circle rates should be fixed by expert committees, which include specialists, and should reflect market realities. It also stated that concerned authorities should fix circle rates scientifically and in accordance with the law, ensuring they are neither inflated nor disproportionately low.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO.12009 OF 2024

case_details.subject_matter: This appeal concerns the enhancement of compensation awarded in a motor vehicle accident case, specifically regarding the calculation of 'loss of future earning' and 'future prospects'.

judgements.case_summary: This appeal was filed by Madivalappa against the Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation, seeking enhancement of compensation for injuries sustained in a vehicular accident on 11.07.2009. The appellant, then 27 years old, was initially awarded Rs.2,60,200/- by the MACT, which was later increased to Rs.3,05,200/- by the High Court. The appellant argued that both the MACT and High Court erred by not applying the multiplier '18' for 'loss of future earning' and by not including 40% for 'Future Prospects', citing precedents like Sarla Verma and Pranay Sethi. The respondent did not appear despite notice. The Supreme Court found merit in the appellant's arguments, agreeing that the multiplier '18' should be applied (considering the appellant's age of 24 years as assessed by MACT) and that 40% for future prospects should be included. Consequently, the Court recalculated the 'loss of future earning' to Rs.2,41,920/-, leading to a total compensation of Rs.3,83,920/-. The Court allowed the appeal, modifying the Impugned Judgment and directing the respondent to pay the differential amount of Rs.78,720/- with 6% interest, along with a cost of Rs.50,000/- for non-appearance.

petitioner_key_arguments: The High Court failed to enhance compensation under the head of 'loss of future earning' by using the multiplier '18' as per Sarla Verma v Delhi Transport Corporation, 2009 (6) SCC 121.
The High Court and MACT did not grant addition of 'Future Prospects' at 40% as per National Insurance Company Limited v Pranay Sethi, 2017 (16) SCC 680.
The correct calculation for 'loss of future earning' should be Rs.4,000/- (notional income) x 12 x 18 (multiplier) x 1.40 (future prospects) x 20/100 = Rs.2,41,920/-.
The appellant seeks an enhancement of Rs.78,720/- along with interest @ 6% per annum from the date of accident.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the multiplier '18' should be applied for 'loss of future earning' and that 40% for 'Future Prospects' should be added, based on the cited precedents.

outcome.relief_granted: The Civil Appeal is allowed, modifying the Impugned Judgment. The appellant is entitled to Rs.3,83,920/- as compensation, representing a differential amount of Rs.78,720/-. The respondent is directed to pay this amount within 30 days with interest at 6% per annum from the date of filing of the claim petition till realization. Failure to pay within 30 days will incur an additional interest of 8% on the principal and interest for the period of delay. A cost of Rs.50,000/- is imposed on the respondent for failure to appear and assist the Court, to be paid to the appellant within the same timeline.

precedents_cited: Sarla Verma v Delhi Transport Corporation, 2009 (6) SCC 121
National Insurance Company Limited v Pranay Sethi, 2017 (16) SCC 680

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The court's decision is based on the principle that compensation for 'loss of future earning' in motor accident cases must correctly apply the appropriate multiplier based on the victim's age and include a component for 'Future Prospects' as established by binding precedents. The High Court and MACT failed to correctly apply these principles, leading to an underestimation of compensation.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed that the respondent's failure to appear and assist the Court warranted the imposition of costs.

special_directions.special_directions: The respondent must pay the differential amount of Rs.78,720/- within 30 days of receiving a copy of the judgment, with interest at 6% per annum from the date of filing of the claim petition till realization. Failure to do so will result in an additional interest of 8% on the principal and interest for the period of delay. A cost of Rs.50,000/- is imposed on the respondent for non-appearance, to be paid to the appellant within the same timeline. The Registry is directed to dispatch a copy of the judgment to the Managing Director of the respondent-corporation.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS. 5560-5561 OF 2024

respondent_advocates: learned counsel appearing for the State

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the High Court's reversal of an acquittal into a conviction in revisional jurisdiction, alleged violation of natural justice, and the retrospective application of the proviso to Section 372 CrPC. It also addresses compensation for unlawful detention.

judgements.case_summary: The appeals challenge a High Court judgment that reversed the trial court's acquittal of the appellants for murder and convicted them, sentencing them to life imprisonment. The High Court's decision was made in revisional jurisdiction, without issuing notice to the acquitted appellants, and after the original de facto complainant (revisionist) had passed away. The Supreme Court noted that Section 401(3) CrPC explicitly bars converting an acquittal into a conviction in revision. It also found that the High Court violated principles of natural justice by proceeding ex-parte. Furthermore, the Court clarified that the proviso to Section 372 CrPC, which grants victims a right to appeal, is not retrospective and thus did not apply when the revision petition was filed in 2006. The Court also criticized the High Court's reliance on a hostile witness's police statement and the conduct of the Public Prosecutor. Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment and ordered the State Government to pay compensation to the appellants for their unlawful detention.

petitioner_key_arguments: High Court violated the express statutory bar under Section 401(3) CrPC against converting an acquittal into a conviction.
No right of appeal was available to the victim in law at the time the revision was filed (19.01.2006), thus Section 401(5) CrPC conditions were not met.
High Court proceeded ex-parte without issuing notice to the appellants, violating principles of natural justice and constitutional rights to be heard and represented.
High Court improperly relied on police statements (Section 161 CrPC) of a hostile witness, which are not substantive evidence and cannot be used to convert acquittal into conviction.
respondent_key_arguments: High Court could have invoked Section 401(5) CrPC to treat the revision as an appeal.
The proviso to Section 372 CrPC, introduced in 2009, should be given retrospective effect, allowing the victim's revision to be treated as an appeal.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the High Court exceeded its revisional jurisdiction by converting an acquittal into a conviction, violated natural justice by not providing an opportunity of being heard, and that the proviso to Section 372 CrPC is not retrospective in operation.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court is hereby set aside. The State Government shall pay Rs. 5,00,000/- each to the three appellants towards compensation within a period of four weeks. The bail bonds furnished by the appellants herein stand discharged.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO.13834 OF 2024

case_details.subject_matter: This case concerns an appeal against a High Court order that, in review jurisdiction, set aside a bus driver's dismissal and awarded back wages, finding the employer guilty of suppressing evidence in prior proceedings related to a road accident.

judgements.case_summary: Mahadeo, a bus driver for the Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation (MSRTC), was dismissed in 1997 following a fatal road accident. His dismissal was upheld by the Labour Court and a subsequent writ petition in the High Court. Mahadeo later discovered that in Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal (MACT) proceedings concerning the same accident, MSRTC had successfully argued that the accident was solely due to the lorry driver's negligence, thereby absolving Mahadeo. Mahadeo filed a review petition in the High Court, contending that MSRTC had suppressed this crucial evidence and made false representations in the earlier proceedings. The High Court, finding MSRTC guilty of "suggestio falsi" and "suppressio veri," set aside its previous dismissal order and the Labour Court's award, directing MSRTC to pay Mahadeo all benefits and back wages. MSRTC appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that the High Court erred in its review jurisdiction and in awarding full back wages. The Supreme Court affirmed the High Court's finding of MSRTC's misconduct in suppressing evidence. While upholding Mahadeo's entitlement to relief, the Supreme Court modified the back wages from 100% to 75% from the date of termination until superannuation, along with full terminal benefits and interest, noting Mahadeo's admission of engaging in daily wage work.

petitioner_key_arguments: The Corporation committed fraud on the Court by not disclosing the judicial proceedings before the MACT and the pleadings filed therein to obtain favourable orders.
Mahadeo has been fighting this legal battle since 1997, has been unable to find permanent employment as a driver, and has been victimised by the Corporation.

The impugned order granting relief is justified based on the decision in Deepali Gundu Surwase v. Kranti Junior Adhyapak Mahavidyala, which supports awarding full back wages for termination based on frivolous allegations.
respondent_key_arguments: Mahadeo, as a trained driver, was responsible for passenger safety; the extensive damage and high impact suggest negligent driving, as supported by T.N. State Transport Corpn. v. M. Chandrasekaran.
The proceedings before the MACT and the disciplinary proceedings operate on completely different footings.
Judicial review is limited to the analysis of the decision-making process, and the High Court should not have interfered with the Labour Court's decision.
The single judge substituted its view for that of the competent authority and erred in not remanding the matter to the Labour Court.

Full back wages were awarded without evidence of Mahadeo not being gainfully employed, and he had a blemished service record, contrary to the principles in Rajasthan State Road Transport Corporation, Jaipur v. Phool Chand.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted Mahadeo's arguments regarding the Corporation's fraudulent conduct (suggestio falsi and suppressio veri) and the relevance of the MACT findings. It also agreed that Mahadeo was entitled to back wages, though it modified the percentage.

outcome.relief_granted: Mahadeo is entitled to 75% of the back wages from the date of his termination till the date of his superannuation, along with full terminal benefits and interest @ 6% per annum. The amounts are to be released within three months, failing which further interest @ 2% will apply.

precedents_cited: Associate Builders v. Delhi Development Authority
T.N. State Transport Corpn. (Coimbatore) Ltd. v. M. Chandrasekaran
Rajasthan State Road Transport Corporation, Jaipur v. Phool Chand
Deepali Gundu Surwase v. Kranti Junior Adhyapak Mahavidyala
Hindustan Tin Works (P) Ltd. v. Employees
Surendra Kumar Verma v. Central Govt. Industrial Tribunal-cum-Labour Court
J.K. Synthetics Ltd. v. K.P. Agrawal
State of M.P. v. Narmada Bachao Andolan
Union of India v. N. Murugesan
constitutional_provisions: Article 226 of the Constitution of India
Articles 41 and 43 of the Constitution
Article 136 of the Constitution

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that a party engaging in "suggestio falsi" (false representation) and "suppressio veri" (suppression of truth) before a court, especially when it leads to an inequitable outcome for the other party, warrants judicial intervention, including review of previous decisions. Such conduct amounts to fraud on the court and undermines the administration of justice. Furthermore, while back wages are not automatic, they are generally awarded when termination is found to be illegal, with the burden on the employer to prove gainful employment of the employee during the intervening period.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed that while full back wages are the normal rule for wrongful termination, courts have discretion to modify this based on factors like the employee's gainful employment, length of service, and the employer's financial condition. It also reiterated that the burden of proving gainful employment lies with the employer once the employee asserts non-employment.

special_directions.special_directions: The amounts Mahadeo is entitled to shall be released by the Corporation within three months from the date of communication of this order. In default, the said amount shall carry further interest @ 2% from such default till full payment.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. ______ OF 2025 (@S.L.P (C) No.19499 of 2024)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns a batch of appeals challenging a High Court judgment that refused to interfere with an Industrial Court order. The Industrial Court had allowed complaints regarding the revision of salaries of workmen by the Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation in 2015, which cancelled an earlier pay fixation from 2010, alleging it to be an unfair labour practice.

judgements.case_summary: This batch of appeals arose from a High Court judgment that upheld an Industrial Court order. The Industrial Court had allowed complaints filed by workmen against the Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation (MSRTC) regarding a 2015 revision of salaries. This revision cancelled a previous pay fixation from 2010, which the workmen alleged constituted an unfair labour practice under the Maharashtra Recognition of Trade Union and Prevention of Unfair Labour Practices Act, 1971. The MSRTC argued that the 2015 revision was in consonance with the Supreme Court's decision in 'Maharashtra SRTC v. Premlali' and was necessary to prevent discrimination among daily wage workers. The respondents (workmen) contended that the revision prejudiced retired and serving employees, misconstrued the 'Premlali' judgment, and interfered with an unchallenged 2010 pay fixation that was already in compliance with an Industrial Court order and the 'Premlali' dictum. The Court analyzed the historical context of various settlements (1956, 1978, 1985) and the interpretation of 'Premlali'. It found that the 2010 pay fixation was indeed made after the 'Premlali' judgment and in compliance with an unchallenged Industrial Court order. The Court concluded that the 2015 revision was effected without proper notice and did not adequately refer to the 'Premlali' decision or subsequent related judgments. Consequently, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, upholding the Industrial Court's interference with the 2015 pay scale revision.

petitioner_key_arguments: The 2015 salary revision was in consonance with the Supreme Court's order in 'Maharashtra SRTC v. Premlali'.
The revision was necessitated to prevent discrimination regarding the time scale of pay granted to daily wage workers.
respondent_key_arguments: The 2015 revision prejudiced retired and serving employees and misconstrued the 'Premlali' judgment.
The earlier 2010 pay fixation was made after the 'Premlali' judgment and in compliance with an unchallenged Industrial Court order.
The 2015 revision was carried out without notice and without proper reference to 'Premlali'.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the respondents' arguments that the 2015 pay scale revision was invalid because the earlier 2010 fixation was made after the Supreme Court's Premlali judgment and in compliance with an unchallenged Industrial Court order. The court also noted that the 2015 revision was without notice and did not properly refer to Premlali, which had clarified that different settlements operated in different fields (time scale vs. absorption).

outcome.relief_granted: The order of the learned Single Judge, which confirmed the interference made by the Industrial Court to the pay scale revision effected in the year 2015, was upheld.

acts_cited: Maharashtra Recognition of Trade Union and Prevention of Unfair Labour Practices Act, 1971
precedents_cited: Maharashtra SRTC v. Premlali
Quinn vs. Leathem
Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation v. Sh. Arjun Gangaram Wajgikar and Ors.3

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The 2015 pay scale revision was invalid because the earlier 2010 fixation was made after the Supreme Court's Premlali judgment and in compliance with an unchallenged Industrial Court order. The MSRTC's attempt to revise pay in 2015, without notice and based on a 'labored interpretation' of Premlali, was not justified, especially since Premlali itself clarified that different settlements operated in different fields (time scale vs. absorption).
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: A case is only an authority for what it actually decides. It cannot be quoted for a proposition that may seem to follow logically from it, as such reasoning assumes that law is necessarily a logical code, whereas every lawyer must acknowledge that law is not always logical at all.

case_identification.respondent_name: EXIDE LIFE INSURANCE COMPANY LIMITED & ANR.
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 [Arising out of SLP (Civil) No. 2136 OF 2021]

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the repudiation of a life insurance claim by Exide Life Insurance Company Limited on the grounds of alleged material suppression of facts by the deceased insured regarding other existing insurance policies.

judgements.case_summary: Ramkaran Sharma, father of the appellant Mahaveer Sharma, obtained a life insurance policy from Exide Life Insurance Co. Ltd. on 09.06.2014 and subsequently died in an accident on 19.08.2015. The appellant's claim for benefits was repudiated on 03.03.2016, with the insurer citing material suppression of facts by the deceased regarding other existing insurance policies. The State Commission and National Commission upheld the repudiation. The appellant argued that there was no material suppression, as one Aviva policy was disclosed, the application form was filled by an agent, and the death was accidental, not due to illness, making health-related non-disclosure irrelevant. The respondent insurance company contended that the deceased held four policies (one Aviva, three LIC) but only disclosed one, justifying the repudiation. The Supreme Court analyzed whether the non-disclosure of all existing policies constituted 'material suppression' in this context. The Court distinguished the case from Mediclaim policies and cases involving illness-related deaths, noting that a 'substantial disclosure' was made by mentioning one policy. Given the accidental nature of death and the type of policy (life insurance), the Court concluded that the failure to mention all other policies did not amount to a material fact that would influence a prudent insurer's decision. Consequently, the appeal was allowed, and the repudiation was deemed improper. The Court directed the insurer to release all policy benefits with 9% interest.

petitioner_key_arguments: No material suppression on the part of his father while obtaining a life insurance policy.
It was not a policy relating to any Mediclaim nor any material fact regarding health was suppressed.
Inadvertent omission of policies issued by Life Insurance Corporation of India under clause 54.
Father mentioned another policy issued by Aviva in clause 54.
Application form was filled up by the agent and all necessary information was provided to the agent.
Death occurred on account of accident and not on account of any illness.
respondent_key_arguments: Insurance company was justified in repudiating the claim on account of material suppression.
Deceased was holding four policies (one Aviva, three LIC) but only disclosed one.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that the non-disclosure of all existing policies did not constitute material suppression in this specific case, given that one policy was disclosed, the death was accidental, and the nature of the policy was life insurance, not Mediclaim. The court found that the disclosed information was substantial enough for a prudent insurer to assess the risk.

outcome.relief_granted: The respondent insurance company is directed to release all benefits under the policy in question along with an interest of 9% per annum from the date the amount became due till the date of its realization to the appellant.

acts_cited: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority (Protection of Policyholders' Interests) Regulations, 2002
precedents_cited: Reliance Life Insurance Co. Ltd. & Anr. v. Rekhaben Nareshbhai Rathod, (2019) 6 Supreme Court Cases 175
Satwant Kaur Sandhu v. New India Assurance Co. Ltd., (2009) 8 SCC 316
Mahakali Sujatha v. Branch Manager, Future Generali India Life Insurance Company Limited & Another, (2024) 8 SCC 712
Manmohan Nanda v. United India Assurance Company Limited & Another, (2022) 4 SCC
Reynolds v. Phoenix Assurance Co. Ltd., (1978) 2 Lloyd's Rep 440

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: In a life insurance policy, where death is due to an accident and not illness, and there has been substantial disclosure of existing policies (even if not all), the failure to mention all other policies may not constitute material suppression influencing a prudent insurer's decision. The materiality of facts depends on the nature of the policy and the cause of death, and a partial disclosure, especially when the insurer is aware of the insured's capacity to pay premiums, may be deemed sufficient.

special_directions.special_directions: The respondent insurance company is directed to release all benefits under the policy in question along with an interest of 9% per annum from the date the amount became due till the date of its realization to the appellant.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 221 OF 2025 (@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRL.) NO. 11868 OF 2023)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns an appeal against the framing of charges under Section 306 of the Indian Penal Code for abetment of suicide, challenging whether the appellant's actions constituted instigation or creation of circumstances compelling suicide.

judgements.case_summary: The case involves an appeal against a High Court order that declined to discharge the appellant, Mahendra Awase, from charges under Section 306 IPC (abetment of suicide). The deceased, Ranjeet Chauhan, committed suicide after allegedly being harassed by the appellant over the repayment of a loan. A suicide note mentioned the appellant's harassment, and audio recordings of conversations between the deceased and the appellant, containing abusive language and demands for money, were presented as evidence. The appellant, an employee, was attempting to recover a loan guaranteed by the deceased. The High Court upheld the charges framed by the Trial Court. The Supreme Court analyzed the ingredients of Section 306 IPC, particularly 'instigation' as defined in Section 107 IPC, citing precedents like Swamy Prahaladdas, Madan Mohan Singh, and Amalendu Pal. The Court emphasized that for abetment, there must be a clear mens rea and an active or direct act of instigation, or creation of circumstances leaving no other option but suicide. It held that merely demanding repayment of a loan, even with heated exchanges or abusive language, does not amount to instigation or abetment of suicide. The Court concluded that the appellant's actions, viewed realistically and in context, did not create circumstances that left the deceased with no other option but to commit suicide. Consequently, the Supreme Court found the case groundless for framing charges under Section 306 IPC.

petitioner_key_arguments: The appellant's actions, including demanding repayment of a loan and using abusive language, did not constitute 'instigation' or 'abetment' as required by Section 306 read with Section 107 IPC.
There was no mens rea or active/direct act on the part of the appellant to compel the deceased to commit suicide.
The circumstances created by the appellant did not leave the deceased with no other option but to commit suicide, as per established legal precedents.
respondent_key_arguments: The suicide note and audio recordings indicated harassment by the appellant, which led the deceased to commit suicide.
The High Court correctly maintained the charges, implying that the appellant's actions were sufficient to constitute abetment under Section 306 IPC.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that the actions described in the suicide note and audio transcripts, primarily related to demanding loan repayment, did not meet the high threshold for 'instigation' or 'abetment' required under Section 306 IPC, as they did not demonstrate the necessary mens rea or direct act to compel suicide.

outcome.relief_granted: The appellant is discharged from proceedings in Sessions Case No. 19 of 2023 pending on the file of First Additional Sessions Judge, Khargone District, Mandleshwar. The impugned order dated 25.07.2023 passed by the High Court in Criminal Revision No. 1142 of 2023 is set aside, and the said proceedings are quashed.

acts_cited: Section 306 of the Indian Penal Code
Section 45 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
precedents_cited: Swamy Prahaladdas vs. State of M.P. and Another, [1995 Supp (3) SCC 438]
Madan Mohan Singh vs. State of Gujarat and Another, (2010) 8 SCC 628
Amalendu Pal alias Jhantu vs. State of West Bengal, (2010) 1 SCC 707
M. Mohan vs. State, (2011) 3 SCC 626
Ramesh Kumar vs. State of Chhattisgarh, (2001) 9 SCC 618

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that for an offence under Section 306 IPC (abetment of suicide), there must be a clear mens rea and an active or direct act of instigation, or the creation of circumstances that leave the deceased with no other option but to commit suicide. Mere casual words, demands for loan repayment, or heated exchanges, without the intent to drive a person to suicide, do not constitute abetment.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that Section 306 IPC is often casually and readily resorted to by the police, and emphasized the need for investigating agencies and trial courts to be sensitive to the law and exercise caution and circumspection, avoiding a 'play it safe' syndrome by mechanically framing charges.

special_directions.special_directions: The Court directed investigating agencies and trial courts to be sensitive to the law laid down for Section 306 IPC, ensuring that the provision is not deployed against individuals merely to assuage feelings, and to avoid mechanically framing charges without proper consideration of the ingredients of the offence.

case_identification.case_number: Civil Appeal Nos. of 2025 (@ SLP (C) Nos. 10558-59 of 2024)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the validity of property alienations (sale and gift deeds) made by an adoptive mother after adopting the appellant, and the appellant's entitlement to a share in the suit schedule properties based on the 'Doctrine of Relation Back'.

judgements.case_summary:
The case involves an appellant (Mahesh) who was adopted by defendant No.1 (Parvatibai) on 16.07.1994. Defendant No.1 was the widow of Bhavakanna Shahapurkar, who died on 04.03.1982. After Bhavakanna's death, a partition suit resulted in defendant No.1 acquiring a 9/32 share in certain properties. The appellant, claiming to be the legal heir of Bhavakanna through adoption, sought partition and challenged two alienations made by defendant No.1: a sale deed dated 13.12.2007 (for 'A' schedule property) and a gift deed dated 27.08.2008 (for 'B' and 'C' schedule properties). The Trial Court partly decreed the suit, declaring the gift deed null and void and granting 'B' and 'C' properties to the appellant, but upheld the sale deed. The High Court reversed the Trial Court's decision regarding the gift deed, upholding both alienations.

The Supreme Court examined the 'Doctrine of Relation Back' for adoption, Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act, and Section 122 of the Transfer of Property Act. It affirmed that while the 'Doctrine of Relation Back' applies, lawful alienations made by the adoptive mother before adoption are binding. The Court upheld the concurrent findings of the Trial Court and High Court regarding the validity of the sale deed, as defendant No.1 had absolute right over the 'A' schedule property. However, for the gift deed, the Court found that the essential pre-requisites of a valid gift under Section 122 of the TP Act, specifically delivery of possession and acceptance, were lacking. Therefore, the Supreme Court declared the gift deed null and void, restoring the Trial Court's finding that the appellant was entitled to the 'B' and 'C' schedule properties as the sole legal heir of defendant No.1.

petitioner_key_arguments: Appellant, as adopted son, is legal heir of Bhavakanna and entitled to half share in suit schedule properties.
Defendant No.1 was not competent to sell 'A' schedule property without appellant's consent.
Defendant No.1 had no right to execute the gift deed for 'B' and 'C' schedule properties, and it is not binding on the plaintiff.
Dismissal of suit for declaration against sale deed is arbitrary and erroneous.
respondent_key_arguments: Defendant No.1 became absolute owner of properties after Bhavakanna's death and by virtue of compromise decree.
Defendant No.1's ownership was prior to appellant's adoption, making alienations valid.
Defendant Nos.2 & 3 claimed possession of 'A' schedule property from date of purchase.
Defendant Nos.4 & 5 claimed absolute ownership of 'B' & 'C' schedule properties through valid gift deed.
Defendant No.6 denied adoption and claimed half share based on compromise decree.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that the gift deed was invalid due to lack of delivery and acceptance, making the petitioner entitled to the 'B' and 'C' schedule properties. The court rejected the petitioner's challenge to the sale deed, upholding the respondent's argument that the adoptive mother had absolute right over the 'A' schedule property and the sale was valid.

outcome.relief_granted: The gift deed dated 27.08.2008 executed by defendant No.1 in favour of defendant Nos.4 and 5 is declared null and void. The appellant is entitled to the entire 'B' and 'C' schedule properties as the sole heir of deceased defendant No.1. The sale deed dated 13.12.2007 is upheld, and the appellant is not entitled to any share in 'A' schedule property.

acts_cited: Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 16
Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, Section 12(c)
precedents_cited: Mst. Deu and Ors. v. Laxmi Narayan and Ors.1
Kasabai Tukaram Karvar and Others v. Nivruti (Dead) Through Legal Heirs and Others2
Shripad Gajanan Suthankar v. Dattaram Kashinath Suthankar3
Govind Hanumantha Rao Desai v. Nagappa alias Narahari Laxman Rao Deshpande and Sever, (1972) 1 SCC 515
Shripad Gajanan Suthankar v. Dattaram Kashinath Suthankar, (1974) 2 SCC 156

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The court held that while the 'Doctrine of Relation Back' makes an adopted child the legal heir from the date of the adoptive father's death, it does not divest the adoptive mother of property that vested in her before the adoption, especially if acquired through a compromise decree. However, for a gift to be valid, the requirements of Section 122 of the Transfer of Property Act, including delivery of possession and acceptance, must be met. The absence of these elements rendered the gift deed null and void.

special_directions.special_directions: no order as to costs.
special_directions.interim_orders: IA No.1/2018 therein for temporary injunction was held as not surviving and consequently the same was also dismissed.

case_identification.petitioner_name: MANILAL SHAMALBHAI PATEL (DECEASED) THROUGH HIS LEGAL HEIRS & ORS.
case_identification.respondent_name: OFFICER ON SPECIAL DUTY (LAND ACQUISITION) & ANR.
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 14670 OF 2015

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the enhancement of compensation for land acquired by the Government of Gujarat for public purpose, specifically challenging the High Court's dismissal of an appeal for higher compensation and consideration of income from fruit-bearing trees.

judgements.case_summary:
The appellants' land (Survey No. 179/3) in Village Ranoli, Gujarat, was acquired by the Government of Gujarat for the Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation (GIDC). The acquisition notification was published on 24.07.1989, and the Special Land Acquisition Officer (SLAO) awarded compensation at Rs. 11 per sq. mt. on 25.02.1992. Dissatisfied, the appellants sought a reference under Section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act, and the Reference Court enhanced the compensation to Rs. 30 per sq. mt. on 31.12.2011. The High Court, however, dismissed their appeal for further enhancement on 14.08.2015.

Before the Supreme Court, the appellants argued for higher compensation (at least Rs. 450 per sq. mt.) citing GIDC's allotment of a nearby plot (Plot No. 7/1) for a petrol pump at that rate, and also contended that income from fruit-bearing trees on their land was not adequately considered. The respondents maintained that the SLAO's compensation was just.

The Supreme Court analyzed the comparable plot (Plot No. 7/1), noting its commercial purpose versus the agricultural nature of the acquired land. It considered GIDC's own industrial land rate of Rs. 180 per sq. mt. from 25.03.1988, increased it by 5% for the time difference to Rs. 190 per sq. mt., and then applied a total 50% deduction (40% for development costs and 10% for largeness of area). This resulted in a compensation rate of Rs. 95 per sq. mt. The Court found no sufficient evidence to support additional compensation for fruit-bearing trees beyond the Rs. 1,06,300 already offered by the SLAO.

Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment, modified the awards of the SLAO and Reference Court, and fixed the compensation at Rs. 95 per sq. mt. with all statutory benefits and interest. The civil appeal was allowed to this extent.

petitioner_key_arguments: Higher compensation (at least Rs. 450 per sq. mt.) based on GIDC's allotment of Plot No. 7/1 for a petrol pump.
Income from fruit-bearing trees (lemon, mango, guava) not considered by lower courts.
respondent_key_arguments: Compensation determined by the SLAO is just and proper.
No justification for enhancement of the compensation as awarded by the Reference Court.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument for enhanced compensation for the acquired land, but determined a different rate (Rs. 95 per sq. mt.) after applying deductions for development and largeness of area. The argument for additional compensation for fruit-bearing trees was not accepted due to lack of evidence.

outcome.relief_granted: Compensation for the acquired land fixed at Rs.95/- per sq. mt. with all statutory benefits including interest as permissible in law.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The market value of acquired land for compensation is determined by considering comparable sales (like GIDC's industrial plot rate), adjusting for time difference, and applying deductions for development costs (as agricultural land needs conversion for industrial use) and largeness of area. Lack of documentary evidence for income from fruit trees means no additional compensation for them beyond the initial offer.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The determination of the prevalent market value of the acquired land is not an algebraic formula and that cannot be determined in a precise or an accurate manner. Some amount of guess work is always permissible. Therefore, a judge has to sit in an arm chair and without much taxing his mind has to determine the market value in a prudent manner.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S). OF 2025 (ARISING OUT OF SLP(CRL.) NO(S). 15882 OF 2024)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns an appeal against a High Court order that partially upheld a summoning order in a criminal case involving alleged sexual offenses and offenses under the SC/ST Act, stemming from a relationship based on a promise to marry.

judgements.case_summary: The case involves an appeal by Manish Yadav against an order of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, which partially upheld a summoning order against him in a criminal case. The complainant alleged that Manish Yadav befriended her on Instagram, promised marriage, engaged in physical relations, forced an abortion, and later used caste-based slurs while refusing to marry her. An FIR was registered under various sections of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act. The trial court summoned Manish Yadav and his father, but the High Court quashed the summoning order against the father while upholding it against Manish Yadav. The Supreme Court examined the complainant's statement under Section 164 CrPC, noting that the initial physical relationship was consensual and that the complainant herself declined the appellant's proposal to elope. Citing precedents, the Court distinguished between a mere breach of promise and a false promise to marry, concluding that there was no evidence of a fraudulent intention from the outset. Furthermore, the Court found no evidence to support the allegations under the SC/ST Act. Consequently, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, quashing the summoning order and all related proceedings against Manish Yadav, deeming the prosecution an abuse of the process of law.

petitioner_key_arguments: The relationship was consensual and not based on a false promise of marriage from the inception.
The complainant's own statement under Section 164 CrPC indicates initial consent and her refusal to elope, contradicting the 'false promise' theory.
There is no evidence to support the allegations under the SC/ST Act, as the complainant did not mention caste-based abuse in her statement.
respondent_key_arguments: The appellant induced the complainant into physical relations under a false promise of marriage.
The appellant committed sexual offenses and offenses under the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments prevailed, as the court found the relationship to be initially consensual, lacked evidence of a false promise to marry from the inception, and found no basis for the SC/ST Act offenses.

outcome.relief_granted: The summoning order dated 24th August, 2023, passed by learned Special Judge, SC/ST Act Gazipur, and all the proceedings sought to be taken thereunder against the appellant for the offences punishable under Sections 376, 323, 504 and 506, IPC and Sections 3(1)(r), 3(1)(s), 3(2)(5a) and 3(2)(v) of the SC/ST Act are quashed.

acts_cited: Scheduled Castes and the Schedules Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, Sections 3(1)(r)
Scheduled Castes and the Schedules Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, Sections 3(1)(s)
Scheduled Castes and the Schedules Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, Sections 3(2)(5a)
Scheduled Castes and the Schedules Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, Sections 3(2)(v)
precedents_cited: Uday v. State of Karnataka (2003) 4 SCC 46
Deepak Gulati v. State of Haryana (2013) 7 SCC 675
Deelip Singh v. State of Bihar (2005) 1 SCC 88

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that consent for sexual intercourse given on a promise of marriage is not considered a misconception of fact unless the promise was false from its inception with a fraudulent intention. A mere breach of promise due to unforeseen circumstances is distinct from a false promise. In this case, the relationship was initially consensual, and there was no evidence of a false promise to marry from the outset or caste-based abuse, thus the ingredients for the alleged offenses were not met.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court emphasized that each case must be considered on its own peculiar facts and surrounding circumstances, and the burden is on the prosecution to prove every ingredient of the offense, including the absence of consent.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (Arising out of SLP (Criminal) No. 10931 OF 2022)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the quashing of an FIR registered under Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, stemming from an alleged cheating in a commercial transaction involving coal supply.

judgements.case_summary: The Supreme Court heard an appeal against a High Court order that refused to quash an FIR (No. 80/2022) registered under Section 420 IPC against the appellant, Manish. The dispute arose from a commercial transaction where Manish, portraying himself as a creditworthy businessman, procured coal from the 2nd non-applicant (Nitin) between 2015-2017. Manish subsequently defaulted on payments, leading to a notarized agreement in 2020 for repayment in installments, which he also failed to fully honor after an initial payment. Consequently, the 2nd non-applicant initiated criminal proceedings, resulting in the FIR. The High Court had concluded that the allegations prima facie disclosed ingredients of Section 415 IPC, deeming it more than a purely commercial dispute. The Supreme Court, however, focused its analysis on whether dishonest intention existed at the *inception* of the transaction. It noted that Manish's bankers had reposed confidence in his financial liquidity, and there was no evidence of his insolvency or bankruptcy at the time of the coal supply. The Court emphasized that a mere breach of contract or failure to pay due to business setbacks, without initial fraudulent intent, does not constitute a criminal offence of cheating. Finding no evidence of dishonest inducement at the outset, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's order and quashing the FIR.

petitioner_key_arguments: The representation of being a creditworthy businessman cannot be labelled as 'deception' merely because of failure to honour subsequent agreement terms.
Mere breach of promise to repay does not infer dishonest intention.
The case is a commercial dispute, not a criminal offence, as there was no dishonest intention at the inception of the transaction.
Materials collected during investigation do not show the case falls in the category of commercial disputes which would attract penal consequences.
respondent_key_arguments: The appellant induced the 2nd non-applicant to sell coal by projecting himself as a reputed, trustworthy, and creditworthy businessman, which constituted a false representation.
The appellant's failure to adhere to the repayment schedule in the notarized agreement further evidenced his dishonest intent.
The allegations prima facie divulge ingredients of offence under Section 415 IPC.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments prevailed, as the Supreme Court found no evidence of dishonest intention at the inception of the transaction, concluding that mere breach of contract or failure to pay due to business setbacks does not constitute cheating under Section 420 IPC.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned order is set aside and FIR No. 80/2022, dated 11th February, 2022, registered under Section 420 IPC, at the Police Station Lakadganj, Nagpur is hereby quashed.

precedents_cited: State of Haryana vs. Bhajan Lal
Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma and Ors vs State of Bihar and Anr, (2000) 4 SCC 168
Satishchandra Ratanlal Shah vs State of Gujarat and Anr., (2019) 9 SCC 148
Delhi Race Club (1940) Ltd and Ors vs State of Uttar Pradesh and Anr, (2024) 10 SCC 690
Hari Prasad Chamaria vs Bishun Kumar Surekha and others, (1973) 2 SCC 823
Mohsinbhai Fateali vs Emperor
Sarabjit Kaur vs State of Punjab & Anr., (2023) 5 SCC 360
Khoda Bakhsh vs Bakeya Mundari
1992 Supp (1) SCC 335
1931 SCC OnLine Bom 55
1905 SCC OnLine Cal 170

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: For an offence of cheating under Section 420 IPC, dishonest intention must be present at the inception of the transaction, inducing the other party to part with property. A mere breach of contract or failure to pay due to business setbacks, without initial fraudulent intent, does not constitute a criminal offence and remains a civil dispute.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The High Court would sparingly exercise its inherent powers to interdict a criminal proceeding. The principles for quashing a criminal proceeding, as laid down in State of Haryana vs. Bhajan Lal, were reiterated.
