case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 1048/2017

case_details.subject_matter: The appeal concerns the High Court's refusal to grant leave to appeal against an acquittal in a murder case, specifically examining the parameters for granting such leave under Section 378(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code.

judgements.case_summary: This appeal was filed by the original first informant, the brother of the deceased, challenging an order by the High Court of Judicature at Bombay. The High Court had declined to grant leave under Section 378(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code for an appeal against the acquittal of respondent no.1 (the deceased's husband) in a murder case. The prosecution alleged that respondent no.1 fired a shot at his wife, who succumbed to firearm injuries, with their fifteen-year-old son being an eyewitness. The Trial Court acquitted respondent no.1, citing inconsistencies, material omissions, and improvements in prosecution evidence, including the son turning hostile, delayed FIR, and unreliable recovery evidence. The High Court upheld this decision, finding no perversity in the Trial Court's reasoning. The Supreme Court, however, reviewed the principles for granting leave to appeal, emphasizing that a prima facie case or arguable points should warrant granting leave, rather than a pre-determination of the appeal's outcome. The Court found the High Court's reasoning for declining leave unconvincing, especially given the case's reliance on circumstantial evidence and the key eyewitness turning hostile. Consequently, the Supreme Court granted leave to appeal and remitted the matter to the High Court for a full consideration of the criminal appeal on its merits.

petitioner_key_arguments: The High Court erred in declining leave to appeal against the acquittal, as there were arguable points and a prima facie case for appeal.
The High Court's reasoning for refusing leave was unconvincing and did not adhere to the established parameters for granting leave under Section 378(3) Cr.P.C.
respondent_key_arguments: The High Court correctly found no perversity in the Trial Court's judgment of acquittal.
The High Court was justified in declining leave to appeal as the prosecution failed to establish a strong case.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's argument that the High Court should have granted leave to appeal, given the existence of arguable points, prevailed.

outcome.relief_granted: Leave to appeal granted; matter remitted to the High Court for consideration of the criminal appeal on its own merits.

precedents_cited: State of Maharashtra v. Sujay Mangesh Poyarekar reported in (2008) 9 SCC 475
Sita Ram v. State of U.P. reported in (1979) 2 SCC 656

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The High Court, when considering an application for leave to appeal against an order of acquittal under Section 378(3) Cr.P.C., must apply its mind to determine if a prima facie case or arguable points have been raised, rather than pre-judging whether the acquittal would ultimately be set aside. Refusal of leave without adequate reasons, especially when arguable points exist, constitutes an error.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that the mere act of abscondence does not necessarily lead to a conclusion of guilt, as even an innocent person may panic and try to evade arrest when wrongly suspected. It also noted that the principle of a single right of appeal is rooted in the doctrine of human fallibility and the idea that every crime is an offense against society.

special_directions.special_directions: The criminal appeal against the judgment and order of acquittal shall be decided on its own merits by the High Court without being influenced by any observations made by the Supreme Court in this order. The original first informant is permitted to file an appeal under the proviso to Section 372 of the CrPC, which may be clubbed with the State's appeal and heard together.

case_identification.petitioner_name: MANSOOR ALI FARIDA IRSHAD ALI & OTHERS
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (ARISING OUT OF SLP (C) NO.1665 OF 2023); CIVIL APPEAL NO(S). OF 2025 (ARISING OUT OF SLP(C) NO(S). OF 2025) DIARY NO.40035 OF 2024; CIVIL APPEAL NO(S). OF 2025 (ARISING OUT OF SLP(C) NO(S). OF 2025) DIARY NO.49187 OF 2024

case_details.subject_matter: The appeals challenge a High Court order dismissing a writ petition against a notice to vacate premises for slum redevelopment under the Maharashtra Slum Areas (Improvement, Clearance and Redevelopment) Act, 1971.

judgements.case_summary:
The appeals challenge an order dated 04.01.2023 by the High Court of Bombay, which dismissed a writ petition filed against a notice issued by the Slum Rehabilitation Authority (SRA) on 06.12.2022. This notice directed appellants to vacate their premises for redevelopment. A prior SRA notice from 28.01.2019, directing vacation for redevelopment, was upheld by the Apex Grievance Redressal Committee (AGRC) on 12.06.2019. Despite this, appellants did not vacate, leading to the second notice.

The appellants argued that the plot was a MHADA layout, not subject to SRA redevelopment under Regulation 33(10) of DCR, but rather MHADA's jurisdiction under Regulation 33(5). They also claimed a lack of mandatory 70% occupant consent and that the area was not a 'censused slum', asserting they were MHADA tenants. The Court found that the AGRC had rightly dismissed these contentions, noting that MHADA consistently stated the plot was never a MHADA layout and had granted an NOC to SRA. The Court emphasized that the AGRC order was never challenged and attained finality. It also found that the plot was a 'censused slum' as per Regulation 33(10) of DCR, for which no separate notification under the Slum Act was required. The Court concluded that the appellants were using dilatory tactics, were ineligible slum dwellers, and were obstructing a legitimate redevelopment project benefiting a large number of eligible slum dwellers. Consequently, the appeals were dismissed.

petitioner_key_arguments: The plot is a MHADA layout and should be redeveloped by MHADA under Regulation 33(5) of DCR, not SRA under Regulation 33(10) of DCR.
The scheme was being implemented without obtaining the mandatory 70% consent of occupants.
They are tenants of MHADA and pay rent to MHADA.
No notification was issued under the Slum Act declaring the area to be a slum area.
They were unaware of the AGRC order dated 12.06.2019.
respondent_key_arguments: The plot is not a MHADA layout; MHADA has consistently maintained this and granted an NOC to SRA for redevelopment.
The area is a 'censused slum' as per Regulation 33(10) of DCR, thus no separate notification under the Slum Act is required.
Appellants were never MHADA tenants but transit camp tenants, and were ineligible slum dwellers.
The AGRC order dated 12.06.2019, which dismissed appellants' contentions, was never challenged and attained finality.
The project has obtained the necessary 70% consent from eligible slum dwellers.
Appellants are using dilatory tactics to delay a legitimate redevelopment project.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the arguments that the plot was a 'censused slum' falling under SRA's jurisdiction with MHADA's NOC, that the appellants were ineligible transit camp tenants, and that the AGRC's decision was final and unchallenged. The court found the appellants' claims to be without substance and their actions dilatory.

acts_cited: Maharashtra Slum Areas (Improvement, Clearance and Redevelopment) Act, 1971, Sections 33, 38, 3, 4, 4A, 3A, 3B
Maharashtra Housing and Area Development Act, 1976
Development Control Regulations for Greater Mumbai, 1991, Regulations 33(5), 33(10), 33(10)(II)(i), 33(10)(II)(viii)

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The court dismissed the appeals primarily because the appellants' claims regarding the land's classification as a MHADA layout and the SRA's jurisdiction were found to be unsubstantiated, as the land was a 'censused slum' with MHADA's No Objection Certificate. Furthermore, the appellants were deemed ineligible slum dwellers and had failed to challenge a prior adverse order from the AGRC, indicating dilatory tactics to obstruct a legitimate redevelopment project.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed that some appellants were "fence sitters" who directly approached the Supreme Court without being parties before the High Court, and found no merit in their case.

special_directions.interim_orders: Interim order(s), if any, stand(s) vacated.

case_identification.respondent_name: STATE REPRESENTED BY THE INSPECTOR OF POLICE & ANR. RESPONDENTS
case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.367 OF 2025

respondent_advocates: Mr. Amit Anand Tiwari, Sr. A.A.G.

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns an appeal against a High Court judgment that refused to quash a criminal chargesheet against the appellants (parents) for alleged cheating, stemming from their son's relationship with the complainant.

judgements.case_summary: The appellants, Marippan & Anr., challenged a High Court judgment that rejected their plea to quash a criminal chargesheet against them. The complainant alleged a relationship with the appellants' son, claiming the appellants had assured her of marriage, leading to physical relations. The appellants argued that the complaint lacked any allegations of instigation, misrepresentation, or knowledge of their son's intimate relationship on their part. The complainant contended that the parents' assurance was crucial for her physical relationship with their son, who later duped her. The Supreme Court found no evidence of illegal or criminal conduct by the appellants, concluding that the ingredients of cheating under Section 415 IPC were not met. The Court noted that the complainant was 29 and the son 32, both educated, and the main allegations were against the son, who could be proceeded against independently. Citing precedents, the Court emphasized protecting against vexatious prosecution. The Court also disapproved of a High Court observation made against the son, who was not a party to the proceedings, and ordered its deletion. Consequently, the appeal was allowed, the High Court's judgment was set aside, and the criminal proceedings against the appellants were quashed.

petitioner_key_arguments: Nowhere in the entire complaint there is any allegation that the parents had instigated or had misrepresented to the complainant that they would get her married to their son.
There is no allegation that the appellants forced the son to marry another girl and that they had any knowledge of the intimate relationship of their son with the complainant.
respondent_key_arguments: The role of the appellants is crucial since they were the parents and only upon their assurance, the complainant had agreed to a physical relationship.
The son of the appellants had duped her and married another girl.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the complaint did not disclose any illegal or criminal act by the appellants, and specifically, the ingredients of cheating under Section 415 of the IPC were not made out against them.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal is allowed. The Impugned Judgment is set aside. Proceedings in P.R.C. No.16/2022 insofar as they relate to the appellants stand quashed. They are discharged from the liabilities of their bail bonds and sureties.

acts_cited: Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
Section 417 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860
Section 319 of the Criminal Procedure Code
precedents_cited: Vishnu Kumar Shukla v State of Uttar Pradesh, (2023) 15 SCC 502
Pushpendra Mishra v. State of M.P., 2019 SCC OnLine MP 7164
Priyanka Mishra v. State of M.P., (2023) 15 SCC 480
Anu Kumar v State (UT Administration), 2021 SCC OnLine SC 3454

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The court held that the complaint did not contain any allegations or evidence of acts or conduct by the appellants that could be deemed illegal or criminal, specifically lacking the essential ingredients for an offence under Section 415 of the Indian Penal Code. The court found no basis to hold the parents criminally liable for the actions of their adult son.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court strongly disapproved of the High Court's observation made against the appellants' son, who was not a party to the proceedings, and directed that this observation be deleted from the High Court's records, emphasizing that such remarks against third parties without notice or opportunity to be heard are impermissible.

special_directions.special_directions: A copy of this Order be despatched to the Registrar (Judicial), Madurai Bench, Madras High Court. The extract from Para 10 of the Impugned Judgment quoted supra shall stand deleted from the High Court's records.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 [@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRL) NO.13369 OF 2024]

case_details.subject_matter: The case involves a criminal appeal against conviction for homicide and injuries stemming from an altercation over a disputed land and deity worship, where the accused trespassed and attacked the victims with deadly weapons.

judgements.case_summary: This criminal appeal challenges the conviction of the appellants for homicide and causing injuries. The incident originated from a dispute over land and the worship of a deity, where the accused, allegedly instigated, trespassed into the deceased's house armed with deadly weapons. A scuffle ensued, resulting in the death of the grandfather and injuries to three grandchildren. The Trial Court convicted three appellants under Sections 302, 323, and 324 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, sentencing them to life imprisonment for homicide and lesser terms for injuries. The High Court affirmed this decision. The appellants argued lack of premeditation or intent to kill, suggesting the death might have been accidental or that the conviction should be under Part II of Section 304 IPC. The respondent-State countered that the attack was premeditated, intentional, and carried out with deadly weapons, supported by credible injured eye-witness testimony. The Supreme Court, after reviewing the evidence, found the ocular testimony of the injured grandchildren credible and concluded that the prosecution unequivocally proved the accused's premeditated intention to cause harm. The medical evidence, while noting the injury could have been accidental, did not negate the Section 302 finding given the strong ocular testimony and the nature of the attack. The appeal was dismissed, and the conviction and sentence were upheld.

petitioner_key_arguments: There was no premeditation and no intention to cause death.
There was no remotest knowledge of an injury being caused which was likely to cause death.
The injury which resulted in death could have been caused by an accidental fall.
If found guilty, the accused can only be convicted under Part II of Section 304 IPC.
respondent_key_arguments: The injured witnesses (eye-witnesses) have spoken in tandem.
The accused trespassed into the house of the victims and attacked them.
There was absolutely no provocation on the part of the victims.
The attack was with premeditation and intention to cause death, as the accused came armed with deadly weapons.
The fact that the deceased died after 25 days does not alter the finding of murder, as the single blow to the head led to death.
There is no reason to interfere with the conviction or alter the sentence imposed.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The respondent's arguments prevailed, as the court found sufficient evidence of premeditation and intention to cause death, upholding the conviction under Section 302 IPC and dismissing the appeal.

acts_cited: Indian Penal Code, Section 304 Part II

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The court held that the prosecution unequivocally proved premeditation and intention to cause death, based on the accused's armed trespass into the deceased's house, the ensuing altercation, and the fatal blow to the head. The credible ocular testimony of injured witnesses, despite their relation to the deceased, was sufficient to establish the guilt under Section 302 IPC, overriding the possibility suggested by medical evidence that the injury could have been caused by an accidental fall.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed that "motive of enmity is a doubled edged weapon. Animosity alleged can even lead to an accusation of false allegation on the part of the complainant to deliberately implicate the accused."

special_directions.special_directions: The appellants, if on bail, shall appear and surrender before the Sessions Court, within two weeks of this order; failing which the Sessions Court shall take appropriate steps to apprehend them so as to undergo the sentence awarded.
special_directions.interim_orders: Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

case_identification.respondent_name: THE ORIENTAL INSURANCE CO. LTD. AND OTHERS
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (Arising out of S.L.P.(C) No.30398 of 2019)

case_details.subject_matter: This case concerns a motor accident claim, specifically challenging the High Court's reduction of compensation by applying a split multiplier and reducing consortium amounts, and seeking proper calculation of loss of dependency and future prospects.

judgements.case_summary:
This Civil Appeal concerns a motor accident claim where the High Court significantly reduced the compensation awarded by the Tribunal. The deceased, Laxman Das Mahour, a 57-58-year-old BSNL mechanic, died in a bus accident on March 7, 2014. The Tribunal initially awarded ₹28,66,994. However, the High Court reduced this to ₹19,66,833 by applying a "split multiplier" method for calculating loss of dependency and lowering the consortium amount.
The petitioners, the deceased's family, argued that the High Court erred by applying a novel split multiplier without proper justification, failing to account for future prospects (a 15% increase), and unduly reducing the consortium. The respondent, the insurance company, contended that the High Court's assessment was fair, considering the deceased was nearing retirement and would have received a pension, not a full salary.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court's application of the split multiplier was erroneous, as it lacked specific reasons and contradicted precedents like Sarla Verma and Sumathi. The Court emphasized that the deceased, being a technically qualified person, was entitled to future prospects. It also noted the Tribunal's error in the consortium amount.
Consequently, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's order. It modified the Tribunal's award, granting a total compensation of ₹33,03,000, along with interest at the rate previously awarded by the Tribunal. This decision reaffirms the principles for calculating motor accident compensation, particularly regarding the application of multipliers and future prospects.

petitioner_key_arguments: High Court committed grave error in reducing compensation by applying a novel split method for pre and post-retirement income.
Appellants are entitled to 15% increase on account of future prospects.
Tribunal failed to grant compensation for loss of estate.
High Court erred in reducing the amount of consortium.
respondent_key_arguments: The compensation assessed by the High Court is just and fair.
Deceased was close to 58 years of age and would have retired in 2-3 years, thereafter receiving pension and not salary.
Compensation should be calculated with reference to loss to the family post-retirement.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the High Court erred in applying a split multiplier without specific reasons, that the deceased was entitled to future prospects, and that the consortium amount was incorrectly reduced.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal is allowed, the impugned order passed by the High Court is set aside. The award of the Tribunal is modified. The appellants are entitled to total compensation of 33,03,000/- (rounded off) with interest at the same rate as was awarded by the Tribunal.

precedents_cited: National Insurance Company Limited v. Pranay Sethi and Others
Sarla Verma v. DTC
Sumathi v. M/s. National Insurance Company Ltd.
Puttamma & Ors. v. K. L. Narayana Reddy & Anr.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The High Court erred in applying a 'split multiplier' for calculating loss of dependency without recording specific reasons, which is contrary to established precedents like Sarla Verma and Sumathi. The deceased was entitled to future prospects (15% increase), and the consortium amount was incorrectly reduced by the High Court.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: People are generally healthy at that age and continue working even after retirement.

special_directions.special_directions: The appellants are held to be entitled to total compensation of 33,03,000/- (rounded off). They shall be entitled to payment of interest at the same rate as was awarded by the Tribunal.

case_identification.case_number: CONTEMPT PETITION (C) NO. 741 OF 2020 IN CONTEMPT PETITION (C) NO. 1030 OF 2018 IN CIVIL APPEAL NO. 2703 OF 2017

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns alleged non-compliance with a previous court order regarding the absorption of a lecturer, payment of salary arrears, and pension, leading to a contempt petition.

judgements.case_summary: The petitioner, Meera Singh, a lecturer, was absorbed in Tilka Manjhi Bhagalpur University based on a J. Sinha Commission order (03.08.2015), confirmed by the Supreme Court (31.08.2017) in 'Krishna Nand Yadav & others Vs. Magadh University & others'. Her absorption was notified on 17.09.2018. Subsequently, the petitioner filed Contempt Petition (C) No. 1030 of 2018 for non-compliance. On 27.02.2019, the Court disposed of it, noting absorption and payment of admitted claims, with a direction for remaining arrears to be paid after verification. Alleging continued non-compliance, the petitioner filed the present Contempt Petition (C) No. 741 of 2020. The State of Bihar contended that ascertainable arrears were paid and raised issues regarding the verification of absence/working periods and the stoppage of pension, citing previous orders in 'Baidya Nath Choudhary Vs. Dr. Sree Surendra Kumar Singh'. The Court found that the issues of actual working, salary payment, and arrears required a detailed fact-finding inquiry, which was not suitable for resolution in a contempt petition. It clarified that previous orders in 'Baidya Nath Choudhary' did not stop pension for actual work but for periods where salaries were received without working. Consequently, the Court disposed of the contempt petition, directing the Registrar/Vice Chancellor of the University to adjudicate all pending issues regarding salary arrears and pension claims within specified timelines.

petitioner_key_arguments: Alleged non-compliance of the order dated 27.02.2019 passed in Contempt Petition (C) No. 1030 of 2018.
Grievance that directions issued in the main case and previous contempt petition regarding absorption, salary arrears, and pension have not been complied with.
respondent_key_arguments: Ascertainable arrears of salary for actual working days have been paid.
Verification of absence period and actual working period for arrears is complex and requires inquiry, citing orders in 'Baidya Nath Choudhary'.
Pension was put on hold by university vide order dated 03.06.2020, also requiring adjudication.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court acknowledged the petitioner's grievance regarding non-compliance but agreed with the respondent that the issues required a detailed fact-finding inquiry, leading to a directive for adjudication by university authorities rather than a direct contempt finding.

outcome.relief_granted: The contempt petition was disposed of with directions for the Registrar/Vice Chancellor of the University to adjudicate all issues related to salary arrears and pension claims within specified timelines, after conducting a discrete inquiry and affording due opportunity to all parties.

precedents_cited: Krishna Nand Yadav & others Vs. Magadh University & others
Baidya Nath Choudhary Vs. Dr. Sree Surendra Kumar Singh
State of Bihar & others vs Bihar Rajya M.S.E.S.K.K.M & others (2005) 9 SCC 129

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: Complex factual disputes concerning actual working days, salary arrears, and pension entitlement, especially when influenced by previous orders in similar cases, are not suitable for resolution in a contempt petition. Such matters necessitate a detailed fact-finding inquiry by appropriate administrative authorities to ensure a just and reasoned decision.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court clarified that previous orders in 'Baidya Nath Choudhary' did not stop pension payments for periods of actual work, but rather for periods where employees received salaries without actually working.

special_directions.special_directions:
1. The petitioner shall submit her claim along with relevant documents setting up her actual working in college in terms of the orders of absorption claiming salary, and also for pension from the date of absorption upto February 28, 2025 before the Registrar/Vice Chancellor of the University.
2. On receiving the claim of salary, a discrete enquiry be held affording due opportunity to the employee, college concerned and the representative of the State if required, and a reasoned order be passed regarding payment of salary and arrears, if any, within a period of three months thereafter.
3. The claim regarding pension of petitioner which has been withheld be decided counting the period of service, w.e.f. date of absorption notionally uninfluenced by the orders dated 11.07.2019, 07.08.2019 and 12.02.2021 passed in Contempt Petition (C) No. 1188 of 2018 in Baidya Nath Choudhary (supra).
4. After adjudicating the issue of pension and arrears the same be paid adjusting the amount already paid as expeditiously as possible not later than two months from the date of such order.
5. Upon adjudication, if it is found that any excess amount has been paid either in the head of salary or pension, it be quantified and the university/college/state as the case may be, shall be at liberty to take recourse to recover the same following the procedure as prescribed.
6. If the employees have submitted the joint claim of arrears of salary and pension, in that event the issue of arrears of salary be governed by direction No. (ii) and pension be governed by direction (iii).
7. In case, the parties feel dissatisfied by the orders of the Registrar/Vice Chancellor of the University, they shall be at liberty to take recourse as permissible before the High Court.
special_directions.interim_orders: Pending interlocutory application(s), if any, stands disposed of.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.127 OF 2014, CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 126 OF 2014

case_details.subject_matter: The case challenges a High Court judgment that upheld the conviction of the appellants for murder and related offenses, primarily questioning the reliability and corroboration of a sole witness's testimony.

judgements.case_summary:
The case involves an appeal against a High Court judgment dated 17th July 2012, which dismissed criminal appeals and confirmed the conviction of appellants Rajkumar and Mehatar for offenses under Sections 147, 148, 452, and 302 read with Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, sentencing them to life imprisonment. The prosecution's case, based on the testimony of PW-1 Sindhubai, alleged a long-standing enmity and an incident on 20th December 2005 where the accused assaulted her husband and brother-in-law, leading to their deaths. The trial court convicted all ten accused, but the High Court acquitted six, maintaining conviction for Rajkumar, Baburao (who died during the appeal), and Mehatar.
The petitioner (appellants Rajkumar and Mehatar) argued that the High Court erred by disbelieving PW-1's testimony for six accused but relying on it for them, highlighting the testimony's unreliability and lack of corroboration. The respondent (State) contended that PW-1's detailed narration was corroborated by the post-mortem report and that minor omissions should be ignored.
The Supreme Court noted that PW-1's testimony was found "partly reliable and partly unreliable" by the High Court itself, which had raised doubts about her ability to witness parts of the incident. Citing the principle that a partly reliable/unreliable sole witness requires corroboration, the Court found no corroboration for PW-1's testimony from other witnesses (Sitabai, Tekaram Rahagadale, Sarpanch were not examined, and PW-4 Police Patil turned hostile). Consequently, the Court concluded that the conviction could not be sustained due to the lack of corroboration for the largely unreliable testimony of the sole witness. The appeals were allowed, and the appellants were acquitted.

petitioner_key_arguments: High Court erred in dismissing appeals of Rajkumar and Mehatar.
High Court disbelieved Sindhubai (PW-1) for six accused but relied on the same evidence for appellants, making her testimony unreliable.
Conviction based on sole testimony of Sindhubai (PW-1) is not justified given its unreliability.
Various lacunae in prosecution's case, including doubts about FIR genuineness (recorded at 9:45 p.m., station diary entry 3:00 a.m. next morning).
respondent_key_arguments: High Court rightly confirmed conviction.
Sindhubai (PW-1) gave a detailed narration of the incident.
Appellant Rajkumar was attributed the role of assaulting the deceased with an axe, corroborated by the post-mortem report.
FIR is not an encyclopedia; minor omissions/contradictions are irrelevant, especially for a rustic villager like Sindhubai (PW-1).
Sindhubai (PW-1)'s evidence is duly corroborated by PW-4 Police Patil (Narendra Katre).
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments regarding the unreliability of the sole witness (Sindhubai PW-1) and the lack of corroboration for her testimony were accepted by the court.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeals are allowed. The judgments and orders of conviction and sentence passed by the High Court and the trial court are quashed and set aside. The appellants are acquitted of all charges. Appellant Mehatar's bail bonds are discharged. Appellant Rajkumar is directed to be released forthwith if not required in any other case.

precedents_cited: Vedivelu Thevar v. State of Madras

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that when the testimony of a sole witness is found to be partly reliable and partly unreliable, conviction cannot be maintained without corroboration in material particulars by reliable testimony, direct or circumstantial. In this case, the High Court itself found the sole witness's testimony largely unreliable, and no corroboration was found from other witnesses, leading to the acquittal of the appellants.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court reiterated the well-established rule that conviction can be based on the testimony of a single witness if it is wholly reliable and of sterling quality, but if the testimony is doubtful or partly reliable/unreliable, corroboration is necessary. The court also noted that the quality of evidence, not quantity, is paramount.

special_directions.special_directions: Appellant Mehatar's bail bonds shall stand discharged. Appellant Rajkumar is directed to be released forthwith, if his detention is not required in any other case.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 48/2025, CIVIL APPEAL NO. 49/2025, CIVIL APPEAL NO. 50/2025

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the High Court's intervention in Corporate Insolvency Resolution Proceedings (CIRP) and the setting aside of a resolution plan, primarily on grounds of natural justice violation.

judgements.case_summary:
The Corporate Insolvency Resolution Proceedings (CIRP) were initiated against Associate Decor Ltd, leading to the acceptance of a resolution plan by the Committee of Creditors (CoC) on 11.02.2020. The respondent, Farooq Ali Khan, a suspended director of the corporate debtor, challenged this decision before the High Court of Karnataka, alleging a violation of natural justice due to lack of notice for the 19th CoC meeting. The High Court, by an order dated 22.04.2024, allowed the writ petition and set aside the resolution plan, finding a violation of natural justice as 24 hours' notice was not granted.

The petitioner (Mohammed Enterprises), the successful resolution applicant, appealed to the Supreme Court. The petitioner, supported by the Solicitor General, argued that the High Court erred in exercising its jurisdiction under Article 226 to interdict CIRP proceedings, especially given the significant delay (three years) in approaching the High Court and the availability of alternate remedies under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC). The respondent contended that the natural justice violation justified the High Court's intervention and that there was no delay on their part due to other pending proceedings.

The Supreme Court found that the High Court committed an error by entertaining the writ petition. It emphasized that the IBC is a complete code with sufficient checks and balances, and the respondent had already initiated proceedings under the Code for similar relief. The Court concluded that the High Court's intervention, particularly after a substantial delay, breached the discipline of law. Consequently, the appeals were allowed, and the High Court's order was set aside.

petitioner_key_arguments: High Court erred in exercising jurisdiction under Article 226 to interdict CIRP proceedings.
The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) is a complete code with alternate remedies.
There was a significant delay of three years by the respondent in approaching the High Court.
respondent_key_arguments: Violation of natural justice (lack of notice for 19th CoC meeting) justified High Court intervention under Article 226.
The writ petition under Article 226 is not barred when principles of natural justice are violated.
The resolution plan accepted was inferior to the proposal made by the respondent under Section 12(A) of the Code.
There was no delay in filing the writ petition, as other proceedings were pending.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the High Court erred in exercising its discretionary jurisdiction under Article 226 due to the availability of alternate remedies under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and the significant delay by the respondent in approaching the High Court.

outcome.relief_granted: The final judgment and order passed by the High Court in Writ Petition No. 483 of 2023 (GM-RES) dated 22.04.2024 were set aside. The Adjudicating Authority was directed to commence the proceedings from where it was interdicted by the High Court and complete the same expeditiously.

case_identification.case_number: SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION(CRIMINAL) NO. 856/2025

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns a Special Leave Petition seeking interim bail for the petitioner, who is in custody for multiple cases including rioting and murder, to campaign for the Delhi Assembly Election, 2025.

judgements.case_summary: The Special Leave Petition was filed by Mohd. Tahir Hussain, who is in custody in connection with FIR No. 65 of 2020 (related to rioting and murder during the 2020 Delhi riots) and several other cases, including a PMLA case. The petitioner sought interim bail from 14.01.2025 to 09.02.2025 to participate and campaign in the Delhi Assembly Election, 2025, after the High Court had granted him conditional custody parole only for filing nomination papers. Justice Pankaj Mithal dismissed the petition, asserting that the right to campaign is neither a fundamental nor a constitutional right, and granting interim bail for this purpose would open a 'Pandora's box' and conflict with Section 62(5) of the Representation of People Act, 1951, which restricts prisoners from voting. He distinguished the case from Arvind Kejriwal's interim bail. In contrast, Justice Ahsanuddin Amanullah dissented, arguing that the petitioner's long incarceration (nearly 5 years) without conviction, coupled with having secured bail in most other cases, justifies interim bail for campaigning. He emphasized balancing the petitioner's rights as an accused with the gravity of allegations, and proposed granting interim bail with strict conditions, including confining campaigning to the Mustafabad Constituency and refraining from discussing pending cases or the Delhi riots. Due to these differing opinions, the matter was referred to the Chief Justice of India for a final decision.

petitioner_key_arguments: Long incarceration (almost 5 years) without trial progression.
Already granted bail in 8 out of 11 cases.
Permitting filing of nomination is meaningless if not allowed to campaign and canvass.
Right to contest elections requires ability to campaign.
The case of Arvind Kejriwal (supra) supports the grant of interim bail.
respondent_key_arguments: Right to campaign or canvass is neither a fundamental, constitutional, nor statutory right.
Granting interim bail for campaigning would open a 'Pandora's box' and lead to misuse.
Petitioner's involvement in multiple serious cases (including PMLA and murder) dilutes his position as a law-abiding citizen.
Risk of tampering with witnesses, especially given the incident location and petitioner's influence as a former Ward Councillor.
Section 62(5) of the Representation of People Act, 1951, restricts prisoners from voting, implying no right to campaign.
The Arvind Kejriwal case is distinguishable as he was a Chief Minister and President of a national party, unlike the petitioner.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The judges had differing opinions on the grant of interim bail for campaigning, leading to the matter being referred to the Chief Justice of India for a final decision. Therefore, no single set of arguments prevailed definitively at this stage.

outcome.judgement_outcome: Referred to Chief Justice of India due to differing opinions
outcome.relief_granted: Justice Pankaj Mithal dismissed the Special Leave Petition, denying interim bail for campaigning. Justice Ahsanuddin Amanullah allowed interim bail for campaigning with specific conditions (confinement to constituency, no discussion of pending cases/riots, deposit passport, surrender by 04/02/2025). The final relief is pending the Chief Justice of India's decision.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: Justice Pankaj Mithal held that interim bail is not permissible for the purposes of contesting elections or campaigning, as it is not a fundamental right and could lead to widespread misuse, conflicting with statutory provisions like Section 62(5) of the Representation of People Act, 1951. Justice Ahsanuddin Amanullah, in his dissenting opinion, reasoned that long incarceration without conviction, coupled with the petitioner having secured bail in most other cases, warrants the grant of interim bail for campaigning, subject to strict conditions, to balance the rights of the accused.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: Justice Pankaj Mithal observed that citizens deserve a clean India and clean politics, implying that people with tainted images should be restricted from participating in elections. Justice Ahsanuddin Amanullah emphasized that his judgment is specific to the facts and circumstances of this case and should not be treated as a precedent for other litigants, recalling that judgments are not to be read as Euclid's theorems.
judicial_reasoning.dissenting_opinion: Justice Ahsanuddin Amanullah expressed his inability to concur with Justice Pankaj Mithal's opinion. He argued that the petitioner's long incarceration (nearly 5 years) without conviction, the fact that he has secured bail in a majority of other cases, and the need to balance the petitioner's fundamental rights under Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution of India, justify granting interim bail for campaigning. He proposed specific conditions for this interim bail, including confinement to the Mustafabad Constituency, refraining from discussing pending cases or the Delhi riots, and depositing his passport.

special_directions.special_directions: Due to differing opinions between Justice Pankaj Mithal and Justice Ahsanuddin Amanullah, the Registry was directed to place the papers immediately before the Hon'ble the Chief Justice of India for a final decision. case_identification.respondent_name: The State Of Nagaland and others
case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS. 4872-4873 OF 2024

case_details.subject_matter: Challenge to preventive detention orders issued under the Prevention of Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1988, on grounds of mechanical application of mind, lack of material for likelihood of release on bail, and improper communication of grounds.

judgements.case_summary: Mortuza Hussain Choudhury challenged the preventive detention of his brother, Ashraf Hussain Choudhary, and Adaliu Chawang, under Section 3(1) of the Prevention of Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1988. The detenus were arrested on 12.04.2024 and subsequently detained via orders dated 30.05.2024 by the Special Secretary, Home Department, Government of Nagaland. Their representations against detention were rejected, and the Gauhati High Court dismissed their writ petitions on 29.08.2024. The Supreme Court noted that the detenus were already in judicial custody when the detention orders were passed and were later granted statutory bail on 28.11.2024 due to the prosecution's failure to file a charge-sheet. The Court analyzed the legal requirements for preventive detention, particularly when a person is already in custody, emphasizing the need for the detaining authority to apply its mind to the real possibility of release on bail and subsequent prejudicial activities. It also stressed the constitutional mandate for communicating grounds of detention in a language understood by the detenu. The Court found that the detaining authority acted mechanically, lacked material to infer a likelihood of release on bail, and failed to properly communicate the grounds in a language understood by the detenus. Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside the Gauhati High Court's judgment, quashed the detention orders, and ordered the immediate release of the detenus.

petitioner_key_arguments: Detention orders were passed mechanically and without application of mind.
Detenus were already in custody, and there was no mention in the orders that their detention was required as they were likely to be released on bail.
Copies of detention orders were served in a language they were not familiar with, violating Article 22(5) of the Constitution.
No material for the detaining authority to have formed an opinion that there was a likelihood of either detenu being released on bail.
respondent_key_arguments: The authorities claimed that the contents of the orders and grounds of detention were explained orally in Nagamese, which they asserted would suffice.
The Special Secretary, Home Department, Government of Nagaland, claimed satisfaction on careful examination of proposals and supporting documents.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments prevailed. The court accepted that the detention orders were passed mechanically, without proper application of mind regarding the likelihood of release on bail, and that the grounds were not effectively communicated in a language understood by the detenus, violating constitutional and statutory norms.

outcome.relief_granted: The detention orders dated 30.05.2024, confirmed and continued by extension orders, were quashed. The detenus, Ashraf Hussain Choudhary and Adaliu Chawang, were ordered to be set at liberty forthwith, unless their continued incarceration is warranted in connection with any other case.

case_identification.respondent_name: THE THEN RAJENDRA AGRICULTURAL UNIVERSITY (NOW DR. RAJENDRA PRASAD CENTRAL AGRICULTURAL UNIVERSITY) & ORS.
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 ARISING OUT OF SLP (C) No. 4644 OF 2023

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns an appeal against a High Court order dismissing a writ petition seeking inclusion of a university employee in the General Provident Fund-cum-pension-cum-gratuity scheme of retiral benefits, based on the interpretation of the University's statutes regarding default retiral schemes.

judgements.case_summary:
The appellant, Mukesh Prasad Singh, was appointed as a Junior Scientist cum Assistant Professor by the Rajendra Agricultural University in 1987. At the time, the University's statutes (Chapter 16 of the Rajendra Agricultural University Statutes, 19761) provided for two retiral benefit schemes: a Contributory Provident Fund (CPF) for those who opted for it, and a General Provident Fund-cum-pension-cum-gratuity (GPF-cum-pension-cum-gratuity) scheme as the default for those who did not opt for CPF. In 2008, the University issued an Office Order inviting employees to opt for CPF, explicitly stating that those who did not opt would be included in the Pension Scheme. The appellant did not opt for the CPF scheme. However, his name was not included in the GPF-cum-pension-cum-gratuity scheme list. His writ petition and subsequent appeal to the High Court were dismissed, reasoning that he had not exercised his option for retiral benefits.

The Supreme Court found that both the University Statute and the 2008 Office Order clearly established the GPF-cum-pension-cum-gratuity scheme as the default for employees who did not opt into the CPF scheme. The Court noted that the High Court itself had previously ruled in similar cases that the option was only for those desiring CPF, and others would automatically fall under the GPF-cum-pension-cum-gratuity scheme. Therefore, the Supreme Court concluded that the High Court erred in dismissing the appellant's petition. The appeal was allowed, and the High Court's order was set aside. The Court directed that the appellant be provided retiral benefits under the GPF-cum-pension-cum-gratuity scheme, with adjustments for any benefits already received under the CPF scheme, and mandated computation and disbursement within four months.

petitioner_key_arguments: The appellant did not opt for the Contributory Provident Fund (CPF) scheme.

As per Chapter 16 of the University Statute and the Office Order dated 21.02.2008, non-exercise of the option for CPF automatically entitles an employee to be included in the General Provident Fund-cum-pension-cum-gratuity scheme.
The High Court had previously allowed similar writ petitions for other employees based on the same interpretation.
respondent_key_arguments: The appellant did not exercise his option for retiral benefits (as per the High Court's reasoning for dismissal).
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that the University Statute and Office Order established the General Provident Fund-cum-pension-cum-gratuity scheme as the default for employees who did not opt for the Contributory Provident Fund, and therefore, the appellant's non-exercise of the option for CPF automatically entitled him to the default scheme.

outcome.relief_granted: The appellant is to be provided retiral benefits under the General Provident Fund-cum-pension-cum-gratuity scheme, subject to adjustments for any benefits availed by the appellant under the Contributory Provident Fund scheme.

precedents_cited: Arjun Kumar v. State of Bihar and ors
Dr Vijay Kumar Jaiswal v. Bihar Agriculture University and ors, CWJC 12667/2012
Ramjanam Prasad v. Rajendra Agricultural University, Bihar, Pusa and ors, CWJC 2377/2006
Dr Surendra Bahadur Singh v. Bihar Agriculture University Sabore, Bhagalpur and ors, CWJC 1941/2014
constitutional_provisions: Article 226 of the Constitution

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that where an employer's governing statutes and subsequent official orders establish a default retiral benefit scheme for employees who do not opt into an alternative scheme, the non-exercise of the option for the alternative scheme automatically entitles the employee to the default scheme. An explicit option for the default scheme is not required if the framework clearly designates it as such.

special_directions.special_directions: Necessary computation and disbursement of retiral benefits shall be made within a period of four months from the date of the judgment.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NOS. 7463-7464 OF 2023

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the jurisdiction of the Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission (DERC) to approve a tariff for a Waste-to-Energy project initiated by the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) and whether MCD, as a local authority, can invoke Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003 for tariff adoption.

judgements.case_summary:
The Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) initiated a Waste-to-Energy (WTE) project and, following a bidding process, sought approval for the bid tariff from the Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission (DERC). DERC dismissed a petition challenging MCD's authority and approved the tariff of Rs. 7.38/KWh. Respondent No. 1, Mr. Gagan Narang, appealed to the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL), which set aside DERC's orders, holding that DERC lacked jurisdiction as MCD was neither a distribution licensee nor a generating company under Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003.
MCD appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that APTEL erred by narrowly interpreting Section 63 and ignoring MCD's statutory obligations under the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016, and the broader regulatory powers of the State Commission under Section 86(1)(b) of the Electricity Act. MCD contended that the Act's provisions should be read harmoniously and in addition to other laws, not in derogation. The respondent maintained that only Discoms or generating companies could invoke Section 63.
The Supreme Court, applying principles of literal and harmonious construction, found that Section 63 does not restrict its invocation solely to Discoms or generating companies. It emphasized that MCD was fulfilling its statutory duties in establishing the WTE project and that DERC's role under Section 86(1)(b) includes regulating electricity procurement from "other sources." The Court concluded that APTEL's interpretation imposed undue restrictions and failed to consider the public interest and MCD's statutory mandate. Consequently, the Supreme Court allowed MCD's appeals, quashed APTEL's judgment, and affirmed DERC's original orders.

petitioner_key_arguments: APTEL erred in restricting the applicability of Sections 63 and 86(1)(b) of the Electricity Act, 2003, only to distribution licensees or generating companies.
The State Commission has wide power to regulate electricity purchase and procurement processes of Discoms, including from "other sources" under Section 86(1)(b).
MCD has a statutory obligation under Rule 15(v)(b) of the SWM Rules 2016 to set up WTE projects.
The National Tariff Policy 2016 mandates Discoms to procure 100% of power from WTE plants.
Section 175 of the Electricity Act states its provisions are in addition to and not in derogation of any other law, thus MCD's mandate under SWM Rules must be read in consonance with the Act.
DERC exercised its powers under Section 86(1)(b) to approve the bidding process and adopt the tariff, especially when no Central Government guidelines exist for WTE projects.
DERC had previously approved similar bidding processes for other WTE projects.
APTEL failed to consider the larger public interest in processing municipal solid waste.
APTEL erred in treating MCD as a "total stranger" when MCD was establishing the project to fulfill its statutory obligations, and the project ownership was always with MCD.
respondent_key_arguments: APTEL correctly held that MCD was not entitled to make an application for adoption of tariff under Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003.
Only Discoms or generating companies are entitled to invoke the provisions of Section 63 of the Act.
In view of Rule 6.4(2) of the National Tariff Policy, 2016, it is exclusively for the Ministry of Power to provide a mechanism for adoption of tariff for WTE projects.
DERC had no jurisdiction to entertain the application filed by MCD.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Supreme Court accepted the petitioner's arguments, emphasizing the harmonious construction of Sections 63 and 86(1)(b) of the Electricity Act, 2003, and MCD's statutory mandate under the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016, to establish Waste-to-Energy projects. The Court found that APTEL's restrictive interpretation of Section 63 was erroneous and that DERC had the jurisdiction to approve the tariff.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeals filed by Municipal Corporation of Delhi were allowed. The Impugned common final judgment and order of the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity dated 31st August 2023 was quashed and set aside. The orders of the Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission dated 6th March 2023 and 7th March 2023 were affirmed.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The Supreme Court held that Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003, which allows for tariff adoption through a transparent bidding process, is not exclusively limited to distribution licensees or generating companies. By applying the principle of harmonious construction, the Court found that Section 63 must be read in conjunction with Section 86(1)(b), which empowers State Commissions to regulate electricity purchase and procurement from "other sources." Given the Municipal Corporation of Delhi's statutory mandate under the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016, to establish Waste-to-Energy projects, it was within DERC's jurisdiction to approve the tariff for such a project.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court reiterated the settled principles of statutory interpretation, emphasizing literal interpretation when the language is clear and capable of giving meaning without absurdity, and harmonious construction to avoid rendering any provision otiose or creating conflicts between sections. It also noted the importance of considering public interest and the legislative intent behind the statutes.

case_identification.petitioner_name: SRI MUNSHI LAL MAHTO AND ORS.
case_identification.case_number: CONTEMPT PETITION (C) NO. 115 OF 2019 IN CIVIL APPEAL NO. 2703 OF 2017

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns alleged non-compliance of a previous Supreme Court order regarding the absorption and payment of arrears of salary for university employees, specifically addressing issues of date of birth and pay fixation for one petitioner.

judgements.case_summary:
This contempt petition was filed alleging non-compliance with an order dated 31.08.2017 passed in Civil Appeal No. 2703 of 2017, which concerned the absorption of employees. Initially, multiple petitioners were involved, but during the hearing, petitioners 1, 3, and 5 withdrew their claims as they were receiving their dues, leading to the dismissal of the petition for them. The case proceeded solely for petitioner No. 4, who was absorbed as a Typist in P.P.K. College, Bundu, with effect from 01.07.2015, following a recommendation by the J. Sinha Commission and confirmation by the Supreme Court. However, petitioner No. 4 claimed he had not received his arrears of salary.

The State of Jharkhand, as the contemnor, argued that petitioner No. 4's date of birth (05.08.1968) was concealed, making him a minor at his appointment date (09.09.1985) and the cutoff date, thus rendering him ineligible and his appointment void ab-initio. Consequently, his pay fixation was rejected, and the State denied willful non-compliance.

The Court observed that the order rejecting pay fixation was not on record and that petitioner No. 4's absorption had not been de-notified. However, the Court determined that the complex issues of date of birth, pay fixation, and arrears required proper adjudication by a competent authority rather than being resolved within the scope of a contempt petition. Citing the precedent of "State of Bihar & others vs Bihar Rajya M.S.E.S.K.K.M & others (2005) 9 SCC 129," the Court disposed of the contempt petition.

The Court directed petitioner No. 4 to submit his claims and relevant documents to the Registrar/Vice Chancellor of the University by February 28, 2025. The University is mandated to adjudicate these claims, providing due opportunity to all concerned parties, and pass a reasoned order within three months. Parties dissatisfied with this order retain the liberty to approach the High Court.

petitioner_key_arguments: Alleged non-compliance of the order dated 31.08.2017 regarding absorption and payment of arrears of salary for petitioner No. 4.
respondent_key_arguments: Petitioner No. 4 was a minor at the time of appointment and cutoff date, making him ineligible and his appointment void ab-initio due to concealed date of birth.
Pay fixation was rejected due to ineligibility.
No willful non-compliance as the issues require detailed enquiry.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court did not rule on the merits of the arguments but directed the University to adjudicate the issues, effectively accepting the respondent's stance that these matters are beyond the scope of a contempt petition.

outcome.relief_granted: Directions issued for the Registrar/Vice Chancellor of the University to adjudicate the claims of petitioner No. 4 regarding date of birth, pay fixation, and arrears of salary within three months, after receiving the claim by February 28, 2025.

precedents_cited: Krishna Nand Yadav & others Vs. Magadh University & others
Baidya Nath Choudhary Vs. Dr. Sree Surendra Kumar Singh
State of Bihar & others vs Bihar Rajya M.S.E.S.K.K.M & others (2005) 9 SCC 129

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: Complex issues concerning an employee's date of birth, eligibility, pay fixation, and arrears of salary, especially when disputed, require proper adjudication by the designated administrative authorities (Registrar/Vice Chancellor) with due process, rather than being summarily decided in a contempt petition.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court noted that the order rejecting pay fixation for petitioner No. 4 was not on record and that his absorption notification had not been de-notified.

special_directions.special_directions: Petitioner No. 4 is directed to submit his claim regarding date of birth, pay fixation, and arrears of salary along with relevant documents before the Registrar/Vice Chancellor of the University by February 28, 2025. The University shall adjudicate this claim, affording due opportunity to the employee, college concerned, and State representative, passing a reasoned order within three months. Parties dissatisfied may take recourse before the High Court.

case_identification.respondent_name: The State Rep. By The Inspector Of Police
case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 3318 OF 2023

case_details.subject_matter: This case involves an appeal against a conviction for murder (Section 302 IPC) related to the death of a constable who was chasing individuals involved in illegal sand transportation. The Supreme Court reviews the High Court's decision, focusing on the reliability of circumstantial evidence.

judgements.case_summary: The case originated from an incident on 06.05.2018, where deceased constable Jagadeesh Durai chased the appellant (Murugan, A1) and two others (A2, A3) for illegally transporting sand. The constable was later found dead. The Trial Court convicted A1 and A2 under Sections 148 and 302 IPC, while acquitting A3. The High Court acquitted A4-A6 and sustained the conviction of A1 and A2 under Section 302 IPC, but acquitted them of Section 148 IPC. The appellant (A1) appealed to the Supreme Court. The appellant argued that key prosecution evidence, including the last seen evidence (PW12), extra-judicial confessions (PW13), and eye-witness testimony (PW2), was unreliable or inadmissible. They also highlighted an unexplained delay in FIR presentation and the absence of sand at the scene, questioning the motive. The respondent contended that ample evidence, such as call records and recovery of a wheel spanner with fingerprints, connected the appellant to the crime. The Supreme Court found that the High Court erred by not giving the appellant the same benefit of doubt as co-accused when the backbone of the prosecution's case (evidence of PW2, PW12, PW13) had crumbled. The court emphasized that circumstantial evidence must form a complete chain leading solely to the accused's guilt. Given the unreliability of crucial witnesses and the unexplained delay in FIR, the court concluded that the mere recovery of a wheel spanner and slippers was insufficient to sustain the conviction. The appeal was allowed, and the conviction and sentence were set aside.

petitioner_key_arguments: The last seen evidence (PW12) is unreliable due to a 17-day delay in recording the statement, identification issues at night, and the witness's failure to report to the police despite being present at the postmortem.
Extra-judicial confessions of co-accused (A2 and A3) before PW13 were made in police custody and are inadmissible, a finding upheld by the High Court.
There was an unexplained and inordinate delay in presenting the FIR to the Magistrate, casting doubt on the prosecution's case.
No sand was found in the tractor-trailer or at the site, undermining the prosecution's alleged motive for the chase.
The evidence of the alleged eye witness (PW2) was disbelieved by the High Court, and this finding was not challenged.
With the crucial evidence being discarded, the conviction under Section 302 IPC is illegal and unsustainable.
respondent_key_arguments: Ample evidence connects the appellant with the commission of the offence.
Call records indicate the deceased informed PW24 and PW1 about the sand theft by all three accused, establishing motive.
The intention to attack was apparent when the tractor tyre was damaged, leading the accused to assault the deceased to avoid arrest.
Recovery of a wheel spanner with the appellant's fingerprints and three pairs of slippers at the incident site establishes the appellant's presence and involvement.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments regarding the unreliability of key prosecution witnesses (PW2, PW12, PW13), the unexplained delay in FIR presentation, and the incomplete chain of circumstantial evidence were accepted by the court, leading to the conclusion that the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

outcome.relief_granted: The judgment and order of conviction and sentence passed by the Courts below are set aside. The appellant is to be released forthwith, if in custody and not required in any other case.

acts_cited: Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957
precedents_cited: Karakkattu Muhammed Basheer vs. State of Kerala

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: In cases based on circumstantial evidence, the chain of events must be so complete and conclusive that it leads only to the guilt of the accused, leaving no room for any other conclusion. If crucial prosecution evidence crumbles or is found unreliable, and the chain of circumstances is incomplete, the benefit of doubt must be extended to the accused.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed that merely the recovery of a weapon with fingerprints and slippers at the scene is insufficient to establish guilt when other crucial evidence forming the backbone of the prosecution's case has been discarded.

special_directions.special_directions: The appellant be released forthwith, if in custody and not required in any other case.
special_directions.interim_orders: Pending application(s), if any, also stand disposed of.

case_identification.petitioner_name: MY PREFERRED TRANSFORMATION & HOSPITALITY PVT. LTD. & ANR.
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 336 OF 2025 ARISING OUT OF SLP (C) NO. 9996 OF 2024 (2025 INSC 56)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the applicability of the Limitation Act, 1963, and the General Clauses Act, 1897, to the limitation period for filing an application to challenge an arbitral award under Section 34(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, specifically when the prescribed or condonable period expires on a court holiday.

judgements.case_summary:
The appellants received an arbitral award on 14.02.2022. The 3-month limitation period for filing a Section 34 application, extended due to the COVID-19 pandemic, expired on 29.05.2022, which was a working day. The subsequent 30-day condonable period expired on 28.06.2022, during the High Court's summer vacation. The application was filed on 04.07.2022, immediately upon the court's reopening. The High Court dismissed the petition as time-barred.

The key legal issues before the Supreme Court were the extent to which the Limitation Act, particularly Section 4, and Section 10 of the General Clauses Act apply to Section 34(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, especially concerning the distinction between the 3-month 'prescribed period' and the 30-day 'condonable period' when a court is closed.

The petitioner argued that the Limitation Act (including Section 4) should not apply to Section 34(3), and if so, Section 10 of the GCA should extend the condonable period. The respondent contended that the Limitation Act applies, but Section 4 only extends the 3-month prescribed period, not the 30-day condonable period, and Section 10 of the GCA is inapplicable due to the Limitation Act's applicability.

The Supreme Court affirmed that Section 4 of the Limitation Act applies to Section 34(3) of the ACA, but only to the 3-month 'prescribed period' if it expires on a court holiday. It does not extend the 30-day condonable period. Since the 3-month period expired on a working day, Section 4 of the Limitation Act did not benefit the appellants. Furthermore, the Court held that Section 10 of the GCA is excluded because the Limitation Act applies. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed, upholding the High Court's decision that the application was time-barred. The judgment highlights the stringent interpretation of limitation periods for challenging arbitral awards.

petitioner_key_arguments: The Limitation Act, including Section 4, does not apply to Section 34(3) of the ACA.
If the Limitation Act is excluded, Section 10 of the General Clauses Act applies, including when the condonable period expires on a holiday.
The term 'certain day' in Section 10 of the GCA has wider import than Section 4 of the Limitation Act.
Expressed doubt regarding the correctness of Bhimashankar (supra) concerning the inapplicability of Section 10 of the GCA.
Section 4 of the Limitation Act does not apply to the proviso of Section 34(3) as it is not the 'prescribed period'.
Section 10 of the GCA, being beneficial legislation, must apply to the condonable period under the proviso.
respondent_key_arguments: Section 4 of the Limitation Act applies to Section 34(3) of the ACA only to the 3-month limitation period, not the 30-day condonable period.
The entirety of Sections 4 to 24 of the Limitation Act are not excluded from Section 34 proceedings, except Section 5.
Section 10 of the General Clauses Act does not apply to Section 34(3) because the Limitation Act applies, as per its own proviso.
Sridevi Datla (supra) is distinguishable as it was decided in the context of Section 16 of the NGT Act, not Section 34(3) of the ACA.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court accepted the respondent's arguments that Section 4 of the Limitation Act applies only to the 3-month 'prescribed period' under Section 34(3) of the ACA, not the 30-day condonable period. It also affirmed that Section 10 of the General Clauses Act is inapplicable when the Limitation Act applies, thereby excluding its benefit for the appellants.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: Section 4 of the Limitation Act, 1963, applies to Section 34(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, only to the extent that the initial 3-month 'prescribed period' expires on a day when the court is closed. It does not extend the subsequent 30-day condonable period if that period expires on a court holiday. Furthermore, Section 10 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, is inapplicable to Section 34(3) proceedings because the Limitation Act applies, as explicitly stated by the proviso to Section 10 of the GCA.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court expressed concerns that the current stringent construction of limitation statutes unduly curtails the remedy available to arbitrating parties to challenge arbitral awards, suggesting that Parliament should address this. Justice Pankaj Mithal, in a concurring opinion, also highlighted the need for uniform limitation periods across statutes and broader powers for courts to condone delays, similar to Section 5 of the Limitation Act, to prevent good cases from being dismissed on technical grounds.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 4312 OF 2025 (Arising out of SLP (C) No. 698 of 2023)

case_details.subject_matter: Dispute over the nature of a property document (gift, settlement, or Will) and the validity of its subsequent cancellation and sale, involving property rights between a daughter and her brother.

judgements.case_summary:
This appeal arises from a property dispute between a daughter (Respondent No.1) and her brother (Appellant) concerning a document executed by their father in 1985. The daughter claimed this document was a gift deed, while the father later cancelled it in 1993 and executed a sale deed for the same property in favor of the son. The trial court and First Appellate Court dismissed the daughter's suit, holding the 1985 document to be a Will. However, the High Court reversed these findings, construing the document as a settlement deed and declaring the cancellation and subsequent sale deeds invalid, thereby granting a declaratory decree to the daughter.

The Supreme Court examined whether the 1985 document was a gift, settlement, or Will, and if it vested a legal right. The appellant argued it was a Will, citing lack of immediate ownership transfer and retained possession by the father. The respondent contended it was a gift/settlement, with ownership transferred in praesenti, and acceptance implied by registration.

The Court emphasized that the nomenclature is not conclusive, and the substance of the document determines its nature. It analyzed the document's clauses, noting the consideration of love and affection, conveyance, conditions, and reservation of life interest. The Court held that the reservation of a life interest and delayed physical possession do not negate an immediate vesting of rights. It concluded that the 1985 document was a settlement, transferring rights in praesenti, and thus could not be unilaterally revoked. The appeal was dismissed, affirming the High Court's judgment in favor of the daughter.

petitioner_key_arguments: The document executed by the Defendant No.1 / father in 1985 was only a Will and not a gift deed, since there was no immediate transfer of ownership.
Possession of the suit schedule property was retained by the Defendant No.1 / father and was never handed over to the Respondent No.1 / plaintiff (daughter).

The main test to find out whether the document constitutes a Will or a gift is to see whether the disposition of interest in the property is in praesenti in favour of the settlee or whether the disposition is to take effect on the death of the executant. If the disposition is to take effect on the death of the executant, it would be a Will.
The Defendant No.1 / father had retained the title to the enjoyment of the property during his lifetime as full owner with all rights.

Even assuming that the document in question was a gift deed, the same was never accepted by the Respondent No.1 / plaintiff during the lifetime of the Defendant No.1/ father and therefore, the gift was not acted upon.
After execution of the sale deed, revenue record was mutated and he has been in possession of the suit property since then.
respondent_key_arguments: The suit schedule property belongs to the Respondent No.1 as per the gift deed dated 26.06.1985.

The ownership of the existing property has been transferred voluntarily to Respondent No.1 (donee) without any consideration and the same was also accepted by Respondent No.1 during the lifetime of Defendant No.1 by presenting the deed for registration.
The tone and tenor of the document clearly show it was a gift deed, as only limited rights (income, mortgage up to Rs.2,000/-) were reserved for the settlor.
Transfer of possession of property is not necessary for the acceptance of a valid gift deed.
Ext.A1 deed was accepted in 1985 and acted upon by the Respondent No.1.
Ext.A1 is a gift deed and it cannot be unilaterally revoked as per section 126 of the Transfer of Property Act.
Mutation of the property in the revenue record does not create or extinguish title nor has it any presumptive value on title.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the respondent's arguments that the 1985 document was a settlement, transferring rights in praesenti, and could not be unilaterally revoked. The court found that the document satisfied the requirements of a settlement, and that the reservation of a life interest and postponement of physical possession did not negate an immediate vesting of rights.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal is dismissed, confirming the judgment passed by the High Court, which granted a decree in favour of the plaintiff / Respondent No.1 declaring her right, title and interest over the suit schedule property by virtue of Ext.A1 settlement deed dated 26.06.1985 and declared that cancellation deed (Ext.A2) dated 19.10.1993 and sale deed (Ext.A3) dated 19.10.1993 would not bind the plaintiff.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The nomenclature of a document is not decisive; its substance determines its nature. A document that transfers interest in praesenti, even with reserved life interest or conditions, is a settlement or gift, not a Will. Unilateral revocation of a valid settlement/gift is impermissible. In cases of conflicting clauses, the earlier clause prevails if it grants an absolute right.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court discussed the general principles of interpreting Wills, gifts, and settlements, emphasizing that the intention of the testator must be gathered from the document as a whole. It also noted that acceptance for gifts can be express or implied, and that registration and possession of the deed can amount to valid acceptance. The court further observed that mutation of revenue records does not create or extinguish title.
