case_identification.petitioner_name: Naganna (Dead) By Lrs. / Smt. Devamma & Ors.
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO (s). 3688/2024

case_details.subject_matter: The case involves a property dispute concerning ownership, possession, and the cancellation of a sale deed, where the plaintiff failed to prove title.

judgements.case_summary: This appeal arose from a property dispute where the plaintiff, Naganna (represented by LRs), sought permanent injunction, cancellation of a sale deed, and recovery of possession for a vacant site and house. The plaintiff claimed ownership through an oral partition. Initially, the Civil Judge (Junior Division) and J.M.F.C. decreed the suit, which was affirmed by the First Appellate Court. However, the High Court of Karnataka reversed these decisions in a second appeal, finding that the plaintiff failed to prove title and possession, relying only on assessment extracts rather than valid title deeds. The High Court also noted ambiguities in the property description and the lack of conclusive proof of ownership or the alleged oral partition. The Supreme Court, after reviewing the material and arguments, upheld the High Court's judgment. The Court concluded that the plaintiff failed to establish ownership and lawful possession of the suit property with cogent and acceptable evidence, and that revenue records do not confer title. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed, affirming the High Court's decision.

petitioner_key_arguments: Respondent No. 2 (seller) was not connected with the property, and the sale deed to Respondent No. 1 was without lawful title.
Respondent No. 1 admitted Siddegowda and Kalegowda looked after the property, and Respondent No. 2 was not connected.
No record of khata change in favor of the second defendant.
Five witnesses deposed in favor of the appellant.
It is not necessary for a person claiming injunction to prove title, only lawful possession.
High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Section 100 CPC by entering into questions of fact.
respondent_key_arguments: Appellant was never in possession of the property.
Burden of proof for title and possession lies on the plaintiff.
Revenue records do not confer title.
Suit property is in possession of Respondent No. 1, raising a strong presumption in their favor.
Appellant's previous suit against Vedavathi for the northern half of the property (bearing No. 111) was dismissed as the plaintiff failed to prove title.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The respondent's arguments prevailed, as the court found that the plaintiff failed to prove title and possession, and that revenue records do not confer title, thereby upholding the High Court's decision.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal was dismissed, upholding the High Court's judgment which had reversed the lower courts' decisions. The plaintiff's claims for cancellation of sale deed and recovery of possession were denied.

precedents_cited: Union of India and Ors. vs. Vasavi Cooperative Housing Society Limited and Ors1. 2014 (2) SCC 269

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core reasoning is that the plaintiff failed to prove their title and possession over the suit property with cogent and acceptable evidence. The documents relied upon (assessment extracts) were not title deeds and did not conclusively establish ownership, and there were ambiguities in the property description and lack of proof for the alleged oral partition.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The observation that 'The plaintiff must stand or fall on the strength of his own case' was reiterated.

special_directions.special_directions: No order as to costs. Pending application(s), if any, stand(s) disposed of accordingly.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S).475 OF 2025 (ARISING OUT OF S.L.P. (CRIMINAL) NO(S).5215/2021)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the High Court's decision to grant suspension of sentence and bail to an accused convicted under the NDPS Act, pending appeal, and whether this decision is constrained by Section 37 of the NDPS Act or previous Supreme Court rulings.

judgements.case_summary:
The Narcotic Control Bureau (NCB) appealed against a High Court order that granted suspension of sentence and bail to Lakhwinder Singh, who was convicted under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (NDPS Act) and sentenced to 10 years rigorous imprisonment. The High Court had noted that the respondent had already undergone 4.5 years of incarceration and his appeal, filed in 2021, was unlikely to be heard before he completed his full sentence. The learned ASG, representing the NCB, argued that the respondent was not entitled to bail unless he had undergone half of the sentence, citing the Supreme Court Legal Aid Committee case, and that Section 37 of the NDPS Act constrained the court's power even at the appellate stage, referring to the Dadu vs. State of Maharashtra decision.

The Supreme Court clarified that the Supreme Court Legal Aid Committee judgment was a one-time measure for undertrial prisoners and did not curtail the general power of courts to grant bail on merits. While acknowledging the constraints of Section 37 of the NDPS Act on appellate courts, the Supreme Court held that if an accused has undergone a substantial part of their sentence and their appeal is not likely to be heard before the entire sentence is served, the Appellate Court can exercise its power to grant bail to prevent a violation of the accused's rights under Article 21 of the Constitution. Given that the respondent had already served a substantial portion of his 10-year sentence and the appeal was not likely to be heard soon, the Supreme Court found no reason to interfere with the High Court's order. The appeal filed by the NCB was dismissed, with a caveat that the appellant could apply for bail cancellation if the respondent misused the granted liberty.

petitioner_key_arguments: The respondent was not entitled to bail pending the final hearing of the appeal against conviction unless he had undergone a sentence for the one-half period, as per the decision in Supreme Court Legal Aid Committee representing Undertrial Prisoners vs. Union of India & Ors.
The power of the Court was constrained by Section 37 of the NDPS Act, which is applicable even at the stage of an appeal, as per Dadu vs. State of Maharashtra.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the argument that an Appellate Court can grant suspension of sentence and bail, even if half the sentence is not served, if the appeal is not likely to be heard before the accused undergoes the entire sentence, to prevent violation of Article 21 rights. The court also clarified that previous judgments like Supreme Court Legal Aid Committee do not curtail the general power to grant bail on merits.

outcome.relief_granted: The High Court's order granting suspension of sentence and bail to the respondent is upheld.

acts_cited: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985
precedents_cited: Supreme Court Legal Aid Committee representing Undertrial Prisoners vs. Union of India & Ors.1 (1994) 6 SCC731
Dadu vs. State of Maharashtra2 (2000) 8 SCC 437
constitutional_provisions: Article 21 of the Constitution

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The Appellate Court has the power to grant suspension of sentence and bail pending appeal, even if the accused has not undergone half of the substantive sentence, particularly when the appeal is not likely to be heard before the completion of the entire sentence, as denying such relief would violate the accused's rights under Article 21 of the Constitution. This power exists despite the constraints of Section 37 of the NDPS Act.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The directions in Supreme Court Legal Aid Committee representing Undertrial Prisoners vs. Union of India & Ors. were one-time measures for undertrial prisoners and do not curtail the general power of courts to grant regular bail on merits. There cannot be a rigid rule that a convict cannot be released on bail pending appeal unless half of the substantive sentence has been undergone.

special_directions.special_directions: If the respondent misuses the liberty granted to him under the impugned order, the appellant can always apply for cancellation of bail.

case_identification.respondent_name: The State Of Uttar Pradesh & Anr.
case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NOOF 2025 (Arising out of Special Leave Petition (Crl.) No. 1093 of)

case_details.subject_matter: The appeal questions the correctness of a High Court judgment that refused to quash a chargesheet and proceedings under Sections 354 and 506 of the Indian Penal Code, arising from allegations of inappropriate behavior and criminal intimidation in a workplace dispute.

judgements.case_summary: This case involves an appeal against a High Court judgment that declined to quash a chargesheet and criminal proceedings against Naresh Aneja (appellant) under Sections 354 and 506 IPC. The dispute originated from a joint business concern, 'M/s LAJ-IDS Exports Pvt. Ltd.', where the appellant and respondent no. 2 (complainant) were directors. The complainant filed a complaint in July 2019, alleging inappropriate behavior, harassment, and threat of murder by RK Aneja (appellant's brother) and implicating the appellant. An FIR was registered, and a chargesheet was filed. The appellant sought to quash these proceedings, arguing that no prima facie offence was made out against him, the dispute was commercial, and the FIR was motivated. The respondent contended that the appellant and his brother took undue advantage and harassed her. The Supreme Court, after examining the contents of the FIR, preliminary investigation report, and chargesheet, found no direct allegations or evidence attributing intent to the appellant for offences under Section 354 IPC (lack of criminal force with intent to outrage modesty) or Section 506 IPC (lack of intention to cause alarm). The Court reiterated that statements under Sections 161 and 164 CrPC are inadmissible for proving guilt. Consequently, the Court set aside the High Court's judgment and quashed the criminal proceedings against the appellant, Naresh Aneja.

petitioner_key_arguments: An earlier complaint making the same allegations was hidden from the Magistrate.
The preliminary investigating report found no offence under Sections 354 & 506 IPC, indicating the dispute is commercial.
The appellant has been falsely implicated.
The FIR is motivated by the complainant's intentions to commit fraud.
Contents of the FIR or chargesheet do not disclose commission of any offence by the appellant.
There is only a one-line statement in the chargesheet regarding the appellant, with no specific act alleged.
respondent_key_arguments: The appellant and his brother took undue advantage of the complainant and blackmailed her.
The FIR and statements under Sections 161 and 164 CrPC clearly show that A-1 made inappropriate advances and the appellant degraded her with abusive language and harassment.
The appellant concealed relevant facts, including his criminal history.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that no prima facie offence was made out against him under Sections 354 and 506 IPC, as the record lacked evidence of criminal force with intent to outrage modesty or clear intention to cause alarm, and statements under Sections 161/164 CrPC are inadmissible for proving guilt.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned judgment of the High Court is set aside, and criminal proceedings arising out of FIR No. 1074 of 2019 are quashed qua the present appellant (Naresh Aneja).

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 660 OF 2025 (@ SLP Criminal No. 3432 of 2023)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the quashing of criminal proceedings under Section 482 Cr.P.C. for an offense under Section 307 IPC, following a compromise between the parties, and the distinction between compounding and quashing of offenses.

judgements.case_summary: The Supreme Court heard an appeal against a High Court order that refused to quash criminal proceedings under Section 482 Cr.P.C. for an offense under Section 307 IPC, despite a compromise between the parties. The case originated from an incident on 11.08.1991, involving a dispute over irrigation water, leading to a counter-FIR (No. 248-A/91) against the appellants, alleging offenses including Section 307 IPC. Although the police initially filed a closure report, the trial court summoned the appellants. After approximately 33 years, a compromise was reached between the injured party (respondent No.2 Mahmood) and the appellants. The High Court, however, dismissed the quashing application, stating that Section 307 IPC cannot be compounded. The Supreme Court clarified the distinction between compounding and quashing, emphasizing that the High Court's inherent powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. allow quashing of non-compoundable offenses, even Section 307 IPC, if the dispute is primarily private, the injuries are not life-threatening, and a genuine compromise exists. Considering the non-grievous nature of the injury (fracture of distal phalanx of left ring finger), the old age of the case, and the police's initial closure report, the Court found that Section 307 IPC was not made out and that continuing the trial would be an abuse of process. Consequently, the High Court's order was set aside, and the criminal proceedings were quashed.

petitioner_key_arguments: A compromise was reached between the appellants and the injured party (respondent No.2 Mahmood).
The High Court erred by not distinguishing between compounding of an offense and quashing of proceedings under Section 482 Cr.P.C.
The nature of injuries (fracture of distal phalanx of left ring finger) and weapons used (lathis and iron bars) do not warrant the application of Section 307 IPC.
The police initially filed a closure report, disbelieving the entire story.
The incident is very old (33.5 years), and continuing the trial would be futile and an abuse of process.
Quashing the proceedings would promote peace and harmony between the parties, who reside in the same village.
respondent_key_arguments: The State (respondent No.1) fairly left the decision to the court.
Respondent No.2 (Mahmood) was part of the compromise.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court accepted the petitioners' arguments that a genuine compromise had been reached, and that the High Court failed to distinguish between compounding and quashing. It agreed that the nature of the injuries and weapons used did not constitute an offense under Section 307 IPC, and that continuing the proceedings after 33 years, especially given the police's initial closure report, would be an abuse of process and against the ends of justice.

outcome.relief_granted: The order of the High Court dated 19.01.2023 in Application under Section 482 Cr.P.C. No. 1315 of 2023 was set aside, and the proceedings in Complaint Case No. 8023 of 2015 arising out of Case Crime No. 248 of 1991 pending in the Court of Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Court No. 5, Moradabad, were quashed.

precedents_cited: Gian Singh vs. State of Punjab and Another, (2012) 10 SCC 303
State of Madhya Pradesh vs. Laxmi Narayan and Others, (2019) 5 SCC 688
Narinder Singh and Others vs. State of Punjab and Another, (2014) 6 SCC 466
Ramgopal v. State of M.P, (2022) 14 SCC 531
constitutional_provisions: Article 142 of the Constitution

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The High Court, under Section 482 Cr.P.C., can quash criminal proceedings for non-compoundable offenses, even those involving Section 307 IPC, if the dispute is primarily private, the injuries are not life-threatening or on vital organs, and a genuine compromise has been reached, to secure the ends of justice and prevent abuse of process.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court emphasized the distinction between compounding and quashing, and that mere mention of Section 307 IPC should not lead to a 'hands-off' approach. It also noted the importance of considering the age of the case and the promotion of peace between parties in the same village.

special_directions.interim_orders: An interim order was passed staying the order of 05.09.1992 in Criminal Revision No. 1318 of 1992.

case_identification.respondent_name: The State Of West Bengal & Ors.
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 3705 OF 2024

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns whether registration under Section 8 of the MSMED Act, 2006, is a necessary precondition for a Micro, Small and Medium Enterprise to refer a dispute to the Facilitation Council under Section 18 of the Act.

judgements.case_summary: NBCC (India) Ltd (appellant/buyer) challenged the jurisdiction of the Micro and Small Enterprises Facilitation Council to arbitrate a payment dispute with M/s Saket Infra Developers Private Limited (Enterprise/supplier). The Enterprise sought recovery of dues under Section 18 of the MSMED Act, 2006. NBCC argued that the Enterprise was not registered under Section 8 of the Act before contract execution, making the reference impermissible, and that works contracts were outside the Act's scope, relying on *Silpi Industries* and *Mahakali Foods* judgments. The High Court dismissed NBCC's writ petition, allowing jurisdictional objections to be raised before the Arbitral Tribunal. The Supreme Court examined whether prior registration under Section 8 is a precondition for invoking Section 18. The Court noted that Section 18 uses "any party to a dispute," not "supplier," and that Section 8 makes registration discretionary for micro and small enterprises. It distinguished previous judgments, finding they did not directly address this specific precondition. The Court emphasized the MSMED Act's beneficial nature and the constitutional duty to ensure effective remedies. While the Court's preliminary view was that the submission requiring prior registration for Section 18 reference must be rejected, it acknowledged the need for clarity. Therefore, to ensure legal certainty, the Court referred the appeal to a three-Judge Bench for an authoritative pronouncement.

petitioner_key_arguments: The Enterprise was not registered under Section 8 of the MSMED Act before contract execution, thus the Facilitation Council lacks jurisdiction under Section 18.
The subject matter, being works contracts, falls outside the scope and ambit of the MSMED Act.
The term 'any party to a dispute' in Section 18 must be confined to a 'supplier' as defined in Section 2(n), which requires prior registration under Section 8.
Relied on the decisions in *Silpi Industries v. Kerala State Road Transport Corporation* and *Gujarat State Civil Supplies Corporation Ltd. v. Mahakali Foods Pvt. Ltd.*
respondent_key_arguments: Jurisdictional objections can be raised before the Arbitral Tribunal, as directed by the Single Judge and Division Bench of the High Court.
The MSMED Act, being a special legislation, overrides other statutes.
Section 18 is not restrictive and is a remedy for dispute resolution, kept open-ended to enable 'any party' to refer the dispute.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court's preliminary view rejected the petitioner's argument that prior registration under Section 8 is a precondition for invoking Section 18 of the MSMED Act, 2006. The court found that Section 18's use of "any party to a dispute" and the discretionary nature of Section 8 registration for micro and small enterprises support a broader interpretation, aligning with the beneficial purpose of the Act.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal is referred to a three-Judge Bench of the Supreme Court for an authoritative pronouncement on whether registration under Section 8 of the MSMED Act, 2006, is a necessary precondition for referring a dispute under Section 18 of the Act. The High Court's decision allowing the reference to proceed was not overturned.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The Court's preliminary view is that Section 18 of the MSMED Act, 2006, which allows "any party to a dispute" to make a reference to the Facilitation Council, is not restricted to only "suppliers" who have registered under Section 8. Registration under Section 8 is discretionary for micro and small enterprises, and the beneficial nature of the Act supports a broader interpretation to ensure effective access to justice.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed the importance of MSMEs to the country's economy and the constitutional duty of courts to interpret statutory remedies to ensure effective access to justice. It also distinguished between the Supreme Court's functions of decision-making and precedent-making, highlighting the need for clarity and certainty in legal pronouncements.

special_directions.special_directions: The Registry is directed to place the appeal paperbooks along with the detailed judgment before the Hon'ble Chief Justice of India for constitution of an appropriate Bench (three-Judge Bench) for an authoritative pronouncement.

case_details.subject_matter: The case involves quintuplet appeals concerning the quantum of compensation awarded for the death of the appellant's parents and younger brother in a motor vehicle accident, with the insurer seeking reduction and the claimant seeking enhancement.

judgements.case_summary:
This case involves five appeals challenging the compensation awarded for the death of the appellant's parents and younger brother in a motor vehicle accident on June 20, 2007. The Motor Vehicles Accident Tribunal initially granted compensation, which the High Court subsequently enhanced. The insurer (New India Assurance Co. Ltd.) sought a reduction in the enhanced compensation for the parents, arguing that the High Court erred by not deducting one-third for personal expenses, considering income without proof, and granting excessive amounts under conventional heads. The claimant (Sonigra Juhi Uttamchand) sought further enhancement, particularly regarding future prospects for self-employed persons and the correct multiplier for her mother.

The Supreme Court acknowledged the legal principles from Sarla Verma (regarding deduction for personal expenses) and Pranay Sethi (regarding conventional heads and future prospects). While noting that a strict application of these principles might lead to a reduction in compensation, the Court emphasized the principle of 'just compensation' under Section 168 of the Motor Vehicles Act. Considering the appellant's tragic loss of her parents and younger brother at the age of 14, and her subsequent plight, the Court decided not to interfere with the enhanced compensation granted by the High Court. It concluded that the High Court's award was not 'alarmingly excessive' and served the interest of justice. Consequently, all appeals, both from the insurer and the claimant, were dismissed, and the High Court's enhanced compensation was maintained.

petitioner_key_arguments: Sought enhancement of compensation for parents, particularly regarding future prospects for self-employed persons.
Sought correct multiplier for the mother based on Sarla Verma's case.
respondent_key_arguments: High Court erred in not deducting 1/3rd of the deceased's income for personal expenditures, especially when dependents included a minor daughter and old aged parents (referencing Sarla Verma).
High Court erred in considering the deceased's income on an assumption basis without proof.
High Court erred in awarding amounts in excess of Rs. 70,000/- under conventional heads (referencing Pranay Sethi).
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court ultimately upheld the High Court's enhanced compensation, effectively dismissing the respondent's arguments for reduction and the appellant's arguments for further enhancement, based on the principle of 'just compensation' and not disturbing the High Court's decision in the interest of justice.

outcome.relief_granted: The enhanced compensation granted by the High Court is maintained.

precedents_cited: Sarla Verma and Ors. v. Delhi Transport Corporation & Anr.1
Trilok Chandra [(1996) 4 SCC 362]
National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Pranay Sethi & Ors.2
M.A. Murthy v. State of Karnataka and Ors.3
Kishan Gopal and Anr. v. Lala and Others4

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: Despite acknowledging that a strict application of established legal precedents (Sarla Verma for deductions, Pranay Sethi for conventional heads and future prospects) might lead to a different calculation, the Court prioritized the principle of 'just compensation' under Section 168 of the Motor Vehicles Act. Considering the appellant's severe and tragic loss at a young age, the Court found that the High Court's enhanced compensation, though not perfectly aligned with every technicality, was not 'alarmingly excessive' and should be maintained in the interest of justice.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that a principle of law enunciated by the Supreme Court is applicable to all cases irrespective of their stage of pendency, as it is considered the law from inception, but clarified that this does not mean matters that have attained finality should be reopened solely for this purpose.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NOS. 1796-1828 OF 2024

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the correctness of a High Court judgment dismissing writ petitions filed by New Mangalore Port Trust, which challenged a District Judge's order quashing demands for revised license fees on grounds of limitation, specifically regarding the retrospective application of tariff revisions and the applicability of Section 18 of the Limitation Act.

judgements.case_summary: The New Mangalore Port Trust (NMPT) allotted land to respondents (licensees) for loading/unloading goods, subject to a revisable license fee. A revised fee was notified in 2010, retrospectively from 2007, leading to demand for arrears. Licensees challenged this retrospective application in writ petitions, which were dismissed by a Single Judge in 2013, but their appeals are pending before a Division Bench. NMPT issued demand notices, which the licensees resisted, citing the pending appeals. Subsequently, NMPT's Estate Officer initiated recovery proceedings under the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971. The District Judge allowed the licensees' appeal, holding the recovery proceedings time-barred. The High Court upheld this, leading NMPT to appeal to the Supreme Court. NMPT argued that the licensees' replies constituted an acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, extending the limitation period, and that the High Court should have awaited the outcome of the pending intra-court appeals. The respondents contended that Section 18 was not pleaded below and that their replies did not admit liability. The Supreme Court found that the licensees' communication dated 04.02.2015 did acknowledge liability, extending the limitation. It also held that the High Court should have deferred hearing NMPT's writ petitions until the intra-court appeals regarding the retrospective tariff were decided. The Court allowed NMPT's appeals, setting aside the High Court's order and remanding the writ petitions for hearing after the intra-court appeals are resolved.

petitioner_key_arguments: Licensees did not raise the plea of limitation in their reply to the show cause notice under Section 7(3) of the PP Act; they raised it for the first time in the appeal.
No limitation is prescribed for passing an order under Section 7(1) of the PP Act.
Even if limitation applies, the recovery proceedings were within the three-year limitation period due to acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act.
The respondents' reply dated 04.02.2015 to the demand notice dated 15.01.2015 acknowledged the debt, extending limitation until 03.02.2018, and further acknowledgments extended it beyond.
The Division Bench and High Court erred in holding recovery proceedings barred by limitation, miscalculating the cause of action and not accounting for interim orders.
Respondents' consistent defence was that the demand should not be pressed due to pending appeals, implying conditional acceptance of liability.
Respondents cannot now argue that recovery proceedings were barred by limitation given their specific stand.
The High Court should have clubbed NMPT's writ petitions with the pending intra-court appeals or awaited their outcome.
Respondents were aware of tariff revision and would be guilty of unjust enrichment if they succeed on a technical ground of limitation.
respondent_key_arguments: Appellant failed to raise the plea of acknowledgment and extension of limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act before any lower court or in the pleadings before the Supreme Court.
The question of limitation is a mixed question of law and fact, requiring specific pleading and evidence for Section 18 benefit.
The communication dated 04.02.2015 never admitted liability/debt; it denied liability due to the retrospective revision of tariff.
Demands prior to 12.08.2015 were not under statutory provision. The first statutory show cause notice on 12.08.2015 was beyond the three-year limitation period.
The notices under Section 7(3) dated 12.08.2015 and the order under Section 7(1) on 21.07.2016 were beyond the prescribed period of limitation.
It cannot be presumed that previous notices by the Assistant Estate Manager were notices under the PP Act.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the appellant's argument that the respondents' communication dated 04.02.2015 constituted an acknowledgment of liability under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, thereby extending the limitation period. The court also agreed that the High Court should have awaited the outcome of the pending intra-court appeals before deciding the writ petitions related to the retrospective application of revised tariffs.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeals are allowed, the impugned order of the High Court is set aside, and the writ petitions before the High Court are restored to be heard after the disposal of the pending intra-court appeals filed by the respondents.

acts_cited: Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971
precedents_cited: NDMC vs. Kalu Ram
New Delhi Municipal Committee vs. Kalu Ram4

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The court held that the respondents' communication dated 04.02.2015, despite objecting to immediate payment, constituted an acknowledgment of liability under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, thereby extending the limitation period. Furthermore, the High Court erred by not deferring the hearing of the writ petitions until the resolution of the pending intra-court appeals, as their outcome directly impacted the validity of the retrospective tariff application.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed that the respondents were well aware of the revised tariff and were resisting payment primarily on the basis of pending appeals, suggesting an attempt to delay payment and benefit from technical objections, which would amount to unjust enrichment.

special_directions.special_directions: The writ petitions before the High Court are restored and are to be heard after the disposal of the pending intra-court appeals filed by the respondents. If the intra-court appeals are allowed, demands would be withdrawn; if dismissed, respondents would be liable to pay with admissible interest.

case_identification.petitioner_name: NIRMITI DEVELOPERS THROUGH ITS PARTNERS & ANR.
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NOS.3238-3239 OF 2025 (@Petition for Special Leave to Appeal (C) Nos.23308-23309/2017)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the lapsing of land reservation under the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, due to the failure of authorities to acquire the land within statutory timelines, and the rights of subsequent purchasers.

judgements.case_summary: This case involves a vacant plot of land in Amravati, Maharashtra, initially reserved for a Government school and later for a private school under the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966 (MRTP Act). Despite the reservation coming into effect in 1993, no steps were taken for acquisition for 13 years. The original owners served a purchase notice under Section 49 in 2006, which was confirmed in 2007, with a directive for acquisition within one year. However, acquisition proceedings were not completed. Another purchase notice was issued under Section 127 in 2014. The appellants purchased the property in 2015. They filed a Writ Petition seeking a declaration that the reservation had lapsed or for compensation. The High Court disposed of the petition, stating that Section 49 was not for de-reservation followed by sale, and that the developer had not taken fresh steps. The Supreme Court, analyzing Sections 49 and 127 of the MRTP Act and various precedents, found that the statutory timelines for acquisition were not met. The Court emphasized that land cannot be held indefinitely under reservation without acquisition. It concluded that the reservation had lapsed by efflux of time under Sections 126 and 127 of the MRTP Act, and even invoked Article 142 of the Constitution due to the gross delay of almost 33 years.

petitioner_key_arguments: The reservation lapsed under Section 49(7) of the MRTP Act on 02/01/2008 due to the failure of the appropriate authority to make an application to acquire the land within one year of confirmation of the purchase notice.
The reservation also lapsed under Section 127 of the MRTP Act on 13/08/2015, as no steps for acquisition were commenced within twelve months of the service of the purchase notice.
The land cannot be held indefinitely under reservation without acquisition, depriving the owner of their property rights.
respondent_key_arguments: Section 49 is not meant for de-reservation of land to then be sold in the open market.
The petitioner, being a developer and subsequent purchaser, had not taken fresh steps after purchase to issue notice either under Section 49 or Section 127 of the Act.

The benefits of the notice given by the previous land owners under Section 49 cannot accrue to the present petitioners as no advantage of de-reservation was taken for more than 6 years by the original owners.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the reservation had lapsed due to the authorities' failure to acquire the land within the statutory timelines under both Section 49(7) and Section 127 of the MRTP Act, and that the land could not be held indefinitely under reservation.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeals are allowed. The impugned order passed by the High Court is set aside. It is declared that the reservation of the plot in question has lapsed by efflux of time in view of the provisions under Sections 126 and 127 of the MRTP Act respectively. The land is deemed to be released from reservation.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that the statutory timelines for land acquisition under Sections 49 and 127 of the MRTP Act are mandatory and must be strictly adhered to by the authorities. Failure to initiate or complete acquisition proceedings within these prescribed periods results in the automatic lapsing of the land reservation, thereby releasing the land for the owner's development and protecting their property rights from indefinite deprivation.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that even without relying on Section 127 of the MRTP Act, it would have exercised its jurisdiction under Article 142 of the Constitution to declare the reservation lapsed due to the gross and inordinate delay of almost thirty years, emphasizing the need to do complete justice. It also highlighted that property rights are now considered human rights.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 2322 OF 2025 (Arising out of SLP(C)No.21766 of 2024)

case_details.subject_matter: This case concerns an appeal for enhanced compensation under the Motor Vehicle Act, 1988, following a motor accident that caused 100% permanent disability to the claimant. The primary issue is the determination of the claimant's monthly income for calculating compensation.

judgements.case_summary: The Claimant-Appellant, aged 27, sustained injuries in a motor vehicle accident on June 24, 2014, caused by a rashly driven goods vehicle, leading to two months of bedridden treatment. He filed for Rs. 30,00,000/- compensation under the Motor Vehicle Act, 1988, claiming a monthly income of Rs. 10,000/- as a 'Goundy'. The Tribunal awarded Rs. 6,78,000/- with 6% interest, assessing his monthly income at Rs. 7,500/- and permanent disability at 20%. Aggrieved, the Claimant-Appellant appealed to the High Court, which enhanced the compensation by Rs. 18,90,938/-, accepting 100% permanent disability but maintaining the monthly income at Rs. 7,500/-. Still dissatisfied, the Claimant-Appellant approached the Supreme Court, arguing his monthly income should be Rs. 10,000/-. The Supreme Court, relying on precedents, agreed that in the absence of contradictory material, the oral evidence regarding income should be accepted. Consequently, the Court fixed the monthly income at Rs. 10,000/-, recalculated the compensation, and modified the total award to Rs. 37,51,000/-, allowing the appeal.

petitioner_key_arguments: The monthly income of the Claimant-Appellant ought to have been taken as Rs. 10,000/- per month.
The disability has been incorrectly assessed at 20% by the Tribunal, while the Appellant has actually suffered 100% functional disability.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's argument that his monthly income should be Rs. 10,000/- per month was accepted by the Supreme Court. The High Court had already accepted the 100% functional disability argument.

outcome.relief_granted: The Civil Appeal is allowed. The compensation awarded is enhanced to Rs. 37,51,000/-. Interest is to be paid as awarded by the Tribunal.

precedents_cited: Chandra v. Mukesh Kumar Yadav1 (2022) 1 SCC 198
National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Pranay Sethi (2017) 16 SCC 680 Para 42 & 59
Kajal v. Jagdish Chand (2020) 4 SCC 413 Para 19 and 25
Sidram v. Divisional Manager, United India Insurance Ltd. (2023) 3 SCC 439 Para 89
K.S. Muralidhar v. R. Subbulakshmi & Anr. 2024 SCC Online SC 3385 Para 13 and 14
Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar (2011) 1 SCC 343 Para 6

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that in the absence of any material to discard oral evidence regarding income, the stated income of the claimant should be accepted for calculating compensation under the Motor Vehicle Act. The Court also affirmed the 100% permanent disability as determined by the High Court.

special_directions.special_directions: Interest is to be paid as awarded by the Tribunal. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

case_identification.case_number: Criminal Appeal No. 352/2020

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the mechanical application of Section 156(3) Cr.P.C. by a Magistrate to direct FIR registration for alleged offences under IPC Sections 323, 294, 500, 504, and 506, and the High Court's affirmation of this order without proper judicial scrutiny.

judgements.case_summary: This appeal arose from a High Court order that rejected the appellant's application under Section 482 Cr.P.C., thereby affirming a Magistrate's order under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C. The Magistrate had directed police to register an FIR against the appellant (a police officer) for offences under IPC Sections 323, 294, 500, 504, and 506, based on a complaint by an advocate alleging humiliation. The Supreme Court found that the Magistrate's order was passed mechanically, without applying judicial mind to ascertain if the allegations constituted cognizable offences. Specifically, the Court analyzed Section 294 IPC, concluding that mere abusive or humiliating words do not meet the criteria for obscenity. It also found that the ingredients for offences under Sections 504 and 506 IPC were not borne out. The Court criticized both the Magistrate for the mechanical order and the High Court for failing to examine these crucial aspects. The judgment also discussed the changes introduced by the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), which codify procedural safeguards for directing investigations under Section 175(3) BNSS (corresponding to Section 156(3) Cr.P.C.), emphasizing the need for affidavits, prior applications to police, and consideration of police submissions to prevent misuse. Consequently, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside both the High Court's and the Magistrate's orders.

petitioner_key_arguments: The High Court erred in rejecting the application under Section 482 Cr.P.C.
The Magistrate's order directing FIR registration under Section 156(3) Cr.P.C. was mechanical and without application of mind.
The allegations in the complaint did not constitute the offences punishable under Sections 294, 504, 506, and 500 of the IPC.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the Magistrate's order was mechanical and that the ingredients of the alleged offences under Sections 294, 504, 506, and 500 IPC were not made out from the complaint.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned order passed by the High Court is set aside. The order passed by the Magistrate directing police investigation under Section 156(3) of the Cr.P.C. is also set aside.

case_identification.petitioner_name: Om Prakash Gupta Alias Lalloowa (Now ... vs Satish Chandra (Now Deceased)
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 13407 OF 2024, CIVIL APPEAL NO. 13408 OF 2024

petitioner_advocates: Mr. Thomas Joseph, learned senior counsel
Mr. Shekar Devessa, learned senior counsel
respondent_advocates: Mr. Raghenth Basant, learned senior counsel

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns two civil appeals related to specific performance suits, focusing on issues of abatement of appeals due to the death of parties, substitution of legal representatives, and condonation of delay in filing such applications.

judgements.case_summary:
This judgment addresses two civil appeals (13407/2024 and 13408/2024) arising from specific performance suits, both involving the heirs of Om Prakash Gupta Alias Lalloowa as appellants. The core issues revolve around the abatement of appeals due to the death of original parties (Satish Chandra and Smt. Rooprani), the subsequent applications for substitution of legal representatives, and the condonation of delay in filing these applications.

In Civil Appeal No. 13407/2024, the High Court had dismissed the appeal as abated, rejecting the application for condonation of delay and substitution filed by Om Prakash's heirs. The Supreme Court noted that Satish Chandra's heirs had previously filed a substitution application, informing the court of his death. The appellants argued that this application should have sufficed, and a separate application by them was not legally required.

For Civil Appeal No. 13408/2024, concerning Smt. Rooprani, the High Court had also dismissed the appeal as abated. The appellants contended that the information regarding Rooprani's death was not clearly conveyed as mandated by Order XXII Rule 10-A CPC, thus excusing their delay.

The Supreme Court, applying principles from Perumon Bhagvathy Devaswom and Mithailal Dalsangar Singh, emphasized a justice-oriented approach, stating that procedural requirements should not override substantive justice. It held that a prayer for substitution can implicitly include a prayer for setting aside abatement, and courts should be liberal in condoning delay if there's no deliberate negligence. For CA 13407, the Court found that the High Court was duly informed of Satish Chandra's death by his heirs, making a separate application by Om Prakash's heirs unnecessary. For CA 13408, the Court ruled that the information about Rooprani's death was not conveyed in a clear manner under Rule 10-A, thus Om Prakash's heirs were not estopped from pleading ignorance.

Consequently, the Supreme Court allowed both appeals, setting aside the High Court's orders that dismissed the substitution/delay condonation applications and declared the appeals abated. Both appeals are restored, and the substitution of legal representatives is ordered. The High Court is directed to prioritize and decide the appeals within six months.

petitioner_key_arguments: High Court erred in not granting prayers and allowing procedural requirements to override substantive justice.
A previously filed application for substitution by the heirs of Satish Chandra (in CA 13407) should have sufficed, making a separate application by Om Prakash's heirs unnecessary.
A prayer for substitution can be construed as implicitly including a prayer for setting aside abatement.
Information about Rooprani's death (in CA 13408) was not conveyed in a clear and unambiguous manner as required by Rule 10-A CPC, thus Om Prakash's heirs were not negligent.
respondent_key_arguments: No infirmity in the High Court's impugned orders.
Om Prakash was negligent in pursuing the second appeals.
The application filed by Satish Chandra's heirs was merely an intimation of death, not a proper substitution application under Rule 4 CPC.
Lack of due diligence by Om Prakash.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the arguments that procedural requirements should not override substantive justice, that a justice-oriented approach is needed, that a prayer for substitution can implicitly include a prayer for setting aside abatement, and that the information regarding Rooprani's death was not properly conveyed to Om Prakash's heirs, thus excusing the delay.

outcome.relief_granted: The orders dismissing the applications for substitution and condonation of delay, and declaring the appeals abated, are set aside. Both Civil Appeal No. 13407 of 2024 and Civil Appeal No. 13408 of 2024 are restored to their original file and number, with directions for substitution of legal representatives.

acts_cited: Order XXII of the Code of Civil Procedure
precedents_cited: Perumon Bhagvathy Devaswom v. Bhargavi Amma
Union of India v. Ram Charan

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that courts should adopt a justice-oriented approach in matters of abatement and substitution, interpreting procedural rules liberally to advance substantial justice. A prayer for substitution can be deemed to include a prayer for setting aside abatement, and delay in substitution should be condoned if there is no deliberate negligence, especially when the death of a party was not clearly communicated as per Order XXII Rule 10-A CPC.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed that the Supreme Court has powers under Article 136 to correct manifest illegalities and avoid travesty of justice even in the absence of a direct challenge to an order. It also discussed the proper sequence of applications for substitution, setting aside abatement, and condonation of delay.

special_directions.special_directions: The High Court is requested to consider the restored second appeals on priority and decide them, preferably within 6 (six) months from the date of the Supreme Court's judgment.
special_directions.interim_orders: A coordinate bench of the Supreme Court, on 12th July, 2019, granted permission to file the special leave petitions and issued notice, and later made an order allowing the applications for substitution and connected applications, subject to just exceptions.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 4229 OF 2024 (Arising out of SLP (Crl.) No.(s) 2214 of 2022)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the plea of juvenility raised by the appellant, who was convicted of culpable homicide, and the court's duty to adjudicate such claims under the Juvenile Justice Acts, even if raised at a late stage or after previous dismissals.

judgements.case_summary:
The appellant, Om Prakash, was convicted of culpable homicide for an incident that occurred on 15.11.1994. He consistently raised the plea of juvenility, claiming to be 14 years old at the time of the offense, but this plea was not properly adjudicated by the trial court, High Court, or even in subsequent proceedings before the Supreme Court, including a Review Petition and a Curative Petition. Despite documentary evidence (school certificates, ossification test) and an admission by the State in a counter-affidavit confirming his juvenility, his plea was dismissed or not adequately considered. The Presidential Order commuted his death sentence to life imprisonment with a caveat of release only after 60 years of age. The appellant then filed a Writ Petition challenging the Presidential Order and seeking relief under Section 9(2) of the 2015 Act, which was dismissed by the High Court.

The Supreme Court emphasized the judiciary's role in discovering truth and the social welfare nature of juvenile justice legislation. It held that a plea of juvenility, if not duly adjudicated, does not attain finality and can be raised at any stage. The Court found that the previous courts erred in not applying the mandatory provisions of the Juvenile Justice Acts. It clarified that setting aside the sentence due to juvenility is not an interference with the Presidential Order but a fulfillment of a constitutional mandate. The Court allowed the appeal, set aside the sentence (while maintaining the conviction), and ordered the appellant's immediate release, directing the Uttarakhand State Legal Services Authority to assist in his rehabilitation.

petitioner_key_arguments: The High Court erred in not considering the independent prayer sought for by the Appellant.
The age of the Appellant was 14 years at the time of commission of the offence, which is not in dispute.
There is no judicial finality attained regarding the juvenility plea.
The phrase 'any stage' used in Section 9(2) of the 2015 Act must be given an extended meaning.
Grave injustice has been meted out due to the lack of adjudication of juvenility.
The Appellant is entitled to immediate release and compensation for the loss of formative years.
Beneficial and retrospective applicability of change in law post the dismissal of the Curative Petition on 06.02.2006.
Claim of juvenility can be raised and considered even after the President has exercised powers under Article 72, Constitution of India.
respondent_key_arguments: This is an attempt to reopen and re-hear an issue which has attained finality.
The Mercy Petition was considered under the constitutional mandate and does not require any interference.
The Special Leave Petition, as filed, is not maintainable.
The bone ossification test cannot be the sole basis for declaring the appellant as the minor.
There was due compliance of Rule 12(3) of the 2007 Rules.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments regarding the non-finality of the juvenility plea when not properly adjudicated, the mandatory nature of juvenile justice provisions, and their retrospective applicability were accepted by the court.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal is allowed. The sentence imposed against the Appellant in excess of the upper limit prescribed under the relevant Act is set aside, while the conviction is maintained. The Appellant shall be released forthwith, if not required in any other case. The Uttarakhand State Legal Services Authority is directed to assist the Appellant's rehabilitation and reintegration into society.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that a plea of juvenility, being a constitutional mandate and a social welfare objective, does not attain finality if it has not been properly adjudicated under the relevant Juvenile Justice Acts. Courts have a mandatory duty to discover the truth regarding juvenility and apply the beneficial provisions of these Acts retrospectively, even if the plea was previously dismissed without a proper inquiry.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court emphasized the importance of truth in the administration of justice, the 'parens patriae' role of courts, and the active role judges must play in discerning truth. It also discussed the limited scope of judicial review for Presidential pardons but distinguished it from the mandatory duty to apply juvenile justice provisions, stating that the latter is not an interference with the former but a fulfillment of a constitutional obligation.

case_identification.respondent_name: THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH & ANR.
case_identification.case_number: SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRL.) No(s). 17781 OF 2024

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the power of a trial court to summon additional accused under Section 319 CrPC, even when a closure report had previously exonerated them, based on evidence adduced during trial.

judgements.case_summary: This petition challenges a High Court order dated 23-10-2024, which affirmed the Trial Court's decision to summon the petitioners as accused for the offence of murder under Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The First Information Report (FIR) initially named the petitioners, but the Investigating Officer subsequently filed a closure report exonerating them, while a charge-sheet was filed against other accused. During the trial, the original first informant (PW3) deposed against the petitioners, attributing specific overt acts. Based on this oral evidence, an application was filed under Section 319 CrPC, leading to the summoning of the petitioners. The petitioners argued that the Trial Court should have considered the closure report. However, the Supreme Court, relying on precedents like Hardeep Singh and S. Mohammed Ispahani, reiterated that a trial court has discretionary and extraordinary power under Section 319 CrPC to summon persons not initially charged, even if a closure report was filed, provided strong and cogent evidence surfaces during the trial. The Court emphasized that the closure report does not render the trial court powerless. Consequently, the petition was dismissed, affirming the summoning order.

petitioner_key_arguments: The Trial Court and High Court should have taken into consideration the closure report filed by the Investigating Officer exonerating the petitioners from the alleged offence before summoning them under Section 319 CrPC.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the principle that a trial court can summon additional accused under Section 319 CrPC based on evidence adduced during trial, even if a closure report had previously exonerated them. This aligns with the Trial Court and High Court's decisions.

precedents_cited: Ramesh Chandra Srivastava v. State of U.P. & Another (2021) 12 SCC 608
Hardeep Singh v. State of Punjab (2014) 3 SCC 92
Hardeep Singh v. State of Punjab (2014) 2 SCC (Cri) 86
S. Mohammed Ispahani v. Yogendra Chandak (2017) 16 SCC 226

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: A trial court has the discretionary and extraordinary power under Section 319 CrPC to summon persons as accused, even if they were previously exonerated by a closure report, provided strong and cogent evidence surfaces during the trial proceedings. The closure report does not curtail the court's power to act on evidence adduced before it.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed that the closure report filed by the police should be looked into promptly by the court concerned and an appropriate order passed after hearing the de facto complainant, rather than keeping it pending for a long time.

special_directions.special_directions: It shall be open for the petitioners to raise all contentions available to them in law before the Trial Court including placing reliance on the closure report whatever its worth.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 2514 OF 2014

case_details.subject_matter: The case challenges a High Court order that dismissed a petition to quash criminal proceedings (FIR, chargesheet, summons) initiated by the respondent against the appellants, arising from a long-standing civil property dispute.

judgements.case_summary: This appeal challenges a judgment and order dated 14th November 2013 by the High Court of Karnataka, which dismissed a petition to quash criminal proceedings (C.C. No.29027 of 2010) against the appellants. The criminal proceedings stemmed from an FIR lodged by respondent No.2 alleging threats from the appellants to withdraw civil suits related to a property dispute. The appellants are the absolute owners of the property and had filed civil suits for permanent injunction and declaration of ownership, securing a temporary injunction against respondent No.2. The appellants argued that the criminal proceedings were mala fide, absurd, and initiated with an ulterior motive, citing previous instances where respondent No.2's similar allegations were found false or quashed. The Supreme Court noted the long-standing civil dispute and respondent No.2's habit of filing false cases. Applying the principles from State of Haryana and Others v. Bhajan Lal, the Court found that the allegations in the FIR were absurd and the proceedings were manifestly mala fide, falling under categories that warrant quashing to prevent abuse of the process of law. Consequently, the appeal was allowed, and the High Court's order, the chargesheet, summons, and all subsequent proceedings were quashed.

petitioner_key_arguments: The proceedings are totally mala fide and instituted with an ulterior motive.
The appellants are the ones who filed civil suits, so there is no question of them threatening respondent No.2 to withdraw a suit he did not file.
Respondent No.2 is in the habit of filing false cases against the appellants and their family members.
Previous criminal cases filed by respondent No.2 with similar allegations were either acquitted or quashed by the High Court.
respondent_key_arguments: The respondent-State vehemently opposed the appeal, but specific arguments are not detailed in the document.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the criminal proceedings were mala fide, based on absurd allegations, and initiated with an ulterior motive, aligning with the principles for quashing criminal proceedings to prevent abuse of process of law.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned judgment and order dated 14th November 2013 passed by the learned Single Judge of the High Court of Karnataka at Bangalore is quashed and set aside. The chargesheet registered as C.C. No. 29027/2010, the order dated 26th June 2010 issuing summons to the appellants, and the subsequent proceedings arising therefrom are also quashed and set aside.

acts_cited: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2
precedents_cited: State of Haryana and Others v. Bhajan Lal and Others (1992 Supp (1) SCC 335)
constitutional_provisions: Article 226 of the Constitution of India

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The Court found that the criminal proceedings were manifestly mala fide, instituted with an ulterior motive for wreaking vengeance, and based on absurd allegations, thus constituting an abuse of the process of law. This squarely fell under categories 1, 3, 5, and 7 of the guidelines established in Bhajan Lal for quashing criminal proceedings.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court reiterated the caution that the power of quashing a criminal proceeding should be exercised very sparingly and with circumspection, and only in the rarest of rare cases, without embarking on an inquiry into the reliability of allegations.

special_directions.interim_orders: This Court, by an order dated 8th May 2014, stayed the proceedings before the trial court for three months. By an order dated 28th November 2014, while granting leave, the interim order of stay was made absolute by this Court.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO(S). OF 2025 (Arising out of SLP(Civil) No(s). 4036-4038 of 2024) and connected matters

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the seniority of Assistant Executive Engineers (AEEs) in the Panchayat Raj Department, specifically whether the officiating service of temporarily appointed AEEs (1990-1992 batch) should be counted for seniority over regularly appointed AEEs (1997 batch).

judgements.case_summary:
The appellants, initially Work Inspectors, were appointed as temporary Assistant Executive Engineers (AEEs) between 1990-1992 in the Panchayat Raj Department under specific Government Orders (G.O.M. No. 540, 391). Their services were regularized in 2005 via G.O.M. No. 234, but they were placed below AEEs regularly selected in 1997 (private respondents). Aggrieved by this, appellants made representations, leading to a revised G.O.M. No. 262 in 2006, which granted them seniority from their initial appointment date (1990-1992 batch), placing them above the 1997 batch. The private respondents challenged G.O.M. No. 262, and the High Court quashed it.

Appellants contended their appointments were not "de hors" rules, as there was a rule vacuum, and they were appointed under Rule 10(a)(i) for continuous service, not as ad-hoc or stop-gap. They argued the State could revise G.O.M.s and no prior hearing was needed for policy decisions, citing Proposition (B) of Direct Recruit Class II Engg. Officers' Association. Respondents argued their regular 1997 appointments were superior, the State was "functus officio" after G.O.M. No. 234, and G.O.M. No. 262 violated natural justice by not hearing them.

The Supreme Court found appellants' appointments were valid given the rule vacuum and the nature of the G.O.M.s, which indicated intent for continuous service. It applied Proposition (B), holding that uninterrupted officiating service, even if not strictly by rules initially, counts for seniority upon regularization. The Court rejected the "functus officio" doctrine for the State's policy-making power and dismissed the need for prior hearings in such administrative decisions, citing precedents.

The Supreme Court allowed the appeals, quashing the High Court's judgment. It held that the appellants' officiating service from 1990-2005 should be counted for seniority, placing them above the 1997 batch of regularly appointed candidates. This decision restores the seniority of the 1990-1992 batch of AEEs.

petitioner_key_arguments: The appellants hold the qualification of Bachelor in Engineering and were duly selected and appointed as Work Inspectors on 1st January, 1990 in the Andhra Pradesh Scheduled Castes Co-operative Development Corporation against a sanctioned post.

The State Government felt an imminent need for qualified engineers to carry out the Cyclone Emergency Reconstruction Project (CERP) in 1990, leading to the appointment of appellants as temporary AEEs under Rule 10(a)(i)(1) of Andhra Pradesh State and Subordinate Service Rules, which was not de hors the rules or a backdoor appointment.
No challenge was ever laid by the private respondents to G.O.M. No. 234 dated 27th June, 2005, which regularized the services of the appellants, and thus, it has attained finality.
The delay in regularizing services was due to the need for amending the Andhra Pradesh Panchayati Raj and Rural Development Act/Rules, which cannot be attributed to the appellants.
The appellants (1990-1992 batch) have continued to discharge functions uninterruptedly for 31 years and would lose 7 years of seniority if placed below the 1997 batch.
G.O.M. No. 540 (appellants' appointment) did not contain conditions for temporary appointment or reversion, unlike G.O.M. No. 1289.
The appointments, though termed temporary, were not stop-gap or ad-hoc, as G.O.M. No. 391 showed intent to retain services and post personnel to new circles/divisions upon project abolition.
The State Government was not 'functus officio' after G.O.M. No. 234 and could modify it through G.O.M. No. 262, as administrative decisions based on policy considerations can be revised.
The reasoning that G.O.M. No. 262 was issued without hearing affected persons is misplaced, as no prior notice is required for policy decisions conferring benefits.

The case falls under Proposition (B) of Direct Recruit Class II Engg. Officers' Association v. State Of Maharashtra, where officiating service counts for seniority if the initial appointment, though not strictly by rules, continued uninterruptedly until regularization.
respondent_key_arguments: The respondents were appointed as AEEs in 1997 after undergoing a regular selection process in pursuance of Notification No. 8 of 1995 issued by APPSC.

The appellants were appointed purely on a temporary basis (1990-1995) either on promotion, recruitment by transfer, or sponsored by employment exchange, without due adherence to selection procedures or service rules.
The APPSC published Notification No. 4 of 1990 and No. 8 of 1995 for regular selection, but appellants did not avail these opportunities.

G.O.M. No. 234, dated 27th June, 2005, was a final policy decision to regularize appellants' services but place them below the last regularly selected candidate, and the State Government became 'functus officio' thereafter.
The revised G.O.M. No. 262, dated 17th June, 2006, was issued without affording an opportunity of hearing to the respondents, violating principles of natural justice.
The factors forming the basis for G.O.M. No. 262 were known during G.O.M. No. 234's formulation, and no sufficient explanation was given for overlooking them.

The case falls under the corollary to Proposition (A) of Direct Recruit Class II Engg. Officers' Association, where initial appointment is ad hoc and not according to rules, so officiation cannot count for seniority.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments that their initial appointments were not 'de hors' the rules due to a rule vacuum and the nature of the government orders, that the State was not 'functus officio' in revising policy decisions, and that no prior hearing was required for such policy changes. The court applied Proposition (B) of the Direct Recruit Class II Engg. Officers' Association case, which allows officiating service to count for seniority when an appointment, though not strictly by rules, continued uninterruptedly until regularization.

outcome.relief_granted: The High Court's judgment dated 21st September, 2023, is quashed and set aside. The period of officiating service (1990 to 2005) of the appellants and the batch of AEEs appointed between 1990-1992 is to be counted as regular service for determining seniority, entitling them to be placed above the 1997 batch of regularly appointed candidates (private respondents herein) in the seniority list.

acts_cited: Andhra Pradesh (Regulation of Appointments to Public Services and Rationalization of Staff Pattern and Pay Structure) Act, 1994
Rule 10(a)(i) of the Andra Pradesh Subordinate Service Rules
Rule 25 of the Andhra Pradesh State and Subordinate Service Rules, 1996

Orissa Administrative Tribunal Bar Association v. UOI19

Santosh Kumar v. State of A.P.22
Amarendra Kumar Mohapatra v. State of Orissa and Ors.23

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that if an initial appointment, though not strictly made according to rules, leads to uninterrupted service until regularization, the period of officiating service must be counted for seniority (Proposition B of Direct Recruit Class II Engg. Officers' Association). Furthermore, the State's rule-making and policy-making powers are not curtailed by the doctrine of 'functus officio' or a requirement for prior hearing to affected parties in administrative policy decisions.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that applying the doctrine of 'functus officio' to the State's administrative decision-making or rule-making power would cripple executive functions and paralyze governance, as policies are inherently subject to change based on prevailing circumstances. Similarly, requiring prior hearings for policy decisions would impose an undue procedural roadblock, undermining efficient policy implementation.

special_directions.special_directions: The appeals are allowed accordingly. No order as to costs. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 @ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CIVIL) NO.4293 OF 2024

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns an appeal against the impleadment of a legal heir (daughter) as a defendant in a civil suit for declaration and recovery of possession, following the death of the original plaintiff and a dispute over a will.

judgements.case_summary: The original plaintiff, Pappammal, filed a civil suit (O.S. No. 155 of 2017) for declaration and recovery of possession. After her death, the Appellant (her son) was substituted as the plaintiff based on a will. Subsequently, Respondent No. 1 (Pappammal's daughter and Appellant's sister) filed an application (I.A. No. 6 of 2023) to implead herself as a defendant in the suit, alleging the will produced by the Appellant was forged. The Trial Court allowed this impleadment, which was upheld by the Madras High Court in a Civil Revision Petition. The Appellant challenged this decision before the Supreme Court, arguing that a previous Supreme Court order only allowed his substitution as plaintiff and did not permit the impleadment of other parties. The Supreme Court clarified that its prior order did not restrict other legal heirs from raising claims or being impleaded. The Court emphasized the importance of hearing all necessary parties to ascertain the truth, especially when there is a dispute over a will and the impleading party is a direct legal heir. Consequently, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court and Trial Court orders allowing Respondent No. 1's impleadment as a defendant.

petitioner_key_arguments: The High Court erred in upholding the Trial Court's order allowing Respondent No. 1's impleadment as Defendant No. 2.
The previous Supreme Court Order dated 21.07.2022 only allowed the present Appellant to be a plaintiff in the suit, implying no other person has the right to revise a claim or contest the will.
The contention for non-impleadment of Respondent No. 1 is based on logic and law.
respondent_key_arguments: Respondent No. 1 is admittedly the daughter and a legal heir of the deceased plaintiff.
Respondent No. 1 alleges the will produced by the Appellant is forged and fabricated.
As a legal heir, Respondent No. 1 has a right to be heard in the dispute over the property.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the arguments that all necessary parties, especially legal heirs with a claim to the disputed property, must be heard for a fair trial. It clarified that its previous order did not restrict the impleadment of other parties and rejected the Appellant's contention against his sister's impleadment.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal was dismissed, thereby affirming the order allowing the impleadment of Respondent No. 1 as a defendant in the original suit.

acts_cited: Order XXII Rule 5 of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908
Order I Rule 10 (2) of the CPC
precedents_cited: Civil Appeal No. 4832 of 2022 [SLP (C) NO. 13332 of 2021]
Civil Appeal No. 4833 of 2022

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that for a fair trial, all necessary parties, particularly legal heirs with a claim to the disputed property, must be heard. The Court clarified that its previous order allowing the appellant's substitution as plaintiff did not preclude other legal heirs from being impleaded or contesting the will. The genuineness of the will is a matter for trial, and the sister's claim as a legal heir warrants her impleadment to reach the truth of the matter.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The entire purpose of a Trial is to reach the truth of the matter and it is absolutely important that all necessary parties must be heard, before a decision is taken by the Court.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO (S). OF 2025 (Arising out of Special Leave Petition (C) No. 4194 of 2024)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the eligibility criteria for Assistant Teachers in Jharkhand, specifically challenging the High Court's decision to allow candidates with CTET/STET qualifications to participate in the recruitment process, contrary to the state's JTET requirement, and the State Government's power to alter eligibility criteria mid-recruitment.

judgements.case_summary:
The appeals challenge a Jharkhand High Court judgment dated 20.12.2023, which permitted private respondents (residents of Jharkhand with CTET or neighboring states' STET qualifications) to participate in the recruitment process for Assistant Teachers, despite the appellants having cleared the Jharkhand Teacher Eligibility Test (JTET). The core dispute arose because the State of Jharkhand had not conducted JTET since 2016, leading CTET-qualified candidates to seek participation. The High Court, based on a concession from the Advocate General, allowed CTET/STET holders to apply, with a stipulation to clear JTET within three years. This led to amendments in the Recruitment Rules and Advertisement No. 13 to accommodate these candidates.

The appellants argued that only the Central Government can relax minimum qualifications, the JTET is better suited for Jharkhand's specific needs (regional/tribal languages), and changing eligibility criteria mid-recruitment is unlawful, citing precedents like *Tej Prakash Pathak*. The State and private respondents contended that the State had the power to recognize CTET/STET under NCTE Guidelines (Para 10(b)) if it decided not to conduct its own TET, and that expanding the zone of consideration was permissible.

The Supreme Court found that the State Government's stand changed at every stage of litigation and that the Advocate General's concession was contrary to the State's earlier affidavits. The Court reiterated that eligibility criteria cannot be changed mid-way through a recruitment process once the advertisement is issued, unless explicitly permitted by extant rules and satisfying non-arbitrariness. It held that the State Government did not have the power to relax qualifications in the manner done, as relaxation power under Section 23(2) of the RTE Act rests with the Central Government under specific contingencies not met here. The Court allowed the appeals, setting aside the High Court's judgment. It directed that JTET holders with requisite qualifications under the 2022 Rules be eligible for appointment, and CTET/STET holders who applied after the High Court judgment or rule amendment would not be eligible for the ongoing recruitment process.

petitioner_key_arguments: Only the Central Government has the power to relax minimum qualifications for teachers under Section 23 of the RTE Act.
The JTET is better suited for Jharkhand's needs, testing specific regional/tribal languages.
There are sufficient JTET-qualified candidates available, so relaxing qualifications was unnecessary.
Allowing under-qualified teachers (who may not clear JTET later) would compromise teaching quality.
Appellants had a legitimate expectation to be recruited based on their 2016 JTET qualification.
The 2022 Recruitment Rules and Advertisement No. 13 mandated JTET, and this cannot be changed based on an Advocate General's concession.
Changing eligibility criteria after the recruitment process has begun ('changing the rules of the game mid-way') is unlawful.
respondent_key_arguments: The requirement of local language knowledge is addressed in the Recruitment Examination.
Para 10(b) of the NCTE Guidelines permits the State Government to recognize CTET and STET as qualifications if it decides not to conduct TET.
Appellants have no legitimate expectations as rules were amended prior to the examination.
Para 10 of NCTE Guidelines must be read with Para 11, which mandates annual TET by the State.
The State Government made a bona-fide decision to expand the zone of consideration without altering selection criteria, in consonance with NCTE Guidelines.
The eligibility of candidates should be reckoned on the last date of application, which was extended.
Para 10 of NCTE Guidelines does not prohibit the State from considering CTET/STET in prescribed situations.
Expanding the zone of consideration without changing eligibility criteria is permissible.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments that eligibility criteria cannot be changed mid-way through a recruitment process and that the State Government lacked the power to relax qualifications in the manner it did.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned judgment of the High Court permitting CTET and STET holders to participate in the ongoing selection process for Assistant Teacher is set aside. JTET holders with requisite qualifications under the 2022 Recruitment Rules, who participated, shall be eligible for appointment, and their results declared forthwith, with appointments made strictly on merit. CTET holders or STET holders who applied after the High Court judgment or amendment in rules/advertisement are not eligible for recruitment under Advertisement No. 13/2023.
