judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The Supreme Court held that eligibility criteria for a recruitment process cannot be altered mid-way after the advertisement has been issued, especially when such changes are not explicitly permitted by existing rules or are based on concessions contrary to the State's official stand. The power to relax minimum qualifications for teachers under Section 23(2) of the RTE Act rests solely with the Central Government under specific contingencies, which were not met in this case, thus the State Government's actions were ultra vires and arbitrary.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: Justice Rajesh Bindal's concurring opinion emphasizes the pivotal role of teachers in nation-building, shaping young minds, and guiding students through modern challenges like social media and artificial intelligence. He stresses the importance of teachers concentrating on their job rather than being embroiled in litigation.

special_directions.special_directions: The High Court's judgment permitting CTET/STET holders to participate in the selection process for Assistant Teacher under Advertisement No. 13 is set aside. JTET holders who possessed the requisite qualification under the 2022 Recruitment Rules and participated shall be eligible for appointment, and their results declared forthwith, with appointments made strictly on merit. CTET holders or STET holders who applied after the High Court judgment or the amendment in rules/advertisement are not eligible for recruitment under Advertisement No. 13/2023.
special_directions.interim_orders: An interim direction was issued on 26.04.2024, allowing the Jharkhand Primary School Assistant Teacher Joint Competitive Examination, 2023 to continue, but prohibiting the declaration of its result without leave of the Supreme Court.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NOOF 2025 (Arising out of S.L.P. (C) No. 4484 OF 2020)

case_details.subject_matter: Enhancement of motor accident compensation for a victim suffering 100% disability and directions for streamlining compensation payment processes.

judgements.case_summary: The appellant, a 21-year-old student and sportsman, suffered quadriplegia and 100% permanent disability in a motor accident on 03.06.2014. Dissatisfied with the compensation awarded by the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (5,16,000/-) and subsequently enhanced by the High Court (15,25,600/-), the appellant sought further enhancement from the Supreme Court. The appellant argued that his income was assessed too low, future prospects were not granted, and various heads of compensation for his lifelong disability were inadequately covered. The respondent contended that a reasonable amount had already been awarded. The Supreme Court found that the High Court's assessment of the appellant's income was too low, even below minimum wage, and failed to account for future prospects. The Court enhanced the appellant's monthly income for calculation purposes to 7,500/-, applied 40% for future prospects, and significantly increased compensation under heads like attendant charges, special diet, pain & suffering, physiotherapy, future medical expenses, and marriage prospects. The appeal was allowed, and the total compensation was enhanced to 36,84,000/-. Additionally, the Court issued broader directions to streamline the payment of compensation in motor accident cases by mandating direct bank transfers to claimants to reduce delays and procedural hassles.

petitioner_key_arguments: Suffered quadriplegia resulting in 100% disability due to the accident.
Income assessed by lower courts was on the lower side, even below minimum wage.
Was a young person (21 years) aiming to become a veterinary doctor and a State Level volleyball player.
High Court failed to grant future prospects under 'Loss of Income'.
Requires special diet and an attendant for life due to 100% disability.
respondent_key_arguments: Reasonable amount of compensation has already been awarded by the High Court.
No ground for further enhancement of compensation.
In the absence of any proof of income, the High Court already assessed the income at 5,600/- per month.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments regarding the inadequate assessment of income, the failure to grant future prospects, and the insufficient compensation for various heads related to lifelong disability (attendant charges, special diet, pain & suffering, physiotherapy, future medical expenses, and marriage prospects) were accepted by the court.

outcome.relief_granted: Total compensation enhanced to 36,84,000/- with interest. Directions issued for direct bank transfer of compensation by the insurance company to the appellant's bank account within a specified timeframe.

precedents_cited: Haryana State Industrial Development Corporation v. Pran Sukh and others 8 (2010) 11 SCC 175
Haryana State Industrial & Infrastructure Development Corporation Ltd. V. Smt. Krishna Rani & another9

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The court found that the lower courts erred in assessing the appellant's income below the minimum wage and in failing to account for future prospects for a young victim with 100% disability. It reasoned that comprehensive compensation must cover all aspects of the victim's lifelong needs, including attendant care, special diet, pain and suffering, physiotherapy, future medical expenses, and loss of marriage prospects, which were inadequately addressed previously.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed the inefficiencies and delays in the current system of disbursing motor accident compensation, noting that funds often remain deposited in tribunals, causing loss of interest and hassle to claimants. It emphasized the need for streamlining the process through direct bank transfers to claimants' accounts to ensure timely and effective compensation.

special_directions.special_directions: The respondent No.3/Insurance Company is directed to calculate and transfer the enhanced compensation amount to the appellant's bank account within six weeks. The appellant must furnish bank account particulars within two weeks. The Insurance Company must verify and transfer the amount within four weeks thereafter, along with up-to-date interest. Tribunals are directed to require bank account particulars from claimants at the initial stages, direct direct bank transfers, ensure accounts are in the claimant's name (or guardian for minors), and report compliance. Banks are responsible for ensuring specified portions are kept in fixed deposit if directed. The Registry is directed to send a copy of this order to the Registrars General of all High Courts and Directors of National/State Judicial Academies for circulation and compliance.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 1388 OF 2014

case_details.subject_matter: Appeal against conviction under Sections 306 and 114 of the Indian Penal Code for abetment to suicide, where the deceased allegedly committed suicide due to blackmail by the appellants.

judgements.case_summary:
This appeal by special leave challenges a judgment and order dated 17.12.2013 by the High Court of Gujarat, which affirmed the conviction of the appellants (accused Nos. 1-4) under Sections 306 and 114 IPC for abetment to suicide. The appellants were sentenced to 5 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine. The State's appeal for enhancement of sentence was also dismissed by the High Court. The prosecution alleged that the deceased, Dashrathbhai Karsanbhai Parmar, consumed poison and died on 25.04.2009, due to blackmail by the appellants involving compromising photographs and videos, leading him to misappropriate money and ultimately commit suicide. A suicide note (Ex. 33) was presented as evidence.

The appellants argued that the prosecution lacked material evidence, such as recovery of videos, photos, money, or ornaments. They contended there was no discernible intention to aid or instigate suicide, and the suicide note was unreliable due to a 20-day delay in its production. They also highlighted inconsistencies in witness testimonies and suggested other reasons for the deceased's distress. The respondent maintained that the death by poison was proven, the suicide note was in the deceased's handwriting, and the blackmail by appellants led to the suicide.

The Supreme Court found significant inconsistencies in the prosecution's evidence, including the unexplained 20-day delay in lodging the FIR and producing the suicide note. The Court noted that the handwriting expert for the suicide note was not examined, and expert opinion requires corroboration. Crucially, the Court held that even if the suicide note were genuine, no act of incitement proximate to the date of suicide, which would leave the deceased with no alternative but to commit suicide, was attributed to the appellants. Consequently, the Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the conviction and sentence.

petitioner_key_arguments: Prosecution case not supported by material evidence (no recovery of video, photos, money, ornaments).
No intention to aid, instigate, or abet suicide discernible from evidence.
Appellants were not present at the time/place of death.
Suicide note produced 20 days after death, making it unreliable.
PW-7 (elder brother) did not support the prosecution.
Deceased had other reasons for distress (misappropriation case, suspension).
respondent_key_arguments: Death by poison proved by postmortem report.
Suicide note (Ex. 33) was in deceased's handwriting (expert opinion).
Appellants blackmailed deceased with compromising photos, leading to suicide.
Conjoint reading of oral and documentary evidence proves charge beyond reasonable doubt.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments regarding the lack of proximate instigation, inconsistencies in prosecution evidence, and the unreliability of the suicide note due to delayed production and lack of corroboration.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal is allowed. The impugned judgment and order of the High Court dated 17.12.2013 and of the trial court dated 12.05.2011 are hereby set aside. The appellants' bail bonds stand discharged.

Chitresh Kumar Chopra versus State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi) (2009) 16 SCC 605
Amalendu Pal alias Jhantu versus State of West Bengal (2010) 1 SCC 707

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that for a conviction under Section 306 IPC for abetment to suicide, there must be clear proof of direct or indirect acts of instigation or incitement by the accused, coupled with a clear mens rea, and these acts must be proximate to the commission of suicide. The Court found that the prosecution failed to establish such proximate acts or mens rea, and the evidence presented suffered from significant inconsistencies and unreliability, particularly concerning the delayed and uncorroborated suicide note.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court reiterated that instigation requires goading, urging, provoking, inciting, or encouraging an act, and while actual words are not always necessary, the accused's conduct must create a situation leaving the deceased with no other option but to commit suicide. It also emphasized the caution required when relying on handwriting expert opinions without examination, especially when uncorroborated.

special_directions.special_directions: The appellants' bail bonds stand discharged.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NOS. 3640-3642 OF 2025 (ARISING OUT OF SLP (C) NOS. 8490-8492 OF 2020)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the execution of a decree for specific performance and possession of immovable property, dealing with obstructions raised by third parties claiming possessory rights as cultivating tenants, and the High Court's decision regarding the maintainability of execution and amendment applications.

judgements.case_summary: This case involves an appeal against a High Court judgment concerning the execution of a decree for specific performance and possession of immovable property. The original suit was filed in 1983 by Ayyavoo Udayar (predecessor of appellants) against vendors, with respondent Nos. 1 and 2 (nephews of vendors) impleaded as defendants who did not contest. A decree for specific performance and possession was granted in 1986 and affirmed by the High Court in 2004 and the Supreme Court in 2006. When appellants sought to execute the decree in 2008, respondent No. 1 obstructed. Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 then filed an application under Section 47 CPC, claiming possession since 1967 as cultivating tenants and alleging lack of notice. They also sought retrospective inclusion of their names in cultivation accounts, which was partially granted from 2008 based on a 'no objection' from the vendors. The ASJ allowed their application, and the High Court upheld this, dismissing the appellants' amendment applications. The Supreme Court found that the lower courts erred by not properly inquiring into the bona fides of the obstruction. It held that the respondent's claims were collusive and mala fide, noting their failure to contest the original suit or appeals, and that their tenancy claim was belated and based on an invalid 'no objection' from vendors who had lost title. The Court emphasized that executing courts must resolve all execution-related questions, including third-party claims, but cannot go behind a valid decree to entertain frivolous objections. The appeals were allowed, and the lower court orders were set aside.

petitioner_key_arguments: The High Court erred in stating that appellants did not appeal the ASJ's order, as they filed the first revision petition.
No separate notice was required for execution as the petition was filed within two years of decree confirmation under Order 21 Rule 22 CPC.
Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 were aware of the execution proceedings, having appeared through counsel in a previous CRP.
Appellants' application for amending the execution petition should have been allowed, as procedural rules advance justice.
There was clear collusion between vendors and respondent Nos. 1 and 2 to frustrate the decree.
Respondent Nos. 1 and 2's claim of cultivating tenancy was belated and based on a 'no objection' from vendors who had no authority after title transfer.
respondent_key_arguments: The decree travelled beyond the judgment.
No effective proceedings were instituted by appellants against respondent Nos. 1 and 2.
Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 had lawful title and uninterrupted possession since 1967 as cultivating tenants.
Appellants did not institute a separate suit for recovery of possession.
Civil courts inherently lacked jurisdiction to decide the question of possession as respondent Nos. 1 and 2 were cultivating tenants.
A challenge to the validity of a decree can be set up even at the execution stage if the civil court inherently lacked jurisdiction.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the respondent's obstruction was mala fide and collusive, and that the lower courts erred in upholding their objections and dismissing the amendment applications. The Court implicitly rejected the respondent's argument that the civil court lacked jurisdiction or that the decree was a nullity.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeals are allowed, and the impugned judgment passed by the High Court and the order passed by the Executing Court are set aside. The Executing Court is directed to ensure vacant and peaceful possession of the suit property to the appellants within a period of two months, with police aid if necessary.
