judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The executing court, under Section 47 and Order XXI Rules 97-101 of the CPC, has the power and duty to conduct a full inquiry into all questions, including third-party claims of right, title, or interest, arising during execution to prevent multiplicity of suits. However, this power does not extend to going behind a valid decree or entertaining frivolous objections aimed at frustrating its execution, especially when the objectors were parties to the original suit and failed to contest. The Court found the respondent's claims of cultivating tenancy and lack of notice to be mala fide and collusive, and therefore, the decree must be executed.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed the long and inordinate delay in execution proceedings across the country and issued mandatory directions for High Courts to ensure timely disposal of execution petitions (within six months) and continuous training for court personnel. It also reiterated that procedural law is subservient to justice and should not be interpreted to frustrate the recipient of justice.

special_directions.special_directions: The Executing Court shall ensure vacant and peaceful possession of the suit property to the appellants within two months, with police aid if necessary. All High Courts are directed to collect data on pending execution petitions, issue administrative orders/circulars to ensure disposal within six months, and forward data to the Supreme Court Registry. The Registry is to notify the matter after seven months for compliance reporting.

case_identification.petitioner_name: Piramal Capital And Housing Finance Limited
case_identification.case_number: Civil Appeal Nos. 1632-1634 of 2022

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns challenges to a Resolution Plan for Dewan Housing Finance Corporation Limited (DHFL) under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, specifically regarding the treatment of recoveries from avoidance applications, compliance with financial regulations, and the rights of various stakeholders including fixed deposit holders and ex-promoters.

judgements.case_summary:
The Supreme Court heard a batch of appeals challenging various orders of the NCLAT concerning the Resolution Plan (RP) for Dewan Housing Finance Corporation Limited (DHFL) under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC). The primary dispute revolved around the NCLAT's modification of the RP, which had allowed the Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA), Piramal Capital, to appropriate recoveries from avoidance applications filed under Section 66 of the IBC. The NCLAT had set aside this term and remanded the RP to the Committee of Creditors (CoC) for reconsideration.

Piramal Capital and Union Bank of India challenged the NCLAT's interference, arguing that the CoC's commercial wisdom was paramount and judicial review was limited. 63 Moons Technologies Limited, Fixed Deposit Holders (FDHs), and ex-promoters (Kapil Wadhawan and Dheeraj Wadhawan) also filed appeals. 63 Moons argued that Section 66 recoveries should benefit creditors, not the SRA. FDHs contended that the RP violated RBI and NHB Acts by not ensuring full repayment of deposits. Ex-promoters challenged their exclusion from the CIRP and the RP's approval process.

The Supreme Court distinguished between avoidance applications under Chapter III (Sections 43, 45, 50) and Chapter VI (Section 66) of the IBC. It held that the NCLAT had transgressed its jurisdiction by interfering with the CoC's commercial wisdom regarding Section 66 recoveries, which were part of a negotiated bargain and had an ascribed notional value of INR 1 due to uncertainty. The Court reiterated that the commercial wisdom of the CoC is supreme and judicial review is limited. It found no legal infirmity in the NCLAT's dismissal of FDHs' appeals, as RBI and NHB Acts do not mandate full repayment of deposits in such a context. The appeals by ex-promoters were also dismissed, affirming their lack of locus standi post-supersession of the board, though they were entitled to a copy of the approved RP as a public document.

The Court set aside the NCLAT's judgment on avoidance applications and upheld the NCLT's approval of the RP. It directed the NCLT to decide avoidance applications under Sections 43, 45, 50 separately, with recoveries going to the CoC, while recoveries from Section 66 applications would go to SRA-Piramal Capital.

petitioner_key_arguments: The decision on recoveries from avoidance transactions falls within the CoC's commercial wisdom and should not be interfered with by NCLAT.
NCLAT's reliance on Regulation 37A of IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016, and foreign jurisprudence was misplaced as they do not apply to CIRP.
The notional value of INR 1 ascribed to Section 66 Applications was legally sound due to the speculative nature of recoveries.
The impugned NCLAT judgment amounts to a unilateral modification of the Resolution Plan, contrary to the SRA's will and CoC's commercial wisdom.
FD Holders/NCD Holders lack locus standi to challenge the Resolution Plan, as their interests were represented by Authorized Representatives.
The RBI Act and NHB Act do not mandate full repayment of deposits, and the Resolution Plan complies with FSP Rules.
Ex-promoters, having vacated their offices due to RBI's supersession of the board, had no right to participate in CoC meetings or challenge the RP.
respondent_key_arguments: Recoveries from avoidance transactions, especially under Section 66, ought to benefit DHFL's creditors, not the SRA, to prevent unjust enrichment.
The NCLAT rightly set aside the illegal Clause 2.13.3 of the RP that allowed SRA to appropriate Section 66 recoveries.
The Resolution Plan violated provisions of the NHB Act and RBI Act by not ensuring full repayment of deposits to FD Holders.
The NCLAT erred by not striking down the RP as it contravened statutory provisions regarding deposit security.
Monies invested by FD Holders were held in trust, making DHFL liable for full repayment, and public depositors have a statutory right to full repayment.
The CoC's commercial wisdom was flawed as creditors lacked knowledge of the true value of assets involved in Section 66 transactions.
Ex-promoters were wrongly excluded from CIRP proceedings, and the CoC failed to maximize the value of DHFL's assets.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the arguments emphasizing the paramountcy of the CoC's commercial wisdom, the limited scope of judicial review by NCLT and NCLAT, and the distinction between different types of avoidance applications under the IBC, particularly regarding Section 66 recoveries. It also upheld that RBI and NHB Acts do not mandate full repayment of deposits in the context of a resolution plan.

outcome.relief_granted: The NCLAT judgment dated 27.01.2022 concerning avoidance applications was set aside. The NCLT order dated 07.06.2021 approving the Resolution Plan was upheld. The NCLT was directed to decide avoidance applications under Sections 43, 45, and 50 separately from those under Section 66. Recoveries from Sections 43, 45, 50 applications shall be appropriated in favour of the CoC, and recoveries from Section 66 applications shall be appropriated in favour of SRA-Piramal Capital.

acts_cited: IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016
precedents_cited: Arcelormittal India Private Limited vs. Satish Kumar Gupta and Others, (2019) 2 SCC 1
K. Sashidhar vs. Indian Overseas Bank and Others, (2019) 12 SCC 150
Ghanashyam Mishra and Sons Private Limited through the Authorised Signatory vs. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Limited through the Director and Others, (2021) 9 SCC 657
Ebix Singapore Private Limited vs. Committee of Creditors of Educomp Solutions Limited and Another, (2022) 2 SCC 401
Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. Icici Bank, (2018) 1 SCC 407
Macquarie Bank Ltd. v. Shilpi Cable Technologies Ltd., (2018) 2 SCC 674
State of A.P. v. P. Laxmi Devi, (2008) 4 SCC 720
Jaypee Kensington Boulevard Apartments Welfare Association & Others vs. NBCC (India) Limited & Others, (2021) SCC Online SC 253
N. Mani v/s Sangeetha Theatre, (2004) 12 SCC 278
Tata Steel BSL Limited vs. Venus Recruiter Private Limited and Others (LPA No.37 of 2021)

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors (CoC) is paramount and subject to limited judicial review. The NCLAT transgressed its jurisdiction by interfering with the Resolution Plan's commercial aspects, particularly regarding the treatment of Section 66 avoidance application recoveries, which are distinct from other avoidance applications under the IBC.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed a distinction between 'supersession' and 'suspension' of a board of directors, noting that supersession has a permanent effect. It also remarked that ex-promoters, while not having a right to participate in CoC meetings post-supersession, are entitled to a certified copy of the approved Resolution Plan as it becomes a public document.

special_directions.special_directions: The NCLT shall decide the Avoidance Applications filed by the Administrator under Sections 43, 45, and 50 separately from the Applications under Section 66. Recoveries/benefits from Sections 43, 45, 50 applications shall be appropriated in favour of the CoC, and recoveries from Section 66 applications shall be appropriated in favour of SRA-Piramal Capital.
special_directions.interim_orders: NCLAT stayed NCLT order dated 19.05.2021. NCLAT dismissed 63 Moons' interim application for a stay on execution of the approved RP.

case_identification.respondent_name: THE MANAGING DIRECTOR, BANGALORE METROPOLITAN, TRANSPORT CORPORATION
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NOS. 3465-3466 OF 2025 (Arising out of SLP(C)Nos.21450-21451/2023)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns an appeal against a High Court judgment in a motor accident claim, specifically challenging the assessment of contributory negligence and the deceased's monthly income for compensation calculation.

judgements.case_summary: The case involves an appeal against a High Court judgment concerning a motor accident claim. The deceased, Boobalan, died on 6th June 2016 after his motorcycle collided with a BMTC bus. The Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT) awarded Rs. 75,97,060/- with 9% interest, assessing the deceased's income at Rs. 62,725/- and finding the bus driver solely negligent. Aggrieved by the compensation amount, both parties appealed to the High Court. The High Court determined 75% contributory negligence on the bus driver and 25% on the deceased, assessed the monthly income at Rs. 50,000/-, and awarded an enhanced amount of Rs. 77,50,000/- with 6% interest. The claimant-appellants then approached the Supreme Court, challenging the High Court's assessment of contributory negligence and the reduced monthly income. The Supreme Court agreed with the Tribunal, finding no sufficient evidence for contributory negligence by the deceased and affirming the deceased's monthly income as Rs. 62,725/- based on the pay slip. The Court recalculated the compensation, allowing the appeals and modifying the award to Rs. 1,20,84,925/-.

petitioner_key_arguments: High Court wrongly assessed contributory negligence of the deceased to the extent of 25%.
High Court wrongly assessed the monthly income of the deceased at Rs.50,000/- instead of Rs.62,725/- (as per Tribunal) or Rs.70,000/- (as claimed).
respondent_key_arguments: There was no negligence on the part of the driver of the bus.
Notional income should have been considered instead of the actual income.
The deceased was not a permanent employee.
The interest @ 9% awarded by the Tribunal was excessive.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments that there was no contributory negligence on the part of the deceased and that the deceased's monthly income should be assessed at Rs.62,725/- (as per the Tribunal's finding) prevailed.

outcome.relief_granted: The Civil Appeals are allowed. The impugned Award dated 12th December, 2017, as modified by the High Court vide the impugned order dated 1st October, 2020, stands modified. The total compensation payable is recalculated to Rs.1,20,84,925/-. Interest is to be paid as awarded by the Tribunal.

precedents_cited: Jiju Kuruvila v. Kun- jujamma Mohan1
Kumari Kiran v. Sajjan Singh and Ors. 2
Sunita v. Rajasthan SRTC3
Rajwati alias Rajjo & Ors. v. United India Insurance Company Ltd. & Ors. 4
National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Pranay Sethi

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The court held that in the absence of direct or corroborative evidence, contributory negligence cannot be assumed. It also affirmed that in motor accident claim cases, the standard of proof is preponderance of probability, not beyond reasonable doubt, and the Tribunal's assessment of income based on evidence (pay slip) should be upheld over the High Court's lower assessment.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court reiterated that under the Motor Vehicle Act, 1988, strict rules of evidence used in criminal trials do not apply, and the standard of proof is based on the preponderance of probability. It also emphasized the beneficial nature of the Motor Vehicles Act for awarding just and fair compensation.

special_directions.special_directions: Interest is to be paid as awarded by the Tribunal.
special_directions.interim_orders: Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (@ SLP (CRL.) No.6185 OF 2023)

case_details.subject_matter: The case involves an appeal against the High Court's dismissal of a criminal revision application, which sought to quash a Trial Court order rejecting a discharge application in a case for offences under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002. Key issues include the retrospective application of PMLA and the continuing nature of money laundering offences.

judgements.case_summary:
The appellant, Pradeep Nirankarnath Sharma, challenged a High Court order that upheld the Trial Court's rejection of his discharge application in a case under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA). The appellant argued that the alleged predicate offences occurred before PMLA came into force or before they were scheduled offences, making the application of PMLA retrospective and impermissible. He also contended that the allegations did not constitute a continuing offence and that the amount involved did not meet the statutory threshold for PMLA proceedings at the relevant time.

The respondent, Directorate of Enforcement, countered that money laundering is a continuing offence, and the appellant's actions continued well after PMLA's enactment. They asserted that the predicate offences were scheduled under PMLA at the relevant time, and the total proceeds of crime significantly exceeded the monetary threshold. The respondent emphasized that at the charge framing stage, only a prima facie case is required.

The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, holding that the offence of money laundering is a continuing offence, and the appellant's involvement in financial transactions linked to proceeds of crime extended beyond the initial point of commission. The Court found that the material on record indicated prima facie involvement and that the amount involved far exceeded the statutory threshold. It concluded that the appellant failed to establish any legally sustainable ground for interference at a pre-trial stage, emphasizing the need for a thorough trial in economic offences of such magnitude.

petitioner_key_arguments: The alleged predicate offences occurred before PMLA came into force or before they were scheduled offences, making PMLA's application retrospective and impermissible.
The judgment in Vijay Madanlal Chaudhary and others v. Union of India and others does not fully settle the issue of retrospectivity, and a larger bench is currently deliberating on it.
There was no direct evidence linking the appellant to the generation, possession, concealment, or transfer of proceeds of crime.
The prosecution failed to establish a prima facie case, as allegations were based purely on assumptions and conjectures.
The alleged acts do not constitute continuing offences.
The amount involved does not meet the statutory threshold (Rs. 30 lakhs) for initiating PMLA proceedings as it stood prior to amendment.
respondent_key_arguments: The offence of money laundering is a continuing offence, as held by this Court.
At the stage of framing charges, the court only needs to determine if there is sufficient material to raise a 'grave suspicion' of the commission of an offence.
The predicate offences were scheduled under PMLA at the relevant time (e.g., Section 7 of PC Act and Section 467 of IPC were Part B scheduled offences since 2005).
The total value of the alleged offence exceeded Rs. 30 lakhs, satisfying the monetary threshold.
The appellant continued to enjoy and utilize proceeds of crime well after PMLA came into force, and sanction orders for land allotments were passed after PMLA's enactment.
The total proceeds of crime laundered (Rs. 1.32 crores) significantly exceed the threshold.
The reverse burden of proof under Section 24 of PMLA places the onus on the appellant to prove that attached properties are not proceeds of crime.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the respondent's arguments that money laundering is a continuing offence, that the predicate offences were scheduled under PMLA at the relevant time, and that the proceeds of crime exceeded the statutory threshold, thus justifying the continuation of proceedings and dismissal of the appeal.

precedents_cited: Vijay Madanlal Chaudhary and others v. Union of India and others
ED v. M/s Obulapuram Mining Company Pvt. Ltd. (Criminal Appeal No. 1269/2017)

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The court held that the offence of money laundering is a continuing offence, extending as long as the proceeds of crime are concealed, used, or projected as untainted property. It affirmed that the PMLA applies even if the scheduled offence occurred before its enactment, provided the dealing with proceeds of crime continued thereafter. The court also ruled that the determination of the amount involved in money laundering should consider the totality of financial transactions, not isolated instances, and found that the proceeds of crime in this case significantly exceeded the statutory threshold.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed that economic offences require a strict approach and thorough trial to unearth the complete chain of events and ensure accountability, preventing perpetrators from exploiting procedural loopholes. It highlighted that money laundering disrupts the financial system, causes loss to the public exchequer, and erodes public trust.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.........2025 (Arising out of SLP(Crl.) No.3154 of 2024)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns an appeal against a High Court order dismissing a plea for a preliminary inquiry before registering FIRs against a retired IAS officer for alleged corruption and abuse of official position.

judgements.case_summary: The appellant, a retired Indian Administrative Service (IAS) officer, challenged a High Court order that dismissed his plea for a preliminary inquiry before registering further First Information Reports (FIRs) against him. He faced multiple FIRs related to alleged irregularities in land allotment orders passed during his tenure as the Collector of Kachchh District between 2003 and 2006, primarily for abuse of official position, corrupt practices, and financial irregularities. The appellant contended that successive FIRs without a preliminary inquiry violated his fundamental rights under Articles 14, 20, 21, 22, and 226 of the Constitution of India, and were lodged with an ulterior motive. He relied on the judgment in *Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.* to argue for the necessity of a preliminary inquiry. The State of Gujarat opposed the petition, arguing that under Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, FIR registration is mandatory for cognizable offenses, and the exceptions for preliminary inquiry in *Lalita Kumari* did not apply to clear allegations of corruption. The High Court dismissed the plea, holding that a preliminary inquiry is only warranted when a cognizable offense is not disclosed. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, reiterating that FIR registration is mandatory for cognizable offenses and that allegations of abuse of official position and corruption fall squarely within this category, requiring no preliminary inquiry. The Court dismissed the appeal, stating that granting a blanket direction for preliminary inquiry would amount to judicial overreach, but clarified that the appellant could still pursue other legal remedies.

petitioner_key_arguments: Multiple FIRs registered without preliminary inquiry violate Fundamental Rights (Articles 14, 20, 21, 22, 226) and constitute harassment.
Successive FIRs were lodged with an ulterior motive to harass him and prevent him from effectively defending himself.
A preliminary inquiry is mandatory in cases involving allegations of abuse of official position, as per the judgment in Lalita Kumari (supra).
The State's conduct in registering successive FIRs, despite the appellant's superannuation, reflects an ulterior motive rather than a bona fide attempt to investigate.
respondent_key_arguments: The relief sought by the appellant is legally untenable; FIR registration is mandatory under Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, for cognizable offenses.
The exceptions for preliminary inquiry laid down in Lalita Kumari (supra) do not apply to cases with clear allegations of cognizable offenses like corruption and abuse of official position.
Granting a blanket protection against investigation or a mandatory preliminary inquiry would be impermissible and amount to judicial legislation.
There is no statutory provision requiring the accused to be given an opportunity to explain their position before FIR registration.
Adequate legal safeguards, such as the right to seek anticipatory bail and the right to challenge malicious prosecution, are already available to the appellant.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The respondent's arguments that FIR registration is mandatory for cognizable offenses, and that preliminary inquiry is not required when clear allegations of corruption and abuse of official position exist, prevailed.

outcome.relief_granted: null

precedents_cited: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh & Ors., (2014) 2 SCC 1
constitutional_provisions: Article 14 of the Constitution of India
Article 20 of the Constitution of India
Article 21 of the Constitution of India
Article 22 of the Constitution of India
Article 226 of the Constitution of India

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The registration of an FIR is mandatory under Section 154 CrPC if the information discloses the commission of a cognizable offence. A preliminary inquiry is only warranted when the information does not prima facie disclose a cognizable offence. Allegations of abuse of official position and corrupt practices are cognizable offences, and thus do not require a preliminary inquiry before FIR registration.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The appellant's contention that successive FIRs have been registered against him with an ulterior motive is a matter that can be examined during the course of investigation and trial. The appellant has adequate remedies under the law, including the right to seek quashing of frivolous FIRs under Section 482 CrPC, the right to apply for bail, and the right to challenge any illegal actions of the investigating authorities before the appropriate forum.

special_directions.special_directions: The order shall not preclude the appellant from availing any other remedies available to him under the law in respect of the pending FIRs or future proceedings.

case_identification.case_number: SLP (CRL.) NO.354 OF 2019, SLP (CRL.) NO.2812 OF 2019

case_details.subject_matter: The case involves two appeals concerning an FIR against the appellant for alleged misuse of official position in a land allotment case, challenging the dismissal of an FIR quashing petition and the denial of anticipatory bail.

judgements.case_summary:
The appellant, Pradip N. Sharma, an IAS officer, faced an FIR (I-C.R. No. 33 of 2011) registered in 2011 for offences under Sections 409, 219, and 114 of the Indian Penal Code. The FIR alleged misuse of his official position as District Collector, Rajkot, by setting aside an order and restoring government land to allottees who were not cultivating it and were residing abroad, with malicious intent. Two appeals were filed before the Supreme Court: one against the Gujarat High Court's dismissal of his petition to quash the FIR (R/Criminal Misc. Application No. 7960 of 2011), and another against the High Court's rejection of his anticipatory bail application (R/Criminal Misc. Application No. 2367 of 2019).

The appellant argued that his actions were within his quasi-judicial functions, the FIR was motivated, and no criminal misconduct occurred. He also contended that custodial interrogation was unnecessary as evidence was documentary. The State of Gujarat argued that serious allegations of misuse of power, condoning a seven-year delay in appeal, and passing orders favoring ineligible allottees warranted investigation and custodial interrogation.

The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal seeking to quash the FIR, agreeing with the High Court that prima facie cognizable offences were disclosed, requiring a full investigation. However, the Court allowed the appeal for anticipatory bail, reasoning that the allegations primarily involved documentary evidence, custodial interrogation was not essential if the appellant cooperated, and there was no evidence of tampering. The appellant was directed to cooperate with the investigation and could be released on a personal bond of Rs. 1,00,000, with the Investigating Agency retaining the option to seek custodial interrogation if deemed necessary.

petitioner_key_arguments: The alleged acts of omission or commission were done in discharge of his duties in the quasi-judicial proceedings and did not amount to criminal misconduct or breach of trust.
The FIR was lodged by the In short, “CrPC” Mamlatdar, acting on behalf of the State, without proper examination of the factual matrix.
The FIR No. 33/2011, registered under Sections 114, 219, and 409 of the IPC, is frivolous and motivated, having been lodged after an unexplained delay of four years.
The appellant was neither entrusted with the property in question nor had dominion over it, and his decision was in accordance with the powers vested in him under the law.
Passing an erroneous order, if at all, does not constitute a criminal offense.
No offence under Section 409 IPC is made out, as the appellant merely adjudicated an appeal in his official capacity.
The allegations under Section 219 IPC were also unfounded, as the appellant had exercised his judicial discretion in accordance with the principles of natural justice.
The appellant had an unblemished record of over 30 years in the civil services.
The prosecution's case is primarily based on documentary evidence, and given his past cooperation with the investigating agency, custodial interrogation is unnecessary.
respondent_key_arguments: The appellant, who was the District Collector, Rajkot at the relevant time, had, knowing fully well that the said allottees were staying abroad and not cultivating the land as per the order of allotment, and therefore were not eligible to get back the land, set aside the order passed by the Deputy Collector, with a view to unduly favour them and that too without verifying the genuineness of the power of attorney holder.

The appellant acting against the interest of the Government and with a view to unduly favour the allottees, had passed the order with malicious intention, and thereby had committed the offences under Sections 409, 219 and 114 of the IPC.

Serious allegations had been made against the appellant regarding his misuse of powers under the Bombay Land Revenue Code, 1879 by condoning a seven-year delay in filing an appeal and passing orders in favor of certain allottees, despite the land having been taken over by the government.
The appellant had already been transferred from Rajkot to Bhavnagar at the time he issued the impugned order, which the High Court found questionable.
The allottees in question were not cultivating the land and were residing abroad, casting doubt on the legitimacy of the transactions.
The appellant faced similar allegations in another case involving the allotment of government land, reinforcing the perception of misconduct.
The appellant misappropriated government land in favor of private individuals, thereby committing criminal breach of trust under Section 405 of the IPC.
Two of the allottees were deceased, and their power of attorney holder had filed false verifications on their behalf, which the appellant ignored while passing the order.
The appellant failed to remand the matter back for fresh adjudication and instead directly issued directions for handing over possession, thereby exceeding his jurisdiction.
Custodial interrogation was necessary given the nature of allegations and the appellant's involvement in multiple similar cases.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that anticipatory bail could be granted as the case primarily involved documentary evidence and custodial interrogation was not essential if cooperation was assured. However, it rejected the petitioner's arguments for quashing the FIR, agreeing with the respondent that prima facie cognizable offences were disclosed, warranting a full investigation.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal against the dismissal of the FIR quashing petition was dismissed. The appeal against the denial of anticipatory bail was allowed, granting anticipatory bail to the appellant subject to conditions.

precedents_cited: R/Criminal Misc. Application No. 7960 of 2011
R/Criminal Misc. Application No. 2367 of 2019
Special Civil Application No. 14966/2012

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The court held that quashing an FIR is only permissible in exceptional cases where no cognizable offense is disclosed, and in this case, prima facie allegations warranted investigation. For anticipatory bail, the court reasoned that where allegations are based on documentary evidence and custodial interrogation is not strictly necessary for investigation, and the accused is willing to cooperate, anticipatory bail can be granted to ensure participation without pre-trial detention.

special_directions.special_directions: The appellant upon arrest may be released upon furnishing a personal bond of Rs.1,00,000/- (Rupees One Lakh only) to the satisfaction of the Investigating Officer in the present case, subject to following two conditions: i. Firstly, the appellant will extend all cooperation during the investigation; and ii. Secondly, if the Investigating Agency requires custodial investigation, it may apply to the concerned Magistrate for appropriate orders, and the said application will be considered/decided on its own merits without being influenced by any of the observations made by us.
special_directions.interim_orders: The High Court had initially granted a stay on the investigation against the appellant within 20 days of the FIR being registered.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (Arising out of SLP(C)No.3066 OF 2024)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns a motor accident claim where the claimant-appellant, in a comatose state with 100% disability, sought enhanced compensation, challenging the lower courts' assessment of disability and inadequate awards for attendant charges and pain and suffering.

judgements.case_summary: The claimant-appellant, Prakash Chand Sharma, suffered severe injuries in a motor accident on March 23, 2014, leaving him in a comatose state with 100% permanent physical impairment. The Motor Accident Claims Tribunal initially awarded Rs. 16,29,465/-, assessing the disability at 50%. The High Court, while entertaining an appeal, modified the award to Rs. 19,39,418/-, still maintaining the 50% disability assessment but adding future prospects. Aggrieved by this, the claimant-appellant appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that the duly constituted Medical Board had assessed 100% disability, which was ignored by the lower courts, and that the compensation for attendant charges was insufficient. The respondent-Insurance Company contended that there was no evidence to substantiate 100% disability and no proof of hiring a medical attendant. The Supreme Court found force in the appellant's submissions, holding that the Medical Board's opinion of 100% disability, being an expert opinion, should have been accepted, especially given the claimant's comatose state. The Court also found the awards for attendant charges and pain and suffering to be insufficient. Consequently, the Supreme Court enhanced the total compensation to Rs. 48,69,180/- (rounded to Rs. 48,70,000/-) with 7% interest from the date of the claim petition.

petitioner_key_arguments: The opinion of the Medical Board computing 100% disability was ignored by the Tribunal and High Court.
The Tribunal substituted its own view on disability instead of accepting expert medical opinion.
The compensation granted towards attendant charges was insufficient (claimed Rs. 6,000/- per month).
respondent_key_arguments: No evidence was led to substantiate the position that the claimant-appellant suffers from 100% disability.
The opinion of the Medical Board stands disbelieved.
No evidence was led to show that a medical attendant had been hired and a salary of Rs.6,000/- per month is paid.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the Medical Board's assessment of 100% disability should be upheld as an expert opinion, and that the compensation for attendant charges and pain and suffering was inadequate, leading to an enhancement of the total award.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal is allowed, and the total compensation payable to the claimant-appellant is enhanced to Rs. 48,70,000/- with an interest @ 7% per annum due from the date of the claim petition.

precedents_cited: Union of India v. Talwinder Singh (2012) 5 SCC 480
Raj Kumar v. Ajay Kumar (2011) 1 SCC 343
Thresiamma Sebastian v. Dr. Renu Swami Das & Ors. 2024 SCC OnLine Ker 4660
Kajal
Jagdish Chand (2020) 4 SCC 413
Abhimanyu Pratap Singh v. Namita Sekhon (2022) 8 SCC 489
K.S Murlidhar v. R. Subbulakshmi 2024 SCC OnLine SC 3385

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The court held that the opinion of a duly constituted Medical Board regarding 100% permanent disability should be accepted as expert opinion, especially when the claimant is in a comatose state and the Tribunal did not opt for re-assessment. Compensation for attendant charges and pain and suffering must be adequately provided, considering the claimant's complete dependency and severe condition.

special_directions.special_directions: The Insurance Company shall deposit the enhanced amount alongwith the interest @7% from the date of filing the claim petition till the date of payment with the Tribunal within two months from today.
special_directions.interim_orders: Pending applications, if any, shall stand closed.

case_identification.case_number: CONTEMPT PETITION (C) NO. 735 OF 2019 IN CIVIL APPEAL NO. 2703 OF 2017

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns a contempt petition alleging non-compliance with a previous Supreme Court order regarding salary and pension claims for a college employee, specifically addressing pending arrears from the period before the bifurcation of the State of Bihar and Jharkhand.

judgements.case_summary: The Supreme Court addressed a contempt petition filed by Prashant Bandyopadhyay and Hiralal Ram, alleging non-compliance with a previous order dated 31.08.2017 in Civil Appeal No. 2703 of 2017. The petition for Hiralal Ram (Petitioner No. 2) was dismissed as no prior order in his favor by the J. Sinha Commission could be found. For Prashant Bandyopadhyay (Petitioner No. 1), a Routine Clerk, his claim for salary was allowed by the J. Sinha Commission and confirmed by the Supreme Court, subject to a declaration of continuous service. He had received arrears from the date of Jharkhand's creation (15.11.2000) until his superannuation (31.08.2016), but arrears from his absorption (22.10.1986) to the state bifurcation (15.11.2000) remained pending. The State of Jharkhand argued that attendance records had discrepancies, making verification difficult, and thus no deliberate non-compliance occurred. The Court noted that the State of Bihar was not a party, preventing adjudication of pre-bifurcation claims. Recognizing the complexity and the need for factual inquiry, the Court disposed of the contempt petition with directions for the Registrar/Vice Chancellor of the University to adjudicate Petitioner No. 1's claims for salary and pension, including a discrete enquiry and a reasoned order within three months. The Court also clarified that the period of service for pension should be counted notionally from the date of absorption, uninfluenced by previous orders concerning payment for periods not worked.

petitioner_key_arguments: Alleged non-compliance with the Supreme Court's order dated 31.08.2017.
Claim for pending arrears of salary from the date of absorption (22.10.1986) till the bifurcation of the State (15.11.2000).
Claim for pension, with service counted from the date of absorption.
respondent_key_arguments: Discrepancies in attendance registers, making it difficult to verify the actual working period.
No deliberate or willful non-compliance due to verification issues.
Arrears of salary from the date of creation of the State of Jharkhand have already been released.
The State of Bihar was not joined as a contemnor, preventing adjudication of pre-bifurcation claims.
Previous orders (11.07.2019, 07.08.2019, 12.02.2021) in another case directed no further payment for periods not actually worked.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court did not fully accept either party's arguments directly to grant or deny the payment. Instead, it accepted the need for a detailed factual inquiry, aligning partially with the respondent's implicit argument that direct payment could not be ordered without verification, but also acknowledging the petitioner's right to have his claim adjudicated. The court's decision to direct the university authorities to conduct a discrete enquiry and pass a reasoned order indicates a procedural win for the petitioner, ensuring his claims are properly addressed, while also considering the complexities raised by the respondent.

outcome.relief_granted: The Registrar/Vice Chancellor of the University is directed to adjudicate the petitioner's claims for salary and pension, conduct a discrete enquiry, and pass a reasoned order within three months. The period of service for pension is to be counted notionally from the date of absorption, uninfluenced by previous orders concerning payment for periods not worked. The contempt petition for Petitioner No. 2 was dismissed.

precedents_cited: Krishna Nand Yadav & others Vs. Magadh University & others
Baidya Nath Choudhary Vs. Dr. Sree Surendra Kumar Singh
State of Bihar & others vs Bihar Rajya M.S.E.S.K.K.M & others (2005) 9 SCC 129

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The court found that the contempt petition could not directly adjudicate the complex claims of salary and pension, especially for periods involving a different state (Bihar) not party to the current proceedings, and where factual verification (attendance) was disputed. Instead, it directed the appropriate administrative authorities (Registrar/Vice Chancellor) to conduct a detailed inquiry and pass a reasoned order, ensuring due process. The court also clarified that previous orders regarding non-payment for periods not worked should not influence the notional counting of service for pension.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed that previous orders in "Baidya Nath Choudhary (supra)" related to absorbed employees receiving salaries for periods in which they had not actually worked, and had directed no further payment even of pension in such cases. This observation was made while clarifying that the notional counting of service for pension in the present case should be uninfluenced by those specific orders.

special_directions.special_directions:
1. Petitioner No. 1 shall submit his claim along with relevant documents setting up his actual working in college in terms of the orders of absorption claiming salary, and also for pension from the date of absorption upto February 28, 2025 before the Registrar/Vice Chancellor of the University.
2. On receiving the claim of salary, a discrete enquiry be held affording due opportunity to the employee, college concerned and the representative of the State if required, and a reasoned order be passed regarding payment of salary and arrears, if any, within a period of three months thereafter.
3. The claim regarding pension of petitioner No. 1 which has been withheld be decided counting the period of service, w.e.f. date of absorption notionally uninfluenced by the orders dated 11.07.2019, 07.08.2019 and 12.02.2021 passed in Contempt Petition (C) No. 1188 of 2018 in Baidya Nath Choudhary (supra).
4. After adjudicating the issue of pension and arrears the same be paid adjusting the amount already paid as expeditiously as possible not later than two months from the date of such order.
5. Upon adjudication, if it is found that any excess amount has been paid either in the head of salary or pension, it be quantified and the university/college/state as the case may be, shall be at liberty to take recourse to recover the same following the procedure as prescribed.
6. If the employees have submitted the joint claim of arrears of salary and pension, in that event the issue of arrears of salary be governed by direction No. (ii) and pension be governed by direction (iii).
7. In case the parties feel dissatisfied by the orders of the Registrar/Vice Chancellor of the University, they shall be at liberty to take recourse as permissible before the High Court.

case_identification.case_number: CONTEMPT PETITION (C) NOS. 103-104 OF 2019 IN CIVIL APPEAL NOS. 2788-2789 OF 2017

case_details.subject_matter: Contempt petitions alleging non-compliance with a previous Supreme Court order regarding the absorption, salary, and family pension of a deceased employee.

judgements.case_summary: The petitioner filed contempt petitions alleging non-compliance with a Supreme Court order dated 31.08.2017 concerning the absorption of her deceased husband, Ayodhya Prasad, as a Lab In-charge. The deceased's absorption was initially approved by a One Man Commission and upheld by the Supreme Court, subject to declarations of continuous service. While the B.R. Ambedkar University initially absorbed him from 13.05.2016, it later corrected the date to 12.02.1990, with the period until his death (09.02.2012) to be counted notionally for retiral benefits. A subsequent attempt by the University to change the absorption date to the date of death was rejected by the State Government. The Court rejected the argument for absorption from the date the college became constituent and affirmed that the deceased should be treated as absorbed from 12.02.1990, entitling the petitioner to salary, family pension, and retiral benefits. However, acknowledging the need for a fact-finding inquiry into actual working and payment of arrears, the Court directed the Registrar/Vice Chancellor of the University to adjudicate these issues. The petitioner is to submit her claim, and the R/VC must conduct a discrete inquiry, provide an opportunity, and pass a reasoned order on salary and arrears within three months. The family pension claim is to be decided based on notional service from the absorption date, uninfluenced by prior orders regarding payments for non-worked periods. Any excess payments found can be recovered, and dissatisfied parties may approach the High Court. The contempt petitions were disposed of with these directions.

petitioner_key_arguments: Aggrieved by alleged non-compliance of the order dated 31.08.2017.
Claimed entitlement to salary, family pension, and retiral benefits based on absorption from 12.02.1990, with service counted notionally.
Implicitly argued against the University's attempts to change the absorption date to the date of death.
respondent_key_arguments: The University initially absorbed the employee from 13.05.2016, then corrected it to 12.02.1990, counting the period notionally for benefits.
The University later attempted to change the absorption date to 09.02.2012 (date of death), which was not accepted by the State Government.
The State's counter affidavit and previous orders in other contempt petitions raised issues regarding actual working and payment for periods not worked.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court largely accepted the petitioner's claim that the deceased employee should be treated as absorbed from 12.02.1990, entitling her to salary, family pension, and retiral benefits. However, the actual payment of salary and arrears was made subject to a fact-finding inquiry by the University authorities to verify continuous working.

outcome.relief_granted: The Court directed the petitioner to submit her claim for salary and family pension to the Registrar/Vice Chancellor of the University. The Registrar/Vice Chancellor is mandated to conduct a discrete inquiry, provide due opportunity, and pass a reasoned order regarding salary and arrears within three months. The claim for family pension is to be decided counting notional service from the date of absorption (12.02.1990), uninfluenced by prior orders. Any excess amount paid can be recovered. Parties dissatisfied with the R/VC's order may approach the High Court.

precedents_cited: Krishna Nand Yadav & others Vs. Magadh University & others (Civil Appeal No. 2703 of 2017)
Baidya Nath Choudhary Vs. Dr. Sree Surendra Kumar Singh (Contempt Petition (C) No. 1188 of 2018)
State of Bihar & others vs Bihar Rajya M.S.E.S.K.K.M & others (2005) 9 SCC 129

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that the deceased employee's absorption date of 12.02.1990, as previously established and corrected, must be maintained, and his service notionally counted from that date for retiral benefits. However, the actual payment of salary and arrears requires a fact-finding inquiry by the University authorities to verify continuous working, while family pension claims should be decided uninfluenced by prior orders concerning non-worked periods.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that it was not inclined to conduct a fact-finding inquiry into the actual working of the deceased employee within the contempt petitions, instead directing the University authorities to undertake this task. It also clarified that previous orders regarding the stoppage of family pension were due to employees receiving salaries for periods they had not actually worked.

special_directions.special_directions: The petitioner shall submit her claim along with relevant documents to the Registrar/Vice Chancellor of the University for salary and family pension up to February 28, 2025. The Registrar/Vice Chancellor shall hold a discrete inquiry, afford due opportunity to all parties, and pass a reasoned order regarding payment of salary and arrears within three months. The claim for family pension shall be decided counting the period of service notionally from the date of absorption, uninfluenced by prior orders dated 11.07.2019, 07.08.2019, and 12.02.2021. After adjudication, family pension and arrears shall be paid expeditiously, not later than two months. If any excess amount is found to have been paid, the university/college/state is at liberty to recover it. If a joint claim for arrears of salary and family pension is submitted, it will be governed by directions (ii) and (iii). Parties dissatisfied with the Registrar/Vice Chancellor's orders may take recourse before the High Court.
special_directions.interim_orders: Pending interlocutory application(s), if any, stands disposed of.

case_identification.petitioner_name: PRINCIPAL COMMISSIONER OF INCOME TAX-4 & ANR.
case_identification.case_number: SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION NO. 63 OF 2025 (Arising out of Diary No. 39934 of 2024)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns whether the reduction of share capital and proportionate reduction in shareholding, leading to a claim of capital loss by the assessee, constitutes a "transfer" under Section 2(47) of the Income Tax Act, 1961.

judgements.case_summary: This Special Leave Petition was filed by the Revenue challenging a High Court judgment that affirmed an ITAT decision. The central legal question was whether the reduction in share capital of a company, leading to a proportionate reduction in the assessee's shareholding and a claim of long-term capital loss, qualifies as a "transfer" under Section 2(47) of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The assessee, M/s. Jupiter Capital Pvt. Ltd., had invested in Asianet News Network Pvt. Ltd. (ANNPL). Due to ANNPL's financial losses, its share capital was reduced, consequently reducing the assessee's shares from 15,33,40,900 to 9,988, for which the assessee received Rs. 3,17,83,474/-. The Revenue contended that no "transfer" occurred as the proportionate shareholding and face value remained unchanged, and there was no extinguishment of rights. However, the ITAT, High Court, and the Supreme Court, relying on precedents such as Kartikeya V. Sarabhai and Anarkali Sarabhai v. CIT, held that the reduction in share capital and the consequent extinguishment of rights in the original shares amounted to a "transfer" under the inclusive definition of Section 2(47). The Court emphasized that relinquishment or extinguishment of rights, even without a traditional sale, falls within the ambit of "transfer". Consequently, the assessee's claim for capital loss was allowed, and the Revenue's petition was dismissed.

petitioner_key_arguments: Reduction in shares did not result in a "transfer" of a capital asset as envisaged in Section 2(47) of the Income Tax Act, 1961.
There was no extinguishment of rights because the proportionate shareholding percentage remained the same.
The face value of shares remained the same.
respondent_key_arguments: The reduction in share capital and the consequent reduction in the number of shares held by the assessee constituted an extinguishment of rights.
This extinguishment of rights falls within the inclusive definition of "transfer" under Section 2(47) of the Income Tax Act, 1961.
The decision in Kartikeya V. Sarabhai is squarely applicable, allowing the claim for capital loss.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the respondent's arguments, holding that the reduction in share capital and the extinguishment of rights in the original shares constituted a "transfer" under Section 2(47) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, thereby allowing the assessee's claim for capital loss.

outcome.relief_granted: The assessee's claim for capital loss on account of reduction in share capital is allowed.

precedents_cited: Kartikeya V. Sarabhai v. Commissioner of Income Tax (1997) 7 SCC 524
Kartikeya V. Sarabhai v. The Commissioner of Income Tax : 1998 2 ITR 163 SC
Anarkali Sarabhai v. CIT [(1982) 138 ITR 437 (Guj)]
Anarkali Sarabhai v. CIT [(1997) 3 SCC 238 : (1997) 224 ITR 422]
Commissioner of Income Tax v. Vania Silk Mills (P.) Ltd. (1977) 107 ITR 300 (Guj)
Sath Gwaldas Mathuradas Mohata Trust v. CIT [(1987) 165 ITR 620 (Bom)]
Commissioner of Income-Tax v. Jaykrishna Harivallabhdas (1998) 231 ITR 108

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The reduction in share capital of a company, which leads to a proportionate reduction in the number of shares held by an assessee and an extinguishment of rights in those shares, constitutes a "transfer" under the inclusive definition of Section 2(47) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, thereby allowing the assessee to claim capital loss. This is because "extinguishment of any rights therein" is a mode of transfer, irrespective of whether the face value or proportionate shareholding remains constant.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that the expression "extinguishment of any right therein" is of wide import, covering any transaction resulting in the destruction, annihilation, extinction, termination, cessation, or cancellation of rights in a capital asset. It also noted that reduction of share capital or redemption of shares involves the company purchasing its own shares, which falls within the meaning of transfer.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NOS. 2027-2028 OF 2012, CIVIL APPEAL NO.4556 OF 2012, CIVIL APPEAL NOS.2033-2034 OF 2012, CIVIL APPEAL NOS.2031-2032 OF 2012, CIVIL APPEAL NOS.2035-2036 OF 2012

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the entitlement of appellant-companies to a 25% rebate on electricity tariff, challenging demand notices for recovery of previously granted rebates based on various government notifications.

judgements.case_summary: This judgment addresses a batch of civil appeals challenging a High Court order that denied a 25% rebate on electricity tariffs to several appellant-companies. The core issue revolved around whether these companies were covered by a 1991 notification granting the rebate, which was later rescinded in 1995 and subsequently amended in 1996. The appellant-companies argued that their rights to the rebate crystallized upon application for power while the 1991 notification was in force, and that the rescission should not have retrospective effect. They also invoked promissory estoppel, citing investments made based on the promise of incentives. The respondents contended that the 1991 notification was rescinded before most appellants received power supply, and that subsequent amending notifications were declared void ab initio. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision, emphasizing that the 1991 notification had a limited life until 31.03.1995, and most appellants received power connection after this date. The Court also applied the principle of res judicata, noting that previous decisions, particularly in GR Ispat (supra), had settled similar issues and were binding. The argument of promissory estoppel was rejected, as public interest (financial crunch of the State) was deemed to override individual claims. Consequently, the Court dismissed all civil appeals, affirming that the appellant-companies were not entitled to the rebate.

petitioner_key_arguments: The appellant-companies are covered by the notification dated 30.09.1991 and not by the notification dated 01.08.1996.

Rights of the appellant-companies crystallized upon making the application for power while the notification dated 30.09.1991 was in force, entitling them to rebate irrespective of actual power supply date.
New industries were attracted to the region relying on the promise of the State of Goa to grant rebate, and without this lure, they would not have set up industries (promissory estoppel).
A notification cannot be rescinded with retrospective effect, and the decision in GR Ispat Ltd. (supra) supports their claim for rebate.
The impugned demand notices are illegal, arbitrary, and ultra vires the provisions of the 2002 Act.
Discovery of new material (a letter from the Electricity Department) warrants a review of the judgment.
respondent_key_arguments: The notification dated 30.09.1991 was rescinded with effect from 01.04.1995, making it inapplicable to appellants who received power supply thereafter.
The previous order in Manohar Parrikar (supra) binds the appellant-companies, holding that rebate benefits would not be available after the unexpired period of five years.
The impugned demand notices are in consonance with the 2002 Act, whose constitutionality has been upheld.
The High Court rightly concluded that the 30.09.1991 notification does not cover the appellant-companies.
The appellant-companies received benefits from the 1996 notifications, not the 1991 notification as they claim.
The policy of rebate was unviable due to financial crunch, constituting overriding public interest to withdraw the benefit.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the respondent's arguments that the 1991 notification was rescinded before most appellants received power supply, rendering it inapplicable. It also upheld the principle of res judicata, stating that previous judgments on similar issues were binding. The court further ruled that public interest, specifically the State's financial crunch, justified the withdrawal of the rebate, overriding claims of promissory estoppel.

outcome.relief_granted: No relief granted to the appellants; all civil appeals were dismissed. Civil appeal no.4556/2012 was dismissed as not pressed.

acts_cited: Goa (Prohibition of Further Payments and Recovery of Rebate Benefits) Act, 2002
Goa (Prohibition of Further Payments and Recovery of Rebate Benefits) Act, 2002, Section 3
Code of Civil Procedure, Order XLVII Rule 1
Code of Civil Procedure, Order XLVII Rule 7
precedents_cited: GR Ispat Ltd. v. Chief Electrical Engineer, 1999
Manohar Parrikar v. State of Goa
MRF Limited v. Manohar Parrikar & Ors.
Goa Glass Fibre Limited v. State of Goa & Anr.
Pawan Alloys & Casting (P) Ltd. v. UP SEB
Inderchand Jain v. Motilal
Satyadhyan Ghosal v. Deorajin Debi [1960] 3 SCR 590
Hope Plantations Ltd. v. Taluk Land Board (1999) 5 SCC 590
T.P. Moideen Koya v. State of Kerala
constitutional_provisions: Article 166(3) of the Constitution
Article 226 of the Constitution

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that the 1991 rebate notification was rescinded effective 01.04.1995, and appellants who received power supply after this date were not entitled to its benefits. The principle of res judicata applied, as similar issues had been conclusively decided in prior litigation binding on the parties. Furthermore, the State's financial crunch constituted overriding public interest, justifying the withdrawal of the rebate and negating claims of promissory estoppel.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court noted its surprise that the rescinded 1991 notification was amended twice, but refrained from further comment as the position was clarified in GR Ispat (supra). It also observed that no appeal lies against an order rejecting a review petition.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 3160 OF 2023

case_details.subject_matter: This appeal concerns a consumer dispute regarding the redevelopment of a building, the allotment of alternative flats, and the subsequent issue of the limitation period for filing a complaint before the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC).

judgements.case_summary: The case involves a dispute between tenants (appellants) and a partnership firm (respondents) concerning the redevelopment of "Madhav Baug" building in Mumbai. The respondents agreed to demolish the old building and construct a new one, allotting a new flat to the appellants. Due to construction delays, an "Indemnity-cum-Undertaking" was executed in 2015 for alternative flats. The old flats were handed over in 2014, and rent for alternate accommodation was paid until January 2019. Despite ongoing negotiations and the involvement of an escrow agent, the matter remained unresolved, leading the appellants to file a complaint with the NCDRC on February 6, 2019. The NCDRC dismissed the complaint as time-barred, calculating the cause of action from July 10, 2015, and noting the two-year limitation under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986. The Supreme Court, in this appeal, found that the NCDRC erred by not considering the "continuing cause of action" due to persistent efforts, negotiations, and the escrow agent's involvement. The Court held that limitation should not defeat a substantive right and that a holistic view of the situation was necessary. Consequently, the NCDRC's order was quashed, and the complaint was restored for a decision on its merits.

petitioner_key_arguments: The cause of action was a "continuing cause of action" due to ongoing negotiations, letters exchanged, meetings held, and the involvement of an escrow agent.
Efforts to secure possession of the flats cannot be discounted in order to compute the applicable limitation.
Limitation, while important, is not meant to defeat a substantive right.
The complaint sought the security of the title for flats already received and protection against alienation, not just the initial allotment.
respondent_key_arguments: The cause of action for enforcement of the "Indemnity-cum-Undertaking" arose on 10th July 2015.
The complaint, filed on 19th February 2019, was time-barred as it exceeded the two-year limitation period prescribed by Section 24-A of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments regarding a "continuing cause of action" and that limitation should not defeat a substantive right were accepted by the Supreme Court.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned order of the NCDRC dismissing the complaint on grounds of limitation is quashed and set aside. The complaint is restored to its status and number before the NCDRC for a decision on its own merits.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The NCDRC committed an error by dismissing the complaint on limitation grounds without considering the continuous efforts and negotiations between the parties, and the involvement of an escrow agent, which constituted a "continuing cause of action." The Court held that limitation should not be applied in a manner that defeats a substantive right, especially when parties are actively pursuing the implementation of contractual terms.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The NCDRC ought to have taken a holistic view of the situation. Observations made in this judgment are only for determining the issue of limitation, and the Commission shall decide the petition on its own merit.

special_directions.special_directions: The parties are directed to appear before the NCDRC on 17th March 2025. The NCDRC is requested to decide the matter expeditiously, preferably within six months from the date of appearance.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (Arising out of SLP(Crl.) No.14900 of 2024)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns an appeal against a High Court order quashing an FIR related to abetment to suicide (Section 306 IPC) and cheating (Section 420 IPC) following the death of the appellant's husband.

judgements.case_summary:
The appellant's husband died by suicide on April 14, 2024. On May 22, 2024, the appellant found a death note written by her deceased husband, alleging he was cheated and blackmailed by partners (respondent Nos. 2 and 3) of M/s. Soundarya Constructions and that respondent No. 4 was also involved. An FIR was registered for offences under Sections 306, 420, and 506 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. Respondents 2-4 filed a petition in the High Court to quash the FIR, which was allowed. The High Court held that for Section 306, there was no proximate act of instigation, and for Section 420, the deceased should have filed the complaint during his lifetime.
The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court. The petitioner argued that the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction and erred in quashing the proceedings for both sections, especially given the investigation material. The respondents contended that the High Court's order was well-reasoned and no offense was made out. The State supported the appeal.
The Supreme Court partly allowed the appeal. It upheld the quashing of proceedings under Section 306 IPC, agreeing that the allegations were an afterthought and lacked a close proximity between the alleged instigation and the suicide. However, the Court found that the High Court acted casually in quashing the proceedings under Section 420 IPC without providing adequate reasons, despite the investigating agency collecting material. Therefore, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order regarding Section 420 IPC, directing the trial court to proceed further in accordance with law.

petitioner_key_arguments: The High Court conducted a mini-trial and exceeded its jurisdiction under Section 482 Cr.P.C.
The High Court grossly erred in quashing proceedings under Section 306 IPC without giving reasons why allegations, taken at face value, could not make out a case.
The High Court grossly erred in quashing proceedings under Section 420 IPC, as investigation seized sufficient material indicating cheating, breach of trust, and forgery.
The investigating agency found sufficient material to proceed for offenses under Sections 306 and 420 IPC.
respondent_key_arguments: The High Court, after considering the entire material, found that the allegations, taken at face value, do not constitute an offense punishable under Sections 306 and 420 IPC.
No case is made out for interference with the High Court's order.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's argument that the High Court erred in quashing the proceedings under Section 420 IPC without proper reasoning prevailed. The respondent's argument that the High Court correctly quashed the proceedings under Section 306 IPC due to lack of proximate link and the allegations being an afterthought prevailed.

outcome.relief_granted: The High Court's judgment and order dated 3rd September 2024, insofar as it quashes the proceedings under Section 420 of IPC, is quashed and set aside. The learned trial court is directed to proceed further in accordance with law regarding the case under Section 420 of IPC. The High Court's order quashing proceedings under Section 306 of IPC is upheld.

precedents_cited: Prakash and Others v. State of Maharashtra and Another
Sanju @ Sanjay Singh Sengar
2024 SCC OnLine SC 3835

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: For Section 306 IPC, the Court found no close proximity between the alleged instigation and the suicide, and the allegations made by the appellant were an afterthought, thus upholding the quashing. For Section 420 IPC, the High Court's order was set aside because it acted casually and failed to provide reasons for quashing despite the investigating agency collecting material.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court clarified that respondents 2 to 4 are at liberty to file an application for discharge before the trial court if they believe the material collected by the investigating agency is insufficient for the offense under Section 420 IPC, and this application shall be considered without being influenced by the observations of the High Court or the Supreme Court.

special_directions.special_directions: The learned trial court would proceed further in accordance with law insofar as the case under Section 420 of IPC is concerned. Respondents Nos.2 to 4 are at liberty to file an application for discharge, which shall be considered by the trial court in accordance with law without being influenced by the observations made by the learned Single Judge of the High Court and this Court.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (Arising out of SLP(C)No.19182 of 2022)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns a landlord-tenant dispute over two shop rooms, where the tenant claimed adverse possession and an oral gift, while the landlord asserted ownership as an adopted son and sought eviction for non-payment of rent.

judgements.case_summary: The present appeal arises from a landlord-tenant dispute concerning two shop rooms in Berhampur. The appellant, Rabindranath Panigrahi, claimed ownership as the adopted son of the original owner, Smt. Ashalata Devi, and sought eviction of the respondent, Surendra Sahu, for non-payment of rent since July 2001. The respondent denied the landlord-tenant relationship, asserting title through adverse possession and an oral gift from Smt. Ashalata Devi. The Trial Court and the First Appellate Court concurrently found in favor of the appellant, holding that he was the rightful owner, the oral gift was invalid, and the respondent's possession was permissive, thus not ripening into adverse possession. However, the High Court, in a Second Appeal, overturned these concurrent findings, questioning the lower courts' conclusions on the landlord-tenant relationship and the First Appellate Court's discharge of its duties. The Supreme Court examined whether the High Court was justified in overturning concurrent findings of fact in a Second Appeal. It reiterated the limited scope of Section 100 CPC, emphasizing that findings of fact should not be disturbed unless perverse, and that questions of law must be 'substantial'. The Supreme Court found that the High Court's questions were not substantial questions of law and that its interference was unwarranted. It held that the respondent failed to prove adverse possession or a valid oral gift, and the appellant's ownership was unchallenged. Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment, allowing the appeal and directing the respondent to vacate the premises and clear all arrears within three months.

petitioner_key_arguments: Plaintiff is the legally adopted son of Smt. Ashalata Devi and acquired absolute ownership of the suit premises upon her demise.
The defendant failed to establish any rightful claim over the suit premises, as an oral gift of immovable property is invalid and permissive possession cannot be construed as adverse possession.
A landlord-tenant relationship existed, and the defendant defaulted on rent, making him liable for eviction.
respondent_key_arguments: Denied the landlord-tenant relationship.
Claimed perfected title over the suit premises by way of adverse possession.
Asserted acquisition of the suit premises from Smt. Ashalata Devi by virtue of an oral gift.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments, finding that the High Court erred in overturning concurrent findings of fact. It affirmed that the petitioner had established ownership, the respondent's claim of adverse possession based on permissive possession was invalid, and an oral gift of immovable property does not confer title.

outcome.relief_granted: The respondent (tenant) is directed to hand over vacant and peaceful possession of the subject premises within a period of three months from the date of the judgment. The respondent is further directed to clear all arrears (rent, utilities, etc.) within the same timeframe.

precedents_cited: Santosh Hazari v. Purushottam Tiwari
Gurdev Kaur v. Kaki
State Bank of India v. S.N. Goyal
Suresh Lataruji Ramteke v. Sau. Sumanbai Pandurang Petkar
Jaichand v. Sahnulal
Hero Vinoth v. Seshammal
Sir Chunilal case
Nazir Mohamed v. J. Kamala
P. Kishore Kumar v. Vittal K. Patkar
Ramachandra Reddy v. Ramulu Ammal
Murthy v. C. Saradambal

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The High Court erred in overturning concurrent findings of fact by the Trial Court and First Appellate Court in a Second Appeal, as the questions framed were not 'substantial questions of law' under Section 100 CPC. Permissive possession cannot mature into adverse possession without a clear exhibition of hostile animus, and an oral gift of immovable property does not convey title.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court reiterated the well-settled principles governing the scope of Second Appeals under Section 100 CPC, emphasizing that High Courts should not disturb findings of fact unless they are perverse, and clarified what constitutes a 'substantial question of law' for the purpose of such appeals.

special_directions.special_directions: The Registry is directed to communicate a copy of this order to the Registrar General, High Court of Orissa, who shall further communicate the same to the concerned parties.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NOS. 2755-2758/2025 ARISING OUT OF SLP(C) NOS. 10926-10929 OF 2024

case_details.subject_matter: Appeals against a Madras High Court order regarding public interest litigations (PILs) concerning the conduct of Formula 4 racing in Chennai, specifically challenging directions related to financial obligations and the State's role in public-private partnerships.

judgements.case_summary:
This case involves appeals against an order of the Madras High Court that disposed of Public Interest Litigations (PILs) concerning the conduct of Formula 4 racing in Chennai. Racing Promotion Private Limited (RPPL), the appellant, had entered into a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the Sports Development Authority of Tamil Nadu (SDAT) to organize the event, with specified financial obligations for both parties (RPPL: Rs. 202 crores; SDAT: Rs. 42 crores). While the High Court permitted the race, it issued several directions, including that RPPL reimburse Rs. 42 crores to the State, deposit Rs. 15 crores for future events, and bear all future expenses, with the State merely facilitating. The High Court also suggested that the State should conduct such events itself in the future.

The Supreme Court noted that the High Court had acknowledged the event as a policy decision but erred by interfering with the specific contractual terms of the MoU. The Court emphasized that issues like mutual obligations and expenditure apportionment in a public-private partnership are beyond the scope of scrutiny in a PIL. It highlighted that SDAT, as a nodal government authority, was promoting sports and that the arrangement was not a distribution of largesse or defalcation of funds. The Court underscored the principle of public-private partnerships for good governance, considering the State's limited resources and expertise. Consequently, the Supreme Court partly allowed the appeals, setting aside the High Court's directions (iv), (v), (vi), and (vii), thereby upholding the original terms of the MoU regarding financial contributions.

petitioner_key_arguments: The High Court's directions (iv) to (vii) imposed new terms and conditions on an existing Memorandum of Understanding (MoU).
The High Court interfered with the State's policy decision regarding public-private partnerships for sports promotion.
respondent_key_arguments: Public inconvenience, lack of safety measures, noise pollution, and environmental damage caused by the racing event.
Lack of transparency in the use of public funds for the benefit of a private party.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court accepted that the High Court erred in interfering with the specific contractual terms of the MoU between the State instrumentality and a private party in a public interest litigation, especially regarding financial obligations and the nature of public-private partnerships, as such matters fall outside the scope of PIL scrutiny and judicial review of contractual terms.

outcome.relief_granted: Directions 22(iv), (v), (vi), and (vii) of the Madras High Court's order dated 19.02.2024 were set aside.

precedents_cited: Master Marine Services (P) Ltd. v. Metcalfe & Hodgkinson (P) Ltd., (2005) 6 SCC 138
Arun Kumar Agrawal v. Union of India, (2013) 7 SCC 1
Silppi Constructions Contractors v. Union of India, (2020) 16 SCC 489
Orissa State Financial Corporation v. Narsingh Ch. Nayak, (2003) 10 SCC 261
Orix Auto Finance (India) Ltd v. Jagmander Singh, (2006) 2 SCC 598
General Assurance Society Ltd v. Chandumull Jain, AIR 1966 SC 1644
Rajasthan State Industrial Development and Investment Corporation v. Diamond & Gem Development Corporation Ltd, (2013) 5 SCC 470
Shree Ambica Medical Stores v. Surat People's Coop Bank Ltd, (2020) 13 SCC 564
