case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (@Special Leave Petition (Crl.) No.7422 of 2023)

legal_representation.winning_arguments: The Court accepted the petitioner's argument that directions for a CBI investigation should not be issued in a bail application, citing precedents that such actions overstep the High Court's jurisdiction in such matters.

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the High Court's jurisdiction to issue directions for a CBI investigation in a bail application, specifically whether such directions are permissible when the bail application itself has been allowed.

judgements.case_summary: The State of Uttar Pradesh appealed against directions issued by a Single Judge of the High Court in a bail application. The High Court had directed the Director, Central Bureau of Investigation, to register a case based on a Section 161 Cr.P.C. statement and conduct an investigation. The State, represented by Shri K.M. Nataraj, argued that such directions in a bail application were improper and had been deprecated by the Supreme Court. The State also mentioned that a CBI inquiry had previously been requested by the Uttar Pradesh Government but was deemed not feasible by the Government of India. The respondent's counsel did not join issue on this point. The Supreme Court, relying on precedents, held that a High Court's jurisdiction in a bail application ends with granting or refusing bail and that issuing directions for a CBI investigation, especially without exceptional circumstances or verification of allegations, constitutes an overstepping of jurisdiction. The Court found no exceptional circumstances in this case to warrant such directions. Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside the impugned order to the extent it issued directions to the CBI, while clarifying that the bail granted was not objected to by the State.

petitioner_key_arguments: Directions for CBI investigation should not be issued in a bail application.
Such actions have been deprecated by the Supreme Court.
The High Court's jurisdiction in a bail application is limited to granting or refusing bail.
No exceptional or extraordinary circumstances were brought out to justify the CBI directions.
respondent_key_arguments: The learned Counsel appearing for the respondent who is the applicant for bail, does not join issue.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned order of the High Court, to the extent it issued directions to the CBI, is set aside.

acts_cited: Section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
Section 439 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that a High Court, while exercising jurisdiction in a bail application, is limited to granting or refusing bail and lacks the authority to issue directions for a CBI investigation, especially when no exceptional circumstances are demonstrated and allegations are unverified. Such actions constitute an overstepping of judicial limits and have been consistently deprecated by the Supreme Court.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court noted that the State did not object to the bail granted to the respondent. Therefore, the Court refrained from examining the facts leading to the investigation to avoid any interference with the ongoing investigation.

special_directions.special_directions: The impugned order is set aside to the extent the directions are issued to the C.B.I. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

case_identification.petitioner_name: State Rep. By Deputy Superintendent Of Police, Vigilance And Anti Corruption Chennai City-I Department
case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 1405/2019

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the quashing of criminal proceedings under the Prevention of Corruption Act for possessing disproportionate assets, challenging a High Court order that quashed the proceedings after discharge and revision petitions were dismissed.

judgements.case_summary: The Supreme Court heard an appeal against a High Court judgment that quashed criminal proceedings against the respondent, G. Easwaran, under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, for possessing disproportionate assets. The respondent, a government surveyor, was accused of acquiring assets worth Rs. 26,88,057/- disproportionate to his income during a check period. The Special Court had initially dismissed the respondent's discharge application, finding a prima facie case. Subsequently, the High Court also dismissed a revision petition, affirming the Special Court's findings. However, the High Court later quashed the proceedings under Section 482 Cr.P.C., citing issues with asset valuation, non-deduction of certain incomes, and the validity/delay in sanction for prosecution. The Supreme Court held that the High Court erred in re-examining facts and quashing proceedings under Section 482 Cr.P.C. when a prima facie case was established. It reiterated that the inherent powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. should be used sparingly and that the validity of sanction is a matter for trial, not for quashing at an early stage. The Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment, and restored the criminal case for expeditious trial.

petitioner_key_arguments: The High Court erred in exercising its inherent powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to quash criminal proceedings, especially after both the Special Court and the High Court itself had previously found a prima facie case and dismissed discharge and revision petitions.
The High Court conducted a 'mini-trial' by re-appreciating evidence and questioning the validity of the sanction for prosecution, which is a matter to be determined during the course of the trial.

The High Court's findings regarding the invalidity and delay in sanction were premature and potentially based on a typographical error, and mere delay in sanction is not a ground to quash a criminal case.
respondent_key_arguments: The High Court found that the prosecution had accepted explanations regarding asset valuation (e.g., house value revised from Rs.17,19,541/- to Rs.10,48,861/-) and loan for car purchase, which reduced the total disproportionate assets.

The High Court also considered the non-deduction of the wife's income from real estate, a gift to the daughter, and the son's income, which were not interfered with by the Special Court but were implicitly considered by the High Court in its quashing order.
The High Court concluded that the sanction for prosecution was invalid and belated, possibly passed without application of mind, and that the delay itself was fatal to the criminal investigation.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Supreme Court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the High Court overstepped its jurisdiction under Section 482 Cr.P.C. by quashing proceedings after a prima facie case was established and discharge/revision petitions were dismissed. The Court agreed that the validity of sanction is a matter for trial and that the High Court's premature findings on sanction were erroneous.

outcome.relief_granted: The High Court's judgment quashing criminal proceedings was set aside, and C.C. No. 30/2013 was restored to the record of the Court of the Special Judge, Prevention of Corruption Act Cases, Chennai, for the continuation of the trial.

precedents_cited: Amit Kapoor v. Ramesh Chander
Krishnan v. Krishnaveni
Renu Kumari v. Sanjay Kumar
R. P. Kapur v. State of Punjab
State by Karnataka Lokayukta, Police Station, Bengaluru v. M.R. Hiremath

State of T.N. v. N. Suresh Rajan

Parkash Singh Badal
State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal
CBI v. Pramila Virendra Kumar Agarwal
Director, Central Bureau of Investigation v. Ashok Kumar Aswal
constitutional_provisions: Articles 226/227 of the Constitution

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The High Court cannot exercise its inherent powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to quash criminal proceedings when a prima facie case has been established and discharge/revision petitions have been dismissed. The validity of sanction for prosecution is a matter to be examined during the trial, not at the stage of quashing, and mere delay in granting sanction is not a ground to quash a criminal case.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court emphasized that Section 482 Cr.P.C. powers should be exercised sparingly and not to conduct a 'mini-trial' or re-appreciate evidence to determine the likelihood of conviction at an early stage, as this would lead to needless multiplicity of procedure, unnecessary delay in trial, and protraction of proceedings.

special_directions.special_directions: The Trial Court is requested to conclude the trial as expeditiously as possible, given the matter pertains to the check period 2001-2008.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.818/2025 (@Petition for Special Leave to Appeal No.1314/2025

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns an appeal against the denial of regular bail in an economic offense involving cryptocurrency, focusing on the interpretation and application of Section 437(6) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

judgements.case_summary: The Supreme Court heard an appeal against the Chhattisgarh High Court's denial of regular bail to Subhelal @ Sushil Sahu in a cryptocurrency-related economic offense (Crime No. 460/2023, Sections 420, 201, 120-B, 34 IPC). The appellant was in custody since December 2023, and the trial, being conducted by the Chief Judicial Magistrate, involved nearly 2000 investors losing approximately Rs. 4 Crore. The prosecution intended to examine 189 witnesses, leading to a potentially prolonged trial. The Court considered Section 437(6) of the CrPC, which allows for bail if a trial is not concluded within 60 days, but noted it's not an absolute right and Magistrates have discretion to refuse for recorded reasons. The Court emphasized a liberal approach to bail under Section 437(6) to protect individual liberty, especially when the trial is delayed, balancing it with the seriousness of the crime and factors like tampering or abscondence. Ultimately, the Court allowed the appeal, granting bail to the appellant on the condition that he deposits Rs. 35,00,000/- (attributed to him in the scam) with the Trial Court within six months, failing which the bail would be automatically cancelled.

petitioner_key_arguments: Appellant is in custody since December 2023.
Trial is being conducted by the Chief Judicial Magistrate, where the maximum punishment is 7 years.
Section 437(6) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, applies as the trial is not concluded within sixty days from the first date fixed for taking evidence.
respondent_key_arguments: The offense is an economic offense.
The alleged crime is serious.
Almost 2000 investors have lost their money.
The prosecution intends to examine 189 witnesses, indicating a lengthy trial.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments regarding prolonged custody and the spirit of Section 437(6) CrPC, balanced with the seriousness of the crime, led to bail being granted with conditions.

outcome.relief_granted: Bail granted to the appellant subject to depositing an amount of Rs. 35,00,000/- with the Trial Court within a period of six months from today.

precedents_cited: Nehul Prakashbhai Shah v. State of Gujarat reported in (2012) 53 (3) GLR 2685
constitutional_provisions: Article 21 of the Constitution of India

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: Section 437(6) of CrPC is not mandatory and does not grant an absolute right to bail, but Magistrates have discretion to refuse bail for recorded reasons. However, a liberal approach should be taken, especially when trial is prolonged, to protect individual liberty, balancing it with the seriousness of the crime and factors like tampering, abscondence, and the accused's role in delay.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court explains the difference between Section 437(6) and Section 167(2) of CrPC, noting that the latter grants an absolute right to bail if charge-sheet is not filed within the stipulated time, unlike the former. It also states that a decision in principle rendered by a co-ordinate Bench of equal strength would bind another co-ordinate Bench as it lays down a principle of law.

special_directions.special_directions: The appellant is directed to deposit an amount of Rs. 35,00,000/- with the Trial Court within a period of six months from today. If the amount is not deposited within this time period, the bail shall stand automatically cancelled.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 641 OF 2024

case_details.subject_matter: The case involves a challenge to a conviction under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, seeking its conversion to Section 304 Part I or Part II of the IPC, arising from a fatal assault during a boundary dispute.

judgements.case_summary: This appeal challenges the final judgment and order of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay, which affirmed the trial court's conviction of the appellant, Sudam Prabhakar Achat, under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, for the murder of Motiram Deoram Achat. The incident occurred during a boundary dispute where the appellant and a co-accused assaulted the deceased and complainant with a stick and the blunt side of an axe, leading to the deceased's death. The petitioner argued that the conviction was unsustainable, primarily because the prosecution relied on interested witnesses (relatives of the deceased), and contended that the offense, at most, fell under Section 304 IPC. The respondent maintained that the concurrent findings of fact by both lower courts, based on the evidence, should not be interfered with. The Supreme Court, while confirming the homicidal nature of the death and the appellant's involvement, found no evidence of premeditation. It noted that the weapons used (stick and blunt side of an axe) did not indicate an intention to cause death, nor was undue advantage taken. Consequently, the Court concluded that the case fell under Exception IV of Section 300 IPC, converting the conviction from Section 302 to Section 304 Part I IPC. The appellant was sentenced to the period already undergone and ordered to be released.

petitioner_key_arguments: The prosecution relies only on eye witnesses who are relatives of the deceased, making their testimony as interested witnesses not sustainable for conviction.
The offence would not come under the ambit of Section 302 IPC and at the most, it would come under Part I or II of Section 304 of IPC.
respondent_key_arguments: Both the trial court and the High Court concurrently found the accused guilty based on the perusal of the evidence.
In view of the concurrent findings of fact, no interference is warranted in the present appeal.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that the offence should be converted from Section 302 IPC to Section 304 Part I IPC, based on the finding that there was no premeditation, the weapons used (stick and blunt side of an axe) did not suggest an intention to cause death, and no undue advantage was taken, thus falling under Exception IV of Section 300 IPC.

outcome.relief_granted: The conviction under Section 302 IPC is converted to Part I of Section 304 IPC. The appellant is sentenced to the period already undergone and directed to be released forthwith if not required in any other case.

acts_cited: Indian Penal Code, 1860, Section 304 Part I
Indian Penal Code, 1860, Section 300, Exception IV

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The court found that while the death of the deceased was homicidal and caused by the appellant, there was no premeditation. The use of a stick and the blunt side of an axe, coupled with the circumstances of a sudden fight in the heat of the moment, indicated that the intention was not to cause death, nor was any undue advantage taken. Therefore, the case falls under Exception IV of Section 300 of the IPC, warranting conversion of the conviction from Section 302 to Section 304 Part I of the IPC.

special_directions.special_directions: The appellant is directed to be released forthwith if not required in any other case.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS.536-537 OF 2025

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the High Court's revisional power to stay an order of discharge in a criminal case and the application of Section 390 CrPC, specifically addressing the legality of ex-parte stay orders and directions for surrender.

judgements.case_summary: The appellant, Sudershan Singh Wazir, was discharged by a Sessions Judge in a criminal case involving murder and other offenses, and subsequently released on a personal bond. The first respondent, NCT of Delhi, filed a revision application before the High Court challenging the discharge order and sought a stay. The High Court initially granted an ex-parte stay on 21st October 2023, which was later extended. Subsequently, on 4th November 2024, the High Court directed the appellant to surrender to judicial custody, reasoning that the stay on the discharge order restored his status as an accused. The appellant challenged these High Court orders before the Supreme Court. The petitioner argued that a stay on a discharge order is a drastic measure, effectively nullifying the discharge without merits, and that the appellant's presence was secured by bail. The respondents contended that a strong prima facie case existed, the discharge order was perverse, and the High Court had the power under Sections 397, 401, and 390 CrPC to stay the order and direct surrender. The Supreme Court held that an ex-parte stay of a discharge order is entirely illegal due to its grave consequences on liberty, noting that a discharged accused is on a higher pedestal than an acquitted person. While acknowledging the High Court's power under Section 390 CrPC in revision, it clarified that the normal rule should be to admit the accused to bail, not commit them to custody. The Court quashed both impugned High Court orders and directed the High Court to decide the revision application on merits, instructing the appellant to furnish bail before the Sessions Court until the revision's disposal.

petitioner_key_arguments: The High Court ought not to have stayed the order of discharge, as it effectively nullifies the discharge without examining its merits.
Unless the order of discharge is set aside, the trial cannot proceed.
The appellant was discharged for cogent reasons, and a stay amounts to granting final relief.
The appellant complied with bail directions under Section 437A CrPC, securing his presence.
An order of discharge places the accused on a higher pedestal than an acquitted person, making a stay a drastic measure.
Relied on the 154th Report of the Law Commission of India and the precedent of Parvinder Singh Khurana v. Directorate of Enforcement.
respondent_key_arguments: A strong prima facie case was made out to proceed on the charge sheet, and the discharge order was perverse.
The case involves a serious murder, supported by evidence like CCTV footage, CDR, and eye-witnesses.
The High Court, under Sections 397 and 401 CrPC, has the power to stay or suspend the impugned order.
Under Section 401(1) CrPC, the High Court can exercise powers of the Court of Appeal, including those under Section 390 CrPC.
Once a revision against discharge is admitted, the status of the appellant as an accused is revived, allowing for direction to custody under Section 390 CrPC.
Relied on precedents like State of Uttar Pradesh v. Poosu & Ors., Amin Khan v. State of Rajasthan & Ors., and State of Maharashtra v. Mahesh Kariman Tirki & Ors.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments regarding the drastic nature and illegality of an ex-parte stay on a discharge order, and the preference for bail over custody under Section 390 CrPC in such revisional proceedings, were accepted by the Supreme Court.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned orders of the High Court dated 21st October 2023 and 4th November 2024 were quashed and set aside. The High Court was directed to decide the revision application without being influenced by the Supreme Court's observations. The appellant was directed to appear before the Sessions Court within four weeks and furnish bail until the disposal of the revision application, with usual conditions and a condition of cooperating with the High Court for early disposal.

precedents_cited: State of Uttar Pradesh v. Poosu & Ors. (1976) 3 SCC 1
Amin Khan v. State of Rajasthan & Ors. (2009) 3 SCC 776
State of Maharashtra v. Mahesh Kariman Tirki & Ors. (2022) 10 SCC 207
Parvinder Singh Khurana v. Directorate of Enforcement 2024 SCC OnLine SC 1765 : 2024 INSC 546
constitutional_provisions: Article 21 of the Constitution

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: An order staying a discharge order is a very drastic measure that curtails the liberty of the accused and should only be passed in rare and exceptional cases, and never ex-parte. While the High Court in revision can exercise powers under Section 390 CrPC, the normal rule is to admit the discharged accused to bail, not commit them to custody, as a discharge order places the accused on a higher pedestal than an acquitted person.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that the case of State of Maharashtra v. Mahesh Kariman Tirki & Ors. was not relevant to the present case due to its peculiar facts where discharge was based on absence of sanction after conviction.

special_directions.special_directions: The High Court will decide the revision application without being influenced by any observations made in this judgment. The first respondent-NCT of Delhi and the fifth respondent may apply before the High Court for necessary priority to the disposal of the revision application. The appellant must appear before the Sessions Court within four weeks from the judgment date and furnish bail effective until the disposal of the revision application, on terms and conditions fixed by the Sessions Court. If the appellant fails to comply, he shall be taken into custody. While admitting the appellant to bail, the Sessions Court shall impose usual conditions and a condition of cooperating with the High Court for early disposal of the revision application. If the High Court finds the appellant is not cooperating, it may cancel the bail after hearing the appellant.
special_directions.interim_orders: The High Court passed an ex-parte order of stay on 21st October 2023, which was extended from time to time. A second impugned order dated 4th November 2024 directed the appellant to surrender to judicial custody.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 2536 OF 2019 with CIVIL APPEAL NO. 5726 Of 2019

case_details.subject_matter: The case addresses whether a spouse of a marriage declared void under Section 11 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, is entitled to claim permanent alimony and maintenance under Section 25, and maintenance pendente lite under Section 24 of the same Act.

judgements.case_summary: This judgment addresses a reference to a three-judge bench concerning conflicting views on the applicability of Sections 24 and 25 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, to marriages declared void. The appellant-husband argued that void marriages, being non-existent ab initio, should not entitle a 'spouse' to maintenance under Section 25, citing examples of incestuous or bigamous unions and previous judgments against granting alimony. He contended that including a decree declaring a marriage void within the expression 'any decree' in Section 25 was absurd. The respondent-wife supported the view that alimony should be granted, relying on previous decisions and Article 15(3) of the Constitution. The Court analyzed Sections 24 and 25, concluding that 'any decree' in Section 25 encompasses all types of decrees under the Act, including a decree of nullity under Section 11. It emphasized that Section 25 aims to prevent financial destitution and that the grant of alimony is discretionary, considering the parties' conduct. The Court also clarified that maintenance pendente lite under Section 24 can be granted even if a marriage is prima facie void or voidable, with the court considering the conduct of the party seeking relief. The Court criticized the use of terms like 'illegitimate wife' by a High Court, deeming it misogynistic and violative of Article 21. The questions referred were answered, affirming the entitlement to both permanent alimony and maintenance pendente lite for spouses of void marriages, subject to judicial discretion and conduct.

petitioner_key_arguments: Void marriages (e.g., father-daughter, brother-sister) are void ab initio and do not create a 'spouse' relationship, thus Section 25 should not apply.
It is absurd to include a decree declaring a marriage void in the expression 'any decree' used in Section 25.
The view taken in Chand Dhawan and Rameshchandra Rampratapji Daga cases, which support granting maintenance for void marriages, is incorrect.
A wife whose marriage is declared void cannot claim to be a spouse within the meaning of Section 25 of the 1955 Act.
Extending Section 25 benefits to void marriages would go against the Act's object to ban bigamous marriages.
Cited judgments like Yamunabai Anantrao Adhav, Abbayolla Reddy, Navdeep Kaur, Bhausaheb Magar, and Savitaben Somabhai Bhatiya as supporting the stance against granting alimony for void marriages.
respondent_key_arguments: Supported the decisions in Chand Dhawan and Rameshchandra Rampratapji Daga, which held that a spouse of a declared void marriage is entitled to maintenance under Section 25.
Relied upon Article 15(3) of the Constitution of India, arguing that Section 25 is a special provision enacted for women.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the broader interpretation of 'any decree' in Section 25 to include decrees of nullity for void marriages, aligning with the respondent's arguments for the entitlement to alimony and maintenance.

outcome.relief_granted: The Court clarified that a spouse of a marriage declared void under Section 11 of the 1955 Act is entitled to seek permanent alimony and maintenance under Section 25, and maintenance pendente lite under Section 24. The grant of such relief is discretionary and depends on the facts and conduct of the parties. The appeals were directed to be placed before the appropriate Bench for decision on merits.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The Court held that the expression 'any decree' in Section 25 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, is broad enough to include a decree declaring a marriage null and void under Section 11. This interpretation ensures that financially dependent spouses of void marriages are not left destitute, with the grant of alimony being discretionary based on the facts and conduct of the parties. Similarly, maintenance pendente lite under Section 24 can be granted even if a marriage is prima facie void or voidable.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court strongly criticized the use of terms like 'illegitimate wife' and 'faithful mistress' by the Bombay High Court in reference to women in void marriages, stating that such language is misogynistic and violates Article 21 of the Constitution of India, which guarantees the right to a dignified life.

special_directions.special_directions: The Registry is directed to place these appeals before the appropriate Bench for the decision on merits, following the clarification of the legal questions.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 [Arising out of SLP (Crl.) No. 9218 of 2024]

case_details.subject_matter: Appeal against the High Court's dismissal of a quashing application for a chargesheet and cognizance order in a criminal case involving dowry harassment and other IPC sections, filed after a divorce petition.

judgements.case_summary: This appeal challenges an order dated 31.08.2022 by the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, which dismissed an application to quash a chargesheet and cognizance order in FIR No. 733 of 2021. The FIR was registered under Sections 498A, 504, 506 of the Indian Penal Code and Sections 3/4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, against the Appellants, including the husband (Appellant No. 3) and his family. The marriage between Appellant No. 3 and Respondent No. 2 (Priyanka Mishra) was solemnized in 2016. Appellant No. 3 filed for divorce on 17.06.2021, and Respondent No. 2 lodged the FIR on 19.08.2021, two months later, initially including Section 376 IPC (rape) against the brother-in-law. However, the Section 376 IPC charge was dropped after investigation, and no protest petition was filed by the complainant. A divorce decree was subsequently granted, and Appellant No. 3 remarried. The Appellants argued that the FIR was a counter-blast, lacked specific allegations, and was fabricated. The High Court dismissed their application, stating that disputed facts could not be examined under Section 482 CrPC. The Supreme Court found the High Court's analysis cursory, noting the lack of specific allegations, the timing of the FIR after the divorce petition, and the dropping of the rape charge without protest. Citing various precedents, the Supreme Court concluded that the FIR was vexatious and motivated by ulterior motives, and thus, exercised its powers under Article 142 of the Constitution to quash the FIR and chargesheet.

petitioner_key_arguments: The FIR was lodged as a counter-blast to the divorce petition filed by Appellant No. 3.
Respondent No. 2's statement under Section 164 CrPC completely deviated from the allegations made in the FIR.
The FIR is false, fabricated, and contains omnibus allegations against all family members.
No charge-sheet was filed for the alleged offense under Section 376 IPC, and no protest petition was filed against its dropping.
A decree of divorce has been passed, and Appellant No. 3 has remarried.
The High Court conducted only a cursory analysis and failed to underscore reasons for its findings.
respondent_key_arguments: The allegations made in the FIR and the charge-sheet disclose the commission of a cognizable offense.
Disputed questions of fact cannot be looked into by the High Court while exercising powers under Section 482 CrPC.
The scope of interference at the stage of filing of a charge-sheet is quite limited.
The High Court was justified in dismissing the quashing application.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the FIR was a counter-blast to the divorce petition, lacked specific details, and was vexatious, especially considering the dropping of the serious Section 376 IPC charge without protest and the subsequent divorce and remarriage. The Court found the High Court's analysis to be cursory and its dismissal of the quashing application flawed.

outcome.relief_granted: FIR No. 733/2021 and the charge-sheet dated 02.02.2022 in the matter are quashed.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (Arising out of Special Leave Petition (Crl.) No.6898 of 20)

respondent_advocates: learned counsel appearing for the respondent-State

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the quashing of a chargesheet and summoning order against a public servant (appellant) in a criminal case, primarily on the ground of lack of valid sanction for prosecution under Section 197 of the CrPC, where the competent authority had explicitly denied sanction.

judgements.case_summary:
The appellant, Suneeti Toteja, an employee of the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) on deputation to the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), was implicated in a criminal case stemming from a sexual harassment complaint filed by Dr. Manisha Narayan against Dr. S.S. Ghonkrorkta. While not named in the initial FIR, the appellant's name surfaced in the complainant's Section 164 CrPC statement, alleging that the appellant filed a counter-affidavit in a Tribunal case without the complainant's consent, threatened her, and pressured her to withdraw the case. A chargesheet was filed against the appellant, and the Special Chief Judicial Magistrate took cognizance and issued summons. The High Court dismissed the appellant's petition to quash these proceedings.

The appellant argued that as a government servant, her actions were in the course of official duties, thus requiring prior sanction for prosecution under Section 197 CrPC. She contended that the competent authority, BIS, had explicitly denied sanction, and the concept of 'deemed sanction' was not legally valid. The respondents argued that the investigating officer proceeded based on a 'deemed sanction' as the sanction was not granted within the stipulated time, and that the appellant had concealed facts and committed perjury.

The Supreme Court analyzed Section 197 CrPC, emphasizing that sanction is mandatory for public servants acting in their official capacity. It found that the appellant's actions as Presiding Officer of the ICC were within her official duties. The Court rejected the 'deemed sanction' argument, stating it is not statutorily recognized, and noted that BIS had unequivocally denied sanction. Consequently, the Court held that the Magistrate erred in taking cognizance without valid sanction, and the High Court was incorrect in not quashing the proceedings. The appeal was allowed, and the chargesheet and summoning order against the appellant were quashed.

petitioner_key_arguments: The appellant is a government servant who acted in the course of her official duties, therefore, cognizance could not have been taken without a valid sanction for prosecution.
The competent authority to grant sanction, BIS, explicitly denied the sanction for prosecution vide its letter dated 14.11.2022.
The Investigating Officer failed to send the sanction request directly to BIS in a timely manner, leading to a delay beyond the stipulated four months.
The concept of 'deemed sanction' is not tenable under Section 197 CrPC and is not statutorily incorporated.
respondent_key_arguments: The Investigating Officer proceeded with the chargesheet based on a 'deemed sanction' as the sanction was not granted by the competent authority within the stipulated time period.
The appellant concealed material facts before the Court, including filing applications for discharge in the trial court.
The appellant filed a counter-affidavit before the Tribunal without the complainant's knowledge and consent and committed perjury.
The appellant was involved in threatening and pressurizing the complainant to withdraw the case.
The police initially restricted the complainant's statement under Section 161 CrPC, which is why the appellant was not named until the Section 164 CrPC statement.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that sanction under Section 197 CrPC was mandatory for actions performed in official duty, and that the concept of 'deemed sanction' is not legally recognized. The explicit denial of sanction by the competent authority (BIS) was a decisive factor.

outcome.relief_granted: The chargesheet, the summoning order, and the consequent steps taken by the trial court pursuant to the same are quashed qua the appellant.

acts_cited: Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013
Code of Criminal Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1991 (43 of 1991)

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that prior sanction under Section 197 of the CrPC is a mandatory condition precedent for taking cognizance against a public servant for offences committed while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of official duty. The concept of 'deemed sanction' is not recognized by the statute, and an explicit denial of sanction by the competent authority vitiates the criminal proceedings.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that the object of Section 197 CrPC is to protect officers and officials from unjustified criminal prosecution while discharging their duties, ensuring they can act fearlessly with bona fides. It also noted that the question of whether an act is traceable to official functions depends on the facts of each case.

case_identification.respondent_name: Bihar Legislative Council (Through Secretary) and Ors.
case_identification.case_number: WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) No. 530 OF 2024

case_details.subject_matter: Challenge to the expulsion of a Member of Legislative Council (MLC) by the Ethics Committee of the Bihar Legislative Council (BLC) for unparliamentary conduct, and the consequential notification relieving him from membership.

judgements.case_summary:
Dr. Sunil Kumar Singh, an MLC and Chief Whip of the RJD in the Bihar Legislative Council (BLC), challenged his expulsion from the BLC. He was accused of unparliamentary conduct, including using derogatory remarks against the Chief Minister. The BLC's Ethics Committee recommended his expulsion, which was subsequently formalized by a majority vote in the BLC. The Petitioner argued that his expulsion violated natural justice principles, was disproportionate, and that the Ethics Committee's proceedings were flawed. He also contended that the report was selectively circulated. The Respondents argued that the writ petition was not maintainable under Article 212(1) of the Constitution, that the House's decisions on proportionality were not subject to judicial review, and that the Petitioner had ample opportunity to present his case but was defiant.

The Supreme Court held the writ petition maintainable, clarifying that while "Proceedings in the Legislature" are immune from judicial review for procedural irregularities under Article 212(1), "Legislative Decisions" or "administrative actions" (like expulsion) are subject to review for illegality, unconstitutionality, or disproportionality. The Court acknowledged the Petitioner's "abhorrent and unbecoming" conduct and his evasiveness before the Ethics Committee. However, it found the expulsion "highly excessive and disproportionate" to the misconduct, emphasizing that such a severe punishment impacts the democratic process and the electorate.

The Court, exercising its powers under Article 142, set aside the expulsion. It directed that the period already undergone by the Petitioner be considered a suspension and sufficient punishment. He was reinstated as an MLC with immediate effect, though without remuneration for the period of disbandment. The bye-election notification issued by the Election Commission was quashed. The Court cautioned the Petitioner to uphold the dignity of the House, warning of future action for misconduct.

petitioner_key_arguments: The Impugned Report and consequential Notification are illegal and unconstitutional, actuated by mala fide, and suffer from gross illegalities.
Expulsion violates principles of natural justice; relevant material (video clip) was not furnished, denying access to evidence.
The Ethics Committee unilaterally and deliberately advanced the hearing date without notice to the Petitioner.
The Ethics Committee's report was circulated selectively to ruling party members and kept confidential from opposition members.
The punishment of expulsion is disproportionate to the attributed misconduct, especially when compared to another MLC (Md. Sohaib) who received a two-day suspension for similar allegations.
The disproportionate punishment falls foul of the Fundamental Rights enshrined in Articles 14, 19, and 21 of the Constitution of India.
respondent_key_arguments: The Writ Petition is not maintainable in view of Article 212(1) of the Constitution of India, which bars questioning the validity of legislative proceedings on grounds of procedural irregularity.
It is the prerogative of the House to regulate its Business and Procedure; the proportionality of punishment cannot be tested by courts.
The Ethics Committee adhered to the principles of audi alteram partem, providing reasonable opportunity to the Petitioner, who deliberately failed to avail it.
The Petitioner was duly served with charges but questioned the legality and authority of the Ethics Committee.
The Petitioner cannot claim parity with Md. Sohaib, who cooperated and expressed regret, while the Petitioner remained defiant.
The Petitioner has a history of degrading the House's authority, having been suspended previously.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court accepted the Petitioner's arguments regarding the maintainability of the writ petition for judicial review of proportionality in administrative actions by legislative bodies and found the punishment of expulsion to be highly excessive and disproportionate to the misconduct.

outcome.relief_granted: The Impugned Report of the Ethics Committee and the subsequent Notification notifying the expulsion of the Petitioner are set aside to the extent of the nature of punishment. The period of expulsion already undergone by the Petitioner is deemed as a period of his suspension and sufficient punishment. The Petitioner is reinstated as a member of the BLC with immediate effect, but shall not be entitled to claim any remuneration or other monetary benefits for the period of his disbandment. The bye-election notification dated 30.12.2024 is quashed.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The Supreme Court ruled that while Article 212(1) of the Constitution bars judicial review of "Proceedings in the Legislature" for procedural irregularities, "Legislative Decisions" or "administrative actions" by legislative bodies, such as the expulsion of a member, are subject to judicial review on grounds of illegality, unconstitutionality, or disproportionality. The Court further held that the expulsion of the Petitioner was a disproportionate punishment for his misconduct, infringing upon his fundamental rights and impacting the representation of his constituents, thus warranting intervention under Article 142 to ensure justice and fairness.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court emphasized the importance of proportionality as a cornerstone of the judicial system, applicable across various legal contexts (service, administrative, constitutional, criminal law), and highlighted the need for legislative bodies to exercise magnanimity and avoid retributive punishment. It noted that while the Petitioner's conduct was "abhorrent and unbecoming," the punishment must be proportionate and not unduly stifle democratic participation or undermine the representative nature of the institution. The Court also stressed the role of Constitutional Courts in upholding democratic values and preventing arbitrary or excessive actions by legislative bodies.

special_directions.special_directions: The Petitioner is directed to be reinstated as a member of the BLC with immediate effect. He shall not be entitled to claim any remuneration or other monetary benefits for the period of his disbandment, but shall be entitled to such other perks and privileges as any other similarly placed MLC upon completion of their full tenure. For the limited purpose of post-tenure benefits, the Petitioner shall be deemed to have served as MLC for the entire tenure. Should the Petitioner indulge further in such misconduct upon his reinstatement, the Ethics Committee or Chairperson of the BLC is at liberty to take appropriate action in accordance with law. The Press Note dated 30.12.2024 issued by Respondent No. 6, Election Commission, declaring the bye-election for the seat earlier held by the Petitioner is quashed, and any action taken pursuant to such Press Note is annulled.
special_directions.interim_orders: Vide order dated 15.01.2025, the declaration of the result of the bye-election for the seat held by the Petitioner was stayed.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. OF 2025

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns an appeal challenging the compensation awarded in a motor accident claim, seeking enhancement of compensation for the death of Smt. Tarawati, focusing on the correct assessment of income, age, multiplier, and various heads of damages.

judgements.case_summary: This appeal challenges a High Court order dated 24.05.2018, which partly allowed an appeal and enhanced compensation from Rs. 4,31,680/- to Rs. 5,96,761/- with 7.5% interest per annum, for the death of Smt. Tarawati in a motor accident on 07.02.2003. The appellants argued that the compensation was inadequate, contending that the deceased's age was incorrectly determined (should be 45 years as per Post-Mortem Report, not 60 or 42), and her monthly income was wrongly computed, failing to include notional income for a housewife. They also argued that the High Court did not award compensation under various heads as per the decision in Pranay Sethi, seeking a total of Rs. 18,74,630/-. The respondent-Insurance Company argued that the High Court's award was fair, reasonable, and based on evidence and established guidelines, asserting no justification for further enhancement. The Supreme Court found the High Court's assessment of monthly income to be on the lower side and determined the deceased's age as 45 years based on the Post-Mortem Report, applying a multiplier of 14. The Court enhanced the monthly income to Rs. 7,000/- (including family pension and notional wages), awarded Rs. 2,40,000/- for loss of love and affection (for 5 claimants), Rs. 20,000/- for funeral expenses, and 25% for future prospects. The deduction for personal expenses was set at 1/4th as per Sarla Verma. The appeal was allowed, enhancing the total compensation to Rs. 13,82,500/- with 7.5% interest per annum.

petitioner_key_arguments: The compensation awarded by the High Court is inadequate and ought to be modified.
The age of the deceased was incorrectly taken as 60 years (or 42 years by High Court); it should be 45 years as per the Post-Mortem Report.
The High Court erred in computing the income of the deceased; it should include notional income for a housewife (Rs. 5,000/-) in addition to family pension.
The High Court did not award compensation under various heads in terms of the decision in National Insurance Company Limited v Pranay Sethi.
A total of Rs. 18,74,630/- ought to be granted in compensation.
respondent_key_arguments: The High Court applied its mind judiciously and thoughtfully to every aspect of the case.
Every observation in the Impugned Order is based on evidence.
The appellants are entitled to compensation of Rs. 5,96,761/- only and nothing more.
The compensation is based on the guidelines of the Courts, and there is no justification for claiming more.
Sympathies cannot override the applicable law, and the compensation awarded is fair and reasonable.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments regarding the inadequacy of compensation, the incorrect determination of the deceased's age, the need to include notional income for a housewife, and the application of established precedents for various heads of damages and future prospects.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal is allowed, and the total compensation is enhanced to Rs. 13,82,500/-. This amount is to be paid with 7.5% interest per annum from the date of filing of the claim till date of realization within 2 months.

precedents_cited: Sarla Verma v Delhi Transport Corporation, (2009) 6 SCC 121
National Insurance Company Limited v Pranay Sethi, (2017) 16 SCC 680
Rajendra Singh v National Insurance Company Ltd., (2020) 7 SCC 256
Magma General Insurance Co. Ltd. v Nanu Ram, (2018) 18 SCC 130
