Vishal Goyal and Others v. State of Karnataka and Others (2014) 11 SCC 456
Neil Aurelio Nunes (OBC Reservation) and Others v. Union of India and Others (2022) 4 SCC 1
constitutional_provisions: Article 14 of the Constitution of India
Article 15 of the Constitution of India
Article 16 of the Constitution of India
Article 5 of the Constitution

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: Residence-based reservation in Post Graduate Medical Courses is constitutionally invalid and impermissible as it violates Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitution, undermining the principle of equality and merit at higher levels of education. While institutional preference to a reasonable extent is permissible, domicile or residence cannot be a basis for reservation in PG medical admissions due to the paramount importance of merit in specialized medical fields.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court clarified that India recognizes only one domicile, namely, domicile in India, and the concept of a provincial or state domicile is a misconception. It also distinguished between the permissibility of residence-based reservation in undergraduate (MBBS) courses to a certain degree, due to local needs and infrastructure costs, versus its impermissibility in postgraduate medical courses where merit is paramount.

special_directions.special_directions: The Medical College should now fill the remaining State Quota seats (beyond permissible institutional preference) according to the merit position of candidates obtained in their NEET Examination. Students already admitted under the residence category and undergoing their course, particularly those admitted under the interim order dated 09.05.2019, will not be affected by this judgment.
special_directions.interim_orders: An ad-interim stay of the impugned order (High Court's decision) was granted till the next date of hearing on 09.05.2019. It was clarified that the admission process already done on the basis of domicile reservation would be subject to the outcome of these petitions.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL No.738 OF 2025

case_details.subject_matter: This case concerns an appeal against the High Court's decision to deny bail to an accused charged under the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act (UAPA) and other statutes, primarily focusing on the right to a speedy trial due to prolonged incarceration and slow trial progress.

judgements.case_summary: The appellant, Tapas Kumar Palit, was arrested on March 24, 2020, for alleged involvement in Naxalite activities. His vehicle was intercepted, and articles such as shoes, green-black printed cloth, electric wire, LED lens, and a walkie-talkie were recovered. He was charged under Sections 10, 13, 17, 38(1)(2), 40, 22-A and 22-C of the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act, 1967 (UAPA), Sections 8(2), (3) and (5) of the Chhattisgarh Vishesh Jan Suraksha Adhiniyam, 2005, and Sections 120B, 201 and 149 read with 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. The High Court of Chhattisgarh at Bilaspur had declined to grant him bail. The Supreme Court noted that the appellant had been in judicial custody as an undertrial prisoner for five years since his arrest. The prosecution intended to examine 100 witnesses, but only 42 had been examined, and the panch witnesses to the recovery had turned hostile. The Court emphasized the fundamental right to a speedy trial enshrined in Article 21 of the Constitution, stating that prolonged incarceration without a timely trial infringes upon this right, regardless of the seriousness of the crime. It also questioned the necessity of examining an excessive number of witnesses and highlighted the role of the Public Prosecutor and Special Judge in ensuring trial efficiency. Consequently, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and granted bail to the appellant, subject to specific conditions.

petitioner_key_arguments: Prolonged incarceration as an undertrial for 5 years.
Slow pace of trial with only 42 out of 100 proposed witnesses examined.
Panch witnesses to recovery turned hostile.
Infringement of the fundamental right to speedy trial under Article 21 of the Constitution.
respondent_key_arguments: Seriousness of the alleged crimes, including charges under UAPA.
Need to examine all intended witnesses (100) to establish the case.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments regarding prolonged incarceration and the infringement of the fundamental right to a speedy trial under Article 21, coupled with the slow progress of the trial and the prosecution's intention to examine an excessive number of witnesses, were accepted by the court.

outcome.relief_granted: The appellant is ordered to be released on bail forthwith, subject to terms and conditions as may be imposed by the trial court.

acts_cited: Chhattisgarh Vishesh Jan Suraksha Adhiniyam, 2005 (Sections 8(2), (3) and (5))
Indian Penal Code, 1860 (Sections 120B, 201 and 149 read with 34)
precedents_cited: Malak Khan vs. Emperor [AIR 1946 Privy Council 16]
constitutional_provisions: Article 21 of the Constitution

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that the fundamental right to a speedy trial, enshrined in Article 21 of the Constitution, cannot be undermined by prolonged incarceration as an undertrial, even in serious crimes, especially when the trial's progress is unduly slow and the prosecution's witness list is extensive without clear justification. The court must balance the seriousness of the crime with the accused's right to a timely resolution.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court made observations regarding the responsibility of the Public Prosecutor to wisely exercise discretion in calling witnesses and the role of the Special Judge in ensuring efficient trial proceedings. It also highlighted the significant adverse impact of lengthy pre-trial incarceration on accused persons, including financial, personal, and social consequences, and stressed that delays are detrimental to the accused, victims, and the credibility of the justice system.

special_directions.special_directions: The appellant shall not enter into the revenue limits of district Kanker, State of Chhattisgarh. He shall appear online on each date of the hearing before the trial. He shall personally remain present before the Trial Court only when his further statement under Section 313 of the Cr.P.C. is to be recorded, for which limited purpose he shall enter Kanker district. If the appellant commits breach of any condition, the bail shall stand automatically cancelled.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S). 649 OF 2013

case_details.subject_matter: This case involves an appeal against conviction for murder and destruction of evidence, primarily challenging the sufficiency and reliability of circumstantial evidence, specifically disclosure statements and recoveries, in proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

judgements.case_summary: This appeal challenges the conviction of Thammaraya (A-2) and Basappa (A-3) for murder and destruction of evidence, which was upheld by the High Court. The case originated from the murder of Shrishail, allegedly orchestrated by Manoj (A-1) (since deceased) due to an illicit relationship, with the assistance of A-2 and A-3. The prosecution's case against A-2 and A-3 relied solely on circumstantial evidence, particularly "recoveries" made pursuant to their disclosure statements. The Supreme Court analyzed the evidence against the "five golden principles" for circumstantial evidence. It found significant infirmities in the Investigating Officer's testimony regarding the disclosure statements, noting the absence of exact words, failure to exhibit the statements, and lack of clear evidence that the accused led to the recoveries. Crucially, the Court highlighted the complete omission of a Test Identification Parade (TIP) for the recovered articles, deeming it a "material omission" that created "holes in the fabric of the prosecution story." Concluding that the chain of circumstantial evidence was incomplete and inconsistent with the innocence of the accused, the Court quashed the convictions and acquitted Thammaraya (A-2) and Basappa (A-3).

petitioner_key_arguments: The circumstantial evidence presented by the prosecution was insufficient to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
The disclosure statements and subsequent recoveries were not proved in accordance with Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.
There was a crucial omission in conducting a Test Identification Parade (TIP) for the recovered articles, rendering their identification unreliable.
The chain of circumstantial evidence was incomplete and did not exclude the hypothesis of innocence.
respondent_key_arguments: The prosecution successfully established the guilt of the accused through circumstantial evidence, including motive, last seen, and recoveries.
The disclosure statements led to valid recoveries of articles belonging to the deceased, thereby linking the accused to the crime.
The convictions by the trial court and High Court were justified based on the evidence presented.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioners' arguments regarding the insufficiency of circumstantial evidence, particularly the flawed disclosure statements and lack of Test Identification Parade (TIP) for recoveries, prevailed.

outcome.relief_granted: The conviction of Thammaraya(A-2) and Basappa(A-3) recorded by the trial Court and affirmed by the High Court is quashed and set aside. The appellant Thammaraya(A-2) and appellant Basappa(A-3) are acquitted of the charges.

precedents_cited: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra, (1984) 4 SCC 116
Shivaji Sahabrao Bobade v. State of Maharashtra [(1973) 2 SCC 793 : 1973 SCC (Cri) 1033 : 1973 Crl LJ 1783]
Babu Sahebagouda Rudragoudar and Other v. State of Karnataka, (2024) 8 SCC 149
Subramanya v. State of Karnataka (2023) 11 SCC 255
Ramkishan Mithanlal Sharma v. State of Bombay, (1954) 2 SCC 516
Munna Kumar Upadhyay alias 15 (1954) 2 SCC 516 Munna Upadhyaya v. State of Andhra Pradesh through Public Prosecutor, Hyderabad, Andhra Pradesh, (2012) 6 SCC 174

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: Conviction based purely on circumstantial evidence requires the chain of evidence to be complete, conclusive, and exclude every hypothesis except guilt. Flaws in proving disclosure statements (exact words, leading to recovery) and the absence of a Test Identification Parade for recovered articles break this chain, making the evidence insufficient to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court emphasized the importance of proper procedure for recording disclosure statements under Section 27 of the Evidence Act, including the presence of independent witnesses and detailed panchnamas. It also highlighted the significance of conducting a Test Identification Parade (TIP) for recovered articles, especially when recoveries form the sole basis of the prosecution's case, to provide corroborative and confirmatory evidence.

special_directions.special_directions: The appellant Thammaraya(A-2) and appellant Basappa(A-3) are acquitted of the charges. They are on bail and need not surrender.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 13651 OF 2024

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the legality and validity of a High Court judgment that set aside a Standing Order issued by the Auroville Foundation, challenging the powers of the Foundation's Governing Board and the role of the Residents' Assembly under the Auroville Foundation Act.

judgements.case_summary: The Auroville Foundation appealed against a High Court judgment dated 15.03.2024, which had allowed a Writ Petition filed by Natasha Storey and set aside the Foundation's Standing Order No. 01/2022. The Foundation argued that its Governing Board possesses statutory powers under the Auroville Foundation Act (A.F. Act) to issue Standing Orders and constitute committees for Auroville's management, and that the Residents' Assembly's role is merely advisory. The Foundation also highlighted that Natasha Storey had previously filed a similar petition challenging the same order, which was dismissed, and that she suppressed this material fact in the current proceedings. The Supreme Court, after reviewing the A.F. Act and Rules, concluded that the Governing Board is vested with all powers for the Foundation's management and can issue Standing Orders. It found no legal infirmity in the impugned Standing Order and clarified that the Residents' Assembly has no legal right to be part of committees constituted by the Governing Board. The Court also strongly criticized the High Court for entertaining the petition despite the respondent's suppression of material facts, emphasizing the 'clean hands' doctrine. Consequently, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment, and imposed costs on the respondent for abusing the process of law.

petitioner_key_arguments: The High Court misdirected itself by misinterpreting the provisions of the A.F. Act.
The Auroville Foundation is a statutory body, and its Governing Board has general superintendence, direction, and management of Auroville's affairs.
The Governing Board is empowered to issue Standing Orders and constitute committees under the A.F. Act and Rules for efficient discharge of duties.
The Residents' Assembly's functions are advisory, and neither the Assembly nor individual residents have a legal right to be part of committees constituted by the Governing Board.
The respondent suppressed material facts by not disclosing a previously dismissed writ petition seeking similar relief, which constitutes an abuse of the process of law.
respondent_key_arguments: The impugned Standing Order No. 01/2022 was not in consonance with the provisions of the A.F. Act.
The Governing Board did not have the power to appoint committees that replaced nominees of the Residents' Assembly.
The right of the Residents' Assembly was getting affected by the impugned order.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the appellant's arguments that the Governing Board has the statutory power to issue Standing Orders and constitute committees, and that the Residents' Assembly's role is advisory. The court also agreed that the respondent's suppression of material facts (prior dismissed petition) was a serious issue that should have led to the dismissal of her petition.

outcome.relief_granted: The High Court's Judgment and Order dated 15.03.2024 passed in Writ Petition No. 25882 of 2022 was set aside. The appeal was allowed with costs of Rs. 50,000/- to be deposited by the respondent.

acts_cited: THE AUROVILLE FOUNDATION ACT, ACT NO. 54 OF 1988
precedents_cited: S.J.S. Business Enterprises (P) Ltd. Vs. State of Bihar & Ors.1, AIR 2004 SC 2421 (2008) 4 SCC 127 (2007) 8 SCC 449
General Manager, Haryana Roadways Vs. Jai Bhagwan & Anr.2
Prestige Lights Ltd. Vs. State Bank of India3
constitutional_provisions: Article 226 of the Constitution of India

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The Governing Board of the Auroville Foundation, as a statutory body, possesses the inherent power under the Auroville Foundation Act and its Rules to issue Standing Orders and constitute committees for the efficient discharge of its duties and functions. The Residents' Assembly's role is strictly advisory, and neither the Assembly nor its individual members have a statutory right to be part of committees formed by the Governing Board. Furthermore, a litigant's suppression of material facts, such as a previously dismissed petition seeking similar relief, constitutes an abuse of the process of law and warrants dismissal of the subsequent petition.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed that a "small group of disgruntled residents of Auroville" repeatedly filed "ill-motivated petitions" to obstruct the development of Auroville and the smooth functioning of the Governing Board, thereby abusing the process of law.

special_directions.special_directions: The respondent is directed to deposit costs of Rs. 50,000/- before the Supreme Court Legal Service Committee within two weeks from the date of judgment.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO(s). 5781-5782 OF 2022

case_details.subject_matter: Appeals against orders of the National Green Tribunal concerning construction activities and environmental clearance for the Auroville township, specifically regarding the 'Crown Road' project and alleged tree cutting.

judgements.case_summary: This case involves appeals filed by The Auroville Foundation against orders of the National Green Tribunal (NGT) dated 28.04.2022 and 27.07.2022. The respondents (original applicants before NGT) had raised concerns about tree cutting and environmental damage during the construction of the 'Crown Road' in Auroville, alleging the area was a 'deemed Forest' requiring environmental clearance. The NGT, applying the 'Precautionary Principle,' directed the Auroville Foundation to prepare a proper township plan and obtain Environmental Clearance, despite concluding that the area was not a 'Forest' under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980. The Supreme Court found that the NGT had exceeded its jurisdiction, as no 'substantial question relating to environment' arising from the specified enactments was established. The Court held that the NGT misdirected itself by interfering with an already approved Master Plan and quashed the impugned orders, stating they were without jurisdiction and legally untenable.

petitioner_key_arguments: The Master Plan for Auroville was already approved by competent authorities in 2001 and published in 2010.
The area in question was not a 'Forest' or 'deemed Forest' as per government documents and was a man-made plantation, thus not requiring clearance under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980.
The NGT lacked jurisdiction as no 'substantial question relating to environment' arising from the implementation of enactments specified in Schedule I of the NGT Act was involved.
The NGT misdirected itself by applying the 'Precautionary Principle' in an extraordinary manner and interfering with an approved Master Plan.
The Auroville Foundation Act, 1988, has an overriding effect, making the NGT's directions untenable.
respondent_key_arguments: The Auroville Foundation was cutting a large number of trees, causing environmental deterioration in the 'Darkali Forest' area.
The area should be treated as a 'deemed Forest' and protected as mandated in T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad Vs. Union of India and Others.
The Auroville Foundation should be injuncted from felling trees and clearing undergrowth.
The 1st Respondent (Auroville Foundation) should prepare a Detailed Development Plan and obtain necessary Environmental Clearance for its projects.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Supreme Court accepted the Appellant's arguments that the NGT exceeded its jurisdiction by issuing directions without a 'substantial question relating to environment' arising from the implementation of enactments specified in Schedule I of the NGT Act, and by interfering with an already approved Master Plan under the guise of the 'Precautionary Principle.' The Court also agreed that the area was not a 'Forest' as per government records.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned Orders passed by the National Green Tribunal dated 28.04.2022 and 27.07.2022 were quashed and set aside.

acts_cited: The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Cess Act, 1977
The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981
precedents_cited: T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad Vs. Union of India and Others1
State of Madhya Pradesh Vs. Centre for Environment Protection Research and Development2, (2020) 9 SCC 781
H.P. Bus-Stand Management and Development Authority Vs. Central Empowered Committee3
Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum Vs. Union of India & Others4
Essar Oil Ltd. Vs. Halar Utkarsh Samiti & Ors.5
Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India [(1996) 5 SCC 281]
N.D. Jayal & Anr. Vs. Union of India & Ors.6
State of H.P. v. Ganesh Wood Products [(1995) 6 SCC 363]
M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath [(1997) 1 SCC 388]
Vellore Citizens [(1996) 5 SCC 647]
constitutional_provisions: Articles 14 of the Constitution of India
Articles 21 of the Constitution of India

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The National Green Tribunal's jurisdiction under Section 14 of the NGT Act is limited to cases involving a 'substantial question relating to environment' that arises from the implementation of specific enactments listed in Schedule I of the Act. The NGT cannot assume jurisdiction or issue directions, particularly by applying the 'Precautionary Principle,' when no such substantial question or violation of specified enactments has been established, or when it interferes with an already approved statutory Master Plan.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court emphasized that 'Sustainable Development' is a balancing concept between ecology and development, and that both the right to a clean environment and the right to development are fundamental rights under Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution of India. It also highlighted the historical context and statutory framework governing Auroville's development.

special_directions.interim_orders: The Supreme Court passed an interim order on 13.12.2023, staying the NGT's direction contained in Para 125(i) of its judgment, finding it prima facie outside the Tribunal's jurisdiction.

case_identification.petitioner_name: THE CHIEF MANAGER, CENTRAL BANK OF INDIA & ORS.
case_identification.respondent_name: M/s AD BUREAU ADVERTISING PVT. LTD & ANR.
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 7438 OF 2023 WITH CIVIL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (@ DIARY NO. 20192 OF 2024)

respondent_advocates: learned counsel for respondent No. 2, i.e. TransUnion CIBIL Limited

case_details.subject_matter: The case determines whether a borrower of a project loan, availed for commercial purposes like film post-production and brand building, falls within the definition of 'Consumer' under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986.

judgements.case_summary:
The Central Bank of India sanctioned a Rs. 10 crore project loan to M/s Ad Bureau Advertising Pvt. Ltd. for film post-production. Following a default, the account was classified as NPA, and an One-Time Settlement (OTS) was reached. Despite the settlement and issuance of a 'No Dues Certificate', the bank allegedly wrongly reported M/s Ad Bureau Advertising as a 'wilful defaulter' to CIBIL, leading to the loss of a significant advertising tender. The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC) found the bank deficient in service and directed it to pay Rs. 75 lakhs compensation and correct the CIBIL reporting.

The bank appealed this order, arguing that M/s Ad Bureau Advertising was not a 'consumer' under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, as the loan was for a commercial purpose. M/s Ad Bureau Advertising also filed a cross-appeal challenging the quantum of compensation. The Supreme Court examined whether the loan, even if partly for brand building, had a 'dominant intention' of profit generation. Citing precedents, the Court concluded that the transaction was a business-to-business activity with a direct nexus to profit, thus falling under 'commercial purpose'. Consequently, M/s Ad Bureau Advertising was deemed not a 'consumer'. The Supreme Court set aside the NCDRC's order, allowing the bank's appeal, and dismissed the cross-appeal, stating that the NCDRC lacked jurisdiction. The Court clarified that its decision was on maintainability and jurisdiction, not the merits, and the respondent could pursue other legal remedies.

petitioner_key_arguments: Respondent No. 1 does not fall within the definition of 'consumer' under Section 2(1)(d)(ii) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986.
The service availed (sanction of project loan) was purely for a commercial purpose.
It was a business-to-business transaction, not a business-to-consumer transaction.
The dominant intention behind the loan was to generate profits and increase revenue for the company.
respondent_key_arguments: Respondent No. 1 is covered by the Explanation to Section 2(1)(d) of the Act.
The loan was availed for 'self-use' (self-branding exercise for the movie "Kochadaiiyaan").
The sole purpose was building a brand name to earn livelihood, with no nexus to generation of profits.
The bank was grossly negligent and deficient in providing banking services, causing monetary damages and loss of reputation.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that the transaction was for a commercial purpose, as the dominant intention was profit generation, thus the respondent was not a 'consumer' under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986.

outcome.relief_granted: The order dated 30.08.2023 passed by the NCDRC is set aside. Civil Appeal No. 7438 of 2023 is allowed, and Civil Appeal No. of 2025 (@ DIARY NO. 20192 OF 2024) is dismissed.

acts_cited: Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002
precedents_cited: National Insurance Company Limited vs. Harsolia Motors & Ors. (2023) 8 SCC 362
Lilavati Kirtilal Mehta Medical Trust vs. Unique Shanti Developers, (2020) 2 SCC 265
Shrikant G. Mantri vs. Punjab National Bank (2022) 5 SCC 42

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The dominant intention or purpose behind availing a service determines whether it is for a "commercial purpose" under Section 2(1)(d)(ii) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986. If the service has a close and direct nexus with a profit-generating activity, it is considered commercial, thereby excluding the user from the definition of 'consumer'.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court clarified that its decision was solely on the issue of maintainability and jurisdiction of the NCDRC, and it did not express an opinion on the merits of the dispute. Respondent No. 1 is free to pursue other appropriate legal remedies in accordance with law.

special_directions.special_directions: Respondent No. 1 is allowed to pursue appropriate remedies in accordance with law.

case_identification.petitioner_name: The Chief Officer, Nagpur Housing And Area Development Board (A MHADA Unit) And Others
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. of 2025

case_details.subject_matter: The appeal concerns a dispute over a housing project, specifically regarding delayed possession of a flat, refund of deposited amounts, and the applicable interest rate on the refund, following decisions by consumer forums and the High Court.

judgements.case_summary: The case originated from a complaint filed by Manohar Burde (respondent) against The Chief Officer, Nagpur Housing And Area Development Board (petitioner) regarding delayed possession of a 3 BHK flat and demand for additional amounts. The SCDRC initially allowed the complaint, directing possession within six months and 15% p.a. interest. After a remand, SCDRC again directed 15% p.a. interest or refund with 15% p.a. interest and compensation. The NCDRC partly allowed the appeal, directing a refund with 9% p.a. interest and Rs. 50,000/- costs, dismissing a subsequent review. The petitioner (complainant) then filed a Writ Petition in the High Court, which allowed it, setting aside the NCDRC order and restoring 15% p.a. interest. The Chief Officer, Nagpur Housing, appealed to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court found the NCDRC's 9% p.a. interest fair and reasonable, especially as the complainant opted for a refund, and deemed the High Court's 15% p.a. interest excessive. The Court set aside the High Court's order, restored NCDRC's 9% p.a. interest, and reduced the compensation from Rs. 10,00,000/- to Rs. 7,50,000/-. The appeal was partly allowed.

petitioner_key_arguments: The High Court was not justified in exercising its supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution of India to modify the well-reasoned findings of NCDRC.
The enhanced interest @ 15% p.a. is exorbitant and contrary to the principles of law.
When the petitioner (complainant) opted for a refund, interest at a reasonable rate (as awarded by NCDRC at 9%) should have been granted.
Awarding 15% p.a. interest coupled with additional compensation of Rs. 10,00,000/- is unjustifiable.
respondent_key_arguments: There have been repeated defaults on the part of the statutory authorities and explicit deficiency of service on the part of the developer.
Interest @ 15% p.a. on account of inordinate delay is just and appropriate, warranting no interference under Article 136 of the Constitution of India.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that the High Court's enhancement of interest to 15% p.a. was excessive and that NCDRC's award of 9% p.a. was fair and reasonable, especially given the option for refund. The court also agreed to reduce the compensation amount.

outcome.relief_granted: The High Court's order dated 29.01.2024 is set aside. The NCDRC's order dated 27.07.2022 awarding interest @ 9% p.a. on the respective deposit till the date of actual payment is restored. The compensation payable is reduced from Rs. 10,00,000/- to Rs. 7,50,000/-.

precedents_cited: Bangalore Development Authority v. Syndicate Bank, (2007) 6 SCC 711
Rohit Chaudhary and another v. Vipul Ltd., (2024) 1 SCC 8
constitutional_provisions: Article 227 of the Constitution of India
Article 136 of the Constitution of India

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The NCDRC's decision to award 9% interest was fair and reasonable, especially since the petitioner (complainant in lower forums) had opted for a refund. The High Court's enhancement of the interest rate to 15% p.a. was deemed excessive and not justified, particularly when balancing the equities and considering the nature of the delay.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The delay, if any, cannot be attributed to any personal animosity of the officers manning the institution, as they have been discharging their statutory duties.

special_directions.special_directions: The appeal stands partly allowed with no order as to costs. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand consigned to records.
special_directions.interim_orders: The respondent (complainant) would be entitled to receive the amount under the impugned order along with interest at the rate of 9% per annum, and the remaining amount of interest and Rs. 10 Lakhs shall be detained in an account and kept in short term auto renewal fixed deposit.

case_identification.petitioner_name: THE COSMOS CO. OPERATIVE BANK LTD.
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 1565 of 2025 (@SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (C) NO. 11557/2019)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the validity and priority of mortgages created by deposit of title deeds and unregistered agreements of sale, specifically distinguishing between legal and equitable mortgages in the context of bank loans and the enforceability of charges against subsequent transferees without notice.

judgements.case_summary:
The case originated from a loan availed by original borrowers from Central Bank of India (Respondent No. 1) against an unregistered agreement of sale for a flat. Upon default, the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT) held borrowers liable but found Central Bank failed to prove mortgage. The Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal (DRAT) allowed Central Bank's appeal. The appellant, The Cosmos Co-operative Bank Ltd., also granted a loan against an unregistered agreement of sale and a share certificate for the same flat, claiming first charge. The High Court rejected Cosmos Bank's writ petition, affirming DRAT, on the grounds that Cosmos Bank's mortgage was subsequent and lacked valid title deeds.

The appellant argued that Central Bank's mortgage was invalid as an unregistered agreement of sale does not create any interest in property. It contended its own mortgage was valid due to the deposit of a share certificate, which constitutes a legal mortgage. The respondent maintained its first charge.

The Supreme Court analyzed the distinction between legal and equitable mortgages. It reiterated that an unregistered agreement of sale does not create interest in immovable property. The court clarified that a mortgage by deposit of title deeds under Section 58(f) of the Transfer of Property Act is a legal mortgage, while an equitable mortgage (not meeting Section 58 requirements) is a 'charge' under Section 100, which is a right in personam. The court found Central Bank's interest to be an equitable mortgage or charge, as it was based on unregistered agreements of sale. The appellant, having received a share certificate, had a stronger claim. Crucially, Central Bank failed to bring its equitable charge to the notice of the appellant.

Consequently, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's order. It ruled that Central Bank's equitable mortgage was not enforceable against the appellant due to lack of notice. The amount of Rs. 51 lakh in escrow, with interest, was directed to be disbursed to the appellant bank.

petitioner_key_arguments: The first mortgage created in favour of Central Bank of India was invalid or had no force in law because it was based on an unregistered agreement of sale, which does not confer any right, title, or interest in property.
The appellant's mortgage was valid as it involved the deposit of a share certificate of ownership, which has the effect of conveyance of title.
The appellant bank should have the first charge over the mortgaged property.
respondent_key_arguments: The Central Bank of India had the first charge over the mortgaged property.
The High Court's findings regarding the validity and priority of the mortgages were correct.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments prevailed. The court accepted that an unregistered agreement of sale does not create interest in property, rendering the Central Bank's mortgage an equitable charge (right in personam). The court found the appellant's mortgage, supported by a share certificate, to be a legal mortgage by deposit of title deeds. Crucially, the Central Bank's failure to bring its equitable charge to the notice of the appellant bank meant it was not enforceable against the appellant.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned order passed by the High Court is set aside. The amount of Rs. 51 lakh lying deposited with the DRT in an escrow account, along with interest, is to be disbursed in favour of the appellant bank.

In contrast, the appellant bank's mortgage, supported by a share certificate, could be considered a legal mortgage by deposit of title deeds under Section 58(f) of the Transfer of Property Act. Since the Central Bank failed to bring its equitable charge to the notice of the appellant bank, its charge could not be enforced against the appellant, especially given the appellant's legal mortgage.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The judgment extensively discusses the historical and legal evolution of equitable mortgages, distinguishing between English law and Indian law, where a mortgage by deposit of title deeds is a legal mortgage. It emphasizes the importance of registration for providing public notice of transactions involving immovable property and protecting against fraud. The court also noted that while the concept of equitable mortgage has a place in Indian jurisprudence as a 'charge' under Section 100 TPA, it is a right in personam and not enforceable against subsequent transferees without notice.

case_identification.petitioner_name: THE GENERAL MANAGER BUSINESS NETWORK PLANNING (RETAIL) BHARAT PETROLEUM CORPORATION LIMITED & ANR.
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (Arising out of SLP(C) No.7845 of 2024)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns an appeal against a High Court judgment regarding the grant of a retail outlet dealership of Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL) to the respondent, specifically challenging the High Court's direction to consider the respondent's application under Group 1 despite her initial application being under Group 2.

judgements.case_summary:
The case involves an appeal by Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL) against a High Court judgment concerning the grant of a retail outlet dealership. The respondent, P. Soundarya, applied for a dealership under Group 2, but later claimed this was a mistake and sought reclassification to Group 1, asserting she possessed the necessary land. BPCL rejected her request, citing strict application guidelines that prohibit editing details post-registration and emphasize that category is determined by the applicant's declaration and supporting documents.

Following multiple writ petitions by the respondent, the High Court directed BPCL to consider her application under Group 1. BPCL appealed this decision to the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court, emphasizing judicial restraint in contractual matters involving State instrumentalities, held that intervention is warranted only in cases of clear arbitrariness, mala fides, or irrationality, not mere sympathy. It noted that the application process required diligent submission of details and supporting documents, making an incorrect group selection more than a simple error. The Court found that the respondent was aware of the conditions and took a chance by applying under Group 2. It also highlighted the "Public Trust" doctrine applicable to public sector undertakings.

The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court erred in directing a category change, as BPCL's rules provided no such flexibility. Consequently, the appeal was allowed, and the High Court's judgment was set aside. The Supreme Court directed BPCL to proceed with the allotment process according to its rules and regulations. The Court also criticized the respondent for engaging in prolonged and unjustified litigation, which delayed the project and wasted judicial resources.

petitioner_key_arguments: Application guidelines require diligent filling of details, with no scope for editing after registration.
Category is determined by the applicant's declaration and supporting documents.
The respondent's application under Group 2 was not a mere error but a conscious choice, as it required specific documents for Group 1.
The High Court erred in directing a category change, as rules provide no leeway for it.
Interference by Writ Courts in contractual matters should be limited to cases of clear arbitrariness, not sympathy.
Prolonged litigation by the respondent was unjustified and prejudiced public interest.
respondent_key_arguments: Her initial Group 2 classification was a mistake.
She possessed the requisite land for Group 1.
BPCL, as a State instrumentality, should have extended a "helping hand" and guided her application, especially as the advertisement was for the Scheduled Caste Category.
The High Court's direction to consider her under Group 1 was reasonable, especially if other candidates were ineligible.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Supreme Court accepted the petitioner's arguments regarding the strict adherence to application guidelines, the lack of scope for category change, and the limited scope of judicial interference in contractual matters.

outcome.relief_granted: The High Court's judgment and order were set aside. BPCL was allowed to proceed with the allotment process/formalities in accordance with its Rules and Regulations.

case_identification.petitioner_name: THE GENERAL MANAGER PERSONNEL SYNDICATE BANK & ORS
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 6327 OF 2024

case_details.subject_matter: Disciplinary action against a bank branch manager for financial irregularities and misappropriation, and the proportionality of the penalty of dismissal.

judgements.case_summary: The respondent, a branch manager at Syndicate Bank, was dismissed from service following a disciplinary inquiry that found him guilty of fraudulent debits, misappropriation of funds, and other irregularities between 2007 and 2008. The High Court (Single Judge and Division Bench) subsequently set aside the dismissal, citing violations of natural justice and a lack of evidence. The appellants (Syndicate Bank) challenged this decision in the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court found that the High Court erred in concluding 'no evidence' as the respondent had admitted to the allegations in written communications and documentary evidence was available. The Court also reiterated that criminal acquittal does not affect disciplinary proceedings and that the inquiry was fair. However, considering the respondent's unblemished record of 21 years, the pressure of work he faced, and the fact that the financial loss caused to the bank had been reimbursed, the Supreme Court deemed the penalty of dismissal disproportionate. The Court restored the finding of misconduct but modified the penalty to a minor one: reduction to a lower stage in the time scale of pay for one year without cumulative effect and without affecting his pension. It also directed the restoration of necessary retiral dues.

petitioner_key_arguments: The respondent admitted the transactions during vigilance investigation and disciplinary inquiry.
The case was based on admitted documentary evidence and statements of customers, making further witness examination unnecessary.
Branch managers of banks are expected to maintain higher standards of honesty and conduct.
Acquittal in a criminal case is irrelevant to disciplinary inquiry as the standard of proof differs.
89 documents were produced, and the respondent cross-examined the investigating officer, indicating a fair inquiry.
The respondent's admission and the recovery of amounts after vigilance investigation proved misappropriation.
There was no perversity in the findings of the disciplinary inquiry, and the High Court should not have interfered.
respondent_key_arguments: All alleged misappropriated amounts and excess payments were recovered, making good the loss to the bank.
The bank had initially closed the issue with a warning letter in 2010, implying disciplinary proceedings should not have been initiated later.
It was a case of 'no evidence' against the respondent.
The respondent had a clean record from 1985 to 2007.
Mistakes occurred due to immense pressure of work, including renewing over 4,700 SKCC accounts in 60 days and political pressure.
The powers of the Disciplinary Authority must be exercised subject to principles of propriety and fair play.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the disciplinary inquiry was valid, misconduct was established based on admissions and documentary evidence, and the High Court erred in finding 'no evidence.' However, the Court also considered factors raised by the respondent, such as his unblemished record and the recovery of funds, to modify the penalty, thereby partially accepting the argument for proportionality.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned judgments and orders of the High Court are quashed and set aside. The finding recorded in the disciplinary inquiry that the misconduct on the part of the respondent was established is restored. The order of penalty is modified, directing that the respondent shall be subjected to a minor penalty under Regulation 4(e) of the Disciplinary Regulations by reducing him to a lower stage in the time scale of pay for a period of one year, without cumulative effect and not adversely affecting his pension. Necessary retiral dues, if any, are to be restored/paid to the respondent within four months from today.

While misconduct was established through admissions and documentary evidence, the penalty of dismissal was disproportionate given the respondent's unblemished service record, the pressure of work, and the recovery of financial losses, warranting a modified, minor penalty.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: Judicial review is not an appeal from a decision but a review of the manner in which the decision is made. A bank officer is required to exercise higher standards of honesty and integrity. Acquittal in a criminal case is no ground to exonerate a delinquent in disciplinary proceedings as the standard of proof differs in these proceedings.

case_identification.respondent_name: THE SECRETARY, WORTH TRUST WORKERS UNION
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 [@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CIVIL) NO. 20474 OF 2019]

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the applicability of the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965, to a trust engaged in commercial activities and its liability to pay bonus to its workmen, specifically addressing the trust's claim for exemption under Section 32(v)(a) and (c) of the Act.

judgements.case_summary: The Management of Worth Trust, originally a charitable trust for rehabilitating leprosy-cured and differently-abled persons, has been engaged in commercial activities since 1985, manufacturing automobile parts and industrial machinery, generating profits. The Worth Trust Workers Union raised an industrial dispute in 1998, demanding bonus and ex-gratia for 1996-97. The Industrial Disputes Tribunal awarded 8.33% bonus and ex-gratia, which the High Court upheld, with a modification that ex-gratia already paid should be deducted from the bonus. The appellant trust argued for exemption from the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965, under Section 32(v)(a) as an institution like the Indian Red Cross Society, or under Section 32(v)(c) as an institution not for profit. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, affirming that the trust's significant commercial activities and its severance of ties with the Swedish Red Cross Society (by 1989 amendment) negate its claim for exemption. The Court held that the workmen, being employed in factories, are covered by the Bonus Act, and the trust's profit-making commercial venture makes the Act applicable. The Court directed the trust to pay bonus from 1996-97 onwards within one month.

petitioner_key_arguments: The Bonus Act does not apply as its employees are to be treated as employees of 'the Indian Red Cross Society' or an 'institution of a like nature', thus exempted under Section 32(v)(a) of the Bonus Act.
Alternatively, it can be treated as an institution 'established not for the purposes of profit', thus exempted under Section 32(v)(c) of the Bonus Act.
The trust has already been paying ex-gratia as a measure of charity, which should be a ground to avoid paying statutory bonus.
respondent_key_arguments: Workmen are engaged in manufacturing activities in factories run by the appellant.
They fall within the definition of 'workmen' and 'employee' under the Factories Act, 1948, and the Bonus Act.
The Bonus Act is applicable to them, entitling them to bonus, as per Section 1(3)(a) of the Bonus Act.
The trust's commercial activities and profit generation make the Bonus Act applicable.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the respondent's arguments that the trust's commercial activities and profit generation, coupled with its severance from the Swedish Red Cross Society, make the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965, applicable to its workmen, and the trust is not entitled to exemption under Section 32(v)(a) or (c).

outcome.relief_granted: The appellant (Management of Worth Trust) is directed to pay bonus to its workmen, as per provisions of the Bonus Act, from the year 1996-1997 till date, within one month of the order.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: An organization, even if initially charitable, becomes subject to the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965, if it engages in significant commercial, profit-generating activities and operates factories falling under the Factories Act, 1948. Exemption under Section 32(v)(a) or (c) of the Bonus Act does not apply if the organization has severed ties with its original charitable affiliation and operates primarily as a commercial venture, regardless of whether profits are reinvested in charitable work.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court noted that the payment of ex-gratia, while admitted by the appellant, cannot be a ground to avoid paying statutory bonus.

special_directions.special_directions: The appellant is directed to pay bonus to its workmen, as per provisions of the Bonus Act, from the year 1996-1997 till date, within one month of this order.

case_identification.petitioner_name: THE MUNICIPAL CORPORATION OF GREATER MUMBAI & ORS.
case_identification.respondent_name: CENTURY TEXTILES AND INDUSTRIES LIMITED & ORS.
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO.6667 OF 2023

case_details.subject_matter: Appeal against a High Court judgment directing the Municipal Corporation to execute a formal conveyance of a plot of land, involving interpretation of lease conditions, statutory provisions, and the issue of delay and laches.

judgements.case_summary:
The Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai (appellant) appealed against a Bombay High Court judgment dated 14.03.2022, which directed the appellant to execute a formal conveyance of a plot of land (C.S. No.1546 of Lower Parel Division) in favour of Century Textiles and Industries Limited (respondent No.1). The case originated from a 1918 application by the respondent under the Poorer Classes Accommodation Scheme (PCAS) for constructing dwellings for workers. A 28-year lease for Block-A was granted in 1928, expiring in 1955. The respondent continued possession without seeking conveyance for 51 years. In 2006, a legal notice was issued by the respondent, followed by a writ petition in 2016, 61 years after the lease expired.

The appellant argued that the writ petition was barred by delay and laches, and that a harmonious reading of Sections 48(a) and 51(2) of the 1925 Act did not impose a mandatory obligation to convey the land, especially since the respondent had not paid the costs for conveyance. The respondent contended that the lease and statutory provisions mandated conveyance, and that a vested right could not be divested by delay.

The Supreme Court analyzed the statutory provisions and the lease deed, concluding that neither imposed a mandatory obligation for conveyance. It emphasized a harmonious construction of Sections 48(a) and 51(2), where conveyance is contingent upon lease terms and statutory prerequisites, including payment of costs. The Court also found significant delay and laches on the part of the respondent, noting that no legal action was taken for 51 years, and a statutory remedy with a 6-month limitation period was not pursued after a 2006 notice. The High Court's finding that there was no delay was deemed unsustainable.

The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment, and dismissed the writ petition, ruling that the respondent had no vested right to conveyance and was guilty of inordinate delay and laches.

petitioner_key_arguments: The writ petition was highly barred by delay and laches, as Respondent No.1 took no legal action for 61 years after the lease expired in 1955.

After issuing a legal notice in 2006, Respondent No.1 failed to file a suit within the 6-month limitation period prescribed by Section 527 of the 1888 Act, and a writ petition cannot bypass this limitation.
Section 51(2) ('shall convey') of the 1925 Act must be read harmoniously with Section 48(a) (lessee leaves premises in good repair) to mean 'may convey', not a mandatory obligation.
The phrase 'at his cost' in Section 51(2) implies that the lessee must bear separate costs for conveyance, which Respondent No.1 failed to do.
Neither the Board Resolution No. 325 nor the lease deed explicitly stated an obligation to convey Block-A upon lease expiration.
Internal notings or communications within the Corporation do not confer legal rights unless approved by the Competent Authority and duly communicated.
respondent_key_arguments: The lease deed and the accepted request for alteration of Scheme No. 51 conferred a right to conveyance upon Respondent No.1 at the expiration of the lease.
The provisions of Section 51(2) of the 1925 Act, using the word 'shall', make the vesting and execution of conveyance mandatory and cannot be contracted out of.
Section 51 of the 1925 Act is a special provision that should prevail over the general provision of Section 48(a) of the same Act.
Respondent No.1, having discharged all its obligations under the scheme, was entitled to the conveyance of the land and building.
A vested right to conveyance, once accrued, cannot be divested by subsequent conduct, including any alleged delay or laches.
The appellants themselves recognized and acknowledged the ownership rights of Respondent No.1 through internal correspondence and notings.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments regarding the harmonious construction of Sections 48(a) and 51(2) of the 1925 Act, concluding that there was no mandatory obligation to convey the land without further payment. Crucially, the court also upheld the petitioner's argument that the respondent's writ petition was barred by inordinate delay and laches, as no legal action was taken for 51 years after the lease expired, and the statutory remedy was not pursued within the prescribed limitation period.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal was allowed. The judgment and order dated 14.03.2022 passed by the Bombay High Court was set aside. The Writ Petition No. 295 of 2017 filed by the Respondent No.1 was dismissed.

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the entitlement of teachers in engineering and technical institutes to revised pay scales and re-designation as Associate Professors under the 6th Central Pay Commission, specifically examining the mandatory Ph.D. qualification prescribed by AICTE notifications.

judgements.case_summary: The Civil Appeals challenge orders of the Bombay High Court directing the appellant-Society to extend revised pay scales under the 6th Central Pay Commission to respondent-teachers. The core issue is the eligibility of these teachers for higher pay scales and re-designation as Associate Professors, particularly concerning the mandatory Ph.D. qualification prescribed by AICTE. AICTE notifications from 2000, 2005, and 2010 made Ph.D. a mandatory qualification for Assistant Professors, with a seven-year grace period. The appellant argued that many respondent-teachers lacked this qualification and were thus ineligible. The High Court had relied on a previous judgment (Sanjay Shrirangrao Surwase), which the appellant contended was distinguishable. The Supreme Court analyzed the AICTE notifications, including the 2010 notification's Clause (ix) and the 2016 clarificatory notification. It held that only teachers appointed prior to 15.03.2000 (when Ph.D. was not essential) or those appointed after 15.03.2000 who acquired Ph.D. within seven years would be eligible for the benefits. The Court partly allowed the appeal, directing the appellant to release higher pay scales with interest to specific teachers appointed before 15.03.2000 and one teacher who acquired a Ph.D., while denying benefits to others who failed to acquire a Ph.D. within the stipulated time.

petitioner_key_arguments: Respondent-teachers lack the requisite Ph.D. qualification as per AICTE norms, which is mandatory for higher pay scales and re-designation as Associate Professors.
The decision in Sanjay Shrirangrao Surwase is distinguishable because the petitioners in that case were qualified, unlike the present respondents.
The 2016 AICTE clarificatory notification does not have statutory status and merely reiterates the existing position of law from the 2010 notification.

The phrase 'incumbent Assistant Professors and incumbent Lecturers' in the 2010 notification refers only to those with essential qualifications, including Ph.D., or those appointed prior to 15.03.2000 without Ph.D.
respondent_key_arguments: The powers vested with AICTE are statutory under Section 23 of the 1987 Act.

The AICTE clarification of 04.01.2016 has statutory status, and its Clause 53 implies that the only consequence of non-completion of Ph.D. within seven years is the stoppage of increments, not denial of higher pay scales or re-designation.
The High Court's decision was correct in granting relief based on the Sanjay Shrirangrao Surwase case, as there was no difference in qualifications between the two batches of petitioners.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court largely accepted the petitioner's argument that Ph.D. qualification was mandatory for higher pay scales and re-designation for teachers appointed after 15.03.2000, unless acquired within the stipulated seven years. It also clarified the scope of 'incumbent' teachers. However, it sided with the respondents for those appointed prior to 15.03.2000 and one who acquired Ph.D.

outcome.relief_granted: Higher pay scales with 7.5% annual interest on arrears (to be increased to 15% if not paid within four weeks) granted to teachers appointed prior to 15.03.2000 and one specific teacher (Dr. Madhavi Ajay Pradhan) who acquired Ph.D. Benefits denied to other private respondents who failed to acquire Ph.D. within seven years.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The Court held that Ph.D. qualification was a mandatory requirement for Assistant Professors to be eligible for higher pay scales and re-designation as Associate Professors under AICTE notifications, particularly for those appointed after 15.03.2000, unless they acquired the Ph.D. within the stipulated seven years. Teachers appointed before 15.03.2000, when Ph.D. was not essential, were entitled to the benefits.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court emphasized that expert bodies like AICTE are best equipped to decide on academic matters and qualifications, and courts should generally not interfere unless the prescribed qualifications are arbitrary or perverse. It also noted that the law itself creates two classes of Assistant Professors (with and without Ph.D.) and that denying benefits to unqualified teachers maintains the quality of teaching.

case_identification.petitioner_name: THE SECRETARY TO GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH & FAMILY WELFARE & ANR.
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 4356 OF 2025 ARISING OUT OF SLP (C) No. 2793 OF 2023

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns whether the transfer or reappointment of a government employee impacts their seniority in the new post, and if such seniority is contingent upon whether the transfer was made in public interest or at the employee's own request.

judgements.case_summary:
The respondent, K.C. Devaki, a Staff Nurse, requested a cadre change to First Division Assistant on medical grounds due to bronchitis. She explicitly consented to be placed below the last person in the new cadre. The government approved this transfer in 1989. In 2007, when the final seniority list was released, she challenged it before the Karnataka Administrative Tribunal, claiming her seniority should be from her initial appointment as Staff Nurse in 1979, not from the date of transfer to First Division Assistant in 1989. The Tribunal and subsequently the High Court allowed her plea, treating the transfer on medical grounds as being in 'public interest' and granting her seniority from 1979.

The petitioner (the State Government) appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that the transfer was at the respondent's request and with her explicit consent to lose seniority, as per Rule 16 of the Karnataka Civil Services (General Recruitment) Rules, 1977, and Rule 6 of the Karnataka Government Servants (Seniority) Rules, 1957. The Supreme Court analyzed the distinction between transfers made in public interest (where seniority is retained) and transfers made at an employee's request (where seniority is lost). The Court found that the respondent's transfer, despite being on medical grounds, was initiated by her request and accepted with the condition of losing seniority. The Court held that the High Court erred by blurring this distinction and by not properly applying the relevant rules and the respondent's consent. Citing previous judgments, the Supreme Court upheld the principle that an employee transferred at their own request, even for medical reasons, and with consent to lose seniority, will have their seniority fixed from the date of transfer to the new post. Consequently, the appeal was allowed, and the High Court's order was set aside.

petitioner_key_arguments: The transfer of the respondent was made at her own request, not in public interest.
The respondent explicitly consented to be placed below the last person in the new cadre, thereby foregoing her previous seniority.
Rule 16 of the 1977 Recruitment Rules and Rule 6 of the 1957 Seniority Rules govern such transfers and seniority fixation, mandating loss of seniority for transfers made at an employee's request.
The High Court erred by treating a transfer on medical grounds (at employee's request) as a transfer in public interest.
respondent_key_arguments: The transfer on medical grounds should be treated as a transfer made in public interest.
Seniority should be reckoned from the initial date of appointment as Staff Nurse (1979), not from the date of transfer to First Division Assistant (1989).
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the transfer was at the respondent's request and that she had consented to lose seniority, which is governed by specific service rules distinguishing it from transfers made in public interest.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeal is allowed, and the order passed by the High Court of Karnataka dated 25.10.2021 in W.P. No. 42244 of 2019 is set aside. The government's final seniority list dated 01.10.2007, granting seniority from 19.04.1989, is upheld.

acts_cited: Rule 16(a)(iii) of the Karnataka Civil Services (General Recruitment) Rules, 1977
Karnataka Civil Services (Service and Kannada Language Examinations) Rules, 1974
precedents_cited: State of Himachal Pradesh and Ors. v. Raj Kumar and Ors., (2023) 3 SCC 773
State of Karnataka v. Sri. K. Seetharamulu
Geetha V.M. v. Rethnasenan K. 2025 SCC OnLine SC 35

M K Jagadeesh v. The Registrar General, High Court of Karnataka
Writ Appeal No. 1263 of 2007 dated 25.07.2007

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that when a government employee's transfer to a different cadre is made at their own request, even on medical grounds, and they explicitly consent to be placed below the junior-most employee in the new cadre, their seniority in the new post will be reckoned from the date of transfer, not from their original appointment. This is distinct from transfers made in public interest, where original seniority may be retained, and is governed by specific service rules that differentiate between these two types of transfers.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that the fundamental principle underlying the relationship between the State and its employee is that it is governed by administrative rules, rather than contractual agreements, and that the State has the power to unilaterally amend service rules. It also emphasized the importance of drawing a clear distinction between transfers made in public interest and those made at the request of the officer, as their purpose, procedure, and consequences are distinct.

case_identification.petitioner_name: The State, Central Bureau of Investigation.
case_identification.case_number: Criminal Appeal No. of 2024 (@ SLP (Crl.) No. 10737 of 2023) and (@ SLP (Crl.) No. 10038 of 2023)

petitioner_advocates: Shri M. Nataraj, learned Additional Solicitor General

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the jurisdiction of the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) to register First Information Reports (FIRs) and conduct investigations in the newly formed State of Andhra Pradesh after its bifurcation, specifically regarding the requirement of state government consent under the Delhi Special Police Establishment Act, 1946, and the jurisdiction of Special Courts under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988.

judgements.case_summary:
The case involves two criminal appeals filed by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) challenging a common judgment of the High Court of Andhra Pradesh. The High Court had quashed FIRs and subsequent proceedings in two cases (CC No.13/2022 and CC No.15/2022) against A. Satish Kumar and another, who were Central Government employees accused of corruption under the PC Act. The offenses occurred in Kurnool and Ananthapur districts, which remained in Andhra Pradesh after the 2014 bifurcation, but the FIRs were registered by CBI, ACB Hyderabad (in Telangana).

The respondents argued that the CBI lacked jurisdiction to register FIRs and investigate without specific consent from the newly formed State of Andhra Pradesh, and that the CBI Court in Hyderabad lacked jurisdiction to try the cases. They contended that the proceedings were vitiated due to the absence of consent and proper notification for a Special Court.

The Supreme Court, however, found that the High Court erred. It emphasized the continuity of laws after the bifurcation of Andhra Pradesh, as clarified by Circular Memo No.13665/SR/2014, which stated that all laws applicable to the undivided state would continue to apply to the new states. The Court relied on precedents (Kanwal Tanuj, Fertico Marketing) to hold that for Central Government employees committing offenses under a Central Act like the PC Act, specific state government consent under Section 6 of the DSPE Act might not be necessary, especially when the CBI is investigating its own employees. The Court concluded that the High Court's reasoning was flawed, and the proceedings were not vitiated. Consequently, the appeals were allowed, and the criminal cases were restored for trial.

petitioner_key_arguments: The High Court failed to consider Circular Memo No.13665/SR/2014 dated 26.05.2014, which clarified that all 'laws' applicable to the undivided State of Andhra Pradesh would continue to apply to the new States (Telangana and Andhra Pradesh) after bifurcation.
Even after bifurcation, the CBI, Hyderabad office retained its identity as 'Special Police Force'.
Consent for CBI was present at the time of FIR registration, as per Section 6 of the DSPE Act.
The High Court erred in holding that G.O.M.S. Nos.158, 67, 168, and 109 extended general consent only to the State of Andhra Pradesh.
For Central Government employees committing offenses under a Central Act (PC Act), consent from the State Government is not always required, irrespective of the place of posting.
The transfer of cases from Additional CBI Court, Vishakhapatnam to Kurnool was in accordance with law.
respondent_key_arguments: The A.P. Re-Organisation Act, 2014, created two new states, requiring fresh permission from the Government of Andhra Pradesh for CBI to register and investigate FIRs within its limits under the DSPE Act.
The subject FIRs were registered by CBI, ACB, Hyderabad (Telangana) for offenses in Kurnool and Ananthapur (Andhra Pradesh) without express permission from Andhra Pradesh.
The entire investigation and filing of chargesheets are vitiated due to lack of consent.
The Court at Hyderabad lacked jurisdiction to entertain the cases.
A specific notification was required under the PC Act to designate a Judge for Special Courts, which was absent after 02.06.2014.

The State of Andhra Pradesh did not accord consent for prosecution of Central Government servants until December 2017, thus the Special Court for CBI Cases, Hyderabad, could not have entertained the cases.
The inherent lack of jurisdiction vitiated the entire proceedings.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments regarding the continuity of laws after state bifurcation, the interpretation of the DSPE Act concerning consent for Central Government employees, and the validity of the CBI's actions were accepted by the Court.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned common judgment dated 13.04.2023 passed by the High Court in WP No.26990 of 2021 and 5441 of 2022 is set aside. Criminal Case Nos.13 of 2022 and 15 of 2022 are restored to the files of the Court of Special Judge for CBI Cases, Kurnool.

precedents_cited: State of Punjab and Others v. Balbir Singh & Ors.1
C.B.I., A.H.D., Patna v. Braj Bhushan Prasad2
Fertico Marketing and Investment Private Limited and Ors. v. Central Bureau of Investigation and Anr.3
Commissioner of Commercial Taxes, Ranchi and Ors. v. Swarn Rekha Cokes and Coals (P) Ltd. and Ors4
Kanwal Tanuj v. State of Bihar and Ors.5
2020 SCC OnLine SC 395

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core reasoning is that the High Court erred in its interpretation of the continuity of laws and the requirement of state consent for CBI investigations. The Court held that the Circular Memo dated 26.05.2014, issued under Section 3 of the A.P. Re-Organisation Act, ensured that all 'laws' applicable to the undivided State of Andhra Pradesh continued to apply to the new States, including government orders related to CBI jurisdiction. Furthermore, for Central Government employees accused of offenses under a Central Act like the PC Act, consent from the State Government under Section 6 of the DSPE Act is not always necessary, especially when the CBI is investigating its own employees or the offense is committed in a Union Territory.

special_directions.special_directions: The trial Court shall continue with those cases against the respective first respondent in the captioned appeals.

case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO.2350 OF 2025

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the cancellation of a select list for the recruitment of 104 Constables in the Assam Forest PCCF AFPF by the State Government and the High Court's interference with that decision.

judgements.case_summary:
The case originated from a recruitment process for 104 Constables in the Assam Forest PCCF AFPF, initiated in 2014. A select list was prepared in May 2016, but the new government, which came to power in May 2016, cancelled it in July 2016, citing serious anomalies, including violations of reservation policy and disproportionate district representation, as detailed in a note by the Principal Chief Conservator of Forest (PCCF). The respondents, whose names were on the select list, challenged the cancellation in the Gauhati High Court. Both a single Judge and a Division Bench of the High Court allowed their writ petitions, holding that the alleged irregularities were curable and did not warrant the cancellation of the entire selection process. The State of Assam appealed to the Supreme Court.

The appellants (State) argued that empanelled candidates have no indefeasible right to appointment, and the government was justified in cancelling the process due to systemic irregularities. The respondents contended that the cancellation was based solely on the PCCF's note without a proper inquiry, no rules were violated, and any alleged reservation policy breach was limited and did not justify cancelling the entire list, invoking the doctrine of proportionality. The Supreme Court, after reviewing precedents, found that the irregularities highlighted by the PCCF were systemic and tainted the entire selection process, making the government's decision to cancel justified and not arbitrary or disproportionate. The Court distinguished previous cases where irregularities were minor or segregable. Consequently, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, quashed the High Court's judgments, and upheld the State's decision to cancel the select list. The State was granted liberty to initiate a fresh recruitment process, with a concession for the respondents to apply with age bar and minor physical/PET deficiencies waived.

petitioner_key_arguments: The writ petition should not have been entertained as empanelled candidates have no indefeasible right of appointment.
The Government was well within its right to cancel the process due to serious irregularities that tainted it.
The PCCF's note dated 4th July, 2016, provided sufficient justification for cancellation, based on meticulous examination of records.
The High Court erred in making directions that fall within the province of an appellate authority, not a judicial review court.
respondent_key_arguments: The cancellation order was based solely on alleged violation of reservation policy and court judgments, and no new reasons can be urged.
No rules were violated in preparing the select list as no rules were framed to govern the selection process at the time.
Cancellation was based solely on the PCCF's note without any inquiry into the alleged anomalies.
No unsuccessful candidate challenged the select list alleging corrupt practice or fraudulent activity.
Even if there was a violation of reservation policy, it was limited to 34 candidates, not justifying cancellation of the entire list (doctrine of proportionality).
Both the single Judge and Division Bench correctly found that alleged violations were curable defects that could be rectified without disturbing the selection process.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the appellants' arguments that systemic irregularities, including violations of reservation policy and disproportionate district representation, tainted the entire selection process, justifying the government's decision to cancel the select list as neither arbitrary nor disproportionate.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned judgments and orders of the High Court are quashed. The appellants are granted liberty to take forward the process of filling up 104 Constables by publishing a fresh advertisement. Respondents, if they choose to apply, shall have their age bar waived, as well as insignificant minor deficiencies in physical measurement and PET requirements. The PCCF may grant further relaxation as deemed fit and proper. The fresh process is to be initiated and concluded without any delay.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The court found that the selection process was marred by systemic irregularities, including violations of reservation policy, disproportionate district representation, and the inclusion of non-meritorious candidates, as detailed in the PCCF's note. These issues tainted the entire process, making the government's decision to cancel the select list justified and not arbitrary or disproportionate, thus warranting interference with the High Court's decision.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed that conducting recruitment processes based on executive orders without proper rules often leads to avoidable litigation and that it would be prudent to have recruitment rules and written examinations for public employment to ensure fairness and transparency. It also discussed the interplay between the Wednesbury unreasonableness test and the doctrine of proportionality.

special_directions.special_directions: The appellants are granted liberty to take forward the process of filling up 104 Constables in the AFPF by publishing a fresh advertisement. It is desirable that rules be framed for recruitment. If rules are not framed, the selection process should be taken forward in terms of administrative instructions placed in the public domain. The respondents, if they choose to apply in pursuance of such advertisement, shall be considered for appointment waiving their age bar as well as insignificant minor deficiencies in physical measurement and PET requirements (exercising power under Article 142). The PCCF may grant further relaxation. The fresh process is to be initiated and concluded without any delay.
special_directions.interim_orders: A single Judge of the High Court did not grant interim stay of the advertisement dated 14th April, 2017. The co-ordinate bench of the Supreme Court granted stay of operation of the High Court's judgment and order under assail till the next date of hearing.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS.1258-1259 OF 2015

case_details.subject_matter: The case involves appeals filed by the State of Chhattisgarh challenging a High Court judgment that acquitted two accused, Ashok Bhoi and Vikash Khubwani, in a kidnapping and murder case, primarily based on the insufficiency of circumstantial evidence.

judgements.case_summary:
The State of Chhattisgarh filed two appeals against a High Court judgment that acquitted Ashok Bhoi and Vikash Khubwani in a case involving the kidnapping and murder of Suhash. The prosecution's case was based entirely on circumstantial evidence, as there were no eyewitnesses. Key evidence included the testimony of PW-18, who claimed to have seen the deceased with Ashok Bhoi, and the recovery of blood-stained items at Ashok Bhoi's instance. The High Court had upheld the acquittal of Vikash Khubwani due to a lack of evidence and acquitted Ashok Bhoi, overturning his conviction by the Sessions Court.

The Supreme Court observed that for Vikash Khubwani, there was no evidence to connect him to the crime. For Ashok Bhoi, the Court found that the "last seen together" testimony of PW-18 alone was insufficient, especially since the STD-PCO person was not examined, and the recovery of items two days later did not inspire confidence. The Court reiterated that in circumstantial evidence cases, the chain of circumstances must be complete and point irresistibly to the accused's guilt, and suspicion cannot replace proof. While Section 106 of the Evidence Act shifts the burden to the accused if reliably proven to be "last seen together," the prosecution must first establish this fact, and the accused's failure to explain does not automatically lead to conviction without other clinching evidence. The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had correctly appreciated the evidence and legal position. Consequently, both appeals filed by the State were dismissed, upholding the acquittal of both accused.

petitioner_key_arguments: The High Court misappreciated the evidence on record and committed gross error in acquitting both the accused.
Reliance on circumstantial evidence, including the 'last seen together' theory (PW-18's testimony) and recovery of blood-stained items from Ashok Bhoi.
respondent_key_arguments: The circumstantial evidence presented by the prosecution was insufficient and unreliable.
The 'last seen together' theory was not adequately proven.
The recoveries made did not inspire confidence.
The prosecution failed to establish a complete chain of circumstances proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The respondent's arguments that the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt based on insufficient and unreliable circumstantial evidence prevailed.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: In a case based on circumstantial evidence, the prosecution must establish a complete chain of circumstances that leads to the irresistible conclusion of the accused's guilt, excluding any other hypothesis. While the 'last seen together' theory shifts the burden under Section 106 of the Evidence Act, the prosecution must first reliably prove this fact, and the accused's failure to explain alone is insufficient for conviction without other cogent and clinching evidence. Suspicion, however strong, cannot substitute proof.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: Justice cannot be made sterile on the plea that it is better to let hundred guilty escape than punish an innocent. Letting guilty escape on fanciful doubts is not doing justice according to law.
