constitutional_provisions: Article 141 of the Constitution

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The High Court committed a miscarriage of justice by allowing a second appeal ex parte without proper service on the appellant and, crucially, without framing any substantial questions of law as mandated by Section 100 CPC. Furthermore, the principle that fraud vitiates all judicial acts, coupled with the fact that dismissal of SLPs does not attract the doctrine of merger, allows for reconsideration of the matter despite previous dismissals.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court emphasized the fundamental imperative of Section 100 CPC, which requires a second appeal to be admitted and heard only on substantial questions of law, and that failure to do so renders the judgment patently illegal. It also reiterated that the principle of "finality of litigation" cannot be stretched to permit oppression by dishonest litigants, especially when fraud is alleged.

special_directions.special_directions: The parties are directed to appear before the High Court on 18.02.2025 without expecting separate notices. The High Court is requested to dispose of S.A. No.140/2016 by considering the respective contentions, additional pleadings, applications, and evidence, and after framing the substantial questions of law. Liberty is reserved to both sides to place additional evidence.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S). OF 2025 (Arising out of SLP(Crl.) No(s). 4297 of 2023)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the dissolution of a marriage on grounds of irretrievable breakdown, the legality of passport impounding, and the justification of extradition proceedings arising from a marital dispute and multiple legal cases filed by both parties.

judgements.case_summary:
This case involves a marital dispute between Vishal Shah (appellant) and Monalisha Gupta (respondent) that led to numerous legal proceedings and an order for the appellant's extradition. The couple married on 19th February 2018, moved to the USA, and separated after only 80 days, with both parties alleging domestic abuse. The respondent initiated multiple criminal and civil cases against the appellant and his family in India, leading to the impounding of the appellant's passport in 2018. When the appellant failed to appear in a Domestic Violence (DV) Act case, the Judicial Magistrate, Howrah, ordered the initiation of extradition proceedings. The High Court of Calcutta dismissed the appellant's revision against this order.

The appellant approached the Supreme Court, arguing that the marriage had irretrievably broken down, the respondent's actions were vindictive, and the impounding of his passport was illegal as he was not given a hearing. He also contended that personal presence is not mandatory in quasi-criminal DV Act proceedings. The respondent maintained that she was maltreated, her allegations were valid, and the appellant failed to comply with court directions.

The Supreme Court, exercising its powers under Article 142, found that the marriage had irretrievably broken down due to prolonged separation, multiple litigations, and lack of reconciliation. The Court also held that the impounding of the appellant's passport was ex-facie illegal due to a clear violation of natural justice, as he was not given an opportunity to be heard. Furthermore, the Court observed that personal presence is not required in DV Act proceedings unless there is a breach of a protection order. Consequently, the Court quashed the lower court orders, dissolved the marriage, directed the release of the appellant's passport, and ordered the closure of all pending cases between the parties. The appellant was directed to pay Rs. 25 lakhs as permanent alimony to the respondent.

petitioner_key_arguments: The marriage between the appellant and respondent has irretrievably broken down due to a very short cohabitation period (80 days), prolonged separation since May 2018, and numerous litigations filed by the respondent.
The respondent's actions, including filing multiple cases with similar allegations, reflect a vindictive attitude and an abuse of the legal process.
The impounding of the appellant's passport by authorities was illegal as it was done without granting him an opportunity to be heard, violating principles of natural justice.
Personal presence of the appellant is not required in quasi-criminal proceedings under the DV Act, as they do not entail penal consequences unless a protection order is breached.
The appellant is willing to pay a reasonable lump sum as permanent alimony for an amicable settlement.
respondent_key_arguments: The respondent was maltreated and unlawfully turned out of the matrimonial home due to the appellant's and his family's greed for dowry.
None of the cases filed by the respondent are barred by limitation, and the allegations disclose a valid cause of action.

The appellant failed to comply with the Family Court's directions after being granted conditional permission to travel abroad, and sent derogatory e-mails, justifying the Magistrate's order for extradition.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the marriage had irretrievably broken down, justifying dissolution under Article 142. It also agreed that the impounding of the appellant's passport was illegal due to a violation of natural justice and that personal presence was not strictly required in the DV Act proceedings for the purpose of initiating extradition.

outcome.relief_granted: The Supreme Court quashed the orders of the Judicial Magistrate, Howrah (dated 15th September 2022) and the High Court of Calcutta (dated 25th January 2023). The marriage between the appellant and respondent was dissolved on the ground of irretrievable breakdown. All criminal cases/DV Act complaints and civil cases pending between the respondent and the appellant and his family members were closed. The appellant was directed to deposit Rs. 25,00,000/- (Rupees Twenty-Five Lakhs only) as permanent alimony to the respondent within two months. The passport of the appellant was ordered to be released by the concerned authorities within one week.

acts_cited: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
precedents_cited: Shilpa Sailesh v. Varun Sreenivasan (2023 SCC OnLine SC 544)
Kiran Jyot Maini v. Anish Pramod Patel (12 2024 SCC OnLine SC 1724)
Rinku Baheti v Sandesh Sharda (13 2024 SCC OnLine SC 3801)
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India and Anr. (16 (1978) 1 SCC 248)
Rajesh Sharma v. State of U.P. (17 (2018) 10 SCC 472)
Rajnesh v. Neha (14 (2021) 2 SCC 324)
Parvin Kumar Jain v. Anju Jain (15 2024 SCC OnLine SC 3678)
constitutional_provisions: Article 142 of the Constitution of India

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The Court found that the marriage had irretrievably broken down, evidenced by a short cohabitation, prolonged separation, and multiple litigations, making reconciliation impossible. The impounding of the appellant's passport was deemed illegal due to the violation of natural justice principles, as no opportunity to be heard was provided. The Court also clarified that personal presence is not mandatory in quasi-criminal DV Act proceedings unless a protection order is breached, thus rendering the extradition order unjustified.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that the respondent's actions reflected a vindictive attitude and were an abuse of the legal process. It reiterated the importance of personal liberty and the right to a passport, emphasizing that impounding should not be routine and must follow due process. The Court also highlighted that the absence of children weighed in favor of dissolving the marriage.

special_directions.special_directions: The Court directed the appellant to deposit Rs. 25,00,000/- as permanent alimony within two months, to be disbursed to the respondent within two weeks thereafter. An undertaking to this effect must be filed within two weeks. If the respondent refuses the amount, it shall be repaid to the appellant. The passport of the appellant shall be released by the authorities within one week.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 @ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRL) NO.1104 OF 2022

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the quashing of proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act against a director of a corporate debtor, where a moratorium under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code was imposed before the cause of action for the NI Act offense arose.

judgements.case_summary: The Supreme Court heard an appeal challenging the Punjab and Haryana High Court's dismissal of a petition to quash proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (NI Act). The appellant, a director of M/s Xalta Food and Beverages Private Limited (corporate debtor), had issued cheques to the respondent, M/s Shakti Trading Company, which were dishonoured on 07.07.2018. A legal notice under Section 138 NI Act was issued on 06.08.2018. Crucially, insolvency proceedings against the corporate debtor commenced, and a moratorium under Section 14 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC) was imposed on 25.07.2018, *before* the cause of action for the NI Act offense fully matured (15 days after demand notice, i.e., 21.08.2018). The appellant argued that with the moratorium in place and an Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) appointed on 25.07.2018, the management of the corporate debtor vested in the IRP, suspending the board of directors' powers under Section 17 IBC. Consequently, the appellant lost the capacity to make the payment, rendering the Section 138 proceedings unsustainable. The High Court had dismissed the appellant's petition, relying on P. Mohan Raj v. M/S Shah Brothers Ispat Pvt. Ltd., which held that the IBC moratorium applies only to the corporate debtor, not to natural persons. The Supreme Court distinguished P. Mohan Raj, noting that in that case, the cause of action under the NI Act arose *before* the moratorium. In the present case, the cause of action arose *after* the moratorium and the IRP's appointment. The Court reasoned that once the IRP takes over, the director cannot fulfill the payment demand, as all corporate debtor accounts are under the IRP's instructions. Therefore, the High Court erred. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's order and quashing the summoning order and the complaint case against the appellant.

petitioner_key_arguments: Moratorium under Section 14 IBC was imposed on 25.07.2018, prior to the cause of action for the Section 138 NI Act offense.
The cause of action for the Section 138 NI Act offense arose after the moratorium was imposed (demand notice on 06.08.2018, 15-day period ending 21.08.2018).
Upon IRP appointment on 25.07.2018, the appellant, as director, lost management control and powers of the board were suspended under Section 17 IBC.
It was impossible for the appellant to repay the amount as bank accounts were under the IRP's instructions.
The High Court erred in relying on P. Mohan Raj as the facts were distinguishable, where the cause of action arose before the moratorium.
respondent_key_arguments: The High Court's reasoning, relying on P. Mohan Raj, that moratorium under Section 14 IBC applies only to the corporate debtor, not to natural persons (directors) under Section 141 NI Act.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The petitioner's arguments prevailed, specifically that the cause of action for the NI Act offense arose after the IBC moratorium was imposed, and the director had lost control of the corporate debtor's affairs and funds due to the IRP's appointment under Section 17 IBC, making it impossible to fulfill the demand.

outcome.relief_granted: The impugned order dated 21.12.2021 of the High Court is set aside. The summoning order dated 07.09.2018 and complaint case no.15580/2018, pending before the Chief Judicial Magistrate Court, Chandigarh, filed by the respondent against the appellant, are quashed.

acts_cited: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 (54 of 2002)
precedents_cited: P. Mohan Raj v. M/S Shah Brothers Ispat Pvt. Ltd. (2021) 6 SCC 258
Jugesh Sehgal v. Shamsher Singh Gogi (2009) 14 SCC 683

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: When a moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC is imposed on a corporate debtor, and an Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) takes over the management under Section 17, suspending the powers of the board of directors, proceedings under Section 138 of the NI Act cannot be initiated or continued against the director if the cause of action for the NI Act offense arises *after* the imposition of the moratorium, as the director loses the capacity to make payment.

special_directions.special_directions: Pending application(s), if any, stand(s) disposed of.

case_identification.respondent_name: THE STATE OF UTTARAKHAND AND OTHERS
case_identification.case_number: TRANSFER PETITION (C) NOS. 42-43 OF 2025

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the eligibility of applicants holding an 18-month D.El.Ed. qualification from NIOS (Open and Distance Learning mode) for appointment as Assistant Teachers in Primary Schools in Uttarakhand, specifically for those who were in-service as of 10th August 2017.

judgements.case_summary: This application seeks a direction for the State of Uttarakhand to permit applicants holding an 18-month D.El.Ed. qualification from NIOS (Open and Distance Learning mode) to participate in the ongoing counselling and recruitment process for Assistant Teachers. The background involves the 2017 amendment to the RTE Act, which allowed in-service teachers (as of 31st March 2015) to acquire minimum qualifications within four years, leading to the 18-month D.El.Ed. program. While Uttarakhand's 2012 Rules required a 2-year diploma, the High Court had previously held the 18-month D.El.Ed. valid. The Supreme Court, in the Jaiveer Singh case (2023), upheld the 2012 Rules but clarified that the 18-month D.El.Ed. was a one-time opportunity for *in-service* teachers as of 10th August 2017. A subsequent clarification (10th December 2024) further stated that this qualification would be treated as valid for applying in 'other institutions or for promotional avenues.' The applicants argue they are covered by this clarification, especially since the advertisement was issued after the judgment. The State contended that the selection process was almost complete. The Court found that the 10th December 2024 clarification covers the applicants' case, interpreting 'other institutions' to include State Government schools. Consequently, the Court directed the State Government to consider the claims of eligible applicants in accordance with the clarification within three months, without reopening selections already finalized.

petitioner_key_arguments: Applicants are eligible as per the original judgment and the clarification dated 10th December 2024.
The advertisement for recruitment was issued after the Supreme Court's judgment and clarification.
The State of Uttarakhand is not considering their claim despite eligibility.
There are 279 vacant posts and 239 applicants, indicating sufficient opportunity.
respondent_key_arguments: The Supreme Court had upheld the 2012 Rules of the State of Uttarakhand, which required a two-year diploma for teachers.
Any interference at this stage would cause complications in the selection process, which is almost complete.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioners' argument that the clarification dated 10th December 2024 covers their case, and that 'other institutions' includes State Government schools, thereby making eligible applicants with 18-month D.El.Ed. (who were in-service as of 10th August 2017) eligible for consideration.

outcome.relief_granted: The State Government is directed to consider the claim of the applicants in accordance with the clarification dated 10th December 2024 and, if found eligible, to appoint them in accordance with law within a period of three months. The State Government is not to reopen the selection already conducted which has reached finality.

acts_cited: Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009
Right to Free and Compulsory Education (Amendment) Act, 2017
Uttarakhand Government Elementary Education (Teacher) Service Rules, 2012
precedents_cited: Jaiveer Singh and Others v. State of Uttarakhand and Others
Viswanath and Others v. The State of Uttarakhand and Others

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The 18-month D.El.Ed. diploma obtained by persons who were in employment as on 10th August 2017 and completed the diploma course, under the one-time scheme, is to be treated as a valid diploma for the purpose of applying in other institutions, including State Government schools, as per the Supreme Court's clarification dated 10th December 2024.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court clarified that while considering the applicants' claims, the State Government should not reopen the selection already conducted, which has reached finality.

special_directions.special_directions: The State Government is directed to consider the claims of the applicants in accordance with the clarification dated 10th December 2024 and, if found eligible, to appoint them in accordance with law within a period of three months from the date of this order. It is further clarified that the State Government shall not reopen the selection already conducted, which has reached finality.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (@Special Leave Petition (Criminal) No.14809/2024)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the custody of a minor child, with the father seeking custody from the maternal grandparents after the mother's death, challenging a Writ Court order that denied his claim.

judgements.case_summary:
The appellant, a father, challenged a Writ Court order that denied him custody of his minor child, who was residing with his maternal grandparents after the mother's demise. The Single Judge had noted the child's comfort with the grandparents and the father's remarriage. The father argued for his right as the natural guardian, citing Gautam Kumar Das v. NCT of Delhi, emphasizing the child's need to be with the natural guardian, and highlighted financial provisions made for the child. The respondents (grandparents) argued that a detailed inquiry into the child's welfare, as per Nirmala v. Kulwant Singh, should be conducted under the Guardian and Wards Act, and that a Habeas Corpus petition was not maintainable as a Guardian O.P. was already filed.

The Supreme Court distinguished Nirmala based on its specific facts and, relying on Tejaswini Gaud and Gautam Kumar Das, affirmed the maintainability of a Habeas Corpus petition when a natural guardian seeks custody from those without a legal right. The Court found the father, as the natural guardian, educated, and well-employed, had a superior claim, with no allegations of unsuitability. While prioritizing the child's welfare, the Court acknowledged the child's current academic year and comfort with the grandparents.

The Court allowed the appeal, granting custody to the father. However, to ensure academic continuity, it directed the child to remain with the grandparents until April 30, 2025, with the father having visitation rights on alternate weekends. Custody will be formally transferred on May 1, 2025, in the presence of a Station House Officer. The grandparents were also granted visitation rights after the transfer. The pending Guardian O.P. was closed.

petitioner_key_arguments: Father is the natural guardian and has a superior right to custody.
Relied on Gautam Kumar Das v. NCT of Delhi, emphasizing the child's need to be with the natural guardian, especially after the mother's death.
Paternal grandfather has secured the child's financial welfare by conveying property and depositing funds.
Father is well-employed and educated, and his second wife is willing to care for the child.
respondent_key_arguments: Relied on Nirmala v. Kulwant Singh & Ors., arguing for a detailed inquiry into child welfare and preference under the Guardian and Wards Act, 1890.
Habeas Corpus petition was not maintainable as the father had already filed a Guardian O.P.
High Court rightly considered the father's remarriage in refusing custody.
Child is comfortably residing and pursuing education with maternal grandparents.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that the father, as the natural guardian, has a superior legal right to custody, and that a Habeas Corpus petition is maintainable in such circumstances. The court also balanced this right with the child's welfare and academic continuity.

outcome.relief_granted: Custody of the minor child is granted to the father. The child will remain with the maternal grandparents until 30/04/2025 to complete the academic year, with the father having visitation rights on alternate weekends. Custody will be formally handed over to the father on 01/05/2025. The grandparents are also granted visitation rights on the second Saturday of every month starting June 2025 for one year, and thereafter as per the child's desire. The Guardian O.P. filed by the father is closed.

precedents_cited: Gautam Kumar Das Vs. NCT of Delhi and another1
Nirmala Vs. Kulwant Singh & Ors.2
Tejaswini Gaud and others Vs. Shekhar Jagdish Prasad Tewari and others5
constitutional_provisions: Article 226 of the Constitution of India

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The welfare of the minor child is paramount, but the natural guardian (father) has a superior legal right to custody, especially when there are no allegations of unsuitability. A Habeas Corpus petition is maintainable to enforce this right against those without a legal claim, even if a Guardian O.P. is pending, provided the detention is illegal or without authority of law.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The court observed that the learned Single Judge did not endeavor to elicit the child's attitude towards his father. It also distinguished the facts of Nirmala v. Kulwant Singh & Ors. from the present case.

special_directions.special_directions: The child shall be retained in the custody of the grandfather till 30/04/2025. The father (appellant) is permitted to take the child on alternate weekends (Friday evening/Saturday morning to Sunday evening) until 30/04/2025. Custody shall be handed over to the father on 01/05/2025 in the presence of the jurisdictional Station House Officer. The grand-parents shall have visitation rights, permitted to take the child to their residence on every weekend in which the second Saturday falls, starting from June 2025, for one year, and then as per the desire of the child. The Guardian O.P. filed before the jurisdictional Family Court shall stand closed.

case_identification.respondent_name: State Govt. Of Nct Of Delhi
case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.201 OF 2020 WITH CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.202 OF 2020

case_details.subject_matter: This case involves appeals against the conviction of Wahid and Anshu for robbery and related offenses, focusing on the reliability of identification, arrest procedures, and recovery of evidence.

judgements.case_summary: The appeals were filed by Wahid and Anshu against a common judgment of the High Court of Delhi dated 15.11.2018, which had dismissed their appeals against conviction by the Trial Court. Wahid was convicted under Sections 392 and 397 IPC, while Anshu was convicted under Sections 392, 397 IPC, and Section 25 of the Arms Act. The prosecution alleged that on 03.12.2011, four persons, including the appellants, robbed passengers in a mini-bus using weapons. The appellants argued that the FIR did not name them, the incident occurred in darkness, their arrest was doubtful, no test identification parade was conducted, no looted articles were recovered, and there were material contradictions in witness statements. The State contended that conviction could be sustained on the reliable testimony of key witnesses. The Supreme Court, upon analysis, found the prosecution's story regarding the manner of arrest highly improbable due to discrepancies in police and complainant statements, and PW-1's self-contradictory testimony. The Court also deemed the dock identification unreliable given the darkness, the time elapsed, and the fact that several witnesses failed to identify the accused. In the absence of corroborative evidence like recovery of looted articles, the Court concluded that the prosecution failed to prove the case beyond reasonable doubt. Consequently, the appeals were allowed, and the appellants were acquitted.

petitioner_key_arguments: FIR named none of the accused persons.
The incident occurred in the darkness of night.
The accused and the witnesses were not known to each other.
The arrest of four accused from one place and at one time, based on identification by PW-1, is highly doubtful.
No test identification parade was conducted.
No looted articles were recovered from any of the accused.
Recovery of knives, screw driver and country-made pistol is doubtful due to PW-1's statement about signing blank papers.
PW-2, PW-3 and PW-12 stated that the accused were not those who committed the robbery.
PW-14 stated it was too dark to recognise the robbers.
Material contradictions exist in the statement of witnesses.
respondent_key_arguments: Conviction can be sustained on the basis of testimony of other witnesses who had no motive to falsely implicate the accused.
The testimony of PW-1, PW-5 and PW-6 is reliable and sufficient to hold the accused guilty.
Once the courts below, after appreciating the evidence, have held the accused appellants guilty, no case is made out to interfere with the findings under Article 136 of the Constitution of India.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the manner of arrest was highly doubtful, the dock identification was unreliable due to darkness and time elapsed, and there was a lack of corroborative evidence, leading to a failure of the prosecution to prove the identity of the accused beyond reasonable doubt.

outcome.relief_granted: The appeals are allowed. The impugned judgment and order of the High Court is set aside. The appellants are acquitted of the charge(s) for which they were tried and convicted. Their bail bonds stand discharged.

precedents_cited: Manoj and others v. State of Madhya Pradesh, (2023) 2 SCC 353
constitutional_provisions: Article 136 of the Constitution of India

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that in cases where the accused are unknown and the FIR does not name them, the prosecution must establish the identity of the accused beyond reasonable doubt through credible evidence. The court found the arrest procedure highly doubtful, the dock identification unreliable due to darkness and time lapse, and a lack of corroborative evidence, thus failing to prove the accused's involvement.

special_directions.special_directions: The appellants are reported to be on bail and need not surrender. Their bail bonds stand discharged.

case_identification.case_number: Civil Appeal No.2608 of 2025 (@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (C) NO.10088 of 2020)

petitioner_advocates: Mr. Tushar Mehta, learned Solicitor General

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the permissibility of forfeiture of gratuity upon termination for misconduct involving moral turpitude, even without a criminal conviction or proceeding.

judgements.case_summary: This case addresses the forfeiture of gratuity for employees terminated due to misconduct involving moral turpitude, specifically whether a criminal conviction is a prerequisite for such forfeiture. The appellants, Western Coal Fields Limited (a PSU) and Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation (MSRTC), argued that forfeiture is permissible if the misconduct constitutes an offence involving moral turpitude, even without a criminal conviction, based on departmental inquiry findings. The respondent in the PSU case contended that forfeiture requires a criminal conviction or proof of financial loss, citing previous judgments. The Supreme Court analyzed Section 4(6)(b)(ii) of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, clarifying that it does not mandate a criminal conviction. The Court held that an 'offence' refers to an act punishable by law, which can be established through a departmental inquiry, and overruled previous interpretations suggesting otherwise. For the PSU case, where the employee obtained appointment through a fraudulent date of birth, the Court upheld the forfeiture of the entire gratuity, deeming the appointment illegal. For the MSRTC cases involving misappropriation of 'meagre amounts', the Court, adopting a sympathetic approach, limited the forfeiture to 25% of the gratuity payable, directing the release of the balance. The appeals were thus allowed with modifications.

petitioner_key_arguments: Forfeiture of gratuity is permissible if misconduct constitutes an offence involving moral turpitude, even without a criminal conviction.
The statutory provision (Section 4(6)(b)(ii) of the Act) does not require the offence to be 'duly established in a Court of Law'.
Misconduct like fraudulent date of birth or misappropriation constitutes moral turpitude, justifying forfeiture.
respondent_key_arguments: Forfeiture of gratuity is not permissible without a criminal conviction or proof of financial loss, as per previous judgments like C.G. Ajay Babu.
Gratuity is a statutory right and the fruits of service, which cannot be denied on termination without strict adherence to legal requirements.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court accepted the appellants' argument that forfeiture under Section 4(6)(b)(ii) of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, does not require a criminal conviction, but rather that the misconduct constitutes an offence involving moral turpitude, which can be established through a departmental inquiry.

outcome.relief_granted: The forfeiture of the entire gratuity for the PSU employee (fraudulent date of birth) was upheld. For the MSRTC employees (misappropriation), the forfeiture was limited to 25% of the gratuity payable, and the balance amounts were directed to be released.

precedents_cited: Union Bank of India and Ors. vs. C.G. Ajay Babuz
C.G. Ajay Babuz (2018) 9 SCC 529
Jaswant Singh Gill vs. Bharat Coking Coal Ltd.4
Jaswant Singh Gill (2007) 1 SCC 663
Mahanadi Coalfields Ltd. vs. Rabindranath Choubey6
Mahanadi Coalfields Ltd. (2020) 18 SCC 71

Lily Thomas v. Union of India [(2000) 6 SCC 224 : 2000 SCC (Cri) 1056]

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that forfeiture of gratuity under Section 4(6)(b)(ii) of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972, does not require a criminal conviction. Instead, it is sufficient that the misconduct constitutes an 'offence involving moral turpitude' as established through a departmental inquiry, where 'offence' means an act punishable by any law for the time being.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that the interpretation in C.G. Ajay Babuz, which suggested a requirement for misconduct to be 'duly established in a Court of Law' for forfeiture under Section 4(6)(b)(ii), was an obiter dictum because Section 4(6) itself was found inapplicable to the employer bank in that specific case.

special_directions.special_directions: The Appointing Authority for the MSRTC cases is directed to limit the forfeiture of gratuity to 25% of the payable amount and release the balance to the respondent employees.

case_identification.respondent_name: LAKHI ALIAS LAKHWINDER SINGH & ANR. ETC.
case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS. _ OF 2025 [Arising out of SLP (Crl.) Nos.14822-14829 of 2024]

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the power of the court to summon additional accused under Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, specifically challenging a High Court order that set aside summons issued by a Trial Court in a murder case.

judgements.case_summary:
This case involves an appeal against a High Court order dated 18.07.2024, which set aside summons issued by a Trial Court under Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, against private respondents in a murder case (FIR No. 50 of 2020). The appellant, the complainant, argued that the accused were clearly identified in the FIR and that the Trial Court had sufficient material to summon them, highlighting the brutal nature of the crime and consistent eye-witness accounts. The private respondents contended that the power under Section 319 CrPC should be used sparingly, citing a Special Investigation Team (SIT) report that found no evidence against them, and alleging political rivalry. They also pointed to inconsistencies in the complainant's statements and the lack of cross-examination of key witnesses.

The Supreme Court, after reviewing various precedents on Section 319 CrPC, reiterated that this power is discretionary and extraordinary, requiring strong and cogent evidence, but can be exercised even based on examination-in-chief. The Court found that the High Court erred in interfering with the Trial Court's decision, which was based on sufficient material. The Court emphasized that while an innocent person should not be punished, no guilty person should go scot-free.

Consequently, the Supreme Court allowed the Criminal Appeals, set aside the High Court's order, and directed the Trial Court to issue fresh summons against the private respondents, making efforts to secure their appearance if they do not appear voluntarily. The Court also directed a copy of the judgment to be sent to the Legal Remembrancer and Principal Secretary, Department of Legal and Legislative Affairs, Government of Punjab, for information and appropriate remedial steps.

petitioner_key_arguments: Appellant is the complainant/informant and his brother had died.
All respondents/accused were identified in the FIR itself.
It was a brutal murder where the deceased was pulled out from the car and then done to death.
Issuance of summons was based on the tentative view of likely involvement of private respondents.
Identity of accused was discernible despite it being 8:30 pm.
Consistency in the appellant's stand regarding the presence of all persons concerned (came in three cars).
Presence supported by two eye-witnesses, including the appellant.
SIT shielded private respondents due to the political nature of the case.
In the interest of justice, persons should be called upon at the earliest point to avoid trial lingering or reverting to an early stage.
respondent_key_arguments: Not a fit case for the Supreme Court to interfere.
Power to summon under Section 319 CrPC is to be used sparingly and requires a higher test than at the stage of framing charge.
FIR alleged 24 persons came in three different vehicles, which was highly improbable and impractical.
Complainant's initial version (2 persons in car) varied from deposition (3 persons in car), indicating a "building-up" of the case.
SIT found respondents could not have been at the place of occurrence (witnesses, CCTV footage).
The fall-out was due to political rivalry as the deceased was a sitting Sarpanch.
Only two prosecution witnesses (relatives of deceased) were examined, without cross-examination, which is insufficient for invoking Section 319 CrPC.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court accepted the petitioner's argument that the Trial Court had sufficient material to summon the private respondents under Section 319 CrPC and that the High Court erred in setting aside these summons. The Court emphasized that the power under Section 319 CrPC, while discretionary, is meant to ensure that real culprits face trial and can be exercised even based on examination-in-chief.

outcome.relief_granted: The High Court's order dated 18.07.2024 was set aside, the Criminal Appeals were allowed, and the Trial Court was directed to issue fresh summons against the private respondents and secure their appearance.

precedents_cited: Brijendra Singh v State of Rajasthan, (2017) 7 SCC 706
Hardeep Singh v State of Punjab, (2014) 3 SCC 92
Mohd. Shafi v. Mohd. Rafiq, (2007) 14 SCC 544 : (2009) 1 SCC (Cri) 889: AIR 2007 SC 1899
Harbhajan Singh [(2009) 13 SCC 608: (2010) 1 SCC (Cri) 1135]
Ramesh Chandra Srivastava v State of Uttar Pradesh, (2021) 12 SCC 608
Sukhpal Singh Khaira v State of Punjab, (2023) 1 SCC 289
Shishupal Singh v State of Uttar Pradesh, (2019) 8 SCC 682
Yashodhan Singh v State of Uttar Pradesh, (2023) 9 SCC 108
Jamin v State of Uttar Pradesh, 2025 SCC OnLine SC 506
Kranti Associates (P) Ltd. v. Masood Ahmed Khan [Kranti Associates (P) Ltd. v. Masood Ahmed Khan, (2010) 9 SCC 496: (2010) 3 SCC (Civ) 852]
Manoj Kumar Khokhar v. State of Rajasthan [Manoj Kumar Khokhar v. State of Rajasthan, (2022) 3 SCC 501: (2022) 2 SCC (Cri) 1]
Raj Kishore Jha v. State of Bihar, (2003) 11 SCC 519: 2004 SCC (Cri) 212]
Limited v Ravindra Loonkar, (2024) 2 SCC 122
Shashikant Singh [Shashikant Singh v. Tarkeshwar Singh, (2002) 5 SCC 738: 2002 SCC (Cri) 1203]

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core reasoning is that the power under Section 319 CrPC, though discretionary and extraordinary, is meant to ensure that real culprits are brought to trial. It can be exercised even based on examination-in-chief, provided there is strong and cogent evidence indicating complicity, and the High Court erred in setting aside the Trial Court's summons when sufficient material existed.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that the State, as investigator and prosecutor, must be available to assist the Courts in criminal matters. It also noted the work pressure on District and Trial Courts and the importance of clear reasoning in orders.

special_directions.special_directions: Let a copy of this Judgment be despatched to the Legal Remembrancer and Principal Secretary, Department of Legal and Legislative Affairs, Government of Punjab by the Registry, for information and appropriate remedial steps. The Trial Court shall issue fresh summons against the private respondents. If they do not appear, the Trial Court shall make all efforts to secure their appearance and proceed as per law.

case_identification.respondent_name: THE STATE OF ANDHRA PRADESH AND ORS.
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. 4311 OF 2025 (ARISING OUT OF SLP (CIVIL) NO. 3324 OF 2015)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns a dispute over the title and possession of a 3.34-acre parcel of land, claimed by the appellants through a chain of private ownership and by the State as assigned government land resumed for public purpose.

judgements.case_summary:
The case concerns a dispute over a 3.34-acre parcel of land (Survey No. 451/1) in Andhra Pradesh. The appellants, Yerikala Sunkalamma & Anr., claimed ownership through a chain of title originating from a 1943 mortgage, a 1970 court auction, and a subsequent sale deed to their predecessor, who also held a Pattadar Passbook and paid land revenue. They were dispossessed by the State in 1995. The State of Andhra Pradesh contended the land was assigned government property, subject to non-alienation conditions, and was lawfully resumed in 1989 for a public purpose (construction of a DIET building).

The Trial Court ruled in favor of the appellants, citing procedural irregularities in the State's resumption process. The High Court reversed this, holding that the appellants failed to establish title and that the land was assigned. The Supreme Court, in its analysis, noted the State's failure to produce evidence proving the land was assigned or that the original owner, Harijana Govindu, lacked alienable rights. The Court emphasized the presumption of title arising from the appellants' long-standing possession, Pattadar Passbook, and revenue payments, which the State failed to rebut. It also criticized the State's non-responsiveness to the Section 80 CPC notice. While acknowledging the appellants' valid claim to title and illegal dispossession, the Court recognized that the DIET building was already constructed. Therefore, instead of restoring possession, the Supreme Court directed the State to pay Rs. 70 lakhs as compensation to the appellants. The judgment also included directions for wider circulation to emphasize the importance of Section 80 CPC compliance by government authorities.

petitioner_key_arguments: The subject land was private property, not assigned government land.
Appellants' title was established through a 1943 mortgage, a 1970 court auction, and a subsequent registered sale deed.
The appellants' predecessor held a Pattadar Passbook and paid land revenue, indicating ownership and possession.
The State illegally dispossessed the appellants in 1995 without proper notice or compensation.
Assignments made prior to 1954 did not contain non-alienation clauses, making the transfers valid.
The State failed to produce any documents to demonstrate that the land was assigned.
respondent_key_arguments: The subject land was assigned government land, subject to conditions of non-alienation.
Harijana Govindu, the original assignee, had no alienable rights over the land.
The land was lawfully resumed by the Mandal Revenue Officer in 1989 for a public purpose (construction of a DIET building) following due process.
The appellants' suit was barred by limitation.
The appellants failed to establish their title over the subject land.
Petitioner No.1 admitted not knowing the conditions of the assignment.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the appellants' arguments regarding their established possession and the State's failure to prove its claim of assigned land. The State could not rebut the presumption of title arising from the appellants' long-standing possession, Pattadar Passbook, and revenue payments. The court also noted the State's non-compliance with Section 80 CPC notice.

outcome.relief_granted: The State is directed to pay an amount of Rs. 70 lakhs to the appellants by way of compensation within a period of three months from the date of this judgment.

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that long-standing, peaceful possession coupled with documentary evidence like Pattadar Passbooks and revenue receipts creates a strong presumption of title under Section 113 of the Bhartiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, which the State must effectively rebut with credible evidence. When the State fails to prove its claim of assigned land and its lawful resumption, and has already utilized the land for public purpose, monetary compensation is the appropriate remedy for illegal dispossession.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court made observations regarding the importance of Section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, emphasizing the State's obligation to respond to statutory notices and avoid unnecessary litigation. It also discussed the nature of assigned lands, constitutional rights to property and livelihood, and the 'unconstitutional conditions' doctrine in the context of government actions.

case_identification.respondent_name: THE STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH AND OTHERS
case_identification.case_number: CIVIL APPEAL NO. OF 2025 (Arising out of SLP(C) NO.5505 of 2020)

case_details.subject_matter: The case concerns the claim for unpaid salary by stenographers whose appointments were terminated, after the Supreme Court had previously granted them liberty to pursue 'appropriate civil action' for their dues.

judgements.case_summary:
The appellant, Yogesh Kumar, and six others were appointed as Stenographers in the District Court, Saharanpur, in 2002. Their appointments were subsequently terminated in 2005 as they were found to be in excess of the advertised posts. The termination was upheld by the High Court and the Supreme Court in earlier rounds of litigation. However, the Supreme Court, while dismissing the Special Leave Petition in 2012, granted liberty to the petitioners to claim payment of salary for the period they had worked through 'appropriate civil action'. Following this, the appellant's representation for salary was rejected by the District Judge, leading to a writ petition before the High Court, which was dismissed. The Division Bench also dismissed the appeal.

The appellant argued that the High Court erred by adopting a hyper-technical view, insisting that 'appropriate civil action' meant only a Civil Court, and dismissing the writ petition despite the undisputed fact that they had worked for eight years. The respondent contended that the liberty granted was specifically for a Civil Court action, and the High Court was justified in its dismissal. The Supreme Court found the High Court's approach erroneous, emphasizing that under Article 226, courts should not be hyper-technical, especially when the State is expected to be a model litigant. It reiterated that even disputed facts can be resolved in a writ petition based on affidavit evidence. The Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the High Court's judgments, and directed the respondents to pay the appellant and similarly situated persons their salary for the eight years worked, along with 6% interest, within three months, and awarded costs of Rs. 1 lakh.

petitioner_key_arguments: The High Court erred in rejecting the claim for salary.
The appellant and others had actually worked for eight years, which is undisputed.
The Supreme Court's previous order granted liberty for 'appropriate civil action', which should include a writ petition under Article 226.
The High Court should not adopt a hyper-technical approach, especially when the State/High Court is expected to be a model litigant.
A writ petition under Article 226 can be entertained even for disputed questions of fact if they can be decided on affidavit evidence.
respondent_key_arguments: The appellant had lost in the first round of litigation up to the Supreme Court regarding their termination.
The liberty granted by the Supreme Court for 'appropriate civil action' specifically meant proceedings before a Civil Court, not a writ petition.
The District Judge had rightly rejected the representation for salary.
The High Court was justified in dismissing the writ petition and the subsequent appeal.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The Court accepted the petitioner's arguments that the High Court's hyper-technical interpretation of 'appropriate civil action' was erroneous, and that a writ petition under Article 226 is a suitable forum for claiming undisputed salary for services rendered, especially when the State is expected to be a model litigant.

outcome.relief_granted: The respondents are directed to pay the salary of the appellant and other similarly situated persons for the period during which they actually worked in the District Court, along with interest at the rate of 6% per annum from the date on which the salaries ought to have been paid. Costs quantified at Rs.1 lakh are also to be paid to the appellant.

precedents_cited: ABL International Ltd. and Another v. Export Credit Guarantee Corporation of India Ltd. and Others
Zonal Manager, Central Bank of (2004) 3 SCC 553 India v. Devi Ispat Limited and Others
Real Estate Agencies v. State of Goa and Others
Popatrao Vyankatrao Patil v. State of Maharashtra and Others
Unitech Limited and Others v. Telangana State Industrial Infrastructure Corporation (TSIIC) and Others

constitutional_provisions: Article 226 of the Constitution of India

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The High Court, while exercising jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, should not adopt a hyper-technical approach. A writ petition can constitute 'appropriate civil action' for claiming undisputed salary for services rendered, especially when the State and High Courts are expected to be model litigants and even disputed questions of fact can be resolved based on affidavit evidence.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The observation that the State as well as the High Courts are expected to be model litigants.

special_directions.special_directions: The respondents are directed to pay the salary of the appellant and other similarly situated persons for the period worked, along with interest at the rate of 6% per annum, within a period of three months. Additionally, costs of Rs.1 lakh are to be paid to the appellant within three months.

case_identification.case_number: CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 2356 OF 2024

case_details.subject_matter: This case concerns a criminal appeal against the dismissal of discharge applications filed by the appellants, who were accused of culpable homicide not amounting to murder following the electrocution deaths of two employees during work.

judgements.case_summary: The case involves Yuvraj Laxmilal Kanther (Appellant No. 1), an interior decorator, and Nimesh Pravinchandra Shah (Appellant No. 2), a Store Operation Manager. Two employees of Appellant No. 1 died from electrocution and fall injuries while working on a sign board at a shop leased by Appellant No. 2. The employees were provided an iron ladder but no safety equipment. An FIR was lodged, and the appellants were chargesheeted under Sections 304A/182/201 read with Section 34 IPC, but the Magistrate committed the case to Sessions Court under Section 304 Part II IPC. The appellants filed discharge applications under Section 227 CrPC, arguing no prima facie case, no negligence, no intention or knowledge to cause death, and that they had provided compensation to the victims' families. The Trial Court and High Court dismissed these applications, finding a strong suspicion and sufficient material for framing charges. The Supreme Court, however, analyzed the ingredients of Section 304 Part II IPC, emphasizing the requirement of knowledge without intention to cause death. The Court concluded that even if the prosecution's allegations were accepted, there was no material to establish that the appellants had the knowledge that their actions were likely to cause death. Distinguishing the case from Keshub Mahindra, the Court held that no prima facie case for culpable homicide was made out. Consequently, the Supreme Court allowed the appeal, setting aside the orders of the lower courts and discharging the appellants from the Sessions Case.

petitioner_key_arguments: No materials to show that the appellants had committed the alleged offence.
Ingredients of the alleged offence charged were not even prima facie established.
Charge levelled by the prosecution was groundless; FIR was totally silent about any overt act of the appellants.
Appellants were not present at the place of occurrence when the incident took place.
There was no negligence on the part of the appellants; not to speak of having any knowledge or intention to cause the death of the two employees.
Even if all statements of the witnesses were considered and accepted as correct, the trial would not end in conviction.
High Court's observations regarding wooden scaffolding and the 'prudent person' test were 'way off the mark' and cannot justify initiation of criminal proceedings.
It was a case of sudden accident, not a negligent or rash act attributable to appellants.
Appellants paid compensation to the legal heirs of the deceased employees, provided employment to one family member, and took care of educational expenses for children.
No material to justify launch of criminal trial against the appellants.
respondent_key_arguments: Appellants knew fully well about the risk that the two deceased employees had to undertake.
Appellants did not provide any safety equipments to the employees.
There is a strong prima facie case made out against the appellants.

Sufficient material to justify framing of charge against the appellants for the offence punishable under Section 302 Part II IPC (as concluded by the Magistrate) or Section 304A IPC (as initially charged by police).
Relied on the decision of Keshub Mahindra Vs. State of M.P.
legal_arguments.winning_arguments: The court accepted the petitioner's argument that there was no prima facie case for culpable homicide not amounting to murder (Section 304 Part II IPC) as there was no material to establish that the appellants had the knowledge that their actions would likely cause death, nor any intention to cause death or bodily injury likely to cause death.

outcome.relief_granted: The discharge applications (Exhibit Nos. 6 and 10) filed by the appellants in Sessions Case No. 749 of 2014 are allowed, and the appellants are discharged from the said case. The orders of the Trial Court dated 01.04.2017 and the High Court dated 02.11.2017 are set aside and quashed.

acts_cited: Indian Penal Code, Section 304 Part II
Indian Penal Code, Section 302 Part II
precedents_cited: Keshub Mahindra Vs. State of M.P. (1996) 6 SCC 129
constitutional_provisions: Article 142 of the Constitution of India

judicial_reasoning.ratio_decidendi: The core legal principle is that for an offence under Section 304 Part II IPC, the act must be done with the knowledge that it is likely to cause death, but without any intention to cause death or such bodily injury. The Court found that even accepting the prosecution's allegations, there was no material to establish such knowledge or intention on the part of the appellants, thus no prima facie case for culpable homicide was made out.
judicial_reasoning.obiter_dicta: The Court observed that a discharge is at a higher pedestal than an acquittal, implying that when an accused is discharged, it means there are no materials to justify the launch of a criminal trial against them.

special_directions.interim_orders: Stay of further proceedings in Sessions Case No. 749 of 2014 was granted by order dated 09.01.2018.
